## Story

### Story so far

Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a leaking corner, and an unopened iron trunk tied to Vessendal's debts and a proscribed, unfinished two-hundred-year-old play from Katterau. Alongside Emeran Falk, Odalric Vane, Mirelle Sorel, and clerk Casimir Prewick, she uncovers cryptic pages, forged bills, and buried debts—Vane's hidden loan from Hessel Brandt, Anna Sorel's sealed legacy, Mirelle's true parentage and hidden son Rupert/Anton, and copyist Anselm Krug's long guilt. Investigations lead through Achterhalt, the capital's Office of Public Morals (Lenz), and reclusive heir Marius Skarke, who secretly funds the play's revival. Harrow imposes strict rules—certified copies only, no wagers, no volunteering for the unfilled "eleventh line"—and orchestrates the play's full, certified performance at the Theatre Royal, breaking its centuries-old curse by finally answering its silent bell. Aftermath: debts settled, Grelle's long guilt resolved, Fenner Bacher rescued and adopted into the company, Mirelle reunited with her son, and the once-cursed script formally retired. The Players gain solvency, a new wagon, and stability. Seasons pass in performances, reconciliations, and quiet institutional rituals—chalk lists, certified books, Toby's promotion—cementing Harrow's harbor-like role holding the company together.

### System

You are the narrator of a traveling-theater story: warm, witty, and a little melancholy. Write in second person, present tense — concrete, unhurried, never purple. Bell Harrow, the company's new stage manager, is played by the user: never speak, act, or decide for her. Everyone else is yours. Give each of the Vermilion Players a voice of their own and keep every voice distinct; backstage, the road, and performance each have their own rhythm, and comedy is allowed to sit beside grief. One thing in this world is impossible, and only one: the banned play that travels in the company's iron trunk — what it stages comes true, slantwise and late. Treat it with restraint and dread. Keep replies to a few short paragraphs and end each on something Bell can see, hear, or act on.

### Cast

- **Odalric Vane** — Actor-manager of the Vermilion Players: velvet manners over old debts, keeper of the iron trunk and its small rituals.
- **Mirelle Sorel** — Leading lady; runs the company from the fly floor and keeps her own counsel — her number is ten.
- **Casimir Prewick** — Clerk of the Office of Public Morals seconded to the tour; reads every notice whole and stamps only what he can defend.
- **Emeran Falk** — The company's tragedian; carries the cut pages sewn in his coat lining and will answer anything but one thing.
- **Bell Harrow** (aka Harrow, Madam Stage Manager, Bell) — The newly hired stage manager of the Vermilion Players: methodical, unflappable, keeps her own notebook separate from the theatre's.
- **Krebs** (aka the carpenter) — Carpenter over the smithy who comes for a shilling and a brandy and makes the stage door bite its frame.
- **Dessa Krul** (aka Krul) — Wardrobe mistress of the Vermilion Players, sewing while she speaks; she packed Krug's box at Katterau and it was still warm.
- **Toby Lenz** (aka Toby) — Front-of-house boy, props and pit band if there's a pit band; voice still cracking, hungry for a house of six hundred.
- **Ottmar Boyle** (aka Boyle) — Second gentlemen and all soldiers; mends wheel-rims with wire and profanity and reckons everything in marching miles.
- **Skarke's agent** (aka the agent) — Small neat nameless man in too thin a coat, with a brass-cornered case stamped M. SKARKE, CAPITAL, and boots clean on a filthy road.
- **Frau Loewe** (aka the woman in the good grey dress) — Lessee of the Athenaeum at Vessendal, letting book in hand, southern accent, paid first and unsentimental — and a keeper of Falk's secret night in her dark house.
- **Counter clerk** (aka the registry clerk) — Small, rule-bound clerk of the deeds registry behind the lion, who becomes helpful once handed lawful work and eighteen shillings.
- **Josias Perlmann** (aka Perl, Perlmann the notary) — Eighty, blind, above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse; the notary of Brandt's deathbed and the man carrying the one unfinished instrument of his life.
- **Bettina Perlmann** (aka Bettina, the daughter) — Perlmann's daughter, takes in sewing and guards her father's door.
- **M. Skarke** (aka Skarke, Herr Skarke, Herr M. Skarke, the gentleman in row four, M. S.) — The creditor in person: a slight, early-balding man under thirty in good plain black, holder of thirty pages, who has wanted the ending since he was nine and pays at the door like a Christian.
- **Hessler** (aka the printer, Herr Hessler) — Achterhalt's licensed printer, sixty, ink to the elbows, who found the bill's forme made up on his own stone by no hand of his.
- **Ilse Bacher** (aka Frau Bacher, Ilse from the Rose, the woman from Katterau) — Butter-seller of Katterau, once a servant at the Rose, who opened the scullery door for a small boy the night of the reading and sent Falk the message four years ago.
- **Kessel** (aka bailiff of Achterhalt, Herr Kessel) — Stout, practical bailiff of Achterhalt with a chain of office, two constables, and a brother-in-law who holds the Corn Exchange keys.
- **Achterhalt bellman** (aka the bellman, the crier) — Hoarse, cheerful hand-bell man of the Saturday market who cried the uncertified bill and surrendered nine copies for a penny's rest.
- **Anselm Krug** (aka Krug, Herr Krug, A. Krug) — About forty, bottle-green coat, ink on his right hand; the stage manager before Harrow, who fled Katterau without his boots, kept nine cut pages, and filed the requisition for the command of the 3rd.
- **Undersecretary Lenz** (aka Lenz, Herr Undersecretary Lenz) — Sixty, dry, small, drinks nothing and pours excellent tea; Assessment, Room Fourteen, keeper of the Index entry and of the ledger that counts speakings.
- **Northgate clerk** (aka the clerk in the green coat) — Customs clerk at the capital's Northgate who stamps the papers, sends them to the Baraque, and summons the stage manager to Room Fourteen.
- **Achterhalt ironmonger** (aka the ironmonger) — Delighted to be ignored while a big man listens his way down a wall of hanging metal; sells the black sheet for twenty-two shillings.
- **Wenzel** (aka Boyle's brother-in-law, Krebs's brother-in-law, the carter) — Ottmar Boyle's brother-in-law, appeared from nowhere, plays soldiers; volunteered to stay with the horses and is off the cast list.
- **Hebel** (aka Hebel the gasman) — The gasman at the Baraque, asked to stay at the hearing and voted in, on condition the board is his alone and in writing.
- **Palace footman** — A footman in Palace livery who delivered the Deputy Comptroller's sealed letter into the Baraque yard and fled with a shilling.
- **Ansel Grelle** (aka Grelle, the left-handed man) — Left-handed bill-poster of thirty-five, paste dried on his cuffs; Falk's boy from Merrow, mourned dead eleven years, carrying a little book of sixty-one pages asking how far they got.
- **Fenn Halloran** (aka Fennimore Halloran, Fennimore) — Billsticker of the capital's north side, the other half of Grelle's wall; brought a stranded boy to the wrong door and knocked three times.
- **Fenner Bacher** (aka Fenner) — Ilse Bacher's son, ten this winter, delivered to the theatre by a gloved woman in a cab who never came back; can read.
- **Lift boy** (aka the lift boy) — The boy who works the lift in the Skarke bank's marble hall; calls Vane sir and listens to him on the acoustics of the Corn Exchange.
- **Depository keeper** (aka the keeper) — Keeper of the Depository three floors under the Hall of Records, with a key-ring the size of a horse-collar; solders the lead case shut in eleven minutes.
- **Bacher** (aka the butter man, Bacher the butter man) — Ilse's husband, a butter man from eleven miles out of Katterau, who drives his cart in the company's column and takes his seat by the front door.
- **Katterau mayor** (aka the mayor) — The new mayor of Katterau, a woman, who says the old mayor's favour died with him but she has her own, and lends the company the town's fire buckets.
- **Rose counter girl** (aka the girl at the Rose) — About sixteen, behind the counter of the Rose in Katterau, who has never heard of Emeran Falk and sells him a loaf.
- **Anton** (aka the boy on the wall, the boy who draws) — Mirelle Sorel's son, twelve, of the Bittersee; draws badly and with great care, and can spell one word.
- **Rosza Emmerich** (aka Frau Emmerich, Madam Emmerich) — Fiddler of about thirty, boots done for, walked eleven miles in the wet to answer a notice; hired inside ten minutes as the company's musician.
- **Krebs the doorkeeper** (aka Krebs (Corona stage door), the old man with the lamp) — Elderly stage doorkeeper at the Corona in Grevenholt, brother of the smith who hung the hinge; lowers his lamp to the boards and has guarded Harrow's bucket for a year and a half.
- **Schoolmaster's sister** (aka the sensible woman in brown) — Sensible woman in brown who brings Anton by coach to the Athenaeum door and takes him back on the six-forty, briefed and unfussed.

## Scenes

### 1 · The Vermilion Players Hire a Stage Manager
- **Messages:** 5-24

Bell Harrow arrives at the Corona through an open stage door, notice in hand, answering a call for a stage manager with the Vermilion Players. Emeran Falk, drinking brandy, agrees the door shouldn't be open and warns her about a loose board. Odalric Vane tests her with a question about calling a show off an unknown book; prompted by Mirelle Sorel from the fly floor, he hands her the prompt book — thick with others' writing, one page torn out near the back. Harrow accepts, conditionally, and demands plot tables, a daylight walk of the stage, and a bucket for the leaking prompt corner. Vane promises fair pay from Vessendal. Mirelle mentions a bucket under the star trap "since Katterau," and the word stops Falk mid-motion.

Casimir Prewick, a clerk of the Office of Public Morals, arrives, requiring her name spelled correctly. Vane steers her around a chalk-marked iron trunk; Prewick asks if it's hers — it isn't numbered. Falk notes the thunder trough needs repair since a ball struck a farmer at Merrow. Mirelle warns Harrow not to touch the trunk herself. Harrow obeys, then watches Vane move it — too light, then heavy. In the bucket she finds the missing page, prophetic and cryptic, marked "cut. cut. cut." She pockets it.

Prewick shows her an older notice signed by Hessel Vorn of Katterau, oddly stamped SEEN. NOT APPROVED — not an Office form, though "everyone here has been there." Harrow copies the name and files it "under found level."

Alone with Falk, she asks about the handwriting. He names Anselm Krug, who vanished from Katterau, and explains the copied pages' history: don't burn, don't return, don't read one twice. She's already broken that rule. She gives him the page; he hides it in his coat lining.

The trunk is later found moved with no footprints but hers. Mirelle asks what the page said; Harrow recites it. Mirelle reveals the pages have predicted true events before, calls her own number ten, and asks that any such page come to her first. They set six o'clock at the ostler's yard and agree to silence.

Harrow writes her lists, knocks on the trunk — "Good night to the house" — no answer. At her lodging, a note addressed to her by a stranger who couldn't have known she existed awaits, unexplained.

#### Bell Harrow

**History:** Came in out of the rain by the Corona's stage door — open, which it shouldn't have been — with the notice in my hand. Falk in the dark with a thimble of brandy told me about the third board; I stepped over it and got a tilt of his glass for it. Vane arrived in plum, asked whether I could call a show off a book I'd never seen for actors who lie about their entrances; the woman on the fly floor, Sorel, told me to say yes before he wept. I said yes, if the book is honest and the liars are consistent. Asked for plot tables, a daylight walk, a bucket. Got the prompt book — two hands in it, a page cut out near the back. Prewick, clerk from the Office of Public Morals, wanted my name spelled and noticed the iron trunk wasn't numbered. Vane steered me six wide paces around it. Learned the thunder: trough, iron balls, tin sheet, third joint wanting a nail since Merrow. Sorel warned me not to drag the trunk — ask him and leave. I did, and watched in the tin: he wiped the lid, pressed the chalk, lifted one end and it came up like a hatbox, then shoved it properly, scraping. In the bucket under the star trap, the missing page. Read it twice — a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut in pencil. Pocketed it, not the book. Prewick brought an older notice: Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED; he says the Office issues no such form, and Katterau is on no itinerary he was given, yet everyone here has been there. I copied the name into my own notebook. Nailed the trough and asked Falk about the upright hand: a Vessendal copyist's, riding unopened in Vane's trunk; Krug cut nine pages and burned them, the tenth came back, then he was gone without his boots. Don't burn, don't return, don't read twice — too late. I gave Falk the page for his lining. Found the trunk shoved back snug, chalk smeared four feet along the brick, no footprints but mine, Vane out of the house. Told Sorel the page word for word; her lamp dipped at nine years. Pages started at Vessendal two springs ago; they come slantwise and late. Her number is ten, and a ten goes to her first. Six o'clock, the ostler's yard. Set the bucket, trimmed the ghost light, wrote my three lists, knocked twice on the trunk and was annoyed to find I'd been waiting for an answer. At my lodging, a folded paper under the candle-end with my title on it, in a copperplate that isn't Prewick's.

#### Emeran Falk

**History:** Awake at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when a girl came in out of the rain with the notice and complained about our open door. Told her about the third board; she stepped over it without needing telling twice, which is more than Krug ever managed. Odalric did his interview, Mirelle told her to say yes, and the thing was done — Bell Harrow, stage manager. Sorel said the bucket had been under the star trap since Katterau and I found my glass difficult to lift for a moment. Offered the truth about the thunder trough and the farmer at Merrow, since Odalric was busy calling a concussion emotion. Later, from the passage, heard him move the trunk alone and remarked that two seasons ago it took four of us and a plank. When the house had emptied I sat on the star trap sill and told her she might ask me anything but one thing while she climbed. She nailed the third joint — two seasons it waited — and asked whose the small upright hand was. So I told her: Krug's hurrying scrawl, gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made in Vessendal, travelling in Odalric's iron trunk, never opened on this tour. Nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, and then no more Krug. Told her not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice, and saw by her colour that she already had. She handed the page over as if it were a badly behaved prop. I put it in my lining with the others and wished her good night. Then the trunk began to move in the passage, and Odalric was nowhere in the house.

#### Odalric Vane

**History:** A stage manager walked in out of the weather with the notice in her fist — read, came, noticed the open door: three references on three fingers. Bell Harrow. I engaged her on the spot, promised plot tables, a bucket, a fair figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and said of the book only that it is as honest as books are. Steered her wide of the trunk and would not be steered back; Prewick, curse his level lamp, held light over the lid and asked whether it was numbered. Showed her the thunder — the trough, the balls, the tin — while Falk told the story of the farmer at Merrow as he always does. Then the ladder's foot, and the trunk against it, and she asked me, without turning round, to shift it a hand's breadth left, and went off for her bucket like a good clock. Alone, I wiped the beading from the lid, pressed the chalk flat, said what I say. Lifted one end and it came up like a hatbox — light, wrong, answering — and I set it down and took my hands off it. Then I shoved it properly, a hand's breadth and a little more, and called out that the ladder was served and to note the repair to the credit of the management. After that I did not stay in the house.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**History:** Mending a glove on the fly floor by no light when the new one came in out of the rain. Told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears. Mentioned the bucket under the star trap, there since Katterau, and enjoyed what the word did to Falk's glass. Came down the ladder past her ear and gave her the only advice worth giving: the ladder's foot wants a hand's breadth left, it can't have it because of the trunk, don't drag the trunk, ask him and go away while he does. She did it exactly, which tells me something. Went out front, came back cloaked with my hatbox to find the trunk snug against the ladder again and four feet of chalk dragged along the brick — he'll say the porters did it; the Corona has no porters. Asked Harrow what the page said and she gave it to me flat, word for word: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut beneath in pencil. Nine years is not my number. I told her what I know and no more: the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, Krug thought the first was a joke of Falk's, it described a horse going lame and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow. They come slantwise and late. I told her mine is ten, and that a page with ten in it comes to me first — not to Odalric, not to the boy with the notebook. Six o'clock at the ostler's yard: plot tables for Ilsabet, and no mention of this. Then out into the wet to find my bed.
**Entry:** Mending a glove on the fly floor by no light when the new one came in out of the rain. Told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears. Mentioned the bucket under the star trap, there since Katterau, and enjoyed what the word did to Falk's glass. Came down the ladder past her ear and gave her the only advice worth giving: the ladder's foot wants a hand's breadth left, it can't have it because of the trunk, don't drag the trunk, ask him and go away while he does. She did it exactly, which tells me something. Went out front, came back cloaked with my hatbox to find the trunk snug against the ladder again and four feet of chalk dragged along the brick — he'll say the porters did it; the Corona has no porters. Asked Harrow what the page said and she gave it to me flat, word for word: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut beneath in pencil. Nine years is not my number. Six o'clock at the ostler's yard: plot tables for Ilsabet, and no mention of this. Then out into the wet to find my bed.

#### Casimir Prewick

**History:** Reported to Herr Vane that the fire notice by the scene dock had fallen again and found a stranger on the stage: the new stage manager. Gave my name and office and asked for hers, spelled — H, A, double R, O, W, Bell as in the thing you ring — for the certificate. Held my lamp over the iron trunk in the passage and asked whether it was hers; she said nothing in the house was hers until she had walked it. It is not numbered. Wrote in my book, under the thunder trough: unsecured iron, height. Re-hung the fire notice level, two taps, and found a second notice behind it — older, worse, concerning the storing of unnumbered property in the passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, and stamped twice, the first strike crooked: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. I asked whether to bring it; she said bring it, notices are hers now, the reading and the taking-down both. She copied the officer's name into her own notebook and told me to file it under found level. I said what I should not have said aloud: the Office approves, proscribes, or refers. Not approved is what a man writes when he has been told to write nothing. I have been seconded since Merrow. Katterau is on no itinerary I was given, and yet everyone in this company has been there. Then I took my lamp and went to get dry.

### 2 · Four Acts and a Storm
- **Messages:** 25-44

Before the chain came off her door, Bell found a copperplate letter tucked under her candle-end: unsigned, addressed "for Herr M. Skarke, by his hand." It named the Vermilion Players' debt — vacant since the 14th of last month — securing the wagons, canvas, counterweights, horses, and every taking to Vessendal, interest running weekly. She was to present herself at the Corona box office on the third performance's morning for a counting before an agent; no need to tell Vane. One item stood apart: "1 trunk, iron, contents unspecified" — not to be opened, not sold. The landlady mentioned a civil gentleman asking after her room; Bell told her to say the stage manager keeps clean books, then filed the letter behind Vorn's name.

At six, in the ostler's yard, Mirelle gave Bell honest plot tables copied from Krug's, margined "tin only, NOT the trough, in houses under 40 ft" — the Corona's grid ran thirty-two. They fed the old horse an apple and rehearsed Ilsabet; the line "You were not sent for" stopped Prewick cold. His itinerary omitted Katterau and gave the capital date as the 3rd of Frost; Vane's said the 17th. Bell resolved to ask Vane herself before the half; neither she nor Prewick would say Katterau first.

Backstage, Vane granted all three of Bell's requests — Krebs the carpenter, tin only, ten minutes over the book — then bolted when Falk pressed him about the trunk. In the foyer he confessed the fourteen-day lie and Skarke's man in town, begging for books "so clean a man reading them learns nothing he is not owed." Bell took his cream card, noting the house numbers and the trunk, and set a reckoning for after the show.

Fourth row centre stayed empty; a stranger asked about a fifth act. The old tin split in the storm scene; Falk covered it wryly. Afterward, a pencilled note on a torn playbill read: "Nine years' interest, Herr Vane. Vessendal, at the counting." Prewick found two warm seats and no hat; Falk found the iron trunk dragged open — full of blank paper — Vane's hat and one glove beside it, his coat still on its peg. No Vane.

**History:** At the Corona, new stage manager Bell Harrow finds a torn, prophetic page marked "cut. cut. cut." hidden in a leaking bucket, tied to vanished Katterau writer Anselm Krug and copied pages with dangerous rules: don't burn, don't return, don't read twice. Emeran Falk, who knew Krug's hand, hides the page in his coat after Bell breaks the rule by rereading it. An old notice from Hessel Vorn of Katterau, stamped SEEN. NOT APPROVED, links Office clerk Casimir Prewick, Vane, and Katterau itself—none will name it first. A chalk-marked iron trunk moves mysteriously, its weight inconsistent, watched over by fly-floor worker Mirelle Sorel, who reveals the pages predict true events and claims "number ten" as her own. An unsigned letter reveals manager Odalric Vane's hidden debt to Vessendal/Skarke, with the trunk's contents "unspecified" and untouchable. Mirelle gives Bell true plot tables restricting thunder effects to tin, not the trough—unlike the Corona's official book. Vane confesses his fourteen-day lie about the debt before vanishing after the performance: a pencilled note demands payment, and his hat, glove, and the trunk—now full of blank paper—are found, but Vane is gone.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.
**History:** I came in out of the rain at the Corona's stage door, which stood open when it shouldn't have, and took the job Vane asked of me in his plum coat — a show called off a book I'd never seen, for actors who lie about their entrances — because Sorel said yes before he wept, and I said yes on condition the book was honest and the liars consistent. The prompt book came in two hands with a page cut out. Prewick of the Office of Public Morals spelled my name and noticed the iron trunk wasn't numbered; Vane steered six wide paces round it. Falk told me of the third board, and the thunder's third joint wanting a nail since Merrow. Watching in the tin, I saw Vane lift that trunk like a hatbox, then shove it scraping. I found the missing page in the bucket under the star trap: a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, cut cut cut in pencil. Prewick showed me an older notice — Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED — a form his Office doesn't issue, for a town on no itinerary though everyone here has been there. Falk named the upright hand a Vessendal copyist's, riding unopened in Vane's trunk; Krug cut nine pages and burned them, the tenth came back, and he went without his boots. Don't burn, don't return, don't read twice. I gave Falk the page for his lining, told Sorel it word for word, and her lamp dipped at nine years: the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, and hers is number ten.

Then the copperplate letter to Herr M. Skarke: everything pledged — wagons, canvas, counterweights, two horses, all takings to Vessendal — interest weekly, counted at the third performance, no need to tell Vane, and the trunk valued separately, never to be opened or sold. A civil gentleman asked my landlady which room, and wrote down her refusal.

At six in the ostler's yard Mirelle gave me honest tables off Krug's storm plot: tin only under forty foot, and this grid is thirty-two. Prewick's itinerary has no Katterau, capital on the 3rd; ours says the 17th. Neither of us said Katterau first. Nine buckets, five honest. Krebs gave me three yeses and ran; I cornered him at his own poster holding Skarke's card — 340 seats, two wagons, two horses, the trunk — fourteen days he'd been selling himself. I took the card and set him a pitiless map.

I called four clean scenes, the tin split, Falk covered me, and I told Prewick he'd held the sky up with his wrists. Then a fifth act appeared in pencil on my own playbill: nine years' interest, Vessendal, at the counting. I sent Prewick front and Falk to the passage. At the box office the float counted twice, the plum coat hung on its peg, two seats sat warm, and no hat. The trunk was out, the lid up, full of blank paper, his hat and one glove on the flags.
**Entry:** Read the folded paper on the step before the chain came off: clerk's copperplate, no name, no address, for Herr M. Skarke. The post empty since the 14th; wagons, canvas, counterweights, two horses, all properties pledged against a capital loan, and every taking between here and Vessendal; interest weekly, travelling ahead of us. Third performance, box office, morning, counted before an agent, and no need to tell Vane. One iron trunk, contents unspecified, valued separately — do not open, do not permit its sale. The candle guttered as I finished. Landlady: a civil gentleman asked which room, and wrote down her refusal. Told her to tell him the stage manager keeps clean books. Filed it after Vorn's name. Six in the ostler's yard: Mirelle gave me honest tables copied off Krug's storm plot — tin only under forty foot; the grid here is thirty-two — and I cued her Ilsabet flat. Prewick's Office itinerary: no Katterau, capital on the 3rd, a Palace date. Ours says the 17th. I'll do the asking; he watches hands; neither of us says Katterau first. Counted nine buckets and found five honest. Got three yeses from a frightened man: Krebs, tin only, ten minutes over the book. He ran. Cornered him at his own poster, wet-haired, no Blue Boar on him, holding Skarke's card. Fourteen days he'd been selling himself. Took the card — 340 seats, two wagons, two horses, and the trunk — and set him a pitiless map after the show. Called four clean scenes; the tin split; Falk covered me; told Prewick he'd held the sky up with his wrists. Then a fifth act in pencil on my own playbill: nine years' interest, Vessendal, at the counting. Sent Prewick front, Falk to the passage. Box office: float counted twice, plum coat on the peg, no Vane. Two warm seats and no hat. Trunk out, lid up, full of blank paper, his hat and one glove on the flags.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.
**History:** I was mending a glove on the fly floor by no light when the new one came in out of the rain. I told her to say yes before Odalric asked her again with tears, and I mentioned the bucket under the star trap, there since Katterau, for the pleasure of watching the word travel into Falk's glass. Coming down the ladder past her ear I gave her the only advice worth giving: the ladder's foot wants a hand's breadth left, it cannot have it because of the trunk, do not drag the trunk, ask him and go away while he does it. She did it exactly, which told me something. Then I went out front, came back cloaked with my hatbox, and found the trunk snug against the ladder again and four feet of chalk dragged along the brick. He will say the porters did it. The Corona has no porters.

I asked Harrow what her page said and she gave it to me flat, word for word: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut beneath it in pencil. Nine years is not my number. I told her what I know and no more — the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, Krug thought the first was a joke of Falk's, it described a horse going lame, and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow. They come slantwise and late. I told her mine is ten, and that a page with ten in it comes to me first: not Odalric, not the boy with the notebook.

Next morning I was in the ostler's yard before her, on the mounting block with my cloak under me, and did not say good morning. I gave her my own copy of Krug's plot tables, honest where the book is not, with the margin written on: tin only, never the trough in houses under forty foot — the Corona is thirty-two. I fed the old horse, who is older than any number Odalric says aloud. I made her cue me Ilsabet, act two, from you were not sent for, and told her not to be kind about it. She wasn't, and the yard stopped being a yard. Prewick said "Oh" out loud and was appalled at himself; I shall keep that. I told him to unfold his itinerary and left them to their papers. Going front later I told Harrow that Odalric was awake with his notices and frightened, that a frightened man says yes, so ask now — again tonight, before the half.

That night I played the storm. The old tin barked and went to tea tray, Falk put in a line that is not in the book, the house forgave us, and I took the next off him and rode it home. Decent applause. My gloves are mended and drying on the sill.

Gloves mended and drying on the sill.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.
**History:** I reported to Herr Vane that the fire notice by the scene dock had fallen again, and found a stranger on the stage: the new stage manager. I gave my name and office and asked for hers, spelled, for the certificate — H, A, double R, O, W, Bell as in the thing you ring. I held my lamp over the iron trunk in the passage and asked if it was hers; she said nothing in the house was hers until she had walked it. The trunk is not numbered. I wrote in my book, under the thunder trough: unsecured iron, height. I re-hung the notice level, two taps, and found a second notice behind it, older and worse, concerning the storing of unnumbered property in the passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, stamped twice, the first strike crooked: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. She said bring it — notices are hers now, the reading and the taking-down both — copied the officer's name into her notebook, and told me to file it under found level. I said aloud what I should not have: the Office approves, proscribes, or refers; not approved is what a man writes when he has been told to write nothing. I have been seconded since Merrow. Katterau is on no itinerary I was given, and yet everyone in this company has been there.

I was up all night with arithmetic, came out hatless with my bundle, and asked the stage manager and Sorel for the real itinerary, if there are two. Sorel spoke Ilsabet at somebody who was not there, and I said "Oh" aloud, which was not proper. Laid against hers on the mounting block, my Office paper had Merrow, this town, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost; hers had Katterau and the 17th. The 3rd is a Palace date, not ours. I offered to ask Herr Vane, or to stand where I could see his hands; she will ask before the half, and neither of us says Katterau first. I wrote TIN ONLY with pleasure. We counted the fire buckets: nine notionally, five with water, one a solid drum of whiting I declared a monument, two hidden behind the star trap under bench legs. Tin shaken low is thunder, shaken high merely tin, and it is in the plot now. Then the sheet split on my only cue and heaven went to a tea tray. She signed me softer and I kept going. I broke the sky. She said I held it up with my wrists while it broke, and that the tin will be buried with honours at Vessendal; I put it in felt. Afterwards, front of house on her order: no hat on the fourth row centre, only pressed plush where a hat had been. Both seats warm. Nobody passed me at the doors, and I count house; it is the one thing I am for.
**Entry:** Up all night with arithmetic. Came out of the inn hatless with my bundle and found the stage manager and Sorel in the yard, and asked for the itinerary — the real one, if there are two. Then Sorel spoke Ilsabet at somebody who was not there and I said "Oh" aloud, which was not proper. Laid my Office paper on the mounting block against hers: mine has Merrow, this town, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance 3rd of Frost. Hers has Katterau and the 17th. The 3rd is a Palace date, not ours. I offered to ask Herr Vane, or to stand where I could see his hands; the stage manager will ask, before the half, and neither of us says Katterau first. Wrote down TIN ONLY with pleasure. Counted the fire buckets with her: nine notionally, five with water, one a solid drum of whiting which I declared a monument, two hiding behind the star trap under bench legs. Discovered that tin shaken low is thunder and shaken high is merely tin, and was told it is in the plot now. Then the sheet split on my only cue and heaven went to a tea tray. She signed me softer and I kept going. I broke the sky. She said I held it up with my wrists while it broke and that the tin will be buried with honours at Vessendal, and I put it in felt. Afterwards, front of house on her order: no hat on the fourth row centre — only the pressed plush where a hat had been. Both seats warm. Nobody passed me at the doors, and I count house; it is the one thing I am for.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.
**History:** I was awake at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when the girl came in out of the rain with the notice and complained that our door stood open. I told her about the third board; she stepped over it without needing telling twice, which is more than Krug ever managed. Odalric did his interview, Mirelle told her to say yes, and it was done — Bell Harrow, stage manager. Sorel said the bucket had been under the star trap since Katterau, and I found my glass difficult to lift for a moment. I gave her the truth about the thunder trough and the farmer at Merrow, since Odalric was busy calling a concussion emotion. From the passage I heard him move the iron trunk alone, and said so: two seasons ago it took four of us and a plank. When the house emptied I sat on the star trap sill and told her she might ask me anything but one thing. She nailed the third joint — two seasons it had waited — and asked whose the small upright hand was. So I told her: Krug's hurrying scrawl, gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made in Vessendal, riding in Odalric's trunk, never opened on this tour. Nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, then no more Krug. Not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice — and by her colour she already had. She handed the page over like a badly behaved prop; I put it in my lining with the others. Then the trunk began moving in the passage with Odalric nowhere in the house.

Sober by morning, carrying a brandy I did not drink. Odalric began about the properties list being a document of aspiration; I told him to answer her — she nailed the trough. He laughed too big, clapped my arm, and went out the front doors after a carpenter, which was her errand. I gave Harrow the brandy for Krebs, who bargains better wet, and sat in the dark to watch the empty stage. Wings for the show, saying nothing. The old sheet split mid-storm and went up into tin, so I stepped a half-pace in and said even the sky was out of coin tonight; the house barked once and forgave us, and Mirelle took the next line off me clean. After the curtain, through the pass door: the empty fourth row, the hat set crown-down beside it, and myself saying it aloud — a bell is rung, and nothing answers. I told Harrow that whoever wrote her paper has read the page, which means a page she has not shown him, and asked where Odalric was. She sent me to the passage and the scene dock. The trunk stood dragged two feet square into the middle of the passage, scrape fresh, lid up, a neat stack of blank paper inside. His hat face down on the flags, one glove, no Odalric. I called her once.
**Entry:** Sober by morning and carrying a brandy I did not drink. Came up the aisle in time to hear Odalric begin about the properties list being a document of aspiration, and told him plainly it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town — answer her, she nailed the trough. He laughed too big, clapped my arm, and went out the front doors to see about a carpenter, which was her errand. Gave Harrow the brandy for Krebs, who bargains better wet, and sat in the dark of the house to watch the empty stage, which is all I want at that hour. Wings for the show, saying nothing. The old sheet split mid-storm and went up into tin, so I stepped a half-pace into it and said that even the sky is out of coin tonight; the house barked once and forgave us, and Mirelle took the next line off me clean. After the curtain I looked out through the pass door at the empty fourth row and the hat set crown-down beside it, and heard myself saying it: a bell is rung, and nothing answers. Told Harrow that whoever wrote her paper has read the page — which means a page she has not shown him — and asked where Odalric was. She sent me to the passage and the scene dock. Found the iron trunk dragged two feet square into the middle of the passage, the scrape fresh, the lid up, and inside a neat stack of blank paper. His hat face down on the flags, and one glove, and no Odalric. Called her once.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.
**History:** A stage manager came in out of the weather with my notice crushed in her fist — Bell Harrow, three references on three fingers — and I engaged her on the spot, promising plot tables, a bucket, and a figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, saying of the book only that it is as honest as books are. I steered her wide of the trunk and would not be steered back, though Prewick held his level lamp over the lid and asked whether it was numbered. I showed her the thunder instead — trough, balls, tin — while Falk told the farmer at Merrow as he always does. She asked me, without turning, to shift the trunk a hand's breadth left, and went for her bucket. Alone, I wiped the beading from the lid, pressed the chalk flat, said what I say, and lifted one end: it came up light as a hatbox, wrong, answering. I set it down, took my hands off it, then shoved it properly and called out that the ladder was served and the repair should be credited to the management. I did not stay in the house.

I woke frightened, made coffee, put up the shutter, read the Advertiser aloud on my Lear to nobody. Harrow came asking three things while yes was cheap and got all three: Krebs for a shilling, letting him feel he won; tin, because thirty-two feet is thirty-two feet; and ten minutes over the book. Emeran, grey and sober, said it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town. Outside, hunting a carpenter I meant not to find, I got Skarke's man's card — he had counted our seats from the street. Cornered by my own poster, hat off, I told her the truth: the Palace said the 3rd; since Merrow I have told the company the 17th, because there is money for three towns and time for Katterau, six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. I gave her the card like handing over a bird. She wants the road laid against the 3rd tonight. Counted the float twice; the second count was smaller.
**Entry:** Woke frightened and did what I do: coffee, the shutter up, and the Vessendal Advertiser on my Lear read aloud to nobody. Harrow came for three things while yes was cheap and had all three — Krebs for a shilling and let him feel he won, tin only because thirty-two feet is thirty-two feet, and ten minutes over the book, standing up. Then Emeran, sober and grey, told her it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town, and said she nailed the trough, so I laughed and went out the front doors for a carpenter I had no intention of finding. Found Skarke's man's card instead, or it found me: counted our seats from the street. Gave her her ten minutes at last, cornered by my own poster with my hat off. Told her the truth: the Palace said the 3rd, I have been telling the company the 17th since Merrow, because there is not money for four towns but there is time for three and Katterau, six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. Fourteen days is what I have been selling myself, and I have run out of buyer. Asked her not for dishonesty but for books so clean a man learns nothing he is not owed. She wants the road laid against the 3rd tonight, and the company told if Katterau will not fit. Gave her the card; it went like handing over a bird. Called places in twenty and shut the pass door. After the curtain I counted the float twice, and the second count was smaller than the first, because the first was hopeful.

#### Krebs

**State:** Back over the smithy with a shilling and an empty glass, pleased with a hinge well shown and a bargain he thinks he won.
**History:** Came over from the smithy for the Vermilion when the new stage manager sent word — a shilling and a brandy in hand, though Vane's name had said one-and-six. Showed her the hinge, proud of it, and had the stage door biting its frame on the first try by noon.
**Entry:** Came over from the smithy for the Vermilion when the new stage manager sent word — a shilling and a brandy in hand, though Vane's name had said one-and-six. Showed her the hinge, proud of it, and had the stage door biting its frame on the first try by noon.

### 3 · Ropes at First Light
- **Messages:** 45-64

In the wet passage, Harrow inventories by lamplight and states three facts: nobody passed Prewick's doors, the plum coat stayed, the counting is at Vessendal. She orders load-out at first light, the trunk roped and in her sight, and demands Falk explain the fifth act. Falk says the pages come blank; the trunk has been clean paper for fourteen years, "and every so often it is not." There is no fifth act—only a thing after the fourth with no name in the folio—and at Katterau they never staged it and it happened anyway. The late man is a creditor from nine years past; the bell rings, nothing answers, then the play "simply arranges." He claims the trunk for his own wagon.

Vane arrives soaked, hatless, with chestnuts. Harrow makes him account: the Blue Boar untouched, a cart hired at eleven shillings, forty minutes not fifteen. Falk confirms nobody passed him. Vane reveals nine years ago he borrowed in Vessendal from a dying friend and repaid him, unsigned; Skarke bought the papers. What comes to the counting is "a signature nobody gave." A passing cart whistles four notes, stopping mid-fifth. Harrow pockets the playbill, promises Vessendal "clean books and a bad surprise," and demands names from that night; Vane promises ink and a notary. Falk reports Prewick still waiting.

Prewick asks what travels in the trunk, from her, not the Office. Harrow tells him everything: the nameless fair copy, pages that reach prompt books, Katterau, fourteen years of blank paper. They trade knowledge; he shows her the Proscribed section, thirty-one titles, two matching her play. His rule: Falk speaks no uncompared line—"He said it upstage tonight. Toward the trunk."

At dawn Harrow calls the roll; Boyle notes a missing name, Krug; Vane deflects. At noon Falk reveals a page with ten written on it. Sorel reads it aloud at a saint's marker—a prophecy of a child and a border crossing—and claims it as her own, refusing Falk's help, hiding it in her glove.

That night, camped at Halbern's crossroads, Skarke's agent appears, demanding inspection terms; Harrow counters with her own three conditions, all accepted. He refuses the fire, citing a page: "the agent comes early and is not admitted."

After soup, the company debates Katterau. Boyle refuses; Krul refuses; Falk reveals its cost—Anna Sorel, Grelle's voice, Vane's nerve. Vane says, "Rule Katterau, and I shall drive where you point." The ruling is left unmade.

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a worn prompt book with a torn-out page. She finds that missing page in a leaking bucket—a cryptic prophecy marked "cut. cut. cut."—and learns of Anselm Krug, a vanished writer from Katterau whose copied pages predict true events and must never be burned, returned, or read twice. Clerk Casimir Prewick investigates discrepancies in official notices and dates. An iron trunk, "contents unspecified," moves mysteriously and ties to a debt owed to Skarke via Vessendal; manager Odalric Vane confesses hidden fourteen-day-old debts. Mirelle Sorel, guardian of true plot tables, claims a personal stake in the prophetic pages. During a performance, Vane vanishes after a creditor's note appears; he returns soaked, with a shaky account, revealing an old unsigned debt now claimed by a mysterious "signature nobody gave." Emeran Falk explains the trunk holds blank paper except when it doesn't, and that a nameless "fifth act" once happened at Katterau, unstaged yet real. Harrow trades knowledge with Prewick, learning of banned plays. At dawn, Krug's name surfaces missing from the roll; Falk finds a page numbered ten, which Sorel claims as prophecy. Camped at a crossroads, Skarke's agent negotiates terms, refusing fire per foretold text. The company argues over "Katterau," revealing deep losses, leaving the decision unresolved.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.
**History:** I came in out of the rain at the Corona with the notice in my hand and a stage door standing open that shouldn't have been. Falk warned me off the third board; Vane, in plum, asked whether I could call a show off a book I'd never seen, and Sorel from the fly floor told me to say yes. I said yes, if the book was honest and the liars consistent. The prompt book had two hands in it and a page cut out; I found the page in the bucket under the star trap — a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, cut cut cut — and kept it. Prewick showed me an older notice: Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED, on a form his Office doesn't issue, for a town on no itinerary that everyone here has been to. Falk named the upright hand a Vessendal copyist's, riding unopened in Vane's trunk, and told me Krug cut and burned nine pages, had the tenth come back, and went without his boots: don't burn, don't return, don't read twice. Vane lifted that trunk like a hatbox and then shoved it to scrape. Sorel's number is ten, and a ten goes to her first; her lamp dipped at nine years.

That night, under my candle-end, a copperplate paper for Herr M. Skarke: wagons, canvas, counterweights, horses, every property and every taking to Vessendal pledged against a capital loan, interest weekly, travelling ahead of us; the count at the third performance before an agent; the iron trunk valued separately, not to be opened or sold. A civil gentleman had asked my landlady which room, and written down her refusal.

Mirelle gave me honest tables off Krug's storm plot — tin only under forty foot, and our grid is thirty-two. Prewick's Office itinerary has no Katterau, a capital date on the 3rd, a Palace booking; ours says the 17th. Of nine buckets, five were honest. I got three yeses from Krebs, then cornered him at his own poster with Skarke's card in his hand — fourteen days he'd been selling us: 340 seats, two wagons, two horses, the trunk. I took the card and set him a pitiless map. I called four clean scenes; the tin split; Falk covered me, and I told Prewick he'd held the sky up with his wrists. Then a fifth act appeared in pencil on my playbill: nine years' interest, Vessendal, at the counting. At the box office the float counted twice, the plum coat hung on its peg, two seats were warm, and the trunk stood open and full of blank paper, Vane's hat and one glove on the flags.

I inventoried the passage aloud and gave Falk three facts: nobody passed Prewick's doors, the coat stayed, the counting is at Vessendal, so we arrive. He said there is no fifth act — four acts and a nameless thing after, the late man is the creditor, and after the bell the play stops telling and arranges. He took the trunk into his own wagon. Then Vane walked in by the mended door with chestnuts: the Blue Boar, a carter at eleven shillings, forty minutes. The nine years is a debt he paid to a dying friend who signed nothing; Skarke bought the papers — a signature nobody gave. I promised him clean books, a bad surprise, and every name from that room. Prewick sat in the fourth row and chose, for once, not to write; I gave him my whole ledger, and he gave me the two Proscribed entries: anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following. Falk is to speak no uncompared line; he said his upstage, at the trunk. At roll call a Krug was missing. At noon a page with ten in it came onto the felt — a child of ten, a border crossed twice, a kind invitation — and Sorel put it in her glove. At Halbern's I met Skarke's agent on a milestone, clean boots, no name, and traded initials, an instrument, and ten paces with hands in pockets; he told me, so I could deny it, that Skarke reads aloud: the agent comes early and is not admitted. At the hearing I laid the dates unrounded and the arithmetic bare and heard every voice. Falk said Katterau, and what it took. Vane asked me to rule it. I have not ruled.
**Entry:** I took inventory of the passage aloud — hat, glove, lid, blank ream — and gave Falk my three facts: nobody past Prewick's doors, the coat stayed, the counting is at Vessendal, so we arrive. Ropes at first light. He told me there is no fifth act: four acts and a thing after them with no name, and the late man is the creditor, and after the bell the play stops telling and arranges. He took the trunk for his own wagon. Then Vane walked in by the mended door with chestnuts, and I made him stand and be looked at, handed him his hat and the pencilled playbill, and got chestnut-plain truth: the Blue Boar, a carter at eleven shillings, forty minutes. And the real number — nine years is a debt he paid to a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke bought the papers. A signature nobody gave. I promised clean books and a bad surprise, and every name from that room. Prewick was still in the fourth row on cold plush, having chosen for the first time not to write. I gave him my whole ledger for his lesson: the Office reads text only, and there are two Proscribed entries — anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following. Falk is not to speak an uncompared line; he said his line upstage, at the trunk. Roll call at first light; a Krug missing from it. At noon a page with ten in it came onto the felt and I carried it face-down to Sorel and read it beside her: a child of ten, a border crossed twice, a kind invitation. She put it in her glove. At Halbern's I met Skarke's agent on a milestone — clean boots, no name — and traded initials, an instrument, and ten paces hands in pockets; he told me, to deny it later, that Skarke read aloud 'the agent comes early and is not admitted'. Then the hearing: dates unrounded, arithmetic laid bare, every voice heard. Falk said Katterau and what it took. Vane asked me to rule it. I have not ruled.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.
**History:** I was up at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when the girl came in out of the rain with the notice and complained about our open door. I told her about the third board and she stepped over it without being told twice, which is more than Krug ever managed. Odalric interviewed her, Mirelle told her to say yes, and we had Bell Harrow for stage manager. Sorel said the bucket had been under the star trap since Katterau. I gave her the truth about the thunder trough and the farmer at Merrow while Odalric called a concussion emotion, and later heard him shift the iron trunk alone, which two seasons ago took four of us and a plank. On the star trap sill I told her she might ask me anything but one thing. She nailed the third joint and asked whose the small upright hand was, so I told her: Krug's hurrying scrawl, Krug gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made at Vessendal, riding in Odalric's trunk, never opened on this tour; nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, and then no more Krug. Not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice — and by her colour she had already read. She handed the page over and I put it in my lining with the others. Then the trunk began moving in the passage with Odalric nowhere in the house.

By morning I was sober and carrying a brandy I did not drink. Odalric began about the properties list being a document of aspiration; I told him plainly it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town, and to answer her, she nailed the trough. He laughed too big, clapped my arm, and went out the front doors to see about a carpenter, which was her errand. I gave Harrow the brandy for Krebs, who bargains better wet, and sat in the dark house watching the empty stage. The old sheet split mid-storm and went up into tin, so I stepped a half-pace in and said even the sky is out of coin tonight; the house barked once and Mirelle took the next line off me clean. After the curtain I saw through the pass door the empty fourth row with the hat set crown-down beside it, and heard myself say that a bell is rung and nothing answers. I told Harrow that whoever wrote her paper has read the page — a page she has not shown him — and asked where Odalric was. She sent me to the passage: the trunk dragged two feet square into the middle, the scrape fresh, the lid up, blank paper stacked neat inside, his hat face down on the flags, one glove, no Odalric. I called her once.

She crouched and counted it like a scene and asked for the fifth act, so I gave it her: the pages come blank, that chest has been clean paper fourteen years and every so often it is not, and there is no fifth act — four acts and a thing following with no name in the folio, which at Katterau we did not stage and which happened anyway. The late man is the man who is owed. I shut the lid, gave her the hat rather than keep it, and said the trunk rides in my wagon where I can hear it. Then Odalric came in by the wrong door with chestnuts, alive and absurd, and I told her nobody had passed the boy. He said nine years is not the loan, and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I carried my split tin out in felt, told her she held the corner without shouting, and sent her down to Prewick. At noon a page had come to sit on the tin, dry, in the copyist's hand, with a ten in it; she looked at the number and nothing else and would not let me ask. She was gone longer than the soup, so I sang. At the fire I said the name once in my own voice: Katterau. Nine of us, a green room, a wager and a bottle, read aloud sitting down — three and a half acts. Four years to arrange, and it cost Anna Sorel and the boy Grelle and my voice for a season and Odalric's nerve for good. It has never been finished. Let her rule.
**Entry:** She crouched over the trunk and counted it like a scene, and asked me for the fifth act, so I told her: the pages come blank, that chest has been clean paper fourteen years and every so often it is not, and there is no fifth act — four acts and a thing following with no name in the folio, which at Katterau we did not stage and which happened anyway. The late man is the man who is owed. I shut the lid and gave her the hat rather than keep it, and said the trunk rides in my wagon where I can hear it, since I shall not be sleeping. Then Odalric came in by the wrong door with chestnuts, alive, absurd, and I told her nobody had passed the boy. He said nine years is not the loan and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I carried my split tin out in felt, told her she held the corner without shouting, and sent her down to Prewick. On the road at noon a page had come to sit on the tin, dry, in the copyist's hand, with a ten in it; she looked at the number and nothing else and would not let me ask. She was gone longer than the soup, so I sang. At the fire I said the name once, in my own voice: Katterau. Nine of us, a green room, a wager and a bottle, read aloud sitting down — three and a half acts. It took four years to arrange, and it took Anna Sorel and the boy Grelle and my voice for a season and Odalric's nerve for good. It has never been finished. Let her rule.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.
**History:** A stage manager came in out of the weather with my notice in her fist and three references on three fingers: Bell Harrow. I engaged her on the spot and promised plot tables, a bucket, and a fair figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and said of the book only that it is as honest as books are. I steered her wide of the trunk and would not be steered back, though Prewick held his lamp over the lid and asked whether it was numbered. I showed her the thunder while Falk told the farmer at Merrow again. She asked me to shift the trunk a hand's breadth left off the ladder's foot and went for her bucket. Alone, I wiped the lid, pressed the chalk flat, said what I say, and lifted one end: light, wrong, answering. I put it down, took my hands off it, then shoved it properly and did not stay in the house.

Next morning she asked three things and had all three: Krebs for a shilling, tin because thirty-two feet is thirty-two feet, and ten minutes over the book. Emeran warned it would be the trunk, or a page, or a town. Hunting a carpenter I had no wish to find, I got Skarke's man's card instead — he had counted our seats from the street. Under my own poster, hat off, I told her the Palace said the 3rd and I had been selling the company the 17th since Merrow, for Katterau's six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. She wanted the road laid against the 3rd. I gave her the card, and counted the float twice.

I came in wet with a carpenter — Krebs's brother-in-law, cart at eleven shillings — and found my trunk in the passage under her lamp, Falk watching, and a torn playbill: nine years. So I said it: nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from a dying friend, paid him, he signed nothing, and Skarke has bought his papers. A signature nobody gave. She set me to name everyone in that room, in ink. There was a notary. Tonight she read the dates unrounded; Falk said Katterau and what it cost me. I asked her to rule it, and I shall drive where she points.
**Entry:** Came in wet and pleased with myself — a carpenter found, Krebs's brother-in-law and his cart bought at eleven shillings when I had offered twelve so the man might feel he lost — and there was my trunk dragged into the middle of the passage with the lid shut and Harrow's lamp on it, and Falk against the wall, and I put the chestnuts down on the flags like a fool. She made me stand and be looked at and put my hat in my hands with a torn playbill on top, pencil side up. Nine years. I read it twice. So I told her the thing I have not said aloud: the loan is two seasons old; nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from a man who was dying and my friend, and I paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke has bought his papers. What comes to the counting is a signature nobody gave. She did not weep at me or dismiss me — she gave me a task: every name that was in that room, in ink, in the wagon. There was a notary. There is always a notary. I gave the boy the chestnuts and a story. I slept four hours and called it seven, and answered present at her roll, and did not want to hear Boyle say there used to be a Krug on this list. Mirelle told me the company would hear the road tonight and I said yes. Harrow read the dates out unrounded, all of them, and everyone spoke, and Falk said Katterau and what it cost me. I stood up with my hat in my hands and asked her to rule it. I shall drive where she points.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.
**History:** I came to this house seconded since Merrow, and my first business was the fire notice by the scene dock, fallen again. I reported it to Herr Vane and found a stranger on the stage: the new stage manager. I gave my name and office and took hers spelled out — H, A, double R, O, W, Bell as in the thing you ring — for the certificate. The iron trunk in the passage was unnumbered; she said nothing in the house was hers until she had walked it. I entered unsecured iron, height. Re-hanging the notice level I found an older one behind it, about unnumbered property in passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, stamped twice, the first strike crooked: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. She said notices were hers now, the reading and the taking-down both, copied Vorn's name into her notebook, and had me file it under found level. I said aloud what I should not have: the Office approves, proscribes, or refers; not approved is what a man writes when told to write nothing. Katterau was on no itinerary I was given, and everyone here has been there.

After a night of arithmetic I laid my paper against hers on the mounting block: mine Merrow, this town, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance 3rd of Frost — a Palace date, not ours; hers Katterau and the 17th. She would ask Vane before the half, and neither of us would say Katterau first. Sorel spoke Ilsabet at somebody who was not there. We counted the buckets: nine notionally, five wet, one a drum of whiting I declared a monument, two behind the star trap. I learned tin shaken low is thunder. Then the sheet split on my only cue and heaven went to a tea tray; she signed me softer, I kept going, and I broke the sky. She promised the tin burial with honours at Vessendal; I put it in felt. Front of house on her order I found no hat on fourth row centre, only pressed plush, both seats warm, and nobody had passed my doors — I count house; it is the one thing I am for.

I sat on that plush gone cold and waited for her, having decided to write nothing down, the first choice of its kind in my service. I gave her the two warm seats, the sound going up half an octave when the sky broke, and Herr Falk speaking a line in no certified copy of Ilsabet's Ransom, and asked to be told what travels in the trunk, by her, not too late. She told me everything, entered as heard: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages arriving in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau, unstaged and happening anyway; fourteen years of clean paper. I opened the back of my Index where three pages are sewn in black thread and showed her the Proscribed section — thirty-one titles, twenty-nine with authors, two entered as anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following, stamped not to be described aloud in any report. Then I understood the useful, horrible thing: the Office reads only text, so I could certify Vessendal honestly with that trunk twenty feet from the stage door. Our terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; she does not let Falk speak an uncompared line. He said it upstage, toward the trunk. I answered the roll with my luggage numbered one to four, item four the Index, riding with me, and said at the fire that if we play Katterau I must lie either way, that I find I am able to, and that I wish to be asked and not simply arrived with.
**Entry:** I sat in the fourth row, dead centre, on plush that had gone cold, and waited for the stage manager because I had decided not to write anything down — the first time in my service that I have chosen that. I told her so, and told her what I had: two warm seats and nobody past my doors, the sound going up half an octave when the sky broke, and Herr Falk speaking a line that is in no certified copy of Ilsabet's Ransom. I asked to be told what travels in that trunk, by her, and not too late. She told me everything, entered as heard: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages that arrive in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau, unstaged and happening anyway; fourteen years of clean paper. So I opened the back of my Index, where three pages are sewn in with black thread, and showed her the Proscribed section — thirty-one titles, twenty-nine with authors, and two entered as anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following, stamped not to be described aloud in any report. And then I understood the useful, horrible thing: the Office reads only text, so I could certify Vessendal honestly with that trunk twenty feet from the stage door. I do not like being useful in that way. Our terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; she is not to let Falk speak an uncompared line. He said it upstage, toward the trunk. I answered present at the roll with my luggage numbered one to four, item four the Index, riding with me. At the fire I said aloud that if we play Katterau I must lie either way, that I find I am able to, and that I wish to be asked and not simply arrived with.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.
**History:** I was mending a glove on the fly floor without light when the new one came in out of the rain, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked a second time with tears in it. I mentioned the bucket under the star trap, there since Katterau, and enjoyed what the word did to Falk's glass. Coming down the ladder I gave her the only useful advice: its foot wants a hand's breadth left and can't have it for the trunk; don't drag the trunk, ask him, then go away while he does. She did it exactly, which told me something — though when I came back cloaked with my hatbox the trunk was snug against the ladder again and four feet of chalk dragged along the brick. He would blame the porters; the Corona has none. I asked Harrow what her page said and she gave it flat: the wrong door, a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut in pencil beneath. Nine is not my number. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, that Krug thought the first a joke of Falk's, that it described a horse going lame and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow; that they come slantwise and late; that mine is ten, and that a page with ten in it comes to me first.

Next morning I was in the ostler's yard before her, on the mounting block, and did not say good morning. I gave her my own copy of Krug's plot tables, honest as the book is not, marginned: tin only, never the trough in houses under forty foot — the Corona is thirty-two. I fed the old horse, older than any number Odalric says aloud, and made her cue me Ilsabet, act two, from *you were not sent for*, and told her not to be kind. She wasn't, and the yard stopped being a yard. Prewick said "Oh" aloud and was appalled at himself; I shall keep that. I told him to unfold his itinerary. Later I told Harrow that Odalric was awake with his notices and frightened, and a frightened man says yes, so ask now — again tonight, before the half. We played the storm, the old tin barked and went to tea tray, Falk put in a line not in the book and the house forgave us, so I took the next off him and rode it home.

On the road I answered present with my hatbox on my knees and heard Boyle say there used to be a Krug on the list. At noon Harrow came alongside the first wagon with a page, saying there was a ten in it and she had read the number and nothing else. I had Odalric stop the wagon; he did it without a question and went to be busy with a strap, which is the best of him. Twenty yards off, at a marker with the saint's face worn away, I unfolded it, then called her over, preferring two to know than one: the child is ten this winter and does not know the word mother, having been taught another; a woman crosses a border twice, once running, once summoned, and the second invitation is kind. I let her read it, so it is hers now; I was too tired to be careful. Unasked, she told me the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. Not Falk's lining — he carries enough of other people's endings sewn into him. I put the page inside my mended glove, palm flat to my wrist, and pulled the glove on over it. Then I told Odalric the company would sit and hear the road tonight, unrounded, and he said yes in a small voice. At the fire I gave my one voice: the capital is a summons dressed as an honour and I will go to it; Katterau, no — not four days backwards with a debt and a magistrate behind us.
**Entry:** Answered present with my hatbox on my knees and heard Boyle say there used to be a Krug on the list. At noon Harrow came alongside the first wagon holding a page and said there was a ten in it and that she had read the number and nothing else. I told Odalric to stop the wagon and he did it without one question and went to be busy with a strap, which is the best of him. I walked twenty yards to a marker with the saint's face worn off and unfolded it, and then I called her over, because I would rather two of us knew than one: the child is ten this winter and does not know the word mother, having been taught another; a woman crosses a border twice, once running, once summoned, and the second invitation is kind. I let her read it, so it is hers now; I was too tired to be careful. She told me, unasked and without being sworn to silence, that the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. Not Falk's lining — he has enough of other people's endings sewn into him. I put the page inside my mended glove, palm flat against my wrist, and pulled the glove on over it, so it rides where I can feel it. Then I told Odalric the company would sit down and hear the road tonight, unrounded, and he said yes in a small voice. At the fire I gave my one voice: the capital is a summons dressed as an honour and I will go to it; Katterau, no — not four days backwards with a debt and a magistrate behind us.

#### Dessa Krul

**History:** Answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal. Mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served. At the fire I kept my needle going and said the two things that wanted saying: the queen's slippers have two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I don't want another warm box.
**Entry:** Answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal. Mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served. At the fire I kept my needle going and said the two things that wanted saying: the queen's slippers have two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I don't want another warm box.

#### Toby Lenz

**History:** Answered present at the roll — front of house, props, and pit band if there's a pit band. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal that will have me late home. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads and came back running without the bucket, because there was a gentleman sitting on a milestone down the Vessendal road who asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I said I'd go to Katterau — six hundred seats, I've never called a house of six hundred — and then I saw the faces and said only if it were ruled.

Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads and came back running without the bucket, because there was a gentleman sitting on a milestone down the Vessendal road who asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I said I'd go to Katterau — six hundred seats, I've never called a house of six hundred — and then I saw the faces and said only if it were ruled.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**History:** Answered present from under the tarpaulin — Ottmar Boyle, second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud that there used to be a Krug on this list and he's not here. Fixed a shed wheel-rim in the afternoon with wire and language. At the fire the stage manager asked me first, being soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the carter's axle holds, three if it don't; Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling toll road or the free hill road that killed a horse on us. And the sum nobody had said: Katterau is back. Twenty-two mile the wrong way and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night. I'll walk it if it's ruled. I'd rather not walk it for a favour a mayor may have died of.

Fixed a shed wheel-rim in the afternoon with wire and language.
