And the sum nobody had said: Katterau is back. Twenty-two mile the wrong way and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night. I'll walk it if it's ruled. I'd rather not walk it for a favour a mayor may have died of.

#### Skarke's agent

**History:** Came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart and waited on the milestone with the case on my knees; the boy for water told me yes, these were the Vermilion Players, and I told him I was early. The stage manager came alone with a lamp and a book and wrote me down as agent, no name given, boots clean, and I let her. Better to deal with one who owns nothing; Herr Vane weeps. I read the three matters in the order of the letter — takings counted before spent, schedule properties not sold or pledged or repaired at expense, and the trunk valued separately and to be inspected, not opened. Eleven schedules I have carried out and never before been told to look at a thing and not open it, so I asked her whether she knew why. She said the man who gave me the instruction has read something I haven't. Her three: daily counting initialled by me — better practice than I am used to and I shall report it so; the nine-year instrument produced — a certified copy only, the strongbox in the room, and she must say the words about a magistrate on Friday; the inspection at ten paces in daylight, hands in pockets — agreed, gladly. Then I told her the fourth matter, which I will deny: when Herr Skarke gave me the trunk instruction he had a page before him and read from it aloud without meaning to — the agent comes early and is not admitted. So I did not go to their fire. The road back was quite dry.
**Entry:** Came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart and waited on the milestone with the case on my knees; the boy for water told me yes, these were the Vermilion Players, and I told him I was early. The stage manager came alone with a lamp and a book and wrote me down as agent, no name given, boots clean, and I let her. Better to deal with one who owns nothing; Herr Vane weeps. I read the three matters in the order of the letter — takings counted before spent, schedule properties not sold or pledged or repaired at expense, and the trunk valued separately and to be inspected, not opened. Eleven schedules I have carried out and never before been told to look at a thing and not open it, so I asked her whether she knew why. She said the man who gave me the instruction has read something I haven't. Her three: daily counting initialled by me — better practice than I am used to and I shall report it so; the nine-year instrument produced — a certified copy only, the strongbox in the room, and she must say the words about a magistrate on Friday; the inspection at ten paces in daylight, hands in pockets — agreed, gladly. Then I told her the fourth matter, which I will deny: when Herr Skarke gave me the trunk instruction he had a page before him and read from it aloud without meaning to — the agent comes early and is not admitted. So I did not go to their fire. The road back was quite dry.

#### Wenzel

**Entry:** Came at first light for the eleven shillings and took the second wagon on with my cart, the axle honest as promised. Six days of road ahead; by mid-morning I was whistling, four notes and stopping in the middle of the fifth, over and over, without noticing.

### 4 · Behind the Lion
- **Messages:** 65-84

At the fire, Bell Harrow rules with the book shut. Katterau will not be settled "this tour, and not for money" — but "not never." Vessendal must give a matinee across three nights; the 3rd stands; Boyle takes the toll road. From tonight, nothing may be spoken on or off stage unless it's in a certified copy — no wagers, no bottles, no lines invented to cover a broken scene. She tells Prewick he has "also arrived with" and orders Vane to drive for Vessendal. Prewick, having only Ilsabet, The Widow's Toll, and Vane's cut of the Wolf King, demands certified copies of everything and vows to sit up comparing. Falk repeats "Not never," touches Bell's head, and leaves muttering toll distances. Vane weeps himself to sleep in his coat. Mirelle reveals that Anna Sorel was her sister, that she kept Vane's accounts that year, and that any signed receipt went into her box.

Bell joins Falk at the roped trunk, where paper turns inside though "it says nothing — it reads." Falk has heard it twice before, near Katterau and Merrow; there are no mice. It stops mid-page; he keeps watch all night. Bell finds a blank sheet outside the ropes and hides it with the tin.

Two days later, Vane pays the toll exactly. At the Athenaeum, Bell pays Frau Loewe's debts, forbidding inspection before Friday. An agent mentions a gentleman from the capital, lodging at the Swan, who doesn't drink. Loewe recalls Falk once hiring the dark house alone, chalking a great plot, and a woman from Katterau later seeking him — Loewe lied that he'd gone south. Falk admits he drew all four acts from memory to bind it to one man: "It wants an audience... it is a play."

Toby delivers a paid, anonymous card for three nights, fourth row centre. At the river they bury the split tin. Mirelle sends Bell to the registry, unable to go herself. There, Vane's names appear in the ledger; Anna Sorel's sealed box remains unreleased, eighteen shillings owed. Bell pays; Prewick certifies the register. The executor, Josias Perlmann, reveals Brandt never signed the receipt — "between friends" — and died before he could. "Say what you want and be quick."

**History:** At the Corona, Bell Harrow becomes stage manager for the Vermilion Players under Odalric Vane, inheriting a prompt book with a torn page and a rumor of a bucket "since Katterau." Emeran Falk warns of hazards; Casimir Prewick, a Public Morals clerk, scrutinizes paperwork and an unnumbered iron trunk. Harrow finds the missing page—cryptic, marked "cut"—linked to vanished writer Anselm Krug and forbidden copying rules. Mirelle Sorel reveals the pages predict real events; her sister Anna died connected to Katterau. A copperplate letter exposes Vane's hidden debt to Skarke of Vessendal, secured against the company's goods, including the untouchable trunk. Plot tables show the Corona's grid unsafe for the "trough." Vane confesses his lie; after a performance, he vanishes, later returning soaked, claiming an old unsigned debt now haunts him as "a signature nobody gave." Prewick and Harrow trade secrets; Falk reveals the trunk cycles blank paper except when it doesn't, and hints at a nameless "fifth act." Skarke's agent appears at camp with eerie foreknowledge. The company argues over Katterau's cost; Harrow rules disputes unsettled but enforces strict script discipline. The trunk's paper turns and "reads" itself. In town, Bell pays debts, uncovers Falk's solitary staging of the full play, and learns from executor Perlmann that Brandt's debt to Vane was never signed before his death.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.
**History:** I came in at the Corona by a stage door that shouldn't have been open and took the book from Vane in his plum coat: yes, I said, if the book is honest and the liars are consistent. Falk warned me off the third board; Sorel, on the fly floor, warned me not to drag the iron trunk. I watched Vane lift it like a hatbox, then scrape it for show. In the bucket under the star trap I found the cut page — a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat — and pocketed it. Prewick showed me an older notice the Office never issued: Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED. Falk named the upright hand a Vessendal copyist's, riding unopened in the trunk; Krug cut nine pages, burned them, the tenth came back, and he went without his boots. Sorel's number is ten. Under my candle-end, copperplate not Prewick's.

It was Skarke's paper: wagons, canvas, horses, all properties pledged, every taking to Vessendal, interest weekly, counting at the third performance before an agent, the trunk valued separately — do not open, do not sell. Mirelle gave me honest tables off Krug's plot; Krebs had been selling himself fourteen days for a card counting 340 seats. The tin split; Falk covered me. A fifth act in pencil on my own playbill. At the counting: float twice, plum coat on the peg, two warm seats, no hat, the trunk full of blank paper.

Falk said there is no fifth act — four acts and a thing after with no name, the late man the creditor, and after the bell the play arranges. Vane came back with chestnuts: the Blue Boar, a carter at eleven shillings, and nine years owed to a dying friend who signed nothing, Skarke holding papers with a signature nobody gave. I promised clean books, a bad surprise, every name. Prewick lent me the Office's two Proscribed entries: anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following. A page with ten in it — a child, a border crossed twice, a kind invitation — went into Sorel's glove. Skarke's agent on a milestone quoted his master: the agent comes early and is not admitted. Falk said Katterau and what it took, and Vane asked me to rule.

I ruled with the book shut: Katterau no, not this tour, not for money, not never; the 3rd stands; the toll road for Boyle; nothing spoken that isn't in a certified copy. Mirelle told me Anna Sorel was her sister, who kept Odalric's books that year and took every receipt into her box. Under the barn I heard paper reading itself, page by page, till it stopped mid-page; Falk has heard it at Katterau after the wager and at Merrow. I put the blank sheet in the felt, not my book. At the Athenaeum I paid Frau Loewe nine shillings and learned Falk hired her dark house four years ago, chalked a full plot, and a week later a woman came from Katterau with a child. The strongbox's gentleman took the fourth row centre, three nights paid, and did not use the doors. We buried the tin in the river. In the registry behind the lion, Anna's box sits sealed, nine years unpaid — I paid eighteen shillings and stopped the clock; kin's proof or a magistrate opens it. Someone has asked after it twice. Perlmann, blind above the saddler's, knew the man's cuff and said the receipt was never finished.
**Entry:** I ruled it standing with the book shut: Katterau no, not this tour and not for money — but not never. The 3rd stands, a matinee out of Vessendal or a reason, the toll road for Boyle, and company law: nothing spoken on a stage or off it that isn't in a certified copy. Prewick asked to be arrived with; I arrived with him. Vane I pointed at Vessendal. Then Mirelle, glove in her lap: Anna Sorel was her sister, kept Odalric's books that year, and every receipt in the world went into her box.

Falk's lamp was moving under the barn. I gave the night thirty seconds of my own ear and heard paper — page by page, unhurried. "It says nothing. It reads." He's heard it at Katterau after the wager and at Merrow the week Krug cut the ninth. It stopped mid-page, like a man interrupted. Outside the ropes I found one blank sheet; into the felt with the tin, not into my book.

Two days' road, eight shillings unrounded. At the Athenaeum: the agent punctual to the town, Frau Loewe with a letting book and nine shillings owed — paid from my hand, trunk roped in her yard, nothing near her under-stage. Her dates cost me nothing: Falk hired her dark house four years ago for two shillings, chalked a full plot in it, and a week later a woman came from Katterau with a child. The agent gave me a courtesy I did not ask for: the strongbox's gentleman rode ahead and is in this town.

Card at half six — fourth row centre, three nights, paid, no hat wanted, and he did not use the doors. Sold things get service: a programme on the seat, counts only, no staring. We buried the tin in the river and Prewick waded in.

Morning: Vane's names in ink; the registry behind the lion with Prewick's seal for a lamp. Anna's box is there, sealed, nine years unpaid — eighteen shillings paid, clock stopped, register lines certified twice. Kin's proof or a magistrate. The executor is Perlmann, blind, above the saddler's — and someone else has asked after that box twice: "paper, I expect. It usually is." I put Odalric at the door and told him no performance. Perlmann knew his cuff, and told us the receipt was never finished.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.
**History:** I was awake at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when Bell Harrow came in out of the rain with the notice and complained about our open door. I warned her of the third board; Odalric interviewed her, Mirelle told her to say yes, and she was our stage manager. Sorel said the bucket had stood under the star trap since Katterau. She nailed the third joint of the thunder trough, so I told her about Krug's hurrying scrawl, how he left Katterau without his boots, about the copyist's fair copy made at Vessendal and riding unopened in Odalric's iron trunk — nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, then no more Krug. I told her not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice, and saw by her colour she already had. Her page went into my lining with the others. Then the trunk moved in the passage with Odalric nowhere in the house, though he had shifted it alone that took four of us and a plank two seasons back.

Next day I sent him to answer her; he laughed and went out on her carpenter's errand. That night the sheet split and I said the sky was out of coin. After the curtain: an empty fourth row, a hat crown-down. In the passage the trunk stood dragged out, lid up, full of blank paper, his hat face down, one glove, no Odalric.

I told her there is no fifth act — four acts and a thing following, and the late man is the man who is owed. Odalric came back with chestnuts, saying nine years is not the loan, and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. A page came dry onto my tin with a ten in it. At the fire I said Katterau aloud and let her rule it: no, then not never.

The trunk does not speak; it reads. She found a sheet outside the ropes. Loewe still holds the house; Harrow gave me work instead of pity. It wants a house. It is a play.
**Entry:** She ruled it: Katterau no — and then not never, which is a different sentence entirely, and I found I had a use for the rest of my life after all. I blessed her head like a gatepost and went off counting toll miles in verse.

Then I had the tarpaulin off and stood listening, and she came across the camp on the sides of her feet and asked. I told her the truth: it does not speak, it reads. Twice before — Katterau, the night after the wager; Merrow, the week Krug cut the ninth page. Not mice. It stopped mid-page, the way a man stops when someone comes in, and I put the felt down against it like bedding and sat the night on the box, and once I said a line into the dark and stopped myself. She found a sheet lying outside the ropes; she says it was outside, and I believe her, which is the worst of it.

Two days' road and then the stone front with my name spelled right on the bills. Loewe still holds the house. I could not get down. Harrow came to my wheel and gave me a job instead of sympathy, which is why she is the harbor. So I told her what I chalked on that stage four years ago: the whole thing from memory, four acts and the matter following, alone, to see whether the arranging would come to one man and be done. It would not come. It wants a house. It is a play.

Load-in, and a proper grid, and a thunder run nailed by somebody who cared. At the river I said the sailors' words over the tin and made the clerk put it in, and he did, boots and all, and the wool warehouses gave the words back. Eleven years, twenty-nine towns, broke honestly in service.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.
**History:** A stage manager came in out of the weather with my notice in her fist and three references on three fingers: Bell Harrow. I engaged her at once and promised plot tables, a bucket, a figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and said of the book only that it is as honest as books are. I steered her wide of the trunk and would not be steered back, though Prewick held his lamp over the lid and asked whether it was numbered. I showed her the thunder while Falk told the farmer at Merrow. She asked me to shift the trunk a hand's breadth left; alone, I wiped the lid, pressed the chalk flat, said what I say, lifted one end — light, wrong, answering — set it down, then shoved it and called out that the repair should go to the credit of the management. I did not stay in the house.

Next morning she asked three things and had all three: Krebs for a shilling, the tin, ten minutes over the book. Emeran said she had nailed the trough. I went out for a carpenter I meant not to find and found Skarke's man's card instead — he had counted our seats from the street. Cornered by my own poster, I told her the truth: the Palace said the 3rd; I had been selling the company the 17th since Merrow, for Katterau's six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. She wanted the road laid against the 3rd. I gave her the card.

Then she set my trunk in the passage, her lamp on it, and a torn playbill in my hat: nine years. So I said it — the loan two seasons old, borrowed nine years ago from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend; I paid him; he signed nothing; Skarke has bought the papers, and a signature nobody gave. She set me to naming everyone in that room in ink. Boyle said there used to be a Krug on this list. She read the dates unrounded, the company spoke, Falk said Katterau and what it cost me, and I asked her to rule.

She ruled standing: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, drive for Vessendal. I wept, slept in my coat, paid eight shillings to the penny at the toll, and went straight to the Athenaeum box office to learn the seats sold. At breakfast I gave the names: Brandt on the Kohlgasse; Perl or Perlmann the notary; Anna Sorel; a doctor whose name I never had; a nun; myself; and the one in the passage I never saw. Then she took me up a leather-smelling stair, said no performance, and I knocked three times. Bettina opened; Josias found my sleeve, rubbed the worn cuff — nine years, the same coat — and told them what I could never prove: I came at eleven at night with the whole of it, saying God forgive me for being late; Hessel laughed, it hurt him, he would not sign, between friends; he died on the Tuesday. The receipt was never finished. I could not speak.
**Entry:** She ruled, standing, and did not spare me: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, and drive for Vessendal. I wept — I am not ashamed of it — quoted my Lear notice at nobody, and slept in my coat. At the toll gate I paid eight shillings to the penny because she was standing there. Vessendal came up out of the flat and the Athenaeum knows what it has; I went straight to the box office to learn the number of seats sold, which is the only prayer I have.

At breakfast I gave her the names in ink as promised: Hessel Brandt on the Kohlgasse; the notary, Perl or Perlmann, inky fingers and a cold; Anna Sorel; a doctor whose name I never had; a nun; myself; and the one in the passage I never saw and have thought of for nine years. Writing it down was worse than saying it.

Then she took me up a stair that smelled of leather with her clerk behind, set me at the door and said: no performance. Three knocks — the smallest sound I have made in my life. Bettina opened it, and then Josias in the doorway with his white eyes past me, finding my sleeve and rubbing the worn place on my cuff: nine years, and I have not changed my coat. He told them what I have never been able to prove: I came at eleven at night with the whole of it and said God forgive me for being late, and Hessel laughed and it hurt him and he would not sign, between friends, and died on the Tuesday. The receipt was never finished. It is the only unfinished instrument of the old man's life. I stood in the doorway and could not speak.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.
**History:** I reported the fallen fire notice by the scene dock to Herr Vane and found a stranger on our stage: the new stage manager, Harrow — H, A, double R, O, W, Bell as in the thing you ring — who said nothing in the house was hers until she had walked it. I noted the unsecured iron trunk, unnumbered, under the thunder trough, and behind the fire notice found an older one about unnumbered property in the passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, stamped twice, SEEN. NOT APPROVED. She took it; I filed it under found level and said aloud that not approved is what a man writes when told to write nothing. I have been seconded since Merrow, and Katterau is on no itinerary I was given, though everyone in this company has been there.

Next morning I laid my paper against hers on the mounting block: mine gave Merrow, this town, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost — a Palace date, not ours; hers gave Katterau and the 17th. She would ask Vane before the half; neither of us would say Katterau first. We counted nine fire buckets, five with water, one solid whiting I declared a monument. I learned tin shaken low is thunder, then split the sheet and broke the sky, and was told the tin would be buried with honours at Vessendal. Front of house I found no hat in the fourth row centre, two warm seats, and nobody past my doors.

Sitting there after, I chose for the first time to write nothing down, and told her so: the warm seats, the sound gone up half an octave, Herr Falk speaking a line in no certified copy of Ilsabet's Ransom. She told me everything, entered as heard — a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages arriving in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau unstaged and happening anyway; fourteen years of clean paper. I opened the back of my Index, the three pages sewn in black thread, and showed her the Proscribed section: thirty-one titles, twenty-nine with authors, two entered as anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following, not to be described aloud. Then I understood the horrible useful thing: the Office reads only text, so I could certify Vessendal honestly with that trunk twenty feet from the stage door. Our terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; she does not let Falk speak an uncompared line — he said it upstage, toward the trunk. At the roll I answered present, luggage one to four, item four the Index riding with me. At the fire I said that if we play Katterau I must lie either way, that I find I am able to, and that I wish to be asked and not arrived with.

The ruling came; I was asked, and told I had also been arrived with, which I shall remember. I demanded certified copies of everything — I hold only Ilsabet, The Widow's Toll and Herr Vane's cut of the Wolf King, and the company plays four, and there are no farces. I compared to line four hundred and twelve and slept upright under four scripts.

At the river Herr Falk said the sailors' words and gave me the tin; I waded in, ruined my boots, and pushed it under, and it made one last small thunder. This morning, collared and sealed, behind the lion with Harrow: the clerk changed his manner at Office of Public Morals, and I asked for the register itself. The lease was there; Brandt's deposits released to an executor with an unreadable scrawl; Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. Told my seal certifies plays and not boxes, I copied the three lines word for word and stamped them crooked, then clean, and gave her both. The probate roll gave us Perlmann, Josias, notary — then a saddler's stair, and an old blind man who could hear my starch.
**Entry:** The ruling came and I was asked and told I had also been arrived with, which I shall remember. I stood up trembling and said what I needed: certified copies of everything. I have Ilsabet, The Widow's Toll and Herr Vane's cut of the Wolf King and nothing else, and the company plays four, and there are no farces. I sat up with a candle and compared to line four hundred and twelve and fell asleep upright with four scripts on my knees, and it is the most work I have ever set myself and I am extremely pleased.

At the river I was fetched from my comparing without knowing why, and Herr Falk said the sailors' words and then handed me the tin and said it was mine. I waded in to the ankle and ruined my boots and pushed it under and it made one last small thunder. I have attended a funeral for an object and it was not ridiculous. I noted it.

This morning, collar and seal and my regulation walk, behind the lion with the stage manager. The counter clerk went from we open at half past to this way, Herr Clerk on the words Office of Public Morals, and I asked for the register itself and not a copy. The lease is there; Brandt's deposits released to an executor with an unreadable scrawl; Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. The clerk told me, correctly, that my seal certifies plays and not boxes, and Harrow turned that into work: I copied the three lines word for word and stamped them, crooked, then again clean, and gave her both. The probate roll gave us Perlmann, Josias, notary. Then up a saddler's stair, and an old blind man who could hear my starch.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.
**History:** The new one came in out of the rain while I was mending a glove on the fly floor, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears. I gave her the bucket under the star trap, there since Katterau, for the pleasure of watching the word travel into Falk's glass, and the only advice worth giving: the ladder's foot wants a hand's breadth left, don't drag the trunk, ask him and go away while he does. She did it exactly. I came back cloaked with my hatbox to find the trunk snug against the ladder again and four feet of chalk along the brick, which he would blame on porters the Corona does not have. Harrow gave me her page flat, word for word — the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, cut cut cut in pencil. Nine years is not my number. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, that Krug thought the first was a joke of Falk's until the near mare went down outside Merrow four weeks later, that they come slantwise and late, that mine is ten and a ten comes to me first.

In the ostler's yard I gave her my own honest copy of Krug's plot tables, margined: tin only, never the trough under forty foot; the Corona is thirty-two. I fed the old horse and made her cue me Ilsabet, unkindly, and Prewick said "Oh" out loud. I told her Odalric was frightened over his notices, and a frightened man says yes.

At noon she brought me a page with a ten in it, having read the number and nothing else. I stopped the wagon; Odalric obeyed and went to fuss with a strap. At the worn marker I opened it: a child ten this winter who does not know the word mother, a woman crossing a border twice, once running, once summoned, the second invitation kind. I let her read it, being too tired to be careful. Unasked, she told me the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. I hid the page in my glove against my wrist, made him sit the company down to hear the road unrounded, and gave my one voice at the fire: the capital is a summons dressed as an honour and I will go to it; Katterau, no, not four days backwards with a debt and a magistrate behind us.

Harrow ruled standing and shut. Katterau went into the ground for this tour and I let out the breath I have held since Halbern. Nobody said aye. While she banked the fire I named the notary at that deathbed, and said aloud for the first time in years that Anna Sorel was my sister, that she kept his accounts that year, and that any receipt with a signature went into Anna's box. Two days of road; I watched the river instead of Vessendal. Coming up the mud from the tin's burial, nine of us with lanterns and Falk's sailors' words, I sent her to the registry behind the lion, eight to noon: the fifth-year lease was Vessendal's, so Anna's box came here. I cannot go in. My name is in that building. She can.
**Entry:** She gave the ruling standing and shut, and Katterau went into the ground for this tour, and I let out the breath I have been holding since Halbern. Nobody said aye; we don't.

I stayed while she banked the fire, my glove off with the page still in it, and gave her the thing she'll need before Friday: the notary at that deathbed. Odalric will not have the name — he remembers notices, not names. So I said it out loud for the first time in years. Anna Sorel was my sister. She kept his accounts that year, and if there is a receipt anywhere in the world with a signature on it, it went into Anna's box, and her box went where the others go.

Two days of road. I did not look at Vessendal once; I watched the river instead, which is a thing you can do with a town.

Coming up the mud from the tin's burial — nine of us, lanterns, and Falk's sailors' words, which were better than the tin deserved and exactly what it deserved — I told Harrow where to go: the registry behind the lion, eight to noon, and the lease in the fifth year was Vessendal's, so Anna's box came here. I cannot go in. My name is in that building on paper I would rather not stand next to. She can.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin — Ottmar Boyle, second gentlemen and all soldiers — and I said out loud what was true, that there used to be a Krug on that list and he isn't on it now. Nobody answered me. That afternoon I fixed a shed wheel-rim with wire and language, which is most of what I'm for.

At the fire the stage manager asked me first, soldiers' sums being my trade: two days to Vessendal if the carter's axle held, three if it didn't; Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling by the toll road or free by the hill road that killed a horse on us once already. And the sum nobody would say aloud: Katterau is back the way we came. Twenty-two mile wrong and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night's playing, and all for a favour to a mayor who may already have died of it. I said I'd walk it if it was ruled. I said I'd rather not.

The ruling came down and I nodded once and went out to look at the axle by lamplight, which is what a ruling amounts to in my hands. Toll road it was — eight shilling, and cheaper than a horse, and I'd said so first. I wired that axle in the morning and it held two days, which is longer than most things hold.

Then I backed the second wagon into the Athenaeum yard and took first watch on the trunk, lantern and a pipe I'm not let smoke in the flies. They relieved me twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river; I grumbled and went anyway. When Krul said a copper kettle would do for thunder I said what wanted saying — kettle's no good, kettle's a bell. And then nobody said anything for half a second. That's how I learned that word's gone bad in this company.
**Entry:** Ruling came down and I nodded once and went to look at the axle by lamplight, which is what a ruling means to me. Toll road, then — eight shilling, and cheaper than a horse, and I said so first. Wired the axle in the morning and it held two days.

Backed the second wagon into the Athenaeum yard, took first watch on the trunk with a lantern and a pipe I'm not let smoke in the flies. Got relieved twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river and grumbled about it and went anyway. When Krul said a copper kettle would do for thunder I said what wanted saying: kettle's no good, kettle's a bell. And then nobody said anything for half a second, which is how I learned that word's gone bad in this company.

#### Dessa Krul

**History:** I answered present from the second wagon, and when the wet chestnut turned up in the queen's slipper I said whoever had put it there could swim to Vessendal. That day was mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served, and nothing else worth keeping. At the fire I kept my needle going and said the two things that wanted saying. First, that the queen's slippers had two more towns in them at best, and I would know, since I am the one who mends them. Second, that Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots. I packed his box myself and it was still warm when I closed it. I said out loud that I did not want another warm box, and I meant it as a vote, and everyone at the fire heard it as one.

She ruled. I bit off my thread, and that was my aye. No Katterau. Good.

After that we came to the Athenaeum, and I carried the queen's slippers into the yard over my head like relics, because that brick is filthy and those slippers cannot afford another insult. Then I went down to the river for the tin. I said there would be new tin at Achterhalt, or a copper kettle at worst, meaning it as comfort, meaning it as arithmetic. Boyle said a kettle's a bell. Everybody stopped on the word. Nobody explained it to me and nobody had to; the stopping was the explanation, and I have carried it since.

So that is where I stand: Katterau refused, Krug's boots still unaccounted for, the slippers good for two towns and no more, Achterhalt ahead of us with its tin or its kettle, and Boyle's word sitting in the middle of us like something waiting to be struck. I keep my needle going. I still do not want another warm box.
**Entry:** She ruled and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye. No Katterau. Good.

Swore at a wet stocking in the frost, carried the queen's slippers into the Athenaeum yard over my head like relics because that brick is filthy. Went down to the river for the tin and said there'd be new tin at Achterhalt or a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and everybody stopped on the word. I keep my needle going. I still don't want another warm box.

#### Toby Lenz

**History:** I answered present at the roll and was put down for front of house, props, and the pit band if there was a pit band. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal long enough to make me late home. When I was sent for water at Halbern's crossroads I came back running and without the bucket, because there was a gentleman sitting on a milestone down the Vessendal road who asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he was early. I told the stage manager. At the fire that night I said I would go to Katterau — six hundred seats, and I had never called a house of six hundred — and then I saw the faces around me and added, only if it were ruled.

She ruled no Katterau, and I sat down hard, and I still do not know whether I was sorry or glad; what I know is that I will be telling people the rest of my life that I nearly called a house of six hundred. In the morning I boiled the water without being asked, and she wrote me into her book under something new.

In the Athenaeum yard I dropped the tailboard first thing. I borrowed Boyle's watch for twenty minutes and had to run to catch up for the tin going into the river, and it made one last thunder as it went under. At half six a gentleman left a cream card at front of house; he did not wait, and he did not come in by my doors — I was on the doors, and I have learned that much. She gave me standing orders after: a programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opens, all three nights, and I am to count row four in and count it out. Counts only, she said. No staring.
**Entry:** She ruled no Katterau and I sat down hard, and I don't know if I was sorry or glad, and I'll be telling people the rest of my life that I nearly called a house of six hundred. Boiled the water in the morning without being asked and she wrote me in her book under something new.

She gave me standing orders: a programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opens, all three nights, and count row four in and count it out. Counts only, no staring.

#### Skarke's agent

**History:** I came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart and sat on the milestone with the case on my knees; the boy who fetched water confirmed these were the Vermilion Players, and I told him I was early. The stage manager came alone, with a lamp and a book, and wrote me down as agent, no name given, boots clean, and I let her have it that way — better to deal with one who owns nothing, since Herr Vane weeps. I read out the three matters in the order of the letter: takings counted before they are spent; the schedule properties neither sold nor pledged nor repaired at expense; the trunk valued separately and inspected, not opened. Eleven schedules I have carried out and never once been told to look at a thing and not open it, so I asked her whether she knew the reason. She said the man who gave me the instruction has read something I haven't.

Her three I granted: the daily counting initialled by me, which is better practice than I am used to and I shall report it so; the nine-year instrument produced, though only a certified copy, the strongbox to stand in the room, and she must say the words about a magistrate on Friday; the inspection at ten paces, in daylight, hands in pockets — that gladly. The fourth matter I told her and will deny: when Herr Skarke gave me the trunk instruction he had a page before him and read aloud from it without meaning to — the agent comes early and is not admitted. So I stayed away from their fire.

Then I waited in the Athenaeum doorway from noon, case on my knees, beside the woman who holds the lease and does not like me. When the wagons came I was looking at the tarpaulined shape on Falk's wagon, and the stage manager put herself between it and me before the horses had stopped: today nobody looks at anything of theirs but the stage and the billing. Friday, ten paces, daylight, hands in pockets — I have it in my instruction book in her words, and it stands, though Herr Skarke will be displeased with me. I stepped back and said I have eyes and the road is where it is. Then I gave her a courtesy she had not bought: the strongbox came up from the capital this morning by coach, and the gentleman who should have come up with it rode ahead and is in the town. I said good afternoon, that I am at the Swan, and that I do not drink. The doorway woman watched me the whole way out.
**Entry:** Waited in the Athenaeum doorway from noon with the case on my knees, next to the woman who holds the lease and does not like me. When the wagons came I was looking at the tarpaulined shape on Falk's wagon, and the stage manager put herself between it and me before the horses had stopped and said today nobody looks at anything of theirs but the stage and the billing. Friday, ten paces, daylight, hands in pockets: I have it written in my instruction book in her words, Herr Skarke will be displeased with me, and it stands. I stepped back from the wagon and said I have eyes and the road is where it is.

Then I gave her a courtesy she had not bought: the strongbox came up from the capital this morning by coach, and the gentleman who should have come up with it rode ahead. He is in the town. I said good afternoon, that I am at the Swan, and that I do not drink. The doorway woman watched me the whole way out.

#### Frau Loewe

**History:** The agent had been in my doorway since noon, so I stood in it too with the letting book, and when the wagons came I told the stage manager the plain facts: I hold the lease, my ledger is the letting book, and I am the one who gets paid first. Nine shillings from the spring and a repaired gas tap, and Vane might open on that debt but he'd not close on it. She counted the nine into my palm on the spot, unrounded, and took the gas man and the counterweights onto herself and swore nothing of theirs would go near my under-stage, and that the trunk would stay roped in the yard and never cross my threshold — it marked my brick once already. I warmed to her by a degree.

Then she asked me to finish a sentence, and wanted it in dates, so she got it. Winter of the fifth year: Emeran Falk came alone, no company, and hired my house for one night at his own cost, two shillings, because he was Falk and I was young enough to be impressed. He never opened it. He sat in it a night and a day with the gas down; I sent a boy in with bread twice; on the second evening he gave back my key and thanked me very kindly. The stage was covered in chalk — marks, numbers, a plot for something big — and I swept it myself rather than let the boy see a man's madness. And a week later a woman came from Katterau asking for him, with a child, and I told her he'd gone south. He'd gone north. I'd tell the same lie again.

Load-in until six. He did not get down off his box for a long while.

#### Counter clerk

**History:** Two of them at the door before we opened, and the one in the collar had the Office of Public Morals on his seal, so I took them through — a search only, he said, and the register itself, not a copy, which is how you know a man who has read a register before. The Athenaeum lease, fifth year: there. Brandt, Hessel, wool factor: three items, released to the executor in the sixth year, and the signature a scrawl. Sorel, Anna: one box, sealed, fifth year, no release, nine years' storage unpaid. I told them what I always tell them — depositor, kin with proof, or an officer with a warrant — and that a seal that certifies plays does not certify boxes.

Then the lady put eighteen shillings on my counter and counted it twice, and asked for lawful things in reverse order, so I did lawful work: stopped the clock, wrote out kin's proof in full, fetched the probate roll. Brandt's executor is Perlmann, Josias, notary, above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse — eighty, blind, doesn't practise, daughter takes in sewing. I decided I liked her, so I gave her the other thing: that box has been asked after twice by the same gentleman, not kin, once with money and once with a lawyer's letter, and got nowhere, and the second time he asked me what was in it and I said I don't know, and he said, paper, I expect. It usually is.

It usually is.

#### Josias Perlmann

**History:** Bettina told me there was somebody on my stair. Three soft knocks — not a creditor's knock. Then a voice I have not heard in nine years saying only, It's Vane.

I found his sleeve, and then his cuff, and the worn shiny place on it, and knew it: nine years and he has not changed his coat. I told him what he came for, since he never could say it himself. He came at eleven at night on Hessel Brandt's last evening with a bag of money and counted it onto the counterpane and said this is the whole of it and God forgive me for being late, and Hessel laughed and it hurt him and made me stop writing. I did not finish the receipt. I said sign, Hessel, and he said no, between friends, and on the Tuesday he died. It is the only unfinished instrument of my life and I have thought of it every week since.

There were others on the stair — a woman breathing steadily, and starch, an officer of some kind. I told them to say what they want and be quick. I am old, and I am not deaf, which is worse.

#### Bettina Perlmann

**History:** Three strangers on our stair before ten, and I stood in the door with the sewing over my arm and weighed them, as I do. Then my father called out from inside and the one with the hat off said a name, and whatever was coming was not mine to stop, so I stepped back and let him have it. He held my father's hand on his own cuff for a long time.

He held my father's hand on his own cuff for a long time.

#### Krebs

**State:** Not present.
**History:** I came over from the smithy for the Vermilion when the new stage manager sent word — a shilling and a brandy in hand, though Vane's name had said one-and-six. I showed her the hinge, proud of it, and had the stage door biting its frame on the first try by noon. Of the second summons, when it came, I remember nothing — I was not present, and whatever passed that day passed without me.
**Entry:** Not present.

### 5 · Unpaid
- **Messages:** 85-104

Harrow lays out three asks; Perlmann agrees in order: he will swear his account Thursday at nine before Registrar Braun, with his own clerk and Bettina writing while he marks. Skarke's assignment is good but the debt is dead — a paid debt is paid — though a magistrate wants corroboration, and since the money came in a bank's bag, banks keep counterfoils. Vane names the bank, then corrects himself: no branch here; he drew it at Achterhalt and carried it two days on his knees. The three executor items were Brandt's wool-loft lease (sold), his marriage certificate, and a sealed packet marked TO THE VERMILION PLAYERS WHEN THEY NEXT COME, AND NOT BEFORE, unopened nine years. Anna Sorel had asked whether a sealed deposit could ever be read by anyone, even the registrar; told no, she wept with relief. Perlmann asks which of them is Sorel — it's only Prewick, who names himself and produces his certified register copy: "It is a record, boy." Bettina brings the tin box; Harrow writes and Perlmann marks a receipt. Perlmann tells Vane to change his coat.

Prewick telegraphs Achterhalt for the counterfoil, paying four shillings himself. At half eleven, nine of the company gather round the tailboard as Harrow opens the packet: a letter, the counterfoil, a copyist's page (unread, given to Falk's lining), and an iron key tagged UNPAID — the Athenaeum green-room cupboard key, Falk says. Vane reads, ashamed: he'd paid the whole loan, but Brandt refused a receipt because the money wasn't his — lent from a fund held for an unnamed party, whose marker was left as security. "He held a play."

In the green room, the cupboard yields an oilcloth parcel: thirty pages, SECURITY LODGED — ONE FOLIO, FOUR ACTS AND A MATTER FOLLOWING. Prewick guesses the Index's two anonymous folios may be halves; Harrow forbids reporting it and hides the parcel.

Boyle announces the agent's visit moved up; counting is now tonight after the show. Skarke, now senior at the Swan, cancels the trunk inspection, demanding delivery against valuation, and sends a letter: he holds thirty pages lodged by his own father; deliver the trunk and all debts are discharged. He reveals he was the child at Katterau whom Falk fed and sent back. Harrow insists the counting proceeds as scheduled.

Between shows, Falk tells Harrow the play only rhymes, not copies, and unfinished in two hundred years is "not a curse... an appetite." Vane bursts in celebrating the take and stops short at their faces.

**History:** At the counting, Skarke's terms are set for tonight regardless of celebration. Harrow, holding both her half and the parcel's half of the same folio, weighs whether completing the play could end the debt for good—or feed the "appetite" Falk fears. Vane, still shaken by Brandt's history and his own near-ruin, defers to her judgment. Falk warns that assembling the whole text might not close the account but open it wider, since the thing "reads" rather than merely sits written. Mirelle's claim on any tenth page, Prewick's insistence on certified copies, and Vane's promise to drive wherever Bell points all converge on the same choice: whether to bring the two halves together before Skarke's counting, risking whatever "matter following" means, or keep them apart and let Katterau remain unsettled "not never." The company, worn from Halbern's crossroads through Vessendal and the Athenaeum's revelations, awaits her ruling as the hour approaches, the trunk roped, the tin buried, the key still marked UNPAID, and Skarke — once the child at Katterau — waiting at the Swan for either delivery or refusal.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.
**Entry:** I put three asks to Perlmann and got all three. He will swear it Thursday at nine before Braun, who was his clerk; Bettina writes, he makes his mark. The assignment will be good and the debt is dead, but a magistrate wants corroboration, and the corroboration is a bank bag with a counterfoil behind it — Achterhalt branch, Farriers' and Merchants', Vane's own memory of the coach seat. The third executor item was a sealed packet for us, unopened nine years; I wrote the receipt in my own hand and he marked it. He told Vane to change his coat. Prewick's certified register lines went on the table beside my receipt, and the old man felt the stamp and softened. Prewick drafted the telegraph and paid the four shillings out of his own purse.

In the yard I opened the packet on the tailboard with nine of them round it: look first, nobody reads aloud, nobody touches. Letter, counterfoil, a copyist's page I turned face-down with the back of my finger and passed unread into Falk's lining, and a key tagged UNPAID that Falk named as the green-room cupboard. Brandt never held papers; he held thirty pages of a play, lodged as security by a party whose name he never gave. I opened the cupboard with three inside and Prewick at the threshold, and the parcel is thirty pages, not two hundred. It is under my coat and it does not cross the yard.

Then the agent, out of turn and honest about it: counting brought forward to tonight, Skarke in the town, inspection cancelled, the trunk to be delivered to the Swan against valuation and every instrument discharged. He signed himself the child in the passage at Katterau. I told Falk flat because he asked flat. I told the agent the counting stands against my book and the trunk's answer will be spoken at the counting, in front of everyone.

Matinee: half a house, honest laughter, a sky better nailed than most. Mirelle gave me the numbers — nine Odalric's, twenty Falk's, ten hers, ring the bell and she'll come. And Falk gave me the arithmetic I asked for: it rhymes, it has never been finished, it is an appetite. Then Vane came in laughing with the take, and the gentleman is in the fourth row early, reading his programme.

#### Josias Perlmann

**History:** Bettina came to tell me there was somebody on my stair. Three soft knocks — not a creditor's knock — and then a voice I had not heard in nine years, saying only, It's Vane. I found his sleeve, and then his cuff, and the worn shiny place on it, and knew him by that: nine years, and he had not changed his coat. Because he never could say it himself, I told him what he had come for. He came at eleven at night, on Hessel Brandt's last evening, with a bag of money, and counted it onto the counterpane, and said this is the whole of it and God forgive me for being late. Hessel laughed, and it hurt him, and I stopped writing. I never finished the receipt. I said sign, Hessel, and he said no, between friends, and on the Tuesday he died. It is the only unfinished instrument of my life, and I have thought of it every week since.

There were others on the stair: a woman breathing steadily, and starch, some kind of officer. I told them to be quick. I am old, and not deaf, which is worse.

I let go of his cuff, found my chair, and Bettina put the shawl over me and stayed, which is her right. I took them in order. My account they may have sworn — Braun sits Thursdays and was my clerk, and I will go on my daughter's arm and make my mark. I told the woman with the book what a magistrate wants: the assignment will be good, the debt will not, and the corroboration is the bank's counterfoil, since the money came in a bag with a bank's mark. Vane named the bank before I had finished the sentence, and sounded surprised at himself.

As executor I had released three items: the wool loft lease, sold; the marriage certificate, to the widow's sister; and Hessel's sealed packet, endorsed in his own hand, to the Players when they next came. They did not next come. Nine years it sat unopened in the tin box with my mother's rings, and I gave it to them and required a receipt, being a notary and not dead.

Then Anna Sorel asked whether a thing deposited sealed could ever be read, not by anyone, not even the registrar, after years, and I said no, madam, it is a box, it will sit there; and she wept with relief, and I did not ask what for. I asked which of them was Sorel, because the breathing at the back had stopped at her name — only a clerk with a stamp, who laid a certified record on my table. Records are the whole of the defence.

I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed, sent them away, and told Vane to change his coat.

They did not next come. Nine years it has sat in the tin box with my mother's rings, unopened, and I gave it to them and required a receipt, being a notary and not dead.

Then Anna Sorel. She asked me whether a thing deposited sealed could ever be read — not by anyone at all, not even by the registrar, after years — and I said no, madam, it is a box, it will sit there, and she wept with relief, and I did not ask what for. I asked which of them was Sorel, because the breathing at the back had stopped moving at her name, and it turned out to be only a clerk with a stamp, who put a certified record on my table. Records are the whole of the defence.

I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed me. I sent them away, and told Vane to change his coat.

#### Bettina Perlmann

**History:** They came before ten, three of them on our stair, and I was in the door with the sewing still over my arm, weighing them the way I weigh everybody. I had a moment when I might have kept them out. Then my father called from inside, and the one who had taken his hat off said a name, and I understood that whatever was coming had already been arranged somewhere I had not been consulted. So I stepped back and let him have it. He took my father's hand and held it against his own cuff a long while, longer than a man holds a hand he means nothing by, and I stood there and let that go on too.

I let them in and I stayed, which was the only part of it that was mine to decide. Father found his chair without help from me; I put the shawl over him and folded my arms and listened to the whole of it. The swearing is to be on Thursday. That means my arm for him to lean on and my hand to write it out, since neither will come from anywhere else. There was the bank bag. There were the three items. When he came to the tin box I went up and fetched it myself, and I put the packet into the woman's hands, the brown paper gone soft as cloth from being handled or from years, I could not tell which. Then I found the place on the receipt where his mark belonged and set his finger on it.

After that he told them to go away, and he told Vane to change his coat, which was fair, and the only thing said in that room all morning that I would have said myself.
**Entry:** I let them in and I stayed. Father found his chair without help; I put the shawl over him and folded my arms and listened to all of it — the swearing on Thursday, which means my arm to lean on and my hand to write it out, and the bank bag, and the three items. When he said the tin box I went up and fetched it and put the packet into the woman's hands, brown paper gone soft as cloth. I set his finger on the receipt where his mark should go. Then he told them to go away, and told Vane to change his coat, which was fair.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.
**History:** I reported the fallen fire notice by the scene dock to Herr Vane and met the new stage manager on the stage — Harrow, spelled with the bell — and noted an unnumbered iron trunk in the passage as unsecured iron, height. Behind the fire notice hung an older one about unnumbered property in the passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, stamped twice: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. I said aloud that not approved is what a man writes when told to write nothing. I have been seconded since Merrow; Katterau is on no itinerary I was given, yet everyone here has been there.

Next morning I laid my Office paper against hers: mine had Merrow, this town, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost; hers had Katterau and the 17th. We agreed she would ask Vane before the half, and neither of us would say Katterau first. We counted nine fire buckets, five with water. I broke the sky on my only cue; the tin went to felt. Front of house I found two warm seats, fourth row centre, and nobody past my doors.

I chose to write nothing down, and she told me everything: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page, pages arriving in prompt books, what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau unstaged and happening anyway. I showed her the sewn-in Proscribed pages — thirty-one titles, two anonymous folios, four acts and a matter following. Terms: I know what she knows within the hour; Falk speaks no uncompared line. He said his to the trunk.

I demanded certified copies of all four plays. At the river Falk gave me the tin and I drowned it. At the registry: Brandt's deposits released to an unreadable scrawl; Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. I certified those three lines for Perlmann, the blind notary, who said records are the whole of the defence. I paid four shillings for the Achterhalt counterfoil myself. Thirty pages in the cupboard, two hundred in the trunk: two halves. She forbade me to report it, and I obeyed on purpose.
**Entry:** I stood very still at the back holding my stamp, and the old man took my breathing for Sorel's. I said my name and rank and put my certified copy of the register lines on his table beside the stage manager's receipt — Sorel, Anna, one box, sealed, fifth year, no release, dated and mine. He felt the stamp with a fingertip and said records are the whole of the defence, and I have written nothing better in my life than that entry.

At the post house I drafted the request for the counterfoil standing up, Achterhalt branch, fifth year, month of Frost, purpose evidence, magistrate's hearing Thursday nine — and added REPLY PAID and paid the four shillings myself, and would not be argued with. Banks love being asked for their own records.

In the yard I saw the packet opened and did not touch anything. At the green room I was put on the threshold with my notebook and told to keep my silence, and I did. Then the arithmetic arrived and went through me: the Index lists two anonymous folios, four acts and a matter following, and I have been counting them for years as one entry duplicated in error. Thirty pages in that cupboard and two hundred in the trunk. Two halves. She has forbidden me to put it in any report until she understands what it adds to, and I obeyed, which is a thing I have begun to do on purpose. I sat in the dark of the stalls through load-in with a script on my knee and did not once look at the trunk in the yard.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.
**History:** A stage manager came in out of the weather with my notice in her fist and three references on three fingers — Bell Harrow — and I engaged her on the spot: plot tables, a bucket, a fair figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and of the book only that it is as honest as books are. I steered her wide of the trunk, though Prewick held his lamp over the lid and asked if it was numbered. She asked me to shift it a hand's breadth left off the ladder's foot. Alone, I wiped the lid, pressed the chalk flat, said what I say, lifted one end — light, wrong, answering — set it down, then shoved it properly and cried that the ladder was served. I did not stay in the house.

Next morning she took Krebs for a shilling, the tin, and ten minutes over the book, and I gave her the truth under my own poster with my hat off: the Palace said the 3rd, and since Merrow I have told the company the 17th, because there is not money for four towns but there is time for three and Katterau — six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. She wanted the road laid against the 3rd and the company told. I gave her Skarke's man's card; it went like handing over a bird. The float counted smaller the second time.

I came back with a carpenter, Krebs's brother-in-law, and found my trunk in the passage under her lamp, and a torn playbill: nine years. So I said it aloud — that nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend, and paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke has bought his papers, so what comes to the counting is a signature nobody gave. She set me a task: every name in that room, in ink.

She ruled standing: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, drive for Vessendal. I wept, and paid eight shillings at the toll to the penny. At breakfast I gave her the names — Hessel on the Kohlgasse; the notary Perl or Perlmann; Anna Sorel; a doctor whose name I never had; a nun; myself; the one in the passage I never saw. She stood me at a door and said: no performance. Bettina opened; Josias found my sleeve and rubbed the worn place on my cuff — nine years, and the same coat — and told them what I could never prove: I came at eleven at night with the whole of it, and Hessel laughed and would not sign, between friends, and died on the Tuesday. The receipt was never finished.

Perlmann said it again, and that the bag bore the Farriers' and Merchants' mark — no branch here then; I drew it at Achterhalt and carried it two days on my knees. He gave Harrow three things: the loft lease, the certificate, and a packet with my company's name, nine years in a tin box. He told me to change my coat. In the yard she made me read the letter twice, standing: Hessel refused the receipt because the money was never his — held out of a fund for a party he never named, whose marker he took as security, put in the green-room cupboard, key tagged unpaid, left for us, God have mercy. Four hundred and twelve marks. The thing behind the debt was the play. In the green room Harrow lifted out thirty pages, which is not a folio. Then load-in, a matinee, a take so good I came through the pass door shouting — and stopped at their two faces.
**Entry:** Perlmann said it all again in front of them, and then said the bag had a bank's mark, and my mouth answered before my head: the Farriers' and Merchants' — and then no, no branch here in the fifth year, I drew it at Achterhalt and carried it two days on my knees, and I remember that coach seat as I remember my mother. Three items: the loft lease, the certificate, and a packet with my company's name on it that has sat in a tin box for nine years because we never came back. He gave it to Harrow. He told me to change my coat, and he was right, and I did not answer.

On the stair I shook. In the yard she opened it and made me read the letter standing, silently, twice, and I did — and it is worse than being owed. Hessel refused the receipt because the money was never his to lend. He held it out of a fund for another party whose name he never told me, and he took that party's marker as security, and put it in the green-room cupboard, and tagged the key unpaid, and left it for us, and asked God to have mercy. Four hundred and twelve marks, the whole of it, and nine years of me saying so, and all the time the thing behind the debt was not paper. It was the play.

I went into the green room with Harrow and Emeran and saw her lift out thirty pages, which is not a folio. Then the day put its boots on: load-in at ten, and a matinee, and a take so good I came through the pass door shouting about it with the bag in my fist, and stopped when I saw their two faces.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.
**History:** I was awake at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when the girl came in out of the rain with the notice; I warned her of the third board and she stepped over it better than Krug ever did. Odalric interviewed, Mirelle said yes, and Bell Harrow became stage manager. Sorel mentioned the bucket under the star trap since Katterau. On the trap sill I told her she might ask anything but one thing, and told her about Krug's hurrying scrawl, Krug gone from Katterau without his boots, the copyist's fair copy made in Vessendal riding in Odalric's iron trunk, nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned. Not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice — and she had already read.

The trunk moved in the passage with Odalric nowhere in the house. Next day he laughed too big and went out for a carpenter. I gave Harrow brandy for Krebs, played the wings, said the storm line into the split sheet. Then the trunk stood dragged into the passage, lid up, full of blank paper, his hat and one glove on the flags.

I told her the truth: pages come blank; there is no fifth act, only four and a thing following; the late man is the man who is owed. Odalric came back with chestnuts, said nine years is not the loan and Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I named Katterau aloud — nine of us, a wager, three and a half acts read sitting down; four years to arrange; it cost Anna Sorel, the boy Grelle, my voice, Odalric's nerve. She ruled: Katterau no — then not never.

I told her the trunk reads, not speaks. At Loewe's stone front I could not get down; I confessed chalking the whole thing alone four years ago. I drowned my split tin in the river: eleven years, twenty-nine towns, broke honestly.

Then Hessel's green-room key, tagged UNPAID; Vane read that Hessel held not papers but a play — thirty pages lodged by a nameless party. Ours is two hundred and whole; someone lodged a piece. Skarke's man came: Skarke, the child at the scullery door, arranging twenty years, wanting no wagons. It does not copy, it rhymes; Anna died at the hour the passage scene falls. Never finished — not a curse, an appetite.
**Entry:** In the yard she opened the merchant's packet and I saw the key before I saw anything else and my own voice went strange: not a registry key — green room, prompt side, the cupboard under the chalk board, where Hessel kept our petty cash the year he bankrolled us, the cupboard I stood in front of four years ago with a stage full of my chalk and no key. The tag turned in the wind and said UNPAID. She gave me the copyist's page face-down and unread and I put it in my lining with the others; they whispered when they met.

Vane read the letter twice standing and told us Hessel had never held papers. He held a play. Thirty pages lodged as security by a party without a name.

I stood in the green-room doorframe with both hands flat on it while she lifted the parcel out, and it was thin, and thin is the whole of the horror: ours is two hundred pages and whole and roped in the yard, and somebody lodged a piece. Then the little man came to the gate and she read his master's letter and I asked her to say the name, and she said it flat: M. Skarke, who was the child in the passage at Katterau, nine years old, and would I remember the door. The scullery door. He stood through the whole reading with his hands behind his back and said is that the finish, and Odalric laughed and said no, boy, that's three and a half, and we gave him bread and sent him back out. He has been arranging for twenty years and he does not want the wagons.

Then I asked what I was in, because there was a call time. Between shows she asked me the other end of the arithmetic and I gave her my twenty years' worth: it does not copy, it rhymes; Anna died of a fever at the hour the passage scene falls; whole, with gas and a house, the rhyme would not stop at nine of us. And it has never been finished. Two hundred years of being interrupted. A play that has never had its ending is not a curse — it is an appetite. Then Vane came in laughing with the take.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.
**History:** The new one, Harrow, came in out of the rain while I was mending a glove on the fly floor, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears, and gave her the only advice worth giving about the ladder's foot and the trunk. She did it exactly. The trunk was back against the ladder within the hour, four feet of chalk dragged along the brick, and he would blame porters the Corona does not have. She recited her page to me flat: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, cut cut cut in pencil. Nine is not my number. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, that Krug thought the first a joke of Falk's until the near mare went down outside Merrow four weeks later, and that mine is ten.

Next morning in the ostler's yard I gave her my honest copy of Krug's plot tables, made her cue me Ilsabet from *you were not sent for*, and told her to ask Odalric now, while he was frightened by his notices. We played the storm; Falk put in a line that is not in the book and I took the next off him.

On the road she brought me a page with a ten in it. I stopped the wagon and read it at a saint's worn marker: the child is ten this winter and does not know the word mother; a woman crosses a border twice, once running, once summoned, and the second invitation is kind. I let her read it, and she told me unasked that the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. I carry the page inside my glove, against my wrist.

At the fire I gave my one voice: the capital, yes; Katterau, no — not four days backwards with a debt and a magistrate behind us. She ruled standing, and Katterau went into the ground for this tour. I have not breathed so freely since Halbern. Then, banking the fire, I said aloud for the first time in years that Anna Sorel was my sister, that she kept his accounts that year, and that any receipt with a signature went into Anna's box. We buried the old tin, nine of us with lanterns and Falk's sailors' words. I sent her to the registry behind the lion, eight to noon — the fifth-year lease was Vessendal's, so Anna's box came here. My name is in that building; I cannot go in.

She came back with brown paper in a merchant's hand, and I heard it from six feet off: Anna asked Perlmann whether a sealed box could ever be read, was told no, and wept; Hessel Brandt never held papers, he held a piece of the play. I dressed for the matinee instead. At the half I found her in the prompt corner with something flat under her coat and told her he will ask a question with a number in it — nine is Odalric's, twenty is Falk's, ten is mine. I will answer it myself. She is not to spare me. Ring the bell and I'll come.
**Entry:** I came last into the yard and stopped six feet off when I saw what was in her hands — brown paper and a merchant's hand. I heard the whole of it from where I stood: Anna asked Perlmann whether a sealed box could ever be read and was told no and wept, and Hessel Brandt never held papers, he held a piece of the play. I did not go into the green room. There was a matinee to dress for and I dressed for it.

At the half I found Harrow in the prompt corner with something flat under her coat and told her the only thing I can do for her tonight: he will ask a question with a number in it. Nine is Odalric's. Twenty is Falk's. Ten is mine, and I will answer it myself, and she is not to spare me. Ring the bell and I'll come.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin — Ottmar Boyle, second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud that a Krug used to be on that list and wasn't. That afternoon I mended a shed wheel-rim with wire and language. At the fire the stage manager asked me first, soldiers' sums being mine: two days to Vessendal if the carter's axle held, three if it didn't; Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling by the toll road or the free hill road that killed a horse on us. And the sum nobody else would say: Katterau is back, twenty-two mile the wrong way and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night. I said I'd walk it if it was ruled, and that I'd rather not walk it for a favour a mayor may have died of.

The ruling came down. I nodded once and went to look at the axle by lamplight, which is what a ruling means to me. Toll road it was, eight shilling, cheaper than a horse, and I said so first. I wired the axle in the morning and it held two days.

I backed the second wagon into the Athenaeum yard and took first watch on the trunk with a lantern and a pipe I'm not let smoke in the flies. They relieved me twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river; I grumbled and went anyway. When Krul said a copper kettle would do for thunder I said what wanted saying: kettle's no good, kettle's a bell. Then nobody spoke for half a second, and that's how I learned that word's gone bad in this company.

I held the watch through the night and woke Toby for his. I stood in the ring round the tailboard while she opened the merchant's parcel, and said nothing, because nothing was wanted. Then the little man with the brass case came to the gate on a Wednesday, asking after her by name. I went and said so, and she had me open it to talking distance and no farther, which I did. The town clock struck the quarter and got it right, and I said load-in for the matinee's at ten. Then I swung the gates and it was ten o'clock, and the day went on being a day.
**Entry:** Took the watch through the night and woke Toby for his. Stood in the ring round the tailboard while she opened the merchant's parcel and said nothing, because nothing was wanted. Then the little man with the brass case was at the gate on a Wednesday, asking after her by name, and I went and said so, and she had me open it to talking distance and no farther, which I did. The town clock struck the quarter and got it right, and I said what wanted saying: load-in for the matinee's at ten. Then I swung the gates and it was ten o'clock and the day went on being a day.

#### Dessa Krul

**History:** I answered present from the second wagon that first day and said whoever put the wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal for the privilege. Mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served. At the fire I kept my needle going and said the two things that wanted saying: the queen's slippers had two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots. I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I said then, and I have said since, that I don't want another warm box.

She ruled. I bit off my thread, and that was my aye — no Katterau. Good.

After that came the frost, and me swearing at a wet stocking, and the queen's slippers carried into the Athenaeum yard over my head like relics, because that brick is filthy. I went down to the river for the tin and said there'd be new tin at Achterhalt, or a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and every one of them stopped on the word. I kept my needle going. I still didn't want another warm box.

Then I came down into the yard with my thimble on and stood in the circle while she untied the tape. There was a letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over without reading, and a key with a word on the tag. I caught myself tapping the thimble against my thumbnail while Vane read it twice, standing up, and I stopped, because the yard was that quiet. Whatever it said, his face went a colour I have not seen on him before.

Then it was ten o'clock, and there was a hem to dress with pins in my mouth, and a matinee, which is what I am for.
**Entry:** Came down into the yard with my thimble on and stood in the circle while she untied the tape. Letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over without reading, and a key with a word on the tag. I caught myself tapping the thimble on my thumbnail while Vane read it twice standing up, and stopped, because the yard was that quiet. Whatever it says, his face went a colour I have not seen on him. Then ten o'clock, and a hem to dress with pins in my mouth, and a matinee, which is what I am for.

#### Toby Lenz

**History:** I answered present at the roll and was put to front of house, props, and the pit band if there was to be a pit band. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal long enough to make me late home. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads, I came back running and without the bucket, because a gentleman was sitting on a milestone down the Vessendal road who asked whether this was the Vermilion Players and said good, he was early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I offered to go to Katterau — six hundred seats, and I have never called a house of six hundred — and then I saw the faces and added, only if it were ruled.

She ruled no Katterau. I sat down hard and still cannot say whether I was sorry or glad, but I will be telling people the rest of my life that I nearly called a house of six hundred. In the morning I boiled the water without being asked, and she wrote me in her book under something new.

At the Athenaeum I dropped the tailboard first thing, then took Boyle's watch for twenty minutes and ran to catch up for the tin going into the river; it made one last thunder going under. At half six a gentleman left a cream card at front of house, did not wait, and did not come in by my doors — I was on the doors, I have learned that much. She gave me standing orders: a programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opens, all three nights, and count row four in and count it out. Counts only, no staring.

Boyle woke me for the watch on the trunk. Afterwards I was in the yard when she opened the packet, and I touched nothing and said nothing, which is new for me. Then load-in, and the programme on fourth row centre, all three nights being all three nights. At the half I called the half hour and reported what I was put there to report: the gentleman was in the fourth row already, come in early, reading his programme.
**Entry:** Boyle woke me for the watch on the trunk, and after that I was in the yard when she opened the packet, and I did not touch anything and did not say anything, which is new for me.
