Then load-in, and I laid a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights being all three nights. At the half I called the half hour and reported the thing I was put there to report: the gentleman is in the fourth row already, come in early, reading his programme.

#### Skarke's agent

**History:** I came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart and waited on the milestone with the case on my knees; the water-boy confirmed these were the Vermilion Players, and I was early. The stage manager came alone with a lamp and a book and entered me as agent, no name, boots clean, and I let her — better to deal with one who owns nothing, since Herr Vane weeps. I read the three matters from the letter: takings counted before spent; schedule properties neither sold nor pledged nor repaired at expense; the trunk valued separately, to be inspected and not opened. Eleven schedules I have carried out and never before been told to look at a thing and not open it, so I asked her why, and she said the man who gave me the instruction has read something I haven't. Her three: daily counting initialled by me, which is better practice than I am used to and I said I would report it; the nine-year instrument produced in certified copy only, strongbox in the room, and her words about a magistrate on Friday; inspection at ten paces, daylight, hands in pockets, which I granted gladly. The fourth matter I gave her I will deny: Skarke read aloud from a page without meaning to — the agent comes early and is not admitted. So I stayed from their fire.

Next I waited in the Athenaeum doorway from noon beside the woman who holds the lease and dislikes me. Looking at the tarpaulined shape on Falk's wagon, I found the stage manager between it and me before the horses stopped: today nobody looks at anything of theirs but stage and billing. I wrote Friday, ten paces, daylight, hands in pockets in her words, and it stands, though Skarke will be displeased. I stepped back and said I have eyes and the road is where it is. Then a courtesy unbought: the strongbox came up from the capital that morning by coach, and the gentleman who should have accompanied it rode ahead and is in the town. I told her I am at the Swan and do not drink; the doorway woman watched me out.

At nine on Wednesday I said first that my instructions had changed by telegraph, since she has been decent and deserved daylight. Skarke had come into town, was at the Swan, and I was no longer the senior man. The counting was brought forward to tonight, after the first performance, in the box office, strongbox present, and I waited while she wrote it, as on the milestone. Then the instruction for her and not Vane: the inspection cancelled and replaced, the trunk delivered to the Swan tonight against valuation. Eleven schedules, and never have I wanted so badly to lose a client, and I said so. I handed her the letter, which I had read, because I read everything I carry; she read it once in the open. Falk came out of the stage door and stopped dead at my case. She said the counting stands against her book, witnesses welcome, and the trunk's answer would come from her mouth at the counting before everyone — that is how valuations are done. I touched my hat and went.
**Entry:** I came at nine on a Wednesday and said so first, because my instructions had changed by telegraph and she has been decent with me and deserved daylight. I gave her the reason: Herr Skarke came into the town last night, he is at the Swan, and I am no longer the senior man here. The counting is brought forward — tonight, after the first performance, in the box office, strongbox present — and I waited while she wrote it, as I did on the milestone. Then the second instruction, which I was to give her and not to Vane: the inspection is cancelled and replaced. The trunk to be delivered to the Swan tonight against valuation. I have carried eleven schedules and I have never wanted so badly to lose a client, and I said so. I handed her the letter, which I had read, because I read everything I carry. She read it once in the open. Falk came out of the stage door and stopped dead at my case. She told me the counting stands against her book, witnesses welcome, and that the trunk's answer will come from her mouth at the counting in front of everyone — that is how valuations are done, she said. I touched my hat and went.

#### Frau Loewe

**History:** The agent had stood in my doorway since noon, so I stood in it too with the letting book under my arm, and when the wagons came I gave the stage manager the plain facts: I hold the lease, my ledger is the letting book, and I am the one who gets paid first. Nine shillings owing from the spring and a repaired gas tap — Vane might open on that debt, but he'd not close on it. She counted the nine into my palm on the spot, unrounded, and took the gas man and the counterweights onto herself, and swore nothing of theirs would go near my under-stage, and that the trunk would stay roped in the yard and never cross my threshold, it having marked my brick once already. I warmed to her by a degree.

Then she asked me to finish a sentence and wanted it in dates, so she got it. Winter of the fifth year: Emeran Falk came alone, no company, and hired my house for one night at his own cost, two shillings, because he was Falk and I was young enough to be impressed. He never opened it. He sat in it a night and a day with the gas down; I sent a boy in with bread twice; on the second evening he gave back my key and thanked me very kindly. The stage was covered in chalk — marks, numbers, a plot for something big — and I swept it myself rather than let the boy see a man's madness. A week later a woman came from Katterau asking for him, with a child, and I told her he'd gone south. He'd gone north. I'd tell the same lie again.

Load-in ran until six. He did not get down off his box for a long while.

Next load-in at ten, and the counterweights exactly as bad as I had warned her, and I said so more than once. Before that there was business in my yard with a parcel and a great deal of standing about in silence, and one of them went into my green room and came out again, and I asked no questions, having swept that stage once already for a man's madness.
**Entry:** Load-in at ten and the counterweights exactly as bad as I warned her they were, and I said so more than once. They had some business in my yard before that with a parcel and a great deal of standing about in silence, and one of them went into my green room and came out again, and I asked no questions, having swept that stage once already for a man's madness.

### 6 · Our Left, and the Man in Row Four
- **Messages:** 105-124

At the Athenaeum, Bell Harrow sends Vane to bank the takings with Boyle and sits by Herr Skarke in row four, a small, hungry man who admits he has waited since age nine to sit among such people, has thirty pages of theatrical inheritance and could never buy the rest, and asks nothing tonight. Bell warns him half a play is hungrier than none.

Backstage, Falk shows Bell that their practical door matches the wrong one from Katterau's folio, and offers to enter upstage right instead. Bell rules: "As blocked. As certified." Falk enters stage left; nothing goes wrong. Skarke leaves before curtain calls, leaving his rug with a note: he doesn't want the trunk, the assignment will be produced and withdrawn, Perlmann's evidence unneeded — he's been given "one for eightpence and a seat in the fourth row." He'll return tomorrow, paying properly, and never come nearer than row four. The rug is for Falk, whose hands were cold — Falk notes bitterly that empresses and mayors gave him gifts, but no one ever noticed his hands before.

In the box office, the assignment is endorsed "withdrawn, this date," witnessed by the agent and Frau Loewe, everything initialled. The agent says: "Discharged tonight. Not forgiven" — the pages return to the capital Saturday regardless of Skarke's wishes. Vane, briefly unafraid, asks what they do now; Bell says: learn solvency, two more nights, then Achterhalt, then the capital.

Afterward, Bell shows Mirelle three routes into Anna's box, warning that opening it may undo Anna's work, though it would bar Skarke's lawyers forever. Mirelle reveals her birth name isn't Sorel — it exists in a capital police file, differs again on her passport — and she won't risk registering days before entering the capital. Instead she asks Bell to learn who came from Katterau four years ago asking for Falk.

Frau Loewe recalls: a dark, thin-faced countrywoman, hands like "your Frau Sorel," asking after Falk, with a silent boy of five or six, saying finally: "Then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his." Mirelle recognizes the coat as her mother's — hers, then — and asks for silence.

Falk reflects that in the folio, a woman's lie about paternity is the play's kindest act — "It rhymes." Skarke returns quietly the remaining nights, sending nothing further. At load-out, Vane hands Bell the float bag and says, "Harrow, ask me for a thing."

**History:** Bell Harrow joins the Vermilion Players as stage manager under Odalric Vane, receiving a battered prompt book with a torn-out page, found by Emeran Falk and Mirelle Sorel to be tied to strange, prophetic "Katterau" pages that reach prompt books and predict real events. Clerk Casimir Prewick investigates alongside her. An unnumbered iron trunk, tied to vanished writer Anselm Krug and moneylender Skarke of Vessendal, proves central: Vane owes nine years' interest on an unsigned loan from the late Brandt, secretly funding an unnamed party's play-security. Vane vanishes and returns; the trunk yields only blank paper that "reads" itself at night. Harrow enforces strict rules—certified copies only, no invented lines—after learning Katterau's cost: Anna Sorel (Mirelle's sister), Grelle's voice, Vane's nerve. Investigating registries and executors, Harrow, Prewick, and Perlmann uncover Brandt's sealed packet: a counterfoil, an unread copyist's page, and a key to thirty pages of the play's folio, held by Skarke's son—the child Falk once fed at Katterau. Skarke discharges the debt without taking the trunk, keeping distance from row four. Mirelle, hiding her true identity, learns a woman resembling her mother once sought Falk, implying Mirelle's true parentage ties to him. The company moves on, uneasy, toward Achterhalt and the capital.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** On the Athenaeum steps at load-out, Saturday morning, book under her arm and Vane's float bag in her hand, tired and clear-headed, watching the strongbox coach out of the square and deciding what to ask Vane for.
**History:** Vane hired me in plum to call a show off a prompt book with a page cut out; I found it in a bucket — a bell, nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat. Prewick showed me a notice his Office never issues: Hessel Vorn, Katterau, NOT APPROVED. The pages come in a Vessendal copyist's hand; Krug cut nine and burned them, the tenth came back, and he went without his boots. Sorel's number is ten. A copperplate letter named Herr M. Skarke, holding everything pledged at weekly interest. At the counting Vane's coat hung on the peg and the trunk held blank paper, a hat, one glove. He came back with chestnuts: nine years was a debt he paid a dying friend who signed nothing, whose papers Skarke bought — a signature nobody gave. Falk said there is no fifth act, only a nameless thing after four, and the late man is the creditor. I promised clean books and every name, and ruled Katterau no, not for money, not never.

Mirelle told me Anna Sorel was her sister and kept Odalric's books. Under Falk's barn I heard paper reading itself, as he had at Katterau and Merrow. Frau Loewe said Falk chalked a full plot in her dark house; a week later a woman came from Katterau with a child. Blind Perlmann swore Anna's receipt was never finished and gave up a nine-year packet: letter, counterfoil, a copyist's page I passed unread into Falk's lining, a key to thirty pages in the green-room cupboard. Skarke's agent signed himself the child in the passage at Katterau.

Then Skarke sat in row four: twenty years, thirty pages, never able to buy the rest; I told him we do finishes. Falk's wrong door was only a door; ours-whole beats theirs-half. He withdrew the claim, kept the counting, left a rug and a note: keep the halves apart, never nearer than row four. Discharged, not forgiven. Mirelle's name was never Sorel. Thursday I banked Perlmann's oath and the Achterhalt counterfoil; Saturday Vane handed me the float bag unasked.
**Entry:** Sent Vane to bank the bag and walked the centre aisle at the half to look at row four. He is small, thirty at most, black coat, walked-in boots, a rug, and he read the programme to the bottom with his lips moving and then looked at the set the way Prewick looked at a broken tin sheet. He spoke first: better nailed than Katterau. So I sat a hat's distance off and told him half a play is hungrier than none, that the counting would be the smallest thing done in the building tonight, and that we do finishes here. He said he is not a wicked man; twenty years, thirty pages, never able to buy the rest; the room is lovely; nine, twenty, ten come from cheap clerks; no questions tonight. Then Falk, grey in the wings: our practical door is stage left, so is Katterau's scullery door, so is the wrong door the creditor comes late by in the folio. I ruled as blocked, as certified — ours-whole beats theirs-half — and he went through it on the hour and it was only a door. Skarke put his face in his hands and went out before the calls, leaving a rug and a pinned note: he withdraws the claim, keeps the counting, needs no Perlmann; got his ending for eightpence and a seat; keep the halves apart, keep her keys, never nearer than row four; back tomorrow, paying at the door. Postscript for Falk's cold hands, and I told him plain. Counting clean and initialled, the assignment endorsed withdrawn, discharged not forgiven, the thirty pages riding to the capital Saturday regardless. Vane owes no man anything and asked what we do now: be solvent, bank Perlmann Thursday anyway, Achterhalt, the capital early. Struck a line through today. On the yard steps Mirelle told me her name has never been Sorel and will not go on any register twelve days before the capital; she chose Odalric's neck over her own and asked me for Loewe's woman instead. Loewe gave me all of it, including it was not his, and a boy nine or ten now. Thursday I banked Perlmann's oath and the Achterhalt counterfoil, and delivered both reports word for word. Saturday, on the steps, Vane handed me the float bag unasked.

#### M. Skarke

**State:** Somewhere in Vessendal or on his way back to the capital, plainly dressed, without his rug, briefly and dangerously happy; his thirty pages locked in a strongbox travelling north by his own arrangement, and his wanting not ended.
**History:** I came in early by no door of theirs and took my seat, fourth row centre, with the rug, and read the programme through — cast, scene list, the note about Frau Loewe's gas — and found the room lovely, which I had not expected. I could not stop counting the joints; the trough is better nailed than Katterau and you can hear it in the run. She came down the aisle and I spoke to her without turning, and apologised, and told her the truth: I have wanted to be in a theatre with these people since I was nine. She sat one seat away, called me Herr Skarke, said half a play is hungrier than none, and that the counting would be the smallest thing done in the building tonight, and that they do finishes here, on the hour, honestly nailed. I told her I do not believe I am wicked; that thirty pages and twenty years of getting richer have bought me nothing; that I found out everything from clerks, because clerks are cheap. I asked nothing. Then the doors went and the drovers came in wet, and I moved my rug onto my own knees, and I watched. Frau Sorel took the house by her fourth line. On the hour the great ruin came through the practical door, stage left, and nothing happened but a door opening and a play going on, and I put my face in my hands. I went out before the calls, because I had had what I came for, and left the rug for Falk with a pin and a note: I do not want the trunk tonight, the claim is withdrawn, keep the halves apart, keep her keys, and never let me nearer than row four. Both remaining nights I paid at the door and sat where I sit and sent nothing further.
**Entry:** I came in early by no door of theirs and took my seat, fourth row centre, with the rug, and read the programme through — cast, scene list, the note about Frau Loewe's gas — and found the room lovely, which I had not expected. I could not stop counting the joints; the trough is better nailed than Katterau and you can hear it in the run. She came down the aisle and I spoke to her without turning, and apologised, and told her the truth: I have wanted to be in a theatre with these people since I was nine. She sat one seat away, called me Herr Skarke, said half a play is hungrier than none, and that the counting would be the smallest thing done in the building tonight, and that they do finishes here, on the hour, honestly nailed. I told her I do not believe I am wicked; that thirty pages and twenty years of getting richer have bought me nothing; that I found out everything from clerks, because clerks are cheap. I asked nothing. Then the doors went and the drovers came in wet, and I moved my rug onto my own knees, and I watched. Frau Sorel took the house by her fourth line. On the hour the great ruin came through the practical door, stage left, and nothing happened but a door opening and a play going on, and I put my face in my hands. I went out before the calls, because I had had what I came for, and left the rug for Falk with a pin and a note: I do not want the trunk tonight, the claim is withdrawn, keep the halves apart, keep her keys, and never let me nearer than row four. Both remaining nights I paid at the door and sat where I sit and sent nothing further.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** In the emptying Athenaeum at load-out with the Marshal's coat and Skarke's rug over his arm, sober, unarmoured and shaken open, wanting brandy after the show and wanting someone to tell him what he is in next.
**History:** A girl came in out of the rain with the notice and by the end of Odalric's interview she was Bell Harrow, stage manager; Mirelle told her to say yes. Sorel said the bucket had sat under the star trap since Katterau. I gave Harrow the thunder trough and the farmer at Merrow, watched Odalric shift alone a trunk that once took four of us and a plank, and on the star trap sill told her she might ask anything but one thing. She nailed the third joint and asked whose the small upright hand was, so I told her: Krug's hurrying scrawl, gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made at Vessendal, riding in Odalric's iron trunk; nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, then no more Krug. Do not burn, do not replace, do not read one twice — and she already had. Her page went into my lining with the others.

Odalric dodged me about the trunk. That night I said the ad-lib into the split tin, saw the hat crown-down by the empty fourth row, and found the trunk dragged into the passage, lid up, full of blank paper, his hat and one glove and no Odalric. I told Harrow the truth: no fifth act, four acts and a nameless thing following; the late man is the man who is owed. Odalric came back with chestnuts, said nine years is not the loan and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. On the road a dry copyist's page sat on the tin with a ten in it. I named Katterau: nine of us, a wager, three and a half acts read sitting down — Anna Sorel, the boy Grelle, my voice for a season, Odalric's nerve. Never finished.

She ruled Katterau not never, which gave me a use for the rest of my life. I told her the trunk does not speak, it reads — Katterau after the wager, Merrow the week Krug cut the ninth page — and it stopped mid-page like a man interrupted; she found a sheet outside the ropes. At the stone house with my name spelled right I could not get down until she gave me work, and I confessed chalking the whole play from memory four years ago, alone: it would not come to one man; it wants a house. I sank the split tin in the river with the sailors' words. Eleven years, twenty-nine towns, broke honestly.

Then the merchant's packet: the key to the green-room cupboard under the chalk board, where Hessel kept our petty cash, tagged UNPAID. Vane read that Hessel never held papers — he held a play, thirty pages lodged as security by a party without a name. The parcel was thin, and thin is the horror. Skarke's man came to the gate; Skarke was the child of nine in the passage at Katterau who came in by the scullery door and asked, is that the finish. Twenty years arranging, and he does not want the wagons. I told Harrow: it does not copy, it rhymes; Anna died of fever at the hour the passage scene falls; whole, with gas and a house, it would not stop at nine. Two hundred years interrupted — an appetite.

Before beginners I saw our practical door was stage left, as the scullery door was, as the creditor's wrong door is, with Skarke in the fourth row. I offered six steps round upstage right and swore not to argue her ruling: as blocked, as certified, ours-whole beats theirs-half. I walked through on my cue and nothing came. She brought me a rug and said my hands were cold in the second act; the debt was discharged, and Vane toasted Hessel Brandt. Thursday she gave me a four-year-old message from a woman out of Katterau — when it comes round again, tell him it was not his — the same word a woman sends in the last act, and a lie, and the kindest thing in the play.
**Entry:** I saw it two minutes before beginners, dressed and cold sober: our practical door is stage left. At Katterau the scullery door was stage left of the green room and the boy came in by it, and in the folio the creditor enters late by the wrong door, and the wrong door is stage left — and the man himself sitting in the fourth row. I offered to go round upstage right, six extra steps, nobody the wiser, and I gave the ruling to Harrow and swore not to argue it. She said: as blocked, as certified; ours-whole beats theirs-half; that door was hung by Boyle and painted by Krul and it opens onto a play with an ending. Our left. I walked through it on my cue for the six hundredth time and it was a door, and the house found me, and nothing came. Twenty years, and nothing came. I do not know what to do with that; I told her I should want telling at intervals. After the calls she brought me a rug off the fourth row and told me plainly that my hands were cold in the second act and the whole house saw it. An empress gave me jewellery and a mayor gave me a horse and neither of them noticed my hands. I wore the coat to the counting and heard the debt discharged, and did not drink my brandy in the green room, and stood in the rug and let Vane toast Hessel Brandt. Thursday, in the empty wings, Harrow gave me a message four years old from a woman out of Katterau: tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. In the last act of the folio a woman sends exactly that word, and it is a lie, and the lie is the kindest thing in the play. It rhymes. I shall never know which this was.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** At load-out in Vessendal, glove drawn over the page at her wrist, outwardly entirely herself and inwardly holding a description of her mother's coat; wanting the Achterhalt road to think, and preparing to ask Harrow for something large.
**History:** I was mending a glove on the fly floor at the Corona when the new one came in out of the rain, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked her again with tears. I gave her the ladder's foot and the trunk, and she did it exactly, which told me something; the trunk was back against the ladder by the time I returned with my hatbox, and four feet of chalk dragged with it, and he would blame porters we do not have. She gave me the page flat, word for word: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, cut cut cut in pencil. Nine is not my number. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, that Krug called the first a joke of Falk's and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow, and that mine is ten.

Next morning I gave her my honest plot tables — tin only under forty foot — cued her Ilsabet until the yard stopped being a yard, and told her a frightened man says yes. We played the storm; Falk put in a line not in the book and I took the next off him.

On the road Boyle said there used to be a Krug on the list. Harrow brought me a page with a ten in it: a child ten this winter who does not know the word mother, a woman crossing a border twice, once running, once summoned, the second invitation kind. I stopped the wagon, read it at a faceless marker, let her read it too. She told me unasked that the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. I put the page inside my glove against my wrist and made the company hear the road unrounded: the capital is a summons dressed as an honour, and I will go; Katterau, no.

Harrow ruled standing, Katterau went into the ground, and I let out the breath I had held since Halbern. So I said it aloud for the first time in years: Anna Sorel was my sister, she kept his accounts that year, and every receipt went into Anna's box. After the tin's burial — nine of us, Falk's sailors' words — I sent her to the registry behind the lion, since the fifth-year lease was Vessendal's; I cannot stand next to my own name in that building.

She came back with brown paper in a merchant's hand: Anna had asked Perlmann whether a sealed box could ever be read, was told no, and wept; Hessel Brandt never held papers, he held a piece of the play. I dressed for the matinee instead. At the half I told her he would ask a question with a number in it — nine is Odalric's, twenty Falk's, ten mine, and I would answer it myself.

I had the house by the fourth line and learned only afterwards that she and Falk had spent the minutes before beginners on the question of a door; he came on stage left as blocked and they stood up for him. In the green room I let them say Hessel Brandt and said And Anna to her alone. On the yard steps she laid it out: a certificate, two ratepayers swearing kinship, or a magistrate's order; nothing promises the box opens; opening it might break Anna's one shelf; a kin claim entered keeps Skarke's lawyers off forever. So I told her what I have told nobody — my name is not Sorel, my born name sits in a police file in the capital under a matter with a date and a magistrate, and my passport spells a third thing over a town I have never seen. I will not register my true name twelve days before walking into the capital by invitation, which is the page, word for word. I want the box shut forever and mine, and I have never had both. I asked instead for Loewe's woman from Katterau and the child's age, and she brought it exact on Thursday: countrywoman's coat, town boots, hands still, standing the way I stand. That is my mother's coat — Anna's, then mine, then someone's. I asked for silence, and the road to Achterhalt to think on it.
**Entry:** I played the first scene to wet wool and drovers and had the house by the fourth line, and never knew, until afterwards, that Harrow and Falk had spent the two minutes before beginners on the question of a door. He came on stage left as blocked and the house stood up for him and nothing in the wings went cold. In the green room I let the room say Hessel Brandt and did not lift my glass with them; I said And Anna to Harrow alone, and drank, and pulled my glove straight over the wrist. On the yard steps she laid out the box: a certificate, two ratepayers swearing kinship, or a magistrate's order — and said honestly that nothing says the box ever opens, that opening it might break Anna's one shelf, and that a kin claim once entered keeps Skarke's lawyers off it forever. So I told her what I have told nobody: my name is not Sorel and never was; the name I was born to sits in a police file in the capital under a matter with a date and a magistrate, and my passport spells a third thing over a town I have never seen. I will not put my true name on a register twelve days before I walk into the capital by invitation, which is the page, word for word. I want the box shut forever and I want it mine, and I have never been able to have both. Thursday belongs to Odalric's neck, not mine; my eighteen shillings' stopped clock does not care about names. I asked her instead for Loewe's woman from Katterau, and the child's age. She brought it back exact on Thursday: countrywoman's coat, town boots, hands still, stood the way I stand. That is my mother's coat — Anna's, then mine, then someone's. I asked for silence, and the road to Achterhalt to think on it.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the Athenaeum square at load-out in his coat, hatless of the plum one, empty-handed now that the float bag is hers; solvent, bewildered by being unafraid, and dreading and wanting Achterhalt where he drew the bag nine years ago.
**History:** I took Bell Harrow on at the door, three references on three fingers, and promised her plot tables, a bucket, and a figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, saying only that the book was as honest as books are. I steered her wide of the trunk; Prewick held his lamp over the lid and asked if it was numbered. When she had gone for her bucket I wiped the beading, pressed the chalk flat, lifted one end and found it light, wrong, answering — and took my hands off it.

She spent her cheap yeses on Krebs, on tin, and on ten minutes over the book, and I told her the truth: the Palace said the 3rd, I had been selling the company the 17th since Merrow, because Katterau had six hundred seats and a mayor who owed me. I gave her Skarke's man's card, who had counted our seats from the street. I found a carpenter and came back to my trunk in the passage under her lamp, and a torn playbill: nine years. So I said it — that nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend, and paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke had bought the papers. She set me to write every name in that room in ink. She ruled Katterau off, held the 3rd, and drove for Vessendal.

There, Josias found the worn place on my cuff and swore I came at eleven with the whole of it. Perlmann said it again, and gave up the packet: the money was never Hessel's to lend, and the marker he took was thirty pages in the green-room cupboard, the key tagged unpaid. Four hundred and twelve marks.

Skarke endorsed the second sheet withdrawn, witnessed by Frau Loewe. Discharged, not forgiven. I toasted Hessel unrounded, swore the oath before Braun, and at load-out gave Harrow the float bag unasked.
**Entry:** She sent me to bank the bag with Boyle at the half and kept the word for the counting, which I obeyed without asking, being a man who has learned that much. Then the house, and Falk through that door on the hour, and the applause coming up out of the stalls over him, and I stood at the back of the wings and wept and told nobody that the Advertiser would not have been generous. Three calls, and a third for Emeran alone that he did not ask for. In the box office with the shutter down I sat with my hat off and my hands flat while the assignment was read out and the second sheet endorsed withdrawn, this date, in Skarke's own hand, witnessed by the agent and by Frau Loewe, who insisted. Every figure initialled against her book. Discharged tonight, said the agent, not forgiven. And then it was nine o'clock on a Wednesday and I owed no man anything, and I sat on a stool too small for me and could not name what I was feeling, and asked her what in God's name we do now. She said: learn to be solvent, two more nights, Perlmann's oath banked Thursday all the same, then Achterhalt, then the capital early. In the green room I stood with the jug and the wrong hat and toasted Hessel Brandt, wool factor of this parish, who would not sign and would not tell and would not open a parcel for nine years, and I did not round the number. Thursday the oath was sworn before Braun and the bank confirmed the draw at Achterhalt in my name. Friday full, Saturday the strongbox gone. At load-out I gave Harrow the float bag without being asked, and asked her to ask me for a thing.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the green room and then at load-out, oilcloth bundle beside him, ink-stained and stamped-out and quietly, ruinously pleased; wanting the copy safely away to the Office and the itinerary to hold.
**History:** I came to this company seconded since Merrow, and began with a fallen fire notice, which I reported to Herr Vane before finding the new stage manager on the stage. I took her name spelled — Harrow — for the certificate, noted the unnumbered iron trunk in the passage as unsecured iron, height, and found behind the notice an older one about unnumbered property in passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, stamped crooked: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. I said aloud that not approved is what a man writes when told to write nothing. Katterau was on no itinerary of mine, though everyone here had been there.

We laid our papers side by side: mine gave Merrow, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost — a Palace date, not ours; hers gave Katterau and the 17th. She would ask Vane; neither of us would say Katterau first. I counted buckets, made thunder of tin, broke the sky when the sheet split, and found two warm seats in the fourth row centre with nobody past my doors.

Then I chose, once, to write nothing, and she told me everything: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages arriving in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau happening unstaged; fourteen years of clean paper. I showed her the Proscribed pages sewn in black thread, and the two anonymous folios, four acts and a matter following. Our terms: I know what she knows within the hour; Falk speaks no uncompared line. I said that at Katterau I must lie either way, and wished to be asked, not arrived with — and was told I had been both.

I demanded certified copies, compared to line four hundred and twelve, ruined my boots sinking the tin at Falk's funeral for it, and at the registry read the lease, Brandt's deposits released to an unreadable scrawl, and Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. I copied those three lines and stamped them crooked, then clean. The probate roll gave Perlmann, Josias, notary; the blind man took my breathing for Sorel's, felt my stamp, and said records are the whole of the defence. I drafted the counterfoil request to the Achterhalt branch for Thursday's hearing and paid the four shillings myself. In the green room I learned the arithmetic: two folios, not one duplicated — thirty pages in the cupboard, two hundred in the trunk, two halves. She forbade me to report it, and I obeyed on purpose.

At the performance the warm seats were paid for, Falk came through the practical door as certified, and nothing occurred outside the book. In the box office I copied the assignment, its second sheet endorsed withdrawn in the creditor's hand, witnessed by the agent and Frau Loewe, and stamped it straight first time. Then Krul's mutton on a crate, and I discovered I was happy, and did not report that either.
**Entry:** I sat the performance in the stalls with my script and my oilcloth and made no note of the two warm seats, since the occupant was in them and paid for. Falk came on stage left through the practical door exactly as blocked and certified, and I observed that nothing occurred that was not in the book. After the curtain I was in the box office for the counting with the shutter down: assignment produced and read, second sheet endorsed withdrawn, this date, in the creditor's hand, witnessed by the agent and by Frau Loewe. I copied the whole instrument for the Office in three-quarters of an hour and stamped it straight the first time. Afterwards I was put on a crate in the green room with a plate of Krul's mutton, and on the third mouthful I discovered that I was happy, which I did not report.

#### Frau Loewe

**State:** In her own dark theatre with the lamp turned low and the letting book squared away, paid in full and grudgingly fond of the stage manager; wanting the trough sheeted, the counterweights respected, and the company out clean on Saturday.
**History:** The agent had stood in my doorway since noon, so I stood in it too with the letting book, and when the wagons came I gave the stage manager the plain facts: I hold the lease, my ledger is the letting book, and I am paid first. Nine shillings from the spring and a repaired gas tap — Vane might open on that debt but he'd not close on it. She counted the nine into my palm unrounded, took the gas man and the counterweights onto herself, and swore nothing of theirs would go near my under-stage, and that the trunk would stay roped in the yard and never cross my threshold, having marked my brick once already. I warmed to her a degree.

Then she asked me to finish a sentence, in dates, and got it. Winter of the fifth year: Emeran Falk came alone, no company, hired my house one night at his own cost, two shillings, and never opened it. He sat in it a night and a day with the gas down; I sent a boy in with bread twice; the second evening he handed back my key and thanked me kindly. The stage was all chalk — marks, numbers, a plot for something big — and I swept it myself rather than let the boy see a man's madness. A week later a woman came from Katterau with a child, asking after him, and I told her he'd gone south. He'd gone north. I'd tell that lie again. Load-in ran to six, and he did not get down off his box for a long while.

Load-in at ten next, and the counterweights exactly as bad as I'd warned, which I said more than once. Before that there was business in my yard with a parcel and a great deal of silent standing, and one of them went into my green room and came out again, and I asked nothing.

I gave them my house for the evening and it went well enough; the counterweights are what I said they were and the trough drips. They wanted a witness at the counting in the box office, and I made sure it was me, and signed under the gentleman's own hand where he wrote that he withdrew it. Then soup in my own green room with two candles on the cupboard, which I did not remark on. Later, locking front of house with the lamp low, the stage manager put me one more question between managers, about the woman from Katterau. I finished the key first, then told the truth: Bauer or Bacher, thirty to thirty-five, countrywoman's coat and town boots, not poor and said so within the minute, dark and thin in the face, hands still the way their Frau Sorel stands. She never asked if Falk was there — she asked whether he still travelled with the Vermilion Players. The boy was five or six, sat on my step without fidgeting, thanked me very correctly for a bun; she never once looked at him. And I told the piece I have told nobody: when I said he'd gone south, she said, then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. Four years I've wondered whether she meant a debt, a fault, or the child. Nine or ten now. I saw the stage manager's face do what it did, said good night, and reminded her the matinee's at two.
**Entry:** I gave them my house for the evening and it went well enough, though the counterweights are what I said they were and the trough drips. They wanted a witness at their counting in the box office, and I made sure it was me, since I am the one who gets paid first and I signed under the gentleman's own hand where he wrote that he withdrew it. Then soup in my own green room with two candles on the cupboard, which I did not remark on. Later, locking front of house with the lamp low, the stage manager put me one more question between managers: the woman who came from Katterau four years ago. I told her the truth, having finished the key first. A name like Bauer or Bacher, thirty to thirty-five, countrywoman's coat and town boots, not poor and said so in the first minute, dark and thin in the face, and she stood with her hands still, the way their Frau Sorel stands. She did not ask if Falk was here; she asked whether he still travelled with the Vermilion Players. The child was a boy, five or six, who sat on my step and did not fidget and thanked me for a bun very correctly, and she never once looked at him while she spoke. And I told her the piece I have never told anybody: when I said he'd gone south, she said, then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. Four years I have wondered whether she meant a debt, a fault, or the child. Five or six then; nine or ten now. I saw the stage manager's face do what it did, and said good night, and reminded her the matinee's at two.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** On the tailboard in the Athenaeum yard, then the load-out, hoarse and blissful with a plate on his knees and the trunk roped beside him; wanting Achterhalt, and to tell somebody that the house stood up.
**History:** I answered present at the roll — front of house, props, and pit band if there was a pit band. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal that would have me late home. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads, I came back running without the bucket, because a gentleman was sitting on a milestone down the Vessendal road and asked was this the Vermilion Players, and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I said I'd go to Katterau — six hundred seats, and I've never called a house of six hundred — then I saw the faces and said only if it were ruled. She ruled no Katterau and I sat down hard, and I still don't know if I was sorry or glad, and I'll be telling people the rest of my life that I nearly called a house of six hundred. In the morning I boiled the water without being asked and she wrote me in her book under something new.

I dropped the tailboard first thing in the Athenaeum yard, took Boyle's watch for twenty minutes and ran to catch up for the tin going into the river; it made one last thunder going under. At half six a gentleman left a cream card at front of house, didn't wait, and didn't come in by my doors — I was on the doors. She gave me standing orders: a programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights, and count row four in and out. Counts only, no staring.

Boyle woke me for the watch on the trunk, and I was in the yard when she opened the packet, and I touched nothing and said nothing. At the half I reported him already in row four, come in early, reading his programme.

The third night he came early with a rug over his arm. I ran the beginners call myself and carried Herr Falk's message down the aisle — one line, about a door. The house stood up for Herr Falk when he came through that door, the loudest thing I have ever stood in. My count came out wrong and right at once: row four went in one and came out none, and he'd left the rug on the seat with a paper pinned to it. I said so at her elbow with my voice gone, and she made everybody take their bows first. I put the chalk back in its tin, took the watch on the trunk till midnight for a penny and a plate, and ate my soup on the tailboard while the lion's bell struck ten and got it right.
**Entry:** Doors and row four, all three nights being all three nights, and the programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opened. Counts only. He came in early again with a rug over his arm, and I ran the beginners call myself and carried Herr Falk's message down the aisle — one line, and it's about a door. Then the show, and the house standing up for Herr Falk when he came through the door, and the loudest thing I have ever stood in. Afterwards I did my count and got it wrong and right at once: row four went in one and came out none, and he'd left the rug on the seat with a paper pinned to it, and I said so at her elbow with my voice gone. She made everybody take their bows first. I put the chalk back in its tin, took the watch on the trunk till midnight for a penny and a plate, and ate my soup on the tailboard while the lion's bell struck ten and got it right.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the yard at load-out with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe in his pocket, satisfied that his door and his knots held; wanting the road to Achterhalt and an axle that behaves.
**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin — Ottmar Boyle, second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud what nobody else would, that there used to be a Krug on that list and he wasn't on it. That afternoon I fixed a shed wheel-rim with wire and language. At the fire the stage manager asked me first, soldiers' sums being my trade: two days to Vessendal if the carter's axle held, three if it didn't; Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling for the toll road or the free hill road that killed a horse on us once. And the sum nobody had said aloud: Katterau was back, twenty-two mile the wrong way and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night. I said I'd walk it if it was ruled, though I'd rather not walk it for a favour a mayor may have died of.

The ruling came down. I nodded once and went to look at the axle by lamplight, which is what a ruling means to me. Toll road it was, eight shilling, cheaper than a horse, and I said so first. I wired the axle in the morning and it held two days.

I backed the second wagon into the Athenaeum yard and took first watch on the trunk with a lantern and a pipe I'm not let smoke in the flies. They relieved me twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river; I grumbled and went anyway. When Krul said a copper kettle would do for thunder I said kettle's no good, kettle's a bell — and nobody spoke for half a second, which is how I learned that word's gone bad in this company.

I took the watch through the night and woke Toby for his. I stood in the ring round the tailboard while she opened the merchant's parcel, and said nothing, because nothing was wanted. Then the little man with the brass case came to the gate on a Wednesday, asking after her by name, and I went and told her, and she had me open it to talking distance and no farther, which I did. The town clock struck the quarter and got it right, and I said what wanted saying: load-in for the matinee's at ten. Then I swung the gates.

I took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it as I was told, no questions. My door held — Falk went through it on his cue, stage left, and it opened like a door and the house came down, and I'll take that. After the curtain I fed the horses, roped the tarpaulin, brought a jug up to the green room, and sold Toby the watch till midnight for a penny and a plate. Saturday I checked the ropes twice, because twice is the number, and we loaded out.
**Entry:** Took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it as I was told, no questions. My door held: Falk went through it on his cue, stage left, and it opened like a door and the house came down, and I'll take that. After the curtain I fed the horses, roped the tarpaulin, brought a jug up to the green room and sold Toby the watch till midnight for a penny and a plate. Saturday I checked the ropes twice, because twice is the number, and we loaded out.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the green room over her pot with a plate going round, thimble on, pleased and saying little; wanting the queen's slippers to last to Achterhalt and no more warm boxes.
**History:** I answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put the wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal. Mud that day, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served. At the fire I kept my needle going and said the two things that wanted saying: the queen's slippers had two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots. I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I said then I didn't want another warm box, and I have not stopped saying it.

She ruled, and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye. No Katterau. Good. I swore at a wet stocking in the frost and carried the queen's slippers into the Athenaeum yard over my head like relics, because that brick is filthy. Down at the river for the tin I said there'd be new tin at Achterhalt or a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and everybody stopped on the word.

Then the yard again, my thimble on, standing in the circle while she untied the tape: a letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over without reading, and a key with a word on the tag. I caught myself tapping the thimble on my thumbnail while Vane read it twice standing up, and stopped, because the yard was that quiet. His face went a colour I have not seen on him. Then ten o'clock struck and there was a hem to dress with pins in my mouth, and a matinee, which is what I am for.

Since then, a pot on from the second act — mutton, barley, and something out of the market nobody needs to hear about. I glared a baby quiet through a gap in the flats. My paint went through that door with Falk on the hour and came back none the worse, and the house stood up. Afterwards the green room full, two candles on the cupboard, Vane on his feet with the jug toasting a wool factor, Prewick on a crate discovering food. No warm boxes that night. Good.
**Entry:** Pot on from the second act — mutton, barley, and something I got in the market that nobody needs to hear about. Glared at a baby through a gap in the flats and it quieted. My paint went through that door with Falk on the hour and came back none the worse, and the house stood up. Then the green room full, two candles on the cupboard, Vane on his feet with the jug toasting a wool factor, and Prewick on a crate discovering food. No warm boxes tonight. Good.

#### Skarke's agent

**State:** On the capital coach out of Vessendal, brass case on his knees and the strongbox at his side, sober as always and privately relieved; wanting to deliver the pages north before his client's happiness wears off.
**History:** I first came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart to meet the Vermilion Players at the milestone, carrying the case and Herr Skarke's three matters: the daily counting initialled by me, the nine-year instrument produced in copy with the strongbox present and words said about a magistrate on Friday, and the trunk inspected at ten paces in daylight, hands in pockets, never opened. The stage manager, owning nothing herself, agreed to all three. I told her of a fourth matter I would later deny — that Herr Skarke had once read aloud, unmeaning, that the agent comes early and is not admitted.

At the Athenaeum I kept my distance from the tarpaulined shape on Falk's wagon as she insisted, and confirmed the Friday inspection terms as written in my book. I told her the strongbox had come up by coach while the man who should have escorted it rode ahead into town, and that I was lodged at the Swan.

Then Herr Skarke himself arrived, and my instructions changed by telegraph. I told her plainly I was no longer senior man on this matter. The counting was brought forward to that same night, after the first performance, and the inspection cancelled, replaced by delivery of the trunk to the Swan for valuation. I said I had never so wanted to lose a client. She held to her book and said the trunk's answer would come from her own mouth at the counting.

That counting, my twelfth ever, was the strangest of my life: the assignment read out, then a second sheet, withdrawn in Herr Skarke's own hand, witnessed by me and the lease-holder both. Every figure was initialled against her book. Discharged, not forgiven, I told them. The thirty pages stayed sealed in the strongbox, returning to the capital that Saturday, made — he wished her to know — while he was happy. I rode beside the box out of the square.
**Entry:** Twelfth schedule, and the strangest counting of my life. Box office, shutter down, strongbox open between the candles, Vane with his hat off and his hands flat. I produced the assignment and read it out, and then the second sheet, endorsed and signed across in my client's own hand, withdrawn, this date — I witnessed it, and so did the woman who holds the lease, because she insisted on it. Her book against mine, every figure initialled: matinee, evening, the lease-holder's cut, eleven shillings for a cart. The officer copied the whole of it for his Office in three-quarters of an hour and stamped it true first time, which I have never seen done. Discharged tonight, I told them; not forgiven, and my client knows the difference better than I do. Then my last instruction, given whole: the thirty pages stay in the strongbox, the strongbox goes back to the capital on Saturday's coach whether or not he changes his mind, and he wished her to know he made that arrangement while he was happy. I closed the case and left. Saturday I rode beside the box out of the square.

#### Josias Perlmann

**State:** Home above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse, in his chair with the shawl over him, spent and lightened; wanting nothing now but to be told, some day, that the paper was enough.
**History:** Bettina told me there was somebody on my stair, three soft knocks, not a creditor's knock, and then a voice I had not heard in nine years saying only, It's Vane. I found his sleeve, his cuff, the worn shiny place on it, and knew him: nine years and the same coat. Because he never could say it himself, I said it for him. He had come at eleven at night on Hessel Brandt's last evening with a bag of money, counted it onto the counterpane, said this is the whole of it and God forgive me for being late; Hessel laughed, and it hurt him, and I stopped writing. I said sign, Hessel, and he said no, between friends, and on the Tuesday he died. The only unfinished instrument of my life, and I have thought of it every week since.

There were others on the stair — a woman breathing steadily, and starch, some kind of officer. I let go of Vane's cuff, took my chair, Bettina put the shawl over me, and I took them in order. I said they might swear my account: Braun sits Thursdays and was my clerk, and I would go on my daughter's arm and make my mark. I told the woman with the book that the assignment would be good and the debt would not, and that corroboration was the bank's counterfoil, since the money came in a bag with a bank's mark — and Vane named the bank before I finished, and sounded surprised at himself.

I set out the three items I released as executor: the wool loft lease, sold; the marriage certificate, to the widow's sister; and Hessel's sealed packet, endorsed in his own hand, to the Players when they next came. They did not next come. Nine years it sat in the tin box with my mother's rings, unopened, and I gave it to them and required a receipt, being a notary and not dead.

Then Anna Sorel asked whether a thing deposited sealed could ever be read, not by anyone, not even the registrar, after years, and I said no, madam, it is a box, it will sit there, and she wept with relief, and I did not ask what for. I asked which of them was Sorel, because the breathing at the back had stopped at her name; it proved to be only a clerk with a stamp, who laid a certified record on my table. Records are the whole of the defence. I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed, sent them away, and told Vane to change his coat.

On the Thursday, on my daughter's arm, before Braun, I swore the account: the eleventh hour, the bag on the counterpane, the whole of it counted out, Hessel laughing and refusing to sign between friends, the receipt I never finished, and the Tuesday he died. It was copied and sealed straight, and I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed. Now it lies on a register where a magistrate can find it, whether the creditor wants it or not.
**Entry:** Thursday, on my daughter's arm, before Braun who was my clerk. I swore the account: the eleventh hour, the bag on the counterpane, the whole of it counted out, Hessel laughing and refusing to sign between friends, the receipt I never finished, and the Tuesday he died. It was copied and sealed straight, and I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed. Nine years I have thought of that instrument every week, and now it is on a register where a magistrate can find it, whether the creditor wants it or not. Records are the whole of the defence.

#### Bettina Perlmann

**State:** Back in the rooms above the saddler's with the sewing taken up again, her father resting in his chair; quietly proud and watchful, wanting no more strangers on the stair.
**History:** They came before ten, three of them on our stair, and I stood in the doorway with the sewing still over my arm and weighed them, the way I always weigh people who come to us. Then my father called out from inside, and the one who had his hat off said a name, and I understood that whatever was coming was not mine to stop. So I stepped back and let him have it. He held my father's hand on his own cuff a long while, longer than a stranger needs to.

I let them in, and I stayed. Father found his chair without help — I gave him that — and I put the shawl over him and folded my arms and heard the whole of it: the swearing to be done on Thursday, which meant my arm for him to lean on and my hand to write it out; the bank bag; the three items. When he named the tin box I went up and fetched it and put the packet into the woman's hands, the brown paper worn soft as cloth by then. I set his finger on the receipt at the place where his mark belonged. Afterwards he told them to go away, and told Vane to change his coat, and that was fair; I thought so too.

Thursday at nine it went as I had known it would go. My arm up the steps, my hand to write it out, my finger on the place for his mark. Braun was civil and quick, which I had not expected of a magistrate, and they took a copy and sealed it. Then I brought my father home and put him back in his chair, and he was tired in the good way, the kind of tired that is finished with something.

That was the whole of my part in it. It was mine.
**Entry:** Thursday at nine, as I knew it would be: my arm for him to lean on up the steps, and my hand to write it out, and my finger on the place for his mark. Braun was civil and quick, which I did not expect of a magistrate. They took a copy and sealed it, and I brought my father home and put him in his chair, and he was tired in the good way. That is the whole of my part in it, and it was mine.

### 7 · Bills for a Road We Have Stopped Walking
- **Messages:** 125-144

On the Athenaeum steps Harrow named her price for the float bag: at Achterhalt Vane must walk her into the Farriers' and Merchants' himself, hat on, and close the fifth-year business he'd owed the town for nine years of avoidance. Vane agreed, admitting they'd once held him four hours in a back room while a boy rode to Vessendal to vouch for him, and promised her a magnificent sky and a rounded-down price. Frau Loewe waved goodbye; Falk lifted Skarke's rug to her; the column rolled.

Twenty miles on, at the Achterhalt milestone, Boyle found dry folded paper under the wet stone. Harrow read it alone: a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who doesn't go in, asking in the fourth act "is that the finish" and unanswered — no number this time. She pocketed it, telling Falk it was not his but theirs.

In the market square a bellman cried a fresh bill: THE VERMILION PLAYERS — FOUR ACTS AND A MATTER FOLLOWING — ONE NIGHT ONLY — BY COMMAND. Harrow forbade repeating it, paid the bellman to stop, and gave the criminal matter to Prewick, who impounded nine bills, declared a forged Palace command meant arrest not fines, and that only his seal could inspect a printer's order book. Mirelle noticed the worn type on the bottom line — kept nine years.

At his shut shop, printer Hessler confessed the forme had made itself up on his stone overnight, paid for under a wet proof with no order recorded; the standing line read a date that Vane's false itinerary would have placed them at Katterau. Prewick called it "bills for a road we have stopped walking." Hessler broke the type; 191 bills and money were sealed.

Boyle spotted a watching woman. Harrow crossed to her alone: Ilse Bacher, once of the Rose in Katterau, confessed she'd sent Falk's old message and named a nameless left-handed man asking "how far did they get?" She named the boy on Loewe's step as her son Fenner. She offered to scout the Rose; Harrow refused, ordering her instead to keep Fenner home on the 14th, giving Loewe's address for word.

Bailiff Kessel arrived with constables; Harrow split jurisdictions, Prewick's account went upward untouched, Kessel lent the strongroom and offered the Corn Exchange — twelve taken. Vane, delighted: "Twelve."

**History:** At the Corona, Bell Harrow becomes stage manager for the Vermilion Players, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a leaking corner, and an iron trunk tied to Katterau, where something once happened involving Anna Sorel (Mirelle's sister), Falk, Vane, and a vanished writer, Anselm Krug. Clerk Prewick investigates alongside her. A cryptic, self-writing "fifth act" haunts the trunk—blank paper that occasionally isn't blank, predicting real events. Harrow discovers Vane's hidden nine-year debt to Vessendal's Skarke, secured against the trunk. Vane vanishes and returns; the company debates Katterau's unresolved tragedy. Harrow imposes strict rules: certified texts only, no invented lines. Investigating executor Perlmann and banker records, they learn Brandt lent Vane money not his own, security being "a play"—thirty pages surface, half of the same folio Skarke's father once held. Skarke, revealed as the child once sheltered by Falk at Katterau, releases his claim on the trunk, keeping only a seat in the audience. Mirelle investigates her mother's connection to Falk and Katterau. Forged "By Command" playbills mysteriously appear, tied again to Katterau's date; printer Hessler and informant Ilse Bacher reveal deeper conspiracy. Bailiffs and Prewick divide jurisdiction as the company presses on toward Achterhalt and the capital, debts settling, mysteries multiplying.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** On the Athenaeum steps at load-out, Saturday morning, book under her arm and Vane's float bag in her hand, tired and clear-headed, watching the strongbox coach out of the square and deciding what to ask Vane for.
**History:** I came in out of the rain at the Corona and said yes to Vane in plum: call a show off a prompt book in two hands with a page cut out. Falk warned me off the third board, Sorel worked the fly floor, Prewick of Public Morals noticed the iron trunk was unnumbered. I found the cut page in a bucket — a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat — and copied down Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED, a form the Office doesn't issue. The pages come in a Vessendal copyist's hand; Krug cut nine, burned them, the tenth came back, and he went without his boots. Then Skarke's letter under my candle: everything pledged, weekly interest, the counting at the third performance, the trunk never to be opened or sold. Krebs had been selling us fourteen days. At the counting the plum coat hung on its peg, Vane gone, the trunk full of blank paper, his hat and one glove on the flags.

Falk told me there is no fifth act, only four and a matter after with no name, and the late man is the creditor. Vane came back with chestnuts and the truth: nine years was a debt he paid a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke bought papers nobody gave. I promised clean books, a bad surprise, and every name. I ruled Katterau no — not this tour, not for money, not never — and made certified copies company law. Mirelle said Anna Sorel was her sister, who kept Odalric's books; later, that her own name was never Sorel. Under the barn I heard the paper reading itself. Falk had hired Frau Loewe's dark house four years back and chalked a full plot in it, and a week later a woman came from Katterau with a child.

At the registry I paid eighteen shillings on Anna's box, nine years unpaid. Blind Perlmann granted my three asks and swore before Braun; his sealed packet held a letter, an Achterhalt counterfoil, a copyist's page I passed unread into Falk's lining, and a key tagged UNPAID — thirty pages in the green-room cupboard, lodged with Brandt as security, now under my coat. The agent, who signed himself the child in the passage at Katterau, brought the counting forward.

Row four was Skarke: small, thirty at most, twenty years and thirty pages and never able to buy the rest. Falk said our stage-left door was Katterau's scullery door and the folio's wrong door; I ruled it blocked and certified, ours-whole over theirs-half, and he went through and it was only a door. Skarke withdrew the claim, kept the counting, got his ending for eightpence and a seat — keep the halves apart, never nearer than row four. Discharged, not forgiven. I banked his oath and the counterfoil, took the float bag from Vane's hand, named my price at Achterhalt, and found paper dry under a wet milestone: a boy asking in the fourth act is that the finish, and no answer. Not Falk's — ours, not yet happened. Then Hessler's bill for the 14th of Frost at Katterau, no order, coin under a pulled proof; forme broken, 191 sacked. And Ilse Bacher, who opened the scullery door at fifteen, with a left-handed man's question — how far did they get — and a boy, Fenner, ten, her own. I ordered her to keep him home on the 14th, gave her Loewe's address, and did not answer her last question. I carry her message for Falk.
**Entry:** I named my price on the steps: Achterhalt, the Farriers' and Merchants', front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed square, the take banked, and then an ironmonger and a sky chosen by ear. He told me about the back room and the drainage pamphlet and said yes. Twenty miles, and paper under the milestone in the copyist's hand — dry under wet stone, which is its signature. I read it once, alone, standing: a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a seat, a programme, nobody asking whose he is, and in the fourth act he asks aloud is that the finish, and nobody answers, and the house does not know him. No number. First time. It went in my coat, not my book. Falk got down and asked me straight if it was his, and I told him no: ours, and not yet happened, and my whole trade is houses that answer. Then the bell in the dip was a market crier with our name on a barrel: four acts and a matter following, by command. I gave the criminal side to Prewick entire and sent Boyle for the printer; Mirelle saw the worn bottom line. Hessler: no order, coin left under a pulled proof, the forme made up on his stone Thursday night, the old Vermilion line nine years standing. The date is the 14th of Frost — Vane's false road, Katterau. Bills for a road we've stopped walking. Forme broken to the case, 191 sacked, coin impounded. Then the coat and the town boots across the way, and it was Ilse Bacher, who opened the scullery door at fifteen. I told her Falk was well and the bill was not ours. She gave me the left-handed man with the little book who asked how far did they get, and the boy: Fenner, ten, her own, a butter man's son. I refused her the Rose and gave her one order instead — keep him home on the 14th, no theatre, no square, no step — and Loewe's address for word. I did not answer her last question. I carry her message for Falk. Kessel got jurisdictions, Prewick's report goes upward, and we have a hall for twelve.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the Athenaeum square at load-out in his coat, hatless of the plum one, empty-handed now that the float bag is hers; solvent, bewildered by being unafraid, and dreading and wanting Achterhalt where he drew the bag nine years ago.
**History:** I took Bell Harrow on as stage manager the day she walked in with the notice in her fist — three references on three fingers — and promised her plot tables, a bucket, and a figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, saying only that the book is as honest as books are. I steered her wide of my trunk, though Prewick held his lamp over the lid and asked whether it was numbered; alone, I lifted one end and it came up light, wrong, answering, and I took my hands off it.

She asked for Krebs, for tin, and for ten minutes with the book, and got all three. Cornered by my own poster, I confessed: the Palace said the 3rd, and I had been telling the company the 17th since Merrow, because there was no money for four towns and Katterau had six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. I handed over Skarke's man's card — he had counted our seats from the street. Then she set my trunk in the passage with a torn playbill on it, pencil side up: nine years. So I said the thing aloud. Nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend; I paid him; he signed nothing; Skarke has bought his papers. She asked me for every name in that room, in ink. Falk named Katterau and what it cost me, and I asked her to rule it. She ruled: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, drive for Vessendal.

I gave her the names — Brandt on the Kohlgasse, the notary Perl or Perlmann, Anna Sorel, a doctor I never had a name for, a nun, myself, and the one in the passage I never saw. Josias found the worn place on my cuff and swore I came at eleven at night with the whole of it; Hessel laughed, would not sign between friends, and died on the Tuesday, the receipt unfinished. Perlmann said the same, remarked the bag's bank mark — the Farriers' and Merchants', drawn at Achterhalt because there was no branch in the fifth year, carried two days on my knees — and gave Harrow the loft lease, a certificate, and a packet with my company's name that had sat nine years in a tin box. Hessel's letter, which I read standing, twice: the four hundred and twelve marks were never his. He held them out of a fund for a party he never named, took that party's marker as security, put it in the green-room cupboard, tagged the key unpaid, and asked God's mercy. The marker was thirty pages. The play.

Then load-in, a matinee, a fine take. Wednesday, Falk through the door on the hour, three calls, a third for Emeran alone; and in the box office with the shutter down, the second sheet endorsed withdrawn in Skarke's own hand, witnessed by the agent and by Frau Loewe, who insisted. Discharged, not forgiven. I toasted Hessel Brandt, wool factor of this parish, and did not round the number. Thursday I swore Perlmann's oath before Braun and the bank confirmed the Achterhalt draw in my name; Saturday the strongbox went, and I gave Harrow the float bag unasked and begged her to ask me for a thing. She asked for the Farriers' and Merchants' at Achterhalt, front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed. I promised her a sky, and to round a price down aloud. Achterhalt had our name in the biggest type, by command; the bailiff came; twelve shillings, and the happiest day of my life.
**Entry:** She asked for a thing I did not expect and it cost me more than money: the Farriers' and Merchants' at Achterhalt, front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed. I told her about the four hours in the back room and the boy on the horse and the drainage pamphlet nineteen times, and then I said yes, and promised her a sky and to round the price down aloud in front of her. Loewe raised a hand and Falk raised the rug and we were out of Vessendal. On the road I talked about kettles versus a hung sheet to nobody at all. At the crest she read a page and put it in her coat and Falk got down off his box and asked her a question; then a crier in Achterhalt with our name in the printer's biggest type and by command under it, and I stood three feet behind her with my hat off and said nothing, which is new for me and cost something. Bailiff came, and she divided us like a woman dealing cards, and gave the man the Office's shilling and my name only for dull certified things. Then he said his brother-in-law asks eighteen and takes twelve, and I heard myself say twelve like a lover. Bank, ironmonger, haggle. The happiest day of my life.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the green room and then at load-out, oilcloth bundle beside him, ink-stained and stamped-out and quietly, ruinously pleased; wanting the copy safely away to the Office and the itinerary to hold.
**History:** I came in over a fallen fire notice and met the new stage manager on the stage: Harrow, H-A-double-R-O-W, Bell as in the thing you ring, and an unnumbered iron trunk she would not claim until she had walked the house. Behind the notice was an older one, unnumbered property in passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, stamped SEEN. NOT APPROVED — which is what a man writes when he has been told to write nothing. I have been seconded since Merrow; Katterau is on no itinerary of mine, and everyone here has been there. Our papers disagreed: mine Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost; hers Katterau and the 17th. Neither of us would say Katterau first.

I broke the sky with a split sheet, counted warm seats with no hats in fourth row centre and nobody past my doors, and heard Falk speak a line in no certified copy of Ilsabet's Ransom. So I chose, once, to write nothing, and she told me everything: a nameless fair copy paid by the page, pages arriving in prompt books, what it stages coming true slantwise and late, Katterau happening unstaged, fourteen years of clean paper. I showed her my sewn-in Proscribed pages, two anonymous folios, four acts and a matter following. Our terms: her knowledge within the hour; Falk never to speak an uncompared line.

I demanded certified copies of all four plays and compared to line 412. Falk gave me the tin at the river and I drowned it. In the registry: Brandt's deposits to an unreadable executor; Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release; Perlmann, Josias, notary, blind, who said records are the whole of the defence. I paid four shillings for the counterfoil myself. Two folios, thirty pages and two hundred: two halves, unreported by her order.

Then Achterhalt's bellman: four acts and a matter following, by command, the Athenaeum, the 14th. I impounded nine copies, type, wax, £1 2s 4d, and wrote to Kessel that forging a Palace command is beyond us both.
**Entry:** Left Vessendal with four numbered pieces of luggage and a report I am not ashamed of. On the road I wrote something and crossed it out. At the milestone she read a page alone and I wrote nothing, which is now habit and choice. In the square: our company name in a printer's biggest type, four acts and a matter following, one night only, by command. She gave the criminal side to me entire, so I crossed the square and took the whole roll off the bellman in the Office voice — nine copies — and certified it on the tailboard: seen this day, uncertified matter announced by public bell, nine copies impounded, C. Prewick, Clerk 3. Stamp straight. I told her the boundaries: I may impound, I may compel a licensed printer's order book, I may not stop a performance nobody has attempted, and by command without warrant is not a fine but an arrest. Hessler had no order, no name, no receipt — the forme made up on his stone Thursday night, coin under the proof. Then the bottom line: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, Thursday the 14th of Frost. The command performance is the 3rd; on the 14th we should be eleven days in the capital, striking. On Vane's false dates we should have been at Katterau. It is bills for a road we have stopped walking, and I said so aloud. Broke-up type, two sacks, wax off Hessler's bench, one pound two shillings and fourpence impounded, his signature. To Kessel I wrote that this is forgery of a Palace command, beyond a district bailiff and beyond a Clerk Third Class, that both of us report upward and neither touches it further, and that it is written in those words so neither can blame the other. He gave us the weigh-house strongroom and kept the key for a lawful shilling.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** At load-out in Vessendal, glove drawn over the page at her wrist, outwardly entirely herself and inwardly holding a description of her mother's coat; wanting the Achterhalt road to think, and preparing to ask Harrow for something large.
**History:** The new one came in out of the rain while I mended a glove on the fly floor, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears, and gave her the ladder and the trunk to prove herself on. She did it exactly. Her page said the wrong door, a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut in pencil. I told her what I knew: the pages started at Vessendal two springs ago, Krug thought the first a joke of Falk's, and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow. Nine is not my number. Mine is ten.

I gave her my honest copy of Krug's tables, cued her Ilsabet in the ostler's yard, and made Prewick say "Oh." Then a page came with a ten in it, and I stopped the wagon: a child ten this winter who does not know the word mother, a woman crossing a border twice, once running, once summoned. She told me the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. I put the page inside my glove and made the company hear the road; I said the capital yes, Katterau never. She ruled it dead, and I let out the breath I have held since Halbern.

Then I said aloud, first time in years, that Anna Sorel was my sister, that she kept his accounts, that every receipt went into her box — and sent Harrow to the registry, because my name is in that building. She brought back Perlmann's no, Anna's weeping, Hessel Brandt holding a piece of the play. On the yard steps I told her my name is not Sorel; the born one sits in a police file in the capital. I want the box shut forever and mine.

Loewe's woman wore my mother's coat. In Achterhalt the pages stopped counting, the bill's bottom line was nine years old, and she crossed the street alone.
**Entry:** Gloves on out of Vessendal with Achterhalt to think about, and at the top of the hill the road gave her another page. She read it standing and said it out for us: a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a question in the fourth act, no answer, a house that does not know him. No number in it at all. Not nine, not twenty, not ten. So it has stopped counting. In the square I came up beside her without saying anything and looked at the bill in the clerk's hand, because type is a thing I can read like a face: the name, the acts, the command all fresh — and the bottom line worn and out of alignment and grey. Somebody kept the forme nine years. Inside the printer's I heard the date read out and heard the clerk put it against Odalric's Katterau road, and I said nothing there either. Then Boyle put his head in and said there was a woman across the way who would not move off: countrywoman's coat, town boots.
