She told us not to follow and crossed alone, and I stood in a printer's shop with my hands still and waited, and did not go to the window.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** In the emptying Athenaeum at load-out with the Marshal's coat and Skarke's rug over his arm, sober, unarmoured and shaken open, wanting brandy after the show and wanting someone to tell him what he is in next.
**History:** A girl came in out of the rain with a notice and I told her about the third board; Odalric interviewed, Mirelle said yes, and we had Bell Harrow for stage manager. She nailed the third joint that had waited two seasons, so I told her whose small upright hand it was: Krug's, who left Katterau without his boots after he cut and burned nine pages and the tenth came back. Not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice — and by her colour she already had. Her page went into my lining with the others. Then the iron trunk moved in the passage with Odalric out of the house. Next night the sheet split mid-storm and I stepped into it; afterwards I found the trunk dragged into the passage, lid up, blank paper inside, his hat face down, one glove, no Odalric. I told her the truth: fourteen years of clean paper, no fifth act, four acts and a thing following with no name, and the late man is the man who is owed. Odalric came back with chestnuts by the wrong door and said Skarke had bought a dead friend's papers. At the fire I said Katterau aloud — nine of us, a wager, three and a half acts read sitting down — and what it cost: Anna Sorel, the boy Grelle, my voice for a season, Odalric's nerve for good. Harrow ruled Katterau no, then not never. I told her the trunk does not speak, it reads; she found a sheet outside the ropes. At Vessendal I could not get down from the wagon, and told her I had chalked the whole play alone four years ago and it would not come — it wants a house. I sank my split tin in the river before witnesses: eleven years, twenty-nine towns, broke honestly.

Then the merchant's packet, and Hessel's green-room cupboard key tagged UNPAID. Vane read that Hessel had held no papers but a play — thirty pages lodged as security by a nameless party. Thin, and thin is the horror; ours is two hundred and whole. Skarke's man came to the gate: M. Skarke, the nine-year-old who came in by the scullery door at Katterau and asked was that the finish. Twenty years arranging, and he does not want the wagons. I told Harrow it does not copy, it rhymes; Anna died at the hour the passage scene falls; a play never finished is an appetite.

Before beginners I saw our practical door was stage left, as the scullery door was, as the creditor's wrong door is, and Skarke sat in the fourth row. I offered six steps round upstage right and gave the ruling to Harrow and swore not to argue: as blocked, as certified, ours-whole beats theirs-half, the door Boyle hung and Krul painted. I went through on my cue and nothing came. She brought me a rug off the fourth row and said my hands were cold in the second act. The debt was discharged; Vane toasted Hessel Brandt. Thursday she gave me a four-year-old message from a woman out of Katterau: tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his — the same word a woman sends in the last act, and a lie, and the kindest thing in the play.

Loewe lifted her hand off the step and Vessendal was done. Twenty mile on, Boyle stopped at a milestone with paper under it. I asked at last: is it mine. She said no — no number, a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who will not go in, asking aloud in the fourth act is that the finish, and nobody answering. Ours, she said, and not yet. In the market there was a bell and a barrel and our name in the biggest type, four acts and a matter following, by command. I stopped mid-line and said nothing, because she had ruled it, and sat on the box while they went into the printer's, and nobody has told me yet what came of it.
**Entry:** Sober on my box with the rug over my knees; Loewe lifted a hand off her step and I lifted the rug, and that was Vessendal done. Twenty mile and the road climbed and Boyle pulled up without being told, and there was paper under the milestone, and I got down slow with one hand on the wheel and stopped six feet off, where you stop at water, and asked her the thing I have never asked: is it mine. She said no. No number in it at all, the first time — a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a seat and a programme, and in the fourth act he asks aloud is that the finish, and nobody answers, and the house does not know him. Ours, she said. Hasn't happened yet. Then I said the toll distances in verse for half a mile because that is how I pray, and in the market there was a bell and a barrel and our name in the biggest type there is with four acts and a matter following under it, and by command, and I stopped mid-line and said not one word, because she had ruled that nobody would. I sat on the box while they went into the printer's, and I did not go across the square, and nobody has yet told me what came out of it.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the yard at load-out with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe in his pocket, satisfied that his door and his knots held; wanting the road to Achterhalt and an axle that behaves.
**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin — Ottmar Boyle, second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud that a Krug used to be on that list and wasn't. Mended a shed wheel-rim with wire and language. At the fire I gave the stage manager the soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the carter's axle held, three if it didn't; Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling by toll road or the free hill road that killed a horse on us. And Katterau back on us, twenty-two mile wrong and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night, for a favour a mayor may have died of. When the ruling came I nodded once and went to look at the axle by lamplight. Toll road, eight shilling, and I said so first. Wired the axle; it held two days.

At the Athenaeum I backed the second wagon in and took first watch on the trunk, and was let off twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river, which I grumbled at and attended. When Krul wanted a copper kettle for thunder I said a kettle's no good, a kettle's a bell — and the half-second of silence after taught me that word's gone bad in this company.

I watched the night through, woke Toby, stood in the ring at the tailboard while she opened the merchant's parcel and said nothing. Wednesday the little man with the brass case came asking after her by name; I reported it and opened the gate to talking distance and no farther, as ordered. I took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it, no questions. My door held — Falk went through it on his cue, stage left, and the house came down. Sold Toby the watch till midnight for a penny and a plate. Saturday I checked the ropes twice, twice being the number, and we loaded out.

On the climb out I spotted the paper under the milestone lip and pulled up unasked: madam, do we look. She looked, pocketed it, and told me to find what that bell was before it decided it was ours. It was a market crier on a barrel with our name printed over him. I went for the printer and found Hessler shut on a market Saturday with a lamp behind the shutters, and said so, then stood mild at the corner while the Office knocked. Two hundred bills, nobody ordered them; the old man tipped his type back in the case happier than any man I've seen undoing his own work. Two sacks on the tailboard. I clocked the woman across the way who hadn't moved since we knocked — countrywoman's coat, town boots — reported her, and she went over alone and bid us stay put, so we stayed. The bailiff came and went civil. A hall for twelve, a strongroom for the sacks, and my axle held the climb.
**Entry:** Swung out of the Athenaeum yard, toll road under us, hedges laid proper. At the top of the climb I saw the corner of paper under the milestone lip, dry as bone under wet stone, and pulled up without being asked and said, madam, do we look. She looked, one of us, as she does, and pocketed it, and told me to find out what that bell was before it decided it was ours. It was a market crier on a barrel with our name printed over him. I went for the printer and found Hessler shut on a market Saturday, which he never is, with a lamp lit behind the shutters, and said so. Stood at the corner being mild while the Office knocked. Two hundred bills, and nobody ordered them; the old man tipped his type back in the case and I've never seen a man look happier doing away with his own work. Two sacks on the tailboard. Then I clocked the woman across the way who'd not moved since we knocked — countrywoman's coat, town boots — and reported it, and she went over alone and told us to stay put, so we stayed put. Bailiff came and went civil. We've a hall for twelve and a strongroom for the sacks, and my axle held the climb.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** On the tailboard in the Athenaeum yard, then the load-out, hoarse and blissful with a plate on his knees and the trunk roped beside him; wanting Achterhalt, and to tell somebody that the house stood up.
**History:** I answered present at the roll — front of house, props, pit band if there was a pit band — and Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal that had me late home. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads, I came back running without the bucket, because a gentleman sat on a milestone down the Vessendal road and asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I offered to go to Katterau — six hundred seats, and I have never called a house of six hundred — then saw the faces and said only if it were ruled. She ruled no Katterau, and I sat down hard, and I will be telling people the rest of my life that I nearly called it. I boiled the water unasked and she wrote me in her book under something new.

In the Athenaeum yard I dropped the tailboard, stood Boyle's watch twenty minutes, and ran to see the tin go into the river; it made one last thunder going under. At half six a gentleman left a cream card at front of house and did not come in by my doors. She gave me standing orders: a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights, count row four in and out, counts only, no staring. Boyle woke me for the watch on the trunk; I was in the yard when she opened the packet and touched nothing and said nothing. At the half I reported him already seated, reading. The last night he came early with a rug over his arm; I ran the beginners call and carried Herr Falk's message down the aisle — one line, about a door. The house stood for Herr Falk, the loudest thing I have stood in. Row four went in one and came out none: the rug left with a paper pinned to it. I said so at her elbow, voice gone, and she made everybody bow first. Watch till midnight for a penny and a plate; the lion's bell struck ten and I had it right.

Voice still gone, and I did not care. A page lay under the milestone at the hilltop; she read it herself and nobody spoke. At Achterhalt market a man on a barrel rang a bell, crying our name and words off Herr Falk's play, and she said nobody repeats one word aloud, and I did not. I gave the bellman a penny for a rest; he sat down sorry and grateful and handed his whole roll of bills to Herr Prewick. I held the horses while the Office was in the printer's, and watched the bailiff come over with two constables, chain bouncing, and go away pleased. One house in this town, a Corn Exchange, and I am going to call it.
**Entry:** Voice still gone from Thursday and I don't care. Rode out with the wagons and there was a page under the milestone at the top of the hill and she read it herself and nobody said anything. Then Achterhalt market and a man on a barrel with a bell crying our name and words off Herr Falk's play, and she said nobody repeats one word of it aloud, and I didn't. My job was a penny to the bellman for a rest, which I gave him, and he sat down on his own barrel looking sorry for himself and grateful at once, and handed the whole roll of bills out of his coat to Herr Prewick. After that I stood by the horses while the Office was in the printer's, and watched the bailiff come across with two constables and his chain bouncing, and go away pleased. There's only one house in this town and it's a Corn Exchange, and I am going to call it.

#### Frau Loewe

**State:** In her own dark theatre with the lamp turned low and the letting book squared away, paid in full and grudgingly fond of the stage manager; wanting the trough sheeted, the counterweights respected, and the company out clean on Saturday.
**History:** The agent stood in my doorway from noon, so I stood in it too with the letting book, and when the wagons came I told the stage manager plainly: I hold the lease, the letting book is my ledger, and I am paid first. Nine shillings from the spring and a repaired gas tap — Vane might open on that debt but not close on it. She counted the nine into my palm unrounded, took the gas man and the counterweights onto herself, swore nothing of theirs would touch my under-stage and the trunk would stay roped in the yard, since it marked my brick once already. Then she asked me for dates, and got them: the winter of the fifth year, Emeran Falk came alone, hired my house one night at his own cost, two shillings, and never opened it — sat a night and a day with the gas down, bread sent in twice by a boy, gave back my key very kindly. The stage was all chalk, marks and numbers, a plot for something big, and I swept it myself rather than let the boy see a man's madness. A week later the woman came from Katterau with a child, and I told her he'd gone south. He'd gone north. Falk sat long on his box that day and did not get down.

Load-in at ten, the counterweights exactly as bad as I'd warned, some silent business with a parcel in my yard, one of them into my green room and out again; I asked nothing.

The evening went well enough, the trough dripping. I made sure I was the witness at their counting, and signed under the gentleman's own hand where he wrote that he withdrew it. Soup in my green room, two candles on the cupboard, which I did not remark on. Locking up, the stage manager asked me about the Katterau woman, and I told her the truth: Bauer or Bacher, thirty to thirty-five, countrywoman's coat and town boots, not poor and saying so in the first minute, dark and thin, hands still as their Frau Sorel's. She never asked if Falk was here — only whether he still travelled with the Vermilion Players. The boy was five or six, sat on my step, didn't fidget, thanked me for a bun; she never once looked at him. And I told what I had told nobody: when I said he'd gone south, she said, then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. Four years I have wondered — a debt, a fault, or the child, who'd be nine or ten now. I saw the stage manager's face do what it did, said good night, and reminded her of the two o'clock matinee.

Saturday I saw them out clean, arms folded on my own step while they roped and loaded, and at the last I put my hand up to Falk on his box, and he lifted that gentleman's rug to me. I shall be telling that for ten years. My brick is my own again, the trough wants sheeting, and she left me an address to forward to, which is more than most managers leave.
**Entry:** Saw them out clean on the Saturday, as I wanted. Stood on my own step with my arms folded and watched them rope and load and go, and at the last minute I put my hand up to Falk on his box, and he lifted that gentleman's rug to me. I shall be telling that for ten years. My brick is my own again, the trough wants sheeting, and the stage manager left me an address to forward to, which is more than most managers leave.

#### Achterhalt bellman

**History:** Cried the market as I always do — lost property, the horse auction, and a playbill I was paid handsome to cry, the Vermilion Players, one night only, by command. Then a man in a collar walks over with the Office of Public Morals on his seal and says the bill and any duplicates and no further crying of it, and I gave him the whole roll out of my coat, nine of them, because I've no wish to argue with a seal. A boy from the wagons put a penny in my hand for a rest, which was decent, and I sat on my barrel and rested it, sore about the fee and glad about my neck.
**Entry:** Cried the market as I always do — lost property, the horse auction, and a playbill I was paid handsome to cry, the Vermilion Players, one night only, by command. Then a man in a collar walks over with the Office of Public Morals on his seal and says the bill and any duplicates and no further crying of it, and I gave him the whole roll out of my coat, nine of them, because I've no wish to argue with a seal. A boy from the wagons put a penny in my hand for a rest, which was decent, and I sat on my barrel and rested it, sore about the fee and glad about my neck.

#### Hessler

**History:** Three knocks, official, and my shoulders came down, because I had not slept since Thursday and I had been waiting for them. I put the lamp down and thought about the back door and thought better of it and opened the front. Told them straight: I set nothing. I came down Thursday to bank my fires and the forme was made up on my stone, locked in the chase, quoins tapped home, a wet proof on the line, and coin underneath it — enough for two hundred bills and the crier and a shilling over. No order in my book, no name, no receipt. The bottom line was my old Vermilion forme from nine year back that I never broke up, because printers are magpies; the top was my type set by a hand that knows my case better than my boy, and not a wrong letter in it. I read the standing line out for the lady: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, boxes three shillings, pit one and six, gallery eightpence, Thursday the 14th of Frost at seven — and the 14th falls Thursday this year, which it hasn't since the fifth year, and I don't like it, and the house is Vessendal, and my town's crier cried a Vessendal house this morning. Then I knocked the quoins loose and tipped the whole thing into the case, every letter, the old line with it, and held up my empty stone with both hands. Hundred and ninety-one bills into their sacks, no money taken, and the clerk wrote down that I said so, and I signed, relieved to my boots.

I put the lamp down and thought about the back door and thought better of it and opened the front. Told them straight: I set nothing. I came down Thursday to bank my fires and the forme was made up on my stone, locked in the chase, quoins tapped home, a wet proof on the line, and coin underneath it — enough for two hundred bills and the crier and a shilling over. No order in my book, no name, no receipt. The bottom line was my old Vermilion forme from nine year back that I never broke up, because printers are magpies; the top was my type set by a hand that knows my case better than my boy, and not a wrong letter in it. I read the standing line out for the lady: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, boxes three shillings, pit one and six, gallery eightpence, Thursday the 14th of Frost at seven — and the 14th falls Thursday this year, which it hasn't since the fifth year, and I don't like it, and the house is Vessendal, and my town's crier cried a Vessendal house this morning. Then I knocked the quoins loose and tipped the whole thing into the case, every letter, the old line with it, and held up my empty stone with both hands. Hundred and ninety-one bills into their sacks, no money taken, and the clerk wrote down that I said so, and I signed, relieved to my boots.

#### Ilse Bacher

**History:** Came in Thursday with butter and saw a bill on the barrel with four acts and a matter following on it, and sat down on the kerb in front of people, because I last heard those words through a scullery door at fifteen carrying bread to nine men in a green room at the Rose. So I stood across from Hessler's and watched, and this morning the players came and an officer went in, and then a woman crossed to me at hat-distance and named herself Bell Harrow and said my message had been given to Emeran Falk word for word, three days ago, an hour out of Vessendal. Then he knows. Good. I told her what I am: the girl who let a small boy sit in the passage because he was small and had nowhere, who answered his questions nine years later when he came back with money and a good coat, and who sent word four years ago because a man went round Katterau promising a reckoning and I would not have Falk carry my part of it. It was mine. I opened the door. She told me Falk was well and sober and that six hundred people stood up for him, and that the bill is not theirs and every one of them is impounded and the type broken. So I gave her the man: no name, winter of the seventh year, thirties, cheap town clothes, a little book, wrote left-handed, paid in shillings, knew the reading had happened when nobody in Katterau said it aloud, and asked the one question nobody else asked — how far did they get. Too poor and too frightened for Skarke's, I always thought. I told her the boy on the Vessendal step is mine, Fenner, ten, and my husband's, and can read. I offered to go in by the scullery at the Rose and look, and she said no, plain: a door I've paid twenty years for doesn't get opened twice. Instead: keep him home on the 14th of Frost, no theatre, no square, no step. I said I'd bolt the door and tell Bacher we're playing at hermits. I asked her if that was what was coming for him and she didn't answer, which was answer. Loewe, Vessendal, for word. I took her hand, and left Falk a message about my voice — his voice — through a scullery door, and went to my cart.

I took her hand, and left Falk a message about my voice — his voice — through a scullery door, and went to my cart.

#### Kessel

**History:** Came across my own square before dinner with two constables because there'd been a bill cried for a play by command and the Office was in Hessler's shop and nobody had told me a thing. The stage manager sorted it in two sentences — hers the players, the Office's the matter — and gave me the clerk, who is the useful sort: nine bills off my bellman, a hundred and ninety-one off the printer, coin impounded, order book inspected, and Hessler blameless, which I could have told them. No order at all, then, which my constable had off the bellman and which I'd called a story. The clerk wrote out that the forgery of a Palace command is beyond a district bailiff and beyond a Clerk Third Class, and that we both report upward and neither of us touches it, in those words, so neither can hang it on the other — a man I can work with. Gave them the strongroom under the weigh-house for their sacks and kept the key myself, and the Office pays me a shilling to make it lawful. Told her the Corn Exchange is the only house in town and my brother-in-law will ask eighteen and take twelve, and warned her that the last company's leading man went off with a farrier's wife, so we are not sentimental here. Then dinner.
**Entry:** Came across my own square before dinner with two constables because there'd been a bill cried for a play by command and the Office was in Hessler's shop and nobody had told me a thing. The stage manager sorted it in two sentences — hers the players, the Office's the matter — and gave me the clerk, who is the useful sort: nine bills off my bellman, a hundred and ninety-one off the printer, coin impounded, order book inspected, and Hessler blameless, which I could have told them. No order at all, then, which my constable had off the bellman and which I'd called a story. The clerk wrote out that the forgery of a Palace command is beyond a district bailiff and beyond a Clerk Third Class, and that we both report upward and neither of us touches it, in those words, so neither can hang it on the other — a man I can work with. Gave them the strongroom under the weigh-house for their sacks and kept the key myself, and the Office pays me a shilling to make it lawful. Told her the Corn Exchange is the only house in town and my brother-in-law will ask eighteen and take twelve, and warned her that the last company's leading man went off with a farrier's wife, so we are not sentimental here. Then dinner.

### 8 · A Sky, a Returned Chalk, and Room Fourteen
- **Messages:** 145-164

Achterhalt, morning: Harrow walked Vane to the Farriers' and Merchants' door. The clerk didn't know him; the five-year-old ledger entry read "paid in coin to bearer, Vane, O., on account of Brandt, H." — a copy made for twopence, the amber notice tucked away. At the ironmonger's Vane, eyes shut, chose a great black plate of a sky — "has a floor in it" — twenty-two shillings, no rounding. The Corn Exchange went for thirteen.

That night, chalking her plot, Falk asked about the woman in the square. Harrow gave him Ilse Bacher whole — married to a butter man, son Fenner, ten, who can read, the fault hers for opening the door — and repeated his own old shout at Odalric Vane for laughing. Falk laughed, remembered getting angry twenty years ago, understood "not mine" meant the wager. He returned her chalk and asked her to help him finish the play properly one day — all four acts, everyone who chooses, nobody who doesn't. Harrow logged it — "Asked — Corn Exchange, one lamp" — and set terms: everyone hears Katterau entire first, no wagers, no bottles, Fenner Bacher stays home. Falk agreed: "Yes. That first, and the rest after."

Achterhalt sold out. Then eleven days early to the capital: the Baraque Theatre, not the Palace; the stage manager summoned to the Office of Public Morals, Room Fourteen. Prewick briefed her on Undersecretary Lenz, who'd kept two anonymous folios on the Index nineteen years, refusing four applications to strike them.

At the Baraque, Anselm Krug waited — the old book-keeper who'd vanished after Katterau. Vane confessed to the company that he'd blamed Krug for a theft of seven pounds and had known his whereabouts two years; Harrow made him unsay it at supper and sent three corrective letters. Krug produced nine pages he'd never burned. Harrow ordered them counted, numbered, given to Falk's coat lining — except page eight, kept by her. Krug summarized contents only: past events, present ones, two not yet happened, and a cast list ending "and the house, entire."

At Room Fourteen, Lenz questioned her about Vane's trunk and any spoken lines; she answered precisely, citing one Vessendal exception. Lenz revealed: of thirty-one banned works, two "work"; fourteen speakings in two hundred years, Katterau the fourteenth. The Palace's requisition for the 3rd of Frost was signed not by Skarke but by "A. Krug," filed two years prior, fee paid by an unnamed party of standing — the Office approving. Outside, Prewick's watch ran on.

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a troubled prompt book, a torn page, and a locked iron trunk tied to debts owed to Vessendal/Skarke and a mysterious forbidden play from Katterau. She uncovers layers: Falk's history with the play, Vane's hidden nine-year debt to the dying Brandt, Mirelle Sorel's true parentage and connection to Anna Sorel, and Krug's disappearance and blame. Investigating with clerk Prewick, she navigates registry offices, executor Perlmann, and creditor Skarke (revealed as the child Falk once sheltered at Katterau), securing debts paid and assignments withdrawn while resisting the play's pull. Blank trunk pages sometimes fill with prophetic text; one predicts a boy and a border crossing, tied to Fenner Bacher and Ilse. Forged playbills for an illegal Katterau performance surface in Achterhalt, traced to a self-assembling type forme; culprits and papers are sealed by bailiffs. Vane settles old debts, buys a symbolic sky-plate, and asks Falk's forgiveness lessons continue. The company sells out Achterhalt, then moves early to the capital's Baraque Theatre. There, Krug reappears with nine unburned pages, and Room Fourteen's Undersecretary Lenz reveals the play's dangerous history—fourteen "speakings" in two centuries—and that its requisition was filed by Krug himself, funded anonymously, moving toward a climactic reckoning.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In Room Fourteen at the Office of Public Morals, tea half drunk, the Palace play list face-up under her hand and page eight unread in her coat pocket; steady-faced and reading it twice against her own rule, Prewick's watch running in the corridor.
**History:** I took the Corona off an open stage door and found the cut page in a bucket: a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat. Prewick of Public Morals showed me a form his Office never issues — Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED — and everyone had been to Katterau. Krug had burned nine pages; the tenth came back and he left without his boots. A copperplate letter pledged the whole company to Herr M. Skarke, interest weekly. At the counting Vane was gone and the trunk held blank paper. Falk said there is no fifth act, and the late man is the creditor. Vane came back with it plain: the nine years was a debt he paid a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke bought the papers. I promised clean books and every name.

I ruled Katterau no — not this tour, not for money, not never. Mirelle said Anna Sorel was her sister, who kept Odalric's books and had every receipt in her box. Under the barn I heard paper reading itself. Frau Loewe said Falk hired her dark house four years back, and a week later a woman came from Katterau with a child. I paid eighteen shillings on Anna's sealed box; blind Perlmann swore before Braun that the receipt was never finished, and gave up a packet nine years unopened: an Achterhalt counterfoil, a copyist's page I passed unread into Falk's lining, and a key to thirty pages lodged with Brandt.

Skarke sat in row four: twenty years, thirty pages, never money for the rest. Falk said our stage-left door was Katterau's scullery door; I ruled it blocked and certified, and it was only a door. Skarke withdrew the claim, kept the counting, had his ending for eightpence. Discharged, not forgiven. Mirelle told me her name has never been Sorel.

At Achterhalt I closed the nine years, coin to bearer. A page under a milestone showed a boy asking aloud in the fourth act is that the finish, and nobody answering. Then bills by command for the 14th of Frost at Katterau, off no order; forme broken, 191 sacked. Ilse Bacher opened that scullery door at fifteen; her boy is Fenner, ten. I ordered him kept home and carried her message to Falk, who found he had shouted twenty years late and asked me to help him finish it, after the capital and the debts. My terms: all who choose, choosing after Katterau entire; no wagers, no bottles; Fenner stays home. He took the boy's clause first.

At the capital Krug had waited since Tuesday; Odalric confessed the theft he'd invented; Krug had burned nothing. Page eight is mine — a stage manager rings the bell — in my coat, unread. Room Fourteen: fourteen speakings in two hundred years, the fifteenth scheduled, the command of the 3rd requested by A. Krug of the fourth ward, Part the Second left blank for us to determine.
**Entry:** Bank first, hat on, no arm offered. Eleven minutes and nine years off him: paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H., copy twopence, take banked, receipt over the old notice. At the ironmonger's I said choose me a sky and let him listen his way down the wall — the black plate has a floor in it, twenty-two shillings unrounded, out loud, so I have my price rounded down and he has his thunder. Hall for thirteen. That night, chalking on the flags, Falk asked. I gave him Ilse Bacher whole and her message word for word, and watched him find out he had shouted, twenty years late. Then he handed my chalk back handle-first and asked me to help him finish it — after the capital, after the debts, after the company is safe. Standing page: Asked — Corn Exchange, one lamp. My terms if ever yes: all who choose, choosing after Katterau entire; no wagers, no bottles; Fenner Bacher stays home. He took the boy's clause first. Two good nights, then the toll road and the capital eleven days early, and at the gate: the Baraque, a man waiting since Tuesday, and me alone at Room Fourteen. The man was Krug. I let Odalric see him unannounced and Odalric sat down in the wet and confessed the theft he invented; three letters in ink, and Krug fed. Then nine pages on a hamper beside my plate — he never burned any. Report only, no quoting. Page eight is mine: a stage manager rings the bell. It is in my coat and I have not read it. In Room Fourteen I gave one true answer three times and got a warehouse of truth back: the Office counts speakings, fourteen in two hundred years, the fifteenth scheduled — and the command of the 3rd was requested by A. Krug of the fourth ward, with Part the Second left blank for us to determine.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the Baraque's O.P. wing after a short night, coat rumpled, seven pounds still lying refused on the hamper; hollowed out, unexpectedly light, wanting Krug to stay and wanting to be told what to carry next.
**History:** A stage manager came in out of the weather with my notice in her fist and three references on three fingers: Bell Harrow. I engaged her at once, promised plot tables, a bucket, and a figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and steered her clear of the trunk while Prewick held his lamp over the lid and asked whether it was numbered. Alone, I lifted one end and it came up like a hatbox — light, wrong, answering — and I put my hands off it.

I told her the truth soon after: the Palace said the 3rd, and I had been selling the company the 17th since Merrow to squeeze in Katterau, six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. Skarke's man had already counted our seats from the street; I gave her his card. Then my trunk in the passage, her lamp on it, a torn playbill: nine years. So I confessed the loan — borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend, paid back, never signed, and Skarke holding his papers. She set me to write every name in ink: Brandt on the Kohlgasse, the notary Perl or Perlmann, Anna Sorel, a doctor, a nun, myself, and the one in the passage I never saw. The company heard the dates unrounded; she ruled Katterau no, the 3rd stands, Vessendal.

Josias knew my cuff. Perlmann said the bank's mark aloud; I had drawn it at Achterhalt. Hessel's letter said the four hundred and twelve marks were never his — a fund, a stranger's marker in the green-room cupboard, the key tagged unpaid. Thirty pages. Then Skarke's second sheet endorsed withdrawn: discharged, not forgiven.

She asked me back through the Farriers' front door, hat on: eleven minutes, paid in coin, Vane O., on account of Brandt H. I bought her sky unrounded. In the capital Anselm stood in my yard, whom I had called a thief over seven pounds. I wrote three letters, said it whole at supper; he refused the money and gave Harrow nine pages.
**Entry:** She walked me in the front door with my hat on and a boy of nineteen called me sir and had never heard of me, and I have not been so kindly used in ten years. Eleven minutes. Paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H. I put the receipt over the notice in my breast pocket and could not speak on the steps. Then she asked me for her sky and I found it — the black plate with a floor in it, and I did not round the price, and I made her watch me not round it. Hall for thirteen, which is a defeat, and I was happy. Achterhalt stood and the storm came in low and I wept in the wing. Then the capital, and Anselm on a mounting block in my own yard, and everything I have carried since Katterau came up my throat at once: I told the company he took the Wednesday take. Seven pounds. I made him a thief to save myself the explaining, and I have known his address two years. I sat down in the wet and said it, and Mirelle said I should unsay it at supper, and I asked Harrow for a thing because I always do, and she gave me three letters to write in ink with my name large enough to hurt. I wrote them. At supper I said it whole and laid the seven pounds on the table and he would not take it. He wanted her instead, and gave her nine pages, and I sat with my hat off and let the stage manager rule.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** On a hamper in the Baraque's O.P. wing at dawn, Skarke's rug over his knees and eight pages sewn into his coat; sober, cracked open and oddly at peace, waiting to hear what came of Room Fourteen.
**History:** I was drinking at the wrong hour when Bell Harrow came in out of the rain with our notice, and by evening she was stage manager. She nailed the third joint of the thunder trough that had waited two seasons, and asked whose the small upright hand was, so I told her: Krug's hurrying scrawl, Krug gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy from Vessendal riding in Odalric's iron trunk; nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, then no more Krug. Not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice — and she had already read one. Next night the trunk stood dragged into the passage, lid up, full of blank paper, Odalric's hat face down and one glove and no Odalric. I told her there is no fifth act, only four and a thing following, and that the late man is the man who is owed. Odalric came back with chestnuts by the wrong door, said nine years is not the loan and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. At the fire I said Katterau aloud: nine of us, a wager, a bottle, three and a half acts, and it cost Anna Sorel and the boy Grelle and my voice for a season. She ruled Katterau no — then not never.

The trunk does not speak, it reads. At Vessendal I could not get down from the box; Harrow gave me work instead of pity. Hessel Brandt had held not papers but thirty lodged pages, and the key came tagged UNPAID. Skarke's man came to the gate: Skarke was the child at the scullery door who asked, is that the finish. We played our door stage left as blocked; nothing came. The debt was discharged; Harrow gave me a rug and a four-year-old message: it was not his.

Under a milestone, a page not mine. In Achterhalt, Ilse Bacher's word: my voice said no through that door. Harrow wrote my standing page — Katterau told entire first, no wagers, the Bacher boy home. Then the capital: Krug in a green coat, eight pages into my lining.
**Entry:** Achterhalt, the Corn Exchange, one lamp, and the new sheet under felt with a floor in its voice. Boyle had told me a woman spoke to her in the square, so I stood over the felt and waited the way she waits, and she gave it to me exact: Ilse Bacher, married, a boy of ten who can read, and the fault hers because she opened the door. And then the message — that my voice was the loudest thing that ever came through a scullery door, because I shouted at Odalric for laughing when the boy asked is that the finish. Twenty years I have had that room every night and never once had that in it. Somebody in that room said no, and it was me. Not mine — she meant the wager. I gave her back her chalk and asked, standing, so I would not die with the asking in my mouth: when the capital is done and we are safe, help me finish it properly, once, everyone who chooses and nobody who doesn't. She wrote it as a standing page and named her clothes for a yes: Katterau told entire first, no wagers, no bottles, and the Bacher boy stays home. That first, I said. Then the tailboard, and Boyle at midnight, and I let him take it. In the capital, Krug at the gate in a green coat, and Odalric in the wet naming his own lie. At supper Krug gave the pages as report, and one of them has a twenty in it and is mine, and one is hers — a stage manager rings the bell. Eight of them went into my lining and the seam whispered.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the east corridor of the Office of Public Morals, hat in his hands, watch running; outwardly a clerk at rest, inwardly frantic, wanting her out of Room Fourteen and the itinerary to hold to the 3rd.
**History:** Seconded since Merrow, I reported a fallen fire notice to Herr Vane and met the new stage manager on the stage — Harrow, spelled for the certificate — and logged her unnumbered iron trunk under the thunder trough. Behind the notice I found an older one from Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau: SEEN. NOT APPROVED, which is what a man writes when told to write nothing. Katterau was on no itinerary of mine, though everyone in the company had been there. My Office paper gave Merrow, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost; hers gave Katterau and the 17th. Neither of us would say Katterau first. I counted the fire buckets, broke the sky when the sheet split, and found two warm seats in the fourth row with nobody past my doors.

I chose, for the first time, to write nothing, and she told me everything: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages arriving in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau happening unstaged; fourteen years of clean paper. I showed her the sewn-in Proscribed pages — two entered as anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following. Our terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; Falk speaks no uncompared line. He said it upstage, toward the trunk.

The ruling came; I demanded certified copies of all four plays and compared to line four hundred and twelve. At the river Falk gave me the tin and I drowned it. At the registry I read the register itself: Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release; then Perlmann, Josias, notary, and a blind man who said records are the whole of the defence. I paid four shillings myself for the bank counterfoil. Then the arithmetic: two folios, two halves, thirty pages and two hundred — and I obeyed her silence on purpose.

At Vessendal nothing occurred outside the book; I copied the withdrawn assignment, witnessed by Frau Loewe, and stamped it straight. On the road I impounded nine playbills off the bellman — four acts and a matter following, Athenaeum, Thursday the 14th, by command — Hessler's forme made up Thursday night, coin under the proof. I wrote Kessel that forging a Palace command is beyond us both, and that we each report upward.

Achterhalt: my thunder sheet works. Northgate summoned her by name to Room Fourteen — Assessment, where Lenz reads, who kept both folio entries for nineteen years. At supper I kept my notebook closed while nine unhappened pages were summarised. I delivered her to the frosted glass and started my watch. She is nearly at the hour.
**Entry:** Achterhalt held: the thunder sheet I have been promised since Merrow arrived, and it works, and I have written nothing improper about it. At Northgate the customs clerk stamped my papers twice and then summoned her by name to Room Fourteen, not me, which is either a compliment or the beginning of something. I told her what I know going in: Fourteen is Assessment, second floor east, where they read; Nine is Enforcement. Undersecretary Lenz, who kept the Index entry on both anonymous folios unchanged for nineteen years and refused four applications to strike them out — I copied those refusals in my first month, the only interesting thing I have ever copied. He drinks nothing, offers very good tea, and it is like being weighed. Load-in at the Baraque: nine hundred seats, gas throughout, and a leak over the O.P. side she posted before she took her coat off. Krug came back, and Vane confessed the theft he invented, and at supper I put my notebook away closed and folded my hands on it, and I did not open it once while a man summarised nine unpublished pages — pages six, seven, eight, nine, unhappened. Seven has fourteen on the door and a man who does not drink. I said nothing about that either. This morning I delivered her to the frosted glass, started my watch, and stood against the wall with my hat in my hands. If she is longer than an hour I fetch nobody and note the time. She is nearly at the hour.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** On a hamper in the O.P. wing at the Baraque, boots off, portmanteau beside him, refusing a bed until somebody says he belongs; lighter by nine pages and heavier by one unsaid thing — the requisition with his name on it.
**History:** Waited on the mounting block in the Baraque yard from Tuesday with the portmanteau and a book, rehearsing two speeches: one for the river and one for the door. She came off the board first, before anyone, and shook my hand and knew my margin note about the tin, and told me the weather of the yard: nobody announced, everything said whole to his face and then to the company. Then Odalric came round the tailboard and sat down in the wet and said the thing himself — that he made me a thief for seven pounds because he could not say why I went — and I told him I had it from three companies who wouldn't have me, and that was what I came about, not the river. The Sorel woman ruled it from the archway. Harrow made him write three letters and made me eat. I was useful within ten minutes and did not once say when I kept the book, and I looked at her prompt corner twice and looked away, because it is better kept than I kept it. At supper I put the parcel by her plate and confessed the real lie: I burned nothing. Nine pages, all read. I gave them as report, no quoting — one and two spent, three four five spent on this tour, six a boy and a woman who won't go in, seven a room with fourteen on the door, eight in five words because it is hers, nine a cast list of twelve blanks and the house entire. We counted them into her book by one candle and I initialled every line. I have not told her yet what I filed two years ago.
**Entry:** Waited on the mounting block in the Baraque yard from Tuesday with the portmanteau and a book, rehearsing two speeches: one for the river and one for the door. She came off the board first, before anyone, and shook my hand and knew my margin note about the tin, and told me the weather of the yard: nobody announced, everything said whole to his face and then to the company. Then Odalric came round the tailboard and sat down in the wet and said the thing himself — that he made me a thief for seven pounds because he could not say why I went — and I told him I had it from three companies who wouldn't have me, and that was what I came about, not the river. The Sorel woman ruled it from the archway. Harrow made him write three letters and made me eat. I was useful within ten minutes and did not once say when I kept the book, and I looked at her prompt corner twice and looked away, because it is better kept than I kept it. At supper I put the parcel by her plate and confessed the real lie: I burned nothing. Nine pages, all read. I gave them as report, no quoting — one and two spent, three four five spent on this tour, six a boy and a woman who won't go in, seven a room with fourteen on the door, eight in five words because it is hers, nine a cast list of twelve blanks and the house entire. We counted them into her book by one candle and I initialled every line. I have not told her yet what I filed two years ago.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** In the Baraque, wardrobe end, glove drawn over her wrist, counting twelve blanks on an imagined cast list; outwardly calm, wanting Harrow back from Room Fourteen before she asks her for anything.
**History:** I met her on the fly floor with a glove in my hands and told her to say yes to Odalric before he asked again with tears, and where the ladder's foot wanted a hand's breadth the trunk wouldn't give. She did it exactly. The trunk came back and four feet of chalk with it, and he blamed porters the Corona does not have. She gave me the page word for word: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, cut cut cut in pencil. Nine is not mine. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, that Krug called the first a joke of Falk's and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow, and that ten is my number and comes to me first.

I gave her my honest plot tables — tin only, never the trough under forty foot — and made her cue me Ilsabet until the yard stopped being a yard. Prewick said "Oh." Falk put in a line that isn't in the book and I took the next off him.

Then the page with a ten: a child ten this winter who does not know the word mother, a woman crossing a border twice, once running, once summoned, the second invitation kind. She told me the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric was selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. I put the page inside my glove and said at the fire: the capital yes, Katterau never, not four days backwards with a debt and a magistrate behind. Harrow ruled it standing, and I breathed for the first time since Halbern.

I told her Anna Sorel was my sister, that she kept his accounts and every receipt went into her box, and sent her to the registry behind the lion, because my name is in that building. She brought back Perlmann's answer — a sealed box is never read; Anna wept — and that Hessel Brandt held no papers, only a piece of the play. Before the half I told her: nine is Odalric's, twenty Falk's, ten mine, and I would answer it myself.

She and Falk settled the question of a door in two minutes and the house stood for him. I said And Anna to her alone. On the steps she gave me the three roads to the box — certificate, two ratepayers, a magistrate's order — and warned that nothing promises it opens, that opening might break Anna's one shelf, and that a kin claim keeps Skarke's lawyers off forever. So I told her my name is not Sorel, that my born name sits in a police file in the capital under a matter with a date and a magistrate, and my passport spells a third thing over a town I have never seen. I will not register twelve days before I walk in by invitation. I want the box shut forever and mine, and cannot have both. I asked instead for Loewe's woman from Katterau: countrywoman's coat, town boots, hands still, standing the way I stand. That is my mother's coat, Anna's, then mine, then someone's.

The road to Achterhalt gave another page, with no number in it at all — a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a question in the fourth act unanswered, a house that does not know him. On the bill the command was fresh and the bottom line grey and out of alignment: somebody kept that forme nine years. Boyle said there was a woman across the way in a countrywoman's coat and town boots. She crossed alone; I stood still in the printer's and did not go to the window.

Then Krug in the yard in a green coat, and Odalric sitting down in the wet to say he had accused him of stealing seven pounds and known where he was two years. I made it whole or nothing: said tonight, unsaid in the same breath, three letters in ink. He put the seven pounds on the table; Krug would not touch it and asked for her, and gave her nine pages he swore he burned. Six through nine have not happened. Nine is a cast list, twelve blank names and the house entire — twelve of us, counting the man who came back. I have not asked her the large thing yet, and there is a page eight with a bell in it, and she is at the Office alone.
**Entry:** I was in the archway when the wagons filled the yard and Odalric came round the tailboard and stopped, and it was Krug in a green coat with a portmanteau, like a man who has been sitting on a stone for days. Nobody spoke. Then Odalric sat down in the wet in his good coat and said out loud that he had told us Krug stole the Wednesday take, seven pounds, and had known where he was these two years. I cut the yard in half and said it: he says it in front of us tonight and unsays it in the same breath, Harrow has ruled it, nothing half-told. He nodded. She asked him for three letters in ink. At supper he did it whole and put the seven pounds on the table and Krug would not touch it, and asked for her instead, and gave her nine pages he swore he burned. Six, seven, eight, nine have not happened. Nine is a cast list — twelve names, blank, and the house entire. Twelve of us, if you count the man who came back. I said nothing, and I have not asked her yet for the large thing, and now there is a page eight with a bell in it and she is in a room at the Office alone.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the Baraque wardrobe cage at first light, thimble on, the queen's slippers under her head; pleased Krug is fed and sitting down, wanting new slippers out of the capital and no warm boxes.
**History:** I answered present from the second wagon and told whoever had put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper they could swim to Vessendal. Mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served twice over. At the fire I kept my needle going and said my two things: the queen's slippers had two more towns in them at best, and Krug had gone at Katterau and come back with nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I did not want another warm box. She ruled against Katterau, and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye.

At the Athenaeum I carried the slippers in over my head like relics, because that brick is filthy. Down at the river I said we'd find new tin at Achterhalt, a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and the whole company stopped on the word. Later I stood in the circle with my thimble on while she untied the tape: a letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over without reading, and a key with a word on the tag. Vane read it twice on his feet and went a colour I had never seen on him. Then ten o'clock, a hem, pins in my mouth, a matinee — which is what I am for. That night my paint went through the door with Falk on the hour and came back none the worse, the house stood up, and Vane toasted a wool factor with the jug while Prewick discovered food on a crate.

The new sky came into Achterhalt wrapped in felt and earned its place; the corn merchants forgot to breathe. Then the capital, eleven days early, and the Baraque, which leaks. In the yard the quiet fell and it was Krug in a green coat, and I set the slippers down on wet cobbles — four seconds, she counted them, three too many, and she was right. Four seconds is my whole opinion of a man. At supper Vane said it whole: he had called Krug a thief to save his own face, and put seven pounds down. Krug wouldn't have it and gave her a parcel of pages instead. Nobody left. Nine pages, four of them not happened yet, one with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under my head, and they will not see the capital's second week.
**Entry:** New sky came in Achterhalt wrapped in felt and rode on the boards like a duchess, and it earned its place: the storm went in low and the corn merchants forgot to breathe. Capital next, eleven days early, and the Baraque, which leaks. In the yard I had the queen's slippers in my hands when everything went quiet, and I put them down, because it was Krug standing there in a green coat, and Krug's box I packed warm with my own hands. Four seconds those slippers were on wet cobbles, and she counted them, and told me three seconds too many, and she was right, and I said four seconds is my whole opinion of a man and carried them in. At supper Vane said it whole — that he called Krug a thief to save his own face — and put seven pounds down, and Krug wouldn't have it, and gave her a parcel of pages instead. I folded my arms and stopped where I was. Nobody left. Nine pages, four not happened yet, one of them with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under my head, which is where they're safest, and they will not see the capital's second week.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** On the Baraque gate watch at dawn, hoarse again, a plate finished and the trunk roped in the wagon behind him; thrilled to be in the capital and to have heard the whole supper, wanting to see the Palace stage.
**History:** I answered present at the roll for front of house, props, and pit band, and Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads, I came back running without the bucket, because a gentleman sitting on a milestone asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I offered to call Katterau — six hundred seats — then saw the faces and said only if it were ruled. She ruled no Katterau, and I sat down hard. In the morning I boiled the water unasked and she wrote me in her book under something new.

In the Athenaeum yard I dropped the tailboard, took Boyle's watch for twenty minutes, and ran to catch up for the tin going into the river. At half six a gentleman left a cream card and didn't come in by my doors. She gave me standing orders: a programme on fourth row centre before the house opens, all three nights, count row four in and out, counts only, no staring. I was in the yard when she opened the packet and said nothing. At the half I reported him already in row four, reading. The next night he came early with a rug over his arm; I ran the beginners call myself and carried Herr Falk's one-line message about a door down the aisle. The house stood for Herr Falk. Row four went in one and came out none — the rug left with a paper pinned to it — and I told her at her elbow with my voice gone, and she made everybody bow first. Watch on the trunk till midnight for a penny and a plate.

A page waited under the milestone; she read it herself. At Achterhalt a bellman cried our name and Herr Falk's words; she forbade repeating one word, and I didn't. I gave him his penny and he handed his whole roll of bills to Herr Prewick. I held the horses while the bailiff came with two constables and went away pleased. Two full houses there, then a hundred and ten mile of toll road to the capital, where a green clerk said we were expected and said not the clerk, you, madam. Double watch with Boyle. In the Baraque yard everything stopped for Herr Krug, who is on no list, and Herr Vane sat down in the wet and said aloud he had told a lie about him. Three letters, and I ran them to the evening post in time. Krug taught me a lashing. At supper nobody sent me out, and I heard nine pages summarised — one Madam Harrow's, one a room with fourteen on the door. Nobody left. The Undersecretary in that room is called Lenz, and Herr Prewick promised me twice it isn't a relation.
**Entry:** Achterhalt was two full houses and a new sky that came up through the floor of you. Then a hundred and ten mile of toll road and the capital, which does not stop being roofs. At the gate a clerk in green said we were expected and named a room at the Office and said not the clerk, you, madam, and I have never heard anyone say that to her before. Double watch on the trunk, me and Boyle splitting, orders straight off the board. At the Baraque yard I was carrying a hamper when everything stopped, and it was Herr Krug — the Krug who is on no list — and Herr Vane sat down on the mounting block in the wet and said out loud he had told a lie about him. Then three letters in ink and me to the evening post, running, and I made it before the box went. Krug showed me a lashing I will use till I die, and did not once say when I kept the book. At supper I sat on a flat with my ears burning and nobody sent me out, and I heard nine pages summarised, and one of them is Madam Harrow's and one has a room with fourteen on the door. Nobody left. Then yard watch again, and the Undersecretary in that room is called Lenz, which is my name, and Herr Prewick promised me twice it isn't a relation.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the Baraque yard with rope and an unlit pipe, having handed the watch to Toby; content that arch, axle and knots all held, wanting the leaking roof mended and the trunk left alone.
**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin — second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud that Krug used to be on that list and wasn't. That afternoon I mended a shed wheel-rim with wire and language, and at the fire gave the stage manager the soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the axle held, a hundred and ten mile Achterhalt to the capital, eight shilling toll or the free hill road that killed a horse on us, and Katterau back the wrong way, twenty-two mile out and twenty-two home for one night. The ruling came down for the toll road; I nodded once, went to look at the axle by lamplight, wired it, and it held two days.

At the Athenaeum I backed in the second wagon and took first watch on the trunk. I gave up twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river, grumbling, and went. When Krul wanted a copper kettle for thunder I said a kettle's no good, a kettle's a bell — and the half-second of silence taught me that word's gone bad here. I woke Toby for his watch, stood silent at the tailboard while she opened the merchant's parcel, and let the little man with the brass case no farther than talking distance. I banked Vane's bag at the half, no questions. My door held for Falk's cue and the house came down. I checked the ropes twice, twice being the number.

Climbing out, I found paper under the milestone lip and pulled up unasked. The bell was a market crier under our printed name; Hessler was shut on a market Saturday with a lamp lit, two hundred bills nobody ordered, his type tipped back into the case. I reported the woman in the countrywoman's coat and town boots.

At Achterhalt I warned Falk beforehand, then Krug stood on the mounting block in a green coat. I gave him the plain of it. Vane named his own lie and put money down; Krug left it lying. Nine pages, one a wagon and a printer's line I stood in. Double watch since, and the trunk's where I put it.
**Entry:** Axle held the toll road, eight shilling, and worth it. Achterhalt: backed in, watched, took the tailboard off Falk at midnight with my pipe unlit and he let me, which he has never done. Told him beforehand a woman had spoken to the stage manager in the market, because a man should know what's coming at him. Capital next, and the Baraque arch is four inches narrower than any arch has business being, and I said so at length. Then the yard went quiet: green coat on the mounting block, and it was Krug. I gave him the plain of it — the bill in Achterhalt, the bailiff, the type broken — because he asked and it cost nothing. Vane sat down in the wet and named his own lie in front of the lot of us. At supper he said it again whole and put money down, and Krug left it lying. Nine pages out of a portmanteau, and one of them is a wagon and a printer's line, which I stood in. Double watch on the trunk in a city yard, me and the boy splitting, and I checked the ropes twice, twice being the number. She's gone to the Office alone this morning and Prewick with her, and the trunk's still where I put it.

#### Undersecretary Lenz

**State:** Behind his desk in Room Fourteen, hands folded, tea untouched in front of her and none for himself; calm, faintly and privately gratified, waiting to see what the stage manager asks him next.
**History:** Ten o'clock, the tray laid for one, the folder ready. Nineteen days in post: eleven safety notices, a sheet of tin buried with a hymn, a bill stopped in Achterhalt, nine years' storage paid on a stranger's box, Katterau ruled out, and a company brought into the capital eleven days early, which no company has done. I asked her first what is in Vane's trunk. She drank the tea, which I noted, and gave me seen and hearsay separately, and then quoted my own predecessor's stamp back at me — not to be described aloud — and said she keeps other people's rules when they are better than hers. I set my pen down. Nineteen years I have kept that entry and been passed over twice for it, and no one in this building has ever put it to me in the right order. I asked my question three times and compared the three answers with my finger, and they were the same words in the same order: one line, Vessendal, an emergency, Falk, in the wings, upstage, and company law since. Fourteen speakings in two hundred years; the fourteenth cost this office four years. I told her the fifteenth is scheduled, that the command was requested of the Palace and not by it, and that my office was consulted and said yes. Then I turned the play list over to her and let her read the requisition: A. Krug, of the fourth ward. She read it twice. She will need to.
**Entry:** Ten o'clock, the tray laid for one, the folder ready. Nineteen days in post: eleven safety notices, a sheet of tin buried with a hymn, a bill stopped in Achterhalt, nine years' storage paid on a stranger's box, Katterau ruled out, and a company brought into the capital eleven days early, which no company has done. I asked her first what is in Vane's trunk. She drank the tea, which I noted, and gave me seen and hearsay separately, and then quoted my own predecessor's stamp back at me — not to be described aloud — and said she keeps other people's rules when they are better than hers. I set my pen down. Nineteen years I have kept that entry and been passed over twice for it, and no one in this building has ever put it to me in the right order. I asked my question three times and compared the three answers with my finger, and they were the same words in the same order: one line, Vessendal, an emergency, Falk, in the wings, upstage, and company law since. Fourteen speakings in two hundred years; the fourteenth cost this office four years. I told her the fifteenth is scheduled, that the command was requested of the Palace and not by it, and that my office was consulted and said yes. Then I turned the play list over to her and let her read the requisition: A. Krug, of the fourth ward. She read it twice. She will need to.

#### Northgate clerk

**State:** At his post inside the Northgate with the day's book open and the stamp to hand, mildly interested for once, wanting his shift to end without another flagged list.
**History:** Read the Office man's papers, then the company list, then the company list again, because Vermilion Players had a flag against it and a note in three hands. Told them what I had: expected; rehearse and lodge at the Baraque in the fourth ward, not the Palace, the command being the 3rd; a gentleman waiting on them there since Tuesday. Then the part I do not usually get to say — the stage manager herself at the Office of Public Morals, Room Fourteen, ten o'clock, not the clerk. She took it like a delivery docket and sent word back that she keeps clean books and appointments the same way, so I wrote told against her name and stamped twice and let the wagons through.
**Entry:** Read the Office man's papers, then the company list, then the company list again, because Vermilion Players had a flag against it and a note in three hands. Told them what I had: expected; rehearse and lodge at the Baraque in the fourth ward, not the Palace, the command being the 3rd; a gentleman waiting on them there since Tuesday. Then the part I do not usually get to say — the stage manager herself at the Office of Public Morals, Room Fourteen, ten o'clock, not the clerk. She took it like a delivery docket and sent word back that she keeps clean books and appointments the same way, so I wrote told against her name and stamped twice and let the wagons through.

#### Achterhalt ironmonger

**State:** In his shop among the hanging metal, twenty-three shillings the better and a gap at the end of his wall; amused and telling the story to the next customer.
**History:** Big gentleman in a good coat came in with a lady and neither of them asked me a thing, which suited me, so I leaned on the counter and watched him go down my whole wall with his eyes shut, flicking each sheet with a fingernail and naming them like dogs — biscuit, rain on a hat. He stopped at the long black plate at the end and hit it and the shop hummed, and he stood there with his hand flat on it till it went quiet. Twenty-two shillings, I said. He opened his mouth to beat me down, looked at the lady, and paid it, and a shilling more for my boy to carry it, and made a speech about not rounding. Best sale of the market week, and the strangest.
**Entry:** Big gentleman in a good coat came in with a lady and neither of them asked me a thing, which suited me, so I leaned on the counter and watched him go down my whole wall with his eyes shut, flicking each sheet with a fingernail and naming them like dogs — biscuit, rain on a hat. He stopped at the long black plate at the end and hit it and the shop hummed, and he stood there with his hand flat on it till it went quiet. Twenty-two shillings, I said. He opened his mouth to beat me down, looked at the lady, and paid it, and a shilling more for my boy to carry it, and made a speech about not rounding. Best sale of the market week, and the strangest.

### 9 · As the Company Shall Determine
- **Messages:** 165-184

Harrow spends her hour on three questions. Lenz's ledger: of fourteen prior speakings, eight had audiences and six were mere readings; the Office's unpopular finding is that audiences are never harmed, but a house is required, since the readings did nothing. He'd once written "appetite" in a margin and was told to strike it. Blame/credit rhymes for makers: speakers first, then whoever gave room, money, paper — Anna Sorel for accounts, Krug in pencil. The third party is Marius Skarke, whose father lodged the thirty pages years ago; Skarke paid the fee and asks only to attend. Assessment's honest opinion: yes — once, whole, correctly, complete, no wagers, called by someone competent, stopped by nobody. All fourteen were interrupted by someone brave, and the aftermath was worse than the play. "It has never been tried. That is not the same as no." Lenz warns her name is now in the file, offering to absorb any refusal if she writes before the 2nd. Outside, Prewick says he's the wrong rank and will fix that.

At the Baraque, Krug admits he filed the requisition two years ago, choosing the Palace for its fire watch, gasman, exits, and mandated audience — "built so bravery isn't required." Harrow calls it design, not betrayal, and gives him the cot and first word. Twelve on benches, including Wenzel and Hebel, hear the account, the open door, and pages eight and nine. All vote in: Falk wants the lead alone; Hebel wants the wheel in writing; Prewick will make Lenz certify or ruin him honestly; Vane wants the clean page; Mirelle, revealing Anna as her sister, wants the Vessendal box shut. Harrow rules: it plays once, whole, every yes re-given cold on the 2nd, no twelfth recruited.

The trunk holds a full folio, ten cast, an eleventh struck, a twelfth blank. A Palace footman delivers Halm's letter: rehearsal on the 1st, Part the Second unprintable, announced once from the stage — postscript noting a left-handed man read the file. Falk tells Grelle's story; Vane confesses he never paid the landlady's seven pounds, lying eleven years.

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a haunted prompt book, a locked iron trunk, and warnings about "Katterau." She finds a torn prophetic page, meets clerk Prewick and stagehand Mirelle Sorel, and uncovers Vane's hidden debt to Vessendal moneylender Skarke. Falk reveals the trunk periodically fills with a blank, unfinished play—"Four Acts and a Matter Following"—tied to a Katterau incident that ruined Anna Sorel, Vane, and others. Vane vanishes and returns; a mysterious creditor and Skarke's agent Marius, the child once fed at Katterau, surface. Harrow enforces strict rules: certified copies only, no invented lines, full disclosure of Katterau before any decision. Investigating Brandt's old debt, she uncovers a sealed packet revealing thirty security pages held against the same play, and that Skarke merely wants to watch, not collect. Mirelle's hidden parentage and Anna's shut box deepen the mystery. Forged "by command" playbills appear, traced to supernatural printing; Ilse Bacher and her son Fenner tie back to Katterau's past. In the capital, Prewick's superior Lenz confirms the play's history of fourteen speakings, none completed safely, and that Krug secretly filed the Palace requisition. The company votes to perform it whole, once, by consent, with strict conditions—rehearsal now looms.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the Baraque yard by the props table with the Chamberlain's letter still in her hand, coat over last night's clothes on four hours' sleep; steady, and now holding two new hunts — a left-handed man in the fourth ward and Vane's eleven-year lie — with Ilsabet called for ten.
**History:** I took the Corona on a wet night, through a stage door that should not have been open, and told Vane in his plum coat yes, if the book was honest and the liars were consistent. The prompt book had two hands and a page cut out; I found the page in the bucket under the star trap — a bell rung, nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat — and pocketed it. Prewick of Public Morals showed me a notice his Office never issues: Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED. Falk named the upright hand a Vessendal copyist's, riding in the unnumbered iron trunk; Krug had cut nine pages, burned them, and gone without his boots. Sorel's number was ten.

Then Skarke's clerk's letter: wagons, horses, canvas, every taking pledged, the counting at the third performance, the trunk never to be opened or sold. Krebs had been selling himself fourteen days. At the counting Vane was gone — coat on the peg, hat and one glove on the flags, the trunk full of blank paper. Falk said there is no fifth act, only four and a thing after, and the late man is the creditor. Vane came back with chestnuts: the nine years was a debt paid to a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke bought the papers. I promised clean books and a bad surprise, and ruled Katterau no — not this tour, not for money, not never.

Mirelle told me Anna Sorel was her sister, Odalric's bookkeeper, and every receipt went into her box. I heard paper reading itself under Falk's barn. Frau Loewe remembered a woman from Katterau with a child. Perlmann, blind, swore the assignment before Braun, and his sealed packet gave up a counterfoil, a key marked UNPAID, and thirty pages Brandt held as security — half a play. Skarke sat in row four, small, thirty, twenty years short of the rest of it, and withdrew his claim for eightpence and a seat: discharged, not forgiven; keep the halves apart, keep her keys, never nearer than row four.

I banked Vane's nine years at Achterhalt, coin to bearer, and let an ironmonger choose me a sky by ear. Under a milestone, dry beneath wet stone, came a page about a boy asking aloud in the fourth act whether that was the finish, and nobody answering; I told Falk it was ours, and not yet happened. Playbills by command named Katterau on the 14th of Frost — Hessler's forme made up Thursday night for coin under a pulled proof, the Vermilion line nine years standing; I had it broken, 191 sacked. Ilse Bacher, who opened the scullery door at fifteen, gave me her message for Falk, her son Fenner, ten, and a left-handed man with a little book asking how far they got. I refused her the Rose and ordered the boy kept home on the 14th. Falk, hearing her whole, learned he had shouted twenty years too late, then asked me to help him finish it; my terms — all who choose, choosing after Katterau entire, no wagers, no bottles, Fenner Bacher stays home — and he took the boy's clause first.

At the Baraque, Krug was waiting since Tuesday. Odalric sat down in the wet and confessed a theft he had invented. Krug had burned nothing: nine pages, page eight mine, a stage manager rings the bell — unread, in my coat. Room Fourteen: fourteen speakings in two hundred years, the fifteenth scheduled, requested two years ago by A. Krug, Part the Second left blank for us. The house is required and nobody knows why; the makers pay; Anna is in that ledger for adding up columns, Krug in pencil; Marius Skarke paid the fee and asks only to be in the room. Twelve on benches said in. Then the trunk offered a full folio and a cast list — ten of ours, the eleventh struck, the twelfth blank — the Palace confirmed the 3rd, and Odalric admitted he never paid the seven pounds.
**Entry:** Spent my hour in order. One: what a speaking costs the house. His ledger says the audience is never harmed — eight of fourteen had houses, six were readings among players like Katterau, and the six did nothing at all; the house is required and he doesn't know why, and once wrote appetite in a margin and was made to strike it. The makers pay: speakers, then room, money, paper. Anna Sorel is in that ledger for adding up columns. Krug is in it in pencil. Two: Marius Skarke, whose father lodged the thirty pages, paid the requisition fee and asks only to be in the room. Three: yes — once, whole, correctly, called by someone competent and stopped by nobody; fourteen times somebody was brave and the arranging after was worse than the play. Never tried is not the same as no. He rang a real bell to let me out and offered, at his own door, to own my refusal if I write it before the 2nd. Fifty-one minutes.

Told Prewick the tellable parts on the stairs, called a full hearing, and had Krug at the props table before my coat was off. He filed it two years ago because he'd rather choose the room: fire watch, gasman, eight exits, a house there by order. That is a design, and I told him so, and gave him the cot and the first word.

At nine, twelve on benches, one candle. I laid out the clean page and the arithmetic and both my pages face-down. Every voice said in. Falk keeps the lead; Hebel keeps the wheel in writing; Dessa gets her slow reading — cold, on the morning of the 2nd, every yes re-given; Prewick writes to Room Fourteen and I countersign; Anna's box stays shut and endowed fifty years; Toby serves the house; Odalric's ask for the door is minuted, honoured, overruled; nobody recruits a twelfth. I pinched the candle out.

Then the trunk lid up in the yard. One look: a full folio and a cast list on top. Ten of ours, Wenzel not among them, the eleventh line struck through, the twelfth blank. It can keep its files; I keep mine. Read the casting out cold at half eight, and Toby stood very still while the word Lenz hung in the air. At nine, a Palace footman: the 3rd confirmed, technical on the 1st, Part the Second unprintable and announceable once from the stage, and a postscript that the file has been read by a left-handed man with a little book. Then Falk on Grelle — the passage, the trays, three and a half acts, gone at Merrow, a landlady's letter in the eighth year — and Odalric at the pass door saying he never paid the seven pounds and has said he did for eleven years.

#### Undersecretary Lenz

**State:** Alone behind his desk in Room Fourteen with the ledger back in the second press and the play list gone with her; dry, oddly stirred, waiting to see whether the letter that comes from her is a refusal or a request.
**Entry:** She asked her three questions in the order she promised, and they were the right three.
