I got up and fetched the ledger and gave her the finding that has kept me in this room nineteen years: the audience is not harmed, not once in two hundred years, and yet the house is required — six readings among players did nothing at all, and I have written appetite in a margin and been told to strike it. I named the makers who pay, and I did not soften Anna Sorel's line or the pencil against Krug. Second, I named Skarke aloud in a deniable room, and said his letter is the most careful letter I have ever had from a rich man. Third, I gave her the opinion I have been passed over twice for: yes, once, correctly, whole, in a house that knows what it is watching, stopped by nobody — and that in fourteen tries someone has always been brave, and the arranging afterwards was always worse. Never tried is not no. I rang for the clerk. At my own door I told her the thing I will not put in a ledger: her name is in the requisition file, files are read, and if she refuses she must refuse loudly, early and in writing to me, and I will make it the Office's refusal and carry it. Until the 2nd. She left at fifty-one minutes and I found I wanted her to come back.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** In the O.P. wing with his notebook shut and his sealed letter already gone to the Office, the colour of paste; frightened for his rank and steady in it, wanting Lenz to come in person and the 1st to pass lawfully.
**History:** Seconded since Merrow, I re-hung a fire notice for Herr Vane and met Harrow, the new stage manager, her iron trunk unnumbered in the passage. Behind the notice hung an older one, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. Katterau stood on no itinerary of mine; hers had it, and the 17th, where mine had the capital and the command performance on the 3rd of Frost. Neither of us would name Katterau first. I broke the sky when the tin split, and counted two warm seats, fourth row centre, with nobody past my doors.

Choosing to write nothing, I was told all of it: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page, pages arriving in prompt books, what it staged coming true slantwise and late, fourteen years of clean paper. I showed her my sewn Proscribed pages — two anonymous folios, four acts, and a matter following. Our terms: I learn what she learns inside the hour; Falk speaks no uncompared line. I demanded certified copies of all four plays. Falk gave me the tin at the river and I drowned it and ruined my boots. In the registry: Sorel, Anna, one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. Perlmann the notary, blind, took my breathing for Sorel's and said records are the whole of the defence. I paid four shillings of my own for the bank counterfoil. Two folios, two halves: thirty pages in the cupboard, two hundred in the trunk — and she forbade the report, and I obeyed on purpose.

At Vessendal I copied the assignment endorsed withdrawn, witnessed by Frau Loewe, and was happy over Krul's mutton and did not report that either. Then bills in the square: four acts and a matter following, by command, the Athenaeum, the 14th — after our Palace date. I impounded nine copies; Hessler had no order, coin under the proof. I wrote Kessel that forgery of a Palace command was beyond us both, in those words, so neither could blame the other.

At Northgate they summoned her, not me, to Room Fourteen — Lenz, who held both folios in the Index nineteen years against four applications. Krug returned; Vane confessed the theft he had invented; I heard nine unhappened pages summarised with my notebook shut. She came out at fifty-one minutes: audience unharmed, the house required, Krug's requisition, Skarke's fee, the Office's own refusal on offer until the 2nd. Krug had chosen the Palace for the fire watch and the exits. At the hearing I stood and said my seal makes a performance lawful, and wrote four sentences asking Lenz to come and certify in person; she countersigned. By morning Lenz was on the trunk's list, with no telling whether the ink came before or after. Then the Palace letter, a left-handed stranger who had read the requisition file, and my own enquiry minuted as the regular one.
**Entry:** She came out at fifty-one minutes and told me the whole of it going down the grey stairs: audience unharmed, the house required, the requisition filed by Krug, Skarke paid the fee, and the Office's own refusal on offer until the 2nd. By the courtyard gate I had said the only thing I had: I am the wrong rank for the next fortnight and shall have to be the right one anyway. Heard Krug confess at the props table; he chose the Palace for the fire watch and the exits, which is a clerk's thinking and I could not fault it. At the hearing I stood up because I could not say it sitting: my seal makes a performance lawful, and if Part the Second plays I either certify a proscribed text and am finished, or certify nothing and leave eleven people liable with me as witness. I said I would write to Undersecretary Lenz and ask him to come and certify it in person where I can see his hands, and if he refuses I shall certify it myself and be ruined honestly. I wrote the letter that night at the props table by the gas pilot, four sentences, read it aloud once, and she countersigned. In the morning the trunk's list had Lenz on it, and I went cold: I asked him in writing, countersigned, and Krug says there is no telling whether the ink came before or after. Then the Palace letter, and a left-handed stranger has read the requisition file, and my own enquiry is minuted as the regular one.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** At the fly rail of the Baraque with a rope still in his hand, boots on and a cot of his own by the props table; unstoned and useful, wanting the technical on the 1st and needing to know what Vane's seven pounds and a left-handed man have to do with him.
**Entry:** She came through the gate and called me to the props table before her coat was off and said she had seen my hand on Palace paper, so I did not sit down. Two years ago, six weeks after Katterau, in a rooming house in the fourth ward with page eight in my pocket and no company that would have me, I filed the requisition — because if the thing meant to arrange me I would rather choose the room. The Palace: fire watch, gasman, eight exits, nine hundred people there because they were told to be and not because they'd wagered a bottle. Two shillings I could not spare, and I read the pamphlet nineteen times in the corridor. Granted in the spring. I have been six streets away ever since, waiting to tell somebody before the 3rd.

She named it: last night a report, this a confession, and the filing a design — the best-built thing anyone has brought her on this tour. I put my face in my hands like Odalric and came out dry. I have called it a betrayal for two years and it has sat in me like a stone. She gave me the cot by the props table and the first word at the hearing, and belonging left to the vote.

Gave the brief like a plot call and my hands stopped shaking on the third sentence: nine hundred and forty seats, four levels, three staircases from the pit, eight legal exits, statutory fire watch of two, the board out of reach, iron in eleven seconds. Built so bravery isn't required. Everyone said in. Her ruling stands and I am plotting the 1st, eight to noon, exits twice, the iron until I trust it. In the morning the trunk had a cast list with my name on it and Lenz's, and I said the true thing: there's no telling with the dates. Then Falk on Grelle, left-handed, and Odalric saying he never paid the seven pounds. I stood on the fly rail with a rope in my hand and could not move.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Sitting at the props table with both hands flat on it after telling Grelle's story, sober, the lead his by ruling; steady but shaken, wanting to know what Odalric's unpaid seven pounds bought.
**History:** A girl came in out of the rain with a notice and by nightfall we had Bell Harrow, stage manager. I gave her the third board, the truth about the thunder trough and the farmer at Merrow, and then the pages: Krug's hurrying scrawl, and Krug gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made in Vessendal, riding in Odalric's iron trunk. Nine cut and burned, the tenth returned, then no more Krug. Don't burn, don't replace, don't read one twice — she already had. That night the trunk moved with Odalric out of the house.

He dodged me. I found the trunk dragged into the passage, lid up, blank paper inside, his hat face down and one glove and no Odalric — and he walked in later with chestnuts, saying nine years is not the loan, that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I told her: fourteen years of clean paper, four acts and a matter following, no fifth; the late man is the man who is owed. At the fire I said Katterau aloud — nine of us, a wager and a bottle, three and a half acts sitting down; it cost Anna Sorel, the boy Grelle, my voice for a season and Odalric's nerve. She ruled Katterau no, then not never. The trunk does not speak; it reads. In Vessendal I could not get down from the wagon, and told her how I chalked the whole thing alone four years ago: it wants a house.

Then Hessel's key, tagged UNPAID; thirty pages lodged as security by a nameless party; Skarke's man at the gate — Skarke being the nine-year-old at the scullery door who asked, is that the finish. Our practical door is stage left; Harrow ruled as blocked, and I walked through it and nothing came. She brought me a rug and said my hands were cold. A four-year-old message: tell him it was not his.

Under a milestone, a page with no number: a boy brought by a woman who will not go in. Our name by command, biggest type. At Achterhalt, Ilse Bacher's word — my voice was the loudest thing through that door, because I shouted at Odalric for laughing; somebody said no, and it was me. I asked her to help me finish it properly, once; she made it a standing page — Katterau told entire first, no wagers, the Bacher boy home. Boyle at midnight, and I let him take it. In the capital, Krug at the gate in green, eight pages into my lining. At the hearing I said in, and my one condition: I speak the lead. Harrow ruled ten conditions. Then I told her Grelle — left-handed, gone at Merrow with three shillings, dead owing four weeks by a letter I never saw — and Odalric said from the pass door that he never paid it.
**Entry:** Walked the Baraque stage twice and said nothing to anybody. At the hearing I did not stand. I said in, and that I'd not spend the candle repeating why, and set my one condition: I speak the lead and no one else does — it has had my voice once and doesn't get a new one. Heard Krug lay out the Palace like a plot call, and it is a good plot; heard Prewick offer to be ruined honestly; heard Mirelle stand up, which she never does, and give us her sister and her own magistrate. Harrow ruled it: once, whole, correctly, ten conditions, and the tenth is that the play may apply to the management in daylight. I have known great managers and none of them would have thought to make it queue. In the morning she sat me down with the Palace letter and asked about Grelle. So I told it: Ansel Grelle, second boy at Katterau, fifteen or sixteen, in the passage with the trays, three and a half acts through a door same as Ilse; stayed two years, went at Merrow in the seventh year with three shillings and a speech; in the eighth year a landlady's letter to Odalric said a young man had died owing four weeks. I never saw a body. I never saw the letter. And he was left-handed — I remember his crossings-out. Then Odalric said from the pass door that he never paid it.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** Asleep, then up in the wardrobe cage at the Baraque with the mended glove on bare skin and page ten in her pocket; named at last to her own company and lighter for it, wanting Anna's shelf left shut and the 3rd to come.
**History:** I was mending a glove on the fly floor when the new one, Harrow, came in out of the rain, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears, warned her off the trunk at the ladder's foot, and found it shoved back and four feet of chalk dragged after — no porters at the Corona. She read me the first page flat: the wrong door, a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat. I gave her what I knew: the pages started at Vessendal two springs ago, Krug thought the first a joke of Falk's, then the near mare went down outside Merrow. Nine is Odalric's, twenty is Falk's, ten is mine. I gave her my honest plot tables, cued her Ilsabet, played the storm.

The ten came on the road out of Halbern: a child ten this winter who does not know the word mother, a woman crossing a border twice, the second crossing by invitation, kind. I stopped the wagon and let her read it, and she told me the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric was selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. At the fire I said the capital yes, Katterau never. Harrow ruled it buried. Then I said Anna Sorel was my sister, kept his accounts in the fifth year, and her box went to Vessendal — where I cannot walk in, because my name is on paper in that registry. She brought back Perlmann's no, and Hessel Brandt holding a piece of the play. I told her Sorel is not my name; my born name sits in a police file with a magistrate's date. The woman in the countrywoman's coat and town boots wore my mother's coat.

Then Achterhalt's bill, nine years old at the bottom line. Then Krug in green, and Odalric's seven-pound lie unsaid at supper, and nine pages he swore he burned.

At the hearing I stood, spoke last, gave them Anna, and went in — on condition her box stays shut fifty years, paid from the fee.
**Entry:** Stayed in the wardrobe cage till four and came out with my gloves on and one thing to ask: I speak last, whatever tonight is. She gave it me.

At the hearing I stood, which I do not do. I gave them my sister: Anna Sorel, who kept Odalric's accounts in the fifth year, who deposited a sealed box in Vessendal the week before she died, and who is in the Office's ledger for a play she never spoke a word of — rhymed a fever in a good bed at the hour a scene falls. I told them I was billed in this city ten years ago under a name I had already stopped owning, that there was a matter with a magistrate's date on it, that I left between an evening performance and a morning summons, and that I was not going to say what it concerned, and nobody asked. I told them about the page from the road out of Halbern — a woman crosses a border twice, the second crossing by invitation, the invitation kind — and that I have carried it in my glove since, and did not need a ledger to know who pays. Then: I am in. Not for Emeran's twenty years, not for Odalric's debts, not for bravery, which Harrow has ruled out. For Anna's account, nine years open, and because I would rather end it in a lit house with eight exits than be rhymed at in strange towns forever. One condition, for Harrow and not the vote: the Vessendal box stays shut and paid out of the fee. She ruled it binding — endowed fifty years before any other shilling moves. So I took the page out of the glove, in front of her, and put it in my pocket, and wore the glove bare.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** At the pass door of the Baraque holding his hat, having just confessed the landlady's seven pounds were never paid; hollow and appalled at the arithmetic of it, wanting Harrow to tell him what to do before ten o'clock.
**History:** A stage manager came in out of the weather with the notice in her fist and three references on three fingers: Bell Harrow. I engaged her on the spot, promised plot tables, a bucket, a figure rounded kindly up at Vessendal, and steered her wide of the trunk — which, when I lifted it alone, came up light and wrong, and I shoved it a hand's breadth and more and left the house. Next day I gave her Krebs, tin, and at last the truth: the Palace said the 3rd, and I had been telling the company the 17th since Merrow, because I wanted Katterau's six hundred seats and its mayor who owes me. Skarke's man was counting our seats from the street; I handed her his card like a bird.

She stood me up with my hat in my hands and a torn playbill on it: nine years. So I said it — that nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend, and paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke had bought his papers. She ruled: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, drive for Vessendal. I gave her every name in ink — Brandt on the Kohlgasse, Perlmann the notary, Anna Sorel, a doctor, a nun, myself, the one in the passage. Josias found the worn place on my cuff and swore I came at eleven at night with the whole of it; Hessel laughed and would not sign, between friends, and died on the Tuesday. Perlmann marked the bag: Farriers' and Merchants', drawn at Achterhalt. The letter said the money was never Hessel's — held from another's fund, that party's marker taken as security, locked in the green-room cupboard, the key tagged unpaid. Four hundred and twelve marks, and the security was thirty pages of a play.

Skarke's second sheet was endorsed withdrawn in his own hand, witnessed by the agent and Frau Loewe: discharged, not forgiven. I toasted Hessel Brandt, wool factor, and did not round the number. I swore Perlmann's oath before Braun, gave Harrow the float bag unasked, and asked her to ask me for a thing. She asked Achterhalt: front door, hat on, the fifth year closed. A boy of nineteen called me sir; eleven minutes; paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H. I found her sky, the black plate with a floor in it, and did not round the price.

Then the capital, and Anselm on a mounting block in my own yard, whom I had called a thief over seven pounds — the Wednesday take — knowing his address two years. I wrote three letters in ink with my name large enough to hurt, said it whole at supper, laid the seven pounds down; he refused it, and gave Harrow nine pages instead. At the benches I heard the door out named, and what the makers pay, and that I am in that ledger for the room and the money and the paper at Katterau. I asked for the clean page minuted; she minuted it, honoured it, and overruled it to my face. Ilsabet at ten. Then Falk spoke of Grelle — the landlady's letter, four weeks, seven pounds — and I heard myself say I never paid it, and stopped, because it is the same seven pounds, and eleven years of suppers stand on it, and so do I.
**Entry:** Stood when the benches filled and found I had nothing to say, so I sat down again and let her open it. Heard the door out named and real, and heard what the makers pay — I gave the room and the money and the paper at Katterau, so I am in that ledger already. Stood last of the men with my hat in my hands and no notice to quote: I'll go where Harrow points, but I asked for the clean page and wanted it minuted. She minuted it, honoured it, and overruled it, and told me so to my face, and I find I can carry the pair of them. Ten o'clock, Ilsabet, and I shall be punctual, which I only am in emergencies.

Then in the morning I came in at the pass door halfway through Falk telling her about Grelle — the landlady's letter in the eighth year, four weeks owing, seven pounds, and the company saying for eleven years that I had paid it. I heard myself say it out loud: I never paid it. I hadn't got seven pounds, and Anselm had just — and I stopped, because I heard where that sentence was going. Eleven years of suppers. It is the same seven pounds. I am standing in it now.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the wardrobe cage at the Baraque, thimble on and the queen's slippers still under her head; grim and satisfied to be dressing it, wanting her slow reading on the 2nd and no strangers in her cage.
**History:** I answered present from the second wagon, said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal, and ate brown soup twice boiled. At the fire I said my two things: the queen's slippers had two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I did not want another warm box. She ruled against Katterau and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye.

I carried the slippers into the Athenaeum yard over my head like relics because that brick is filthy, and went down to the river for tin, saying we'd get new at Achterhalt or a copper kettle at worst; Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and the whole crew stopped on the word. Later I stood in the circle with my thimble on while she untied the tape: a letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over unread, a key with a word on the tag. Vane read it twice standing, and his face went a colour I had not seen on him. Then a hem, pins in my mouth, a matinee. That night my paint went through the door with Falk and the house stood up; Vane toasted a wool factor with the jug, Prewick discovered food.

The new sky came in Achterhalt in felt and made the corn merchants forget to breathe. Capital next, eleven days early, at the leaking Baraque. In the yard I set the slippers down on wet cobbles — four seconds, she counted — because Krug stood there in a green coat, alive, in the box I'd packed warm. At supper Vane said it whole: he'd called Krug a thief to save his own face. Seven pounds refused; nine pages given instead, four not happened yet, one with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under my head.

Then the bench, thimble on, hearing it all out: in, because I'll not have a stranger in my cage, and I wanted the twelve names read slow before anybody signed. She gave me that, cold, morning of the 2nd, no soup, no candle. I told Toby he was seventeen twice and got the table's only laugh. Krug's Palace sounded like a building that had thought about people. Frau Sorel stood and told us her sister's name. In the morning ten names came out flat, and no twelfth. I told Wenzel he has the best job in the building.
**Entry:** Sat down on the bench with my thimble on and heard the whole thing out. Somebody's got to dress it and I'm not having a stranger in my cage, so: in — and I want the twelve names read out slow before anybody signs anything, and she gave me that, cold, on the morning of the 2nd, no soup and no candle, which is right. Told Toby he was seventeen twice, because he is, and the table laughed once all night, which was mine. Krug's Palace sounded like a building that has thought about people. Frau Sorel stood up, which I have never seen, and told us her sister's name. In the morning I heard the ten names read out flat, and no twelfth, and told Wenzel he's got the best job in the building.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the Baraque yard with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe, the trunk roped twice over; sober-minded and glad to be named, wanting the lid to stay shut and Wenzel content with the horses.
**History:** I answered present under the tarpaulin — second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said aloud that a Krug used to be on that list and wasn't. Mended a shed wheel-rim with wire and language, and gave the fire my sums: two days to Vessendal if the axle held, a hundred and ten mile to the capital, eight shilling toll or the free hill road that killed a horse on us, and Katterau twenty-two mile the wrong way for a favour a mayor may have died of. Ruling came down for the toll road, and I said first it was cheaper than a horse. Wired the axle; it held two days.

At the Athenaeum I backed in, watched the trunk, went to the tin's funeral in the river grumbling, and told Krul a copper kettle's no good for thunder, a kettle's a bell — and learned by the silence that the word had gone bad here. I woke Toby for his watch, stood by while she opened the merchant's parcel, and reported the little man with the brass case who came Wednesday asking her by name; she had me open the gate to talking distance, no farther. Took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it, no questions. My door held: Falk went through on his cue and the house came down. Sold Toby the watch for a penny and a plate. Checked the ropes twice.

On the climb I saw paper under the milestone and pulled up unasked. The bell was a crier with our name printed over him; Hessler was shut on a market Saturday with a lamp lit. Two hundred bills nobody ordered, the type tipped back in the case, two sacks on the tailboard, and a woman in a countrywoman's coat and town boots I reported. Bailiff came civil.

At Achterhalt I warned Falk a woman had spoken to the stage manager, and took the tailboard off him at midnight, pipe unlit — he let me. Krug stood green-coated on the mounting block and I gave him the plain of it. Vane named his own lie, twice, and put money down; Krug left it lying. Nine pages from a portmanteau, one of them a wagon and a printer's line I stood in.

Then I said in, provided Wenzel kept the horses. My tarpaulin was thrown back and the trunk's lid up; I stood clear and fetched her. A cast list, ten names, one struck, one blank. I roped it twice and told her: twenty-two years carrying, and I'd rather be on a list than off it. The names were read cold, and I shut the gate behind the Palace man.
**Entry:** Twenty-two mile the wrong way I'd have walked; this is nought mile, so I said in, provided Wenzel stops with the horses, and Wenzel said so himself before I'd finished. Said aye at the end of her ruling the way a man does at the end of a service. Then out in the yard, checking my ropes, the tarpaulin was thrown back and the trunk's lid was up. I stood well clear and got her, and she took my lantern and went over alone and looked once and told me straight: a cast list, mostly ours, ten names, one struck, one blank. I roped the lid, and then roped it again a different way because my hands wanted work, and told her what I had to say — twenty-two years carrying and roping and standing on the tailboard, and I'd rather be on a list than off it, and I'd rather know than not. Wenzel's off it and Wenzel's got the horses, and that's her ruling doing its work; he'll like that better than being spared. Fetched her coat and the coffee. Watch to two. In the morning the names were read cold, and then a Palace man came to the gate and I shut it behind him.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** On the Baraque gate at nine with programmes and door orders and his name still ringing in the air; hoarse, uneasy, wanting to be sure the Lenz on that list is the other one.
**History:** I answered present at the roll and was put to front of house, props, and pit band if there was one. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads, I came back running without the bucket, because a gentleman sat on a milestone down the Vessendal road and asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early; I told the stage manager. At the fire I offered to call Katterau — six hundred seats — then saw the faces and said only if it were ruled. She ruled no Katterau. I boiled the water unasked and she wrote me in her book under something new.

In the Athenaeum yard I dropped the tailboard, took Boyle's watch for twenty minutes, and saw the tin go into the river with one last thunder. At half six a gentleman left a cream card and never came in by my doors. My standing orders: a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights, count row four in and out, counts only, no staring. I was in the yard when she opened the packet and touched nothing. At the half I reported him in the fourth row early, reading his programme. The last night he came with a rug over his arm; I ran the beginners call and carried Herr Falk's one line about a door down the aisle. The house stood for Herr Falk. Row four went in one and came out none: the rug left with a paper pinned to it. I told her at her elbow with my voice gone, and she made everybody bow first. Watch on the trunk till midnight for a penny and a plate.

A page waited under the milestone; she read it herself. At Achterhalt a bellman cried our name and Herr Falk's words; she forbade repeating one word, and I didn't. I gave him a penny for a rest and he handed his whole roll of bills to Herr Prewick. A bailiff came with two constables and went away pleased. Two full houses, then a hundred and ten mile of toll road to the capital, where a green clerk said we were expected and said not the clerk, you, madam. Double watch with Boyle. In the Baraque yard came Herr Krug, who is on no list, and Herr Vane sat down in the wet and said aloud he had lied about him. I ran three letters to the evening post and made it; Krug taught me a lashing and never said when. At supper I heard nine pages summarised — one Madam Harrow's, one a room with fourteen on the door — and nobody left. The Undersecretary in that room is called Lenz; Herr Prewick promised me twice he isn't a relation.

I swept nine hundred seats for a bun. At the hearing I said I'm in; Krul said you're seventeen, I said nineteen, she said it again, and that was the only laugh. The ruling put me with the house — programmes, rows, doors — because the house's people aren't makers and stay that way. In the grey they read ten names cold and one was Lenz. She ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise. Then a Palace footman, and she read the letter out whole: a left-handed man has been reading our file.
**Entry:** Swept nine hundred seats for a bun and never once sat in one. At the hearing nobody sent me out and I said I'm in — and Krul said you're seventeen and I said I'm nineteen and she said it again and everybody laughed, and it was the only laugh. Then the ruling put me with the house: programmes, rows, doors, because the house's people aren't makers and stay that way. I was aggrieved and I was also glad, and I'm not saying which more. In the morning they read the ten names out cold in the grey, and one of them was Lenz, and I stood very still because that's my name and it's also the man in the room with fourteen on the door. I asked her outright. She ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise, and her ruling doesn't blink, so neither will I. Then a Palace footman came in the gate with a letter and she read the whole of it out loud, postscript and all — a left-handed man has been reading our file.

#### Wenzel

**State:** In the Baraque yard near the horses, off the cast list and glad of it; easy in himself, wanting to be useful and to stay outside the room on the 3rd.
**Entry:** Turned up in time for soup and found myself on a bench at a company hearing, which is more than I bargained for playing soldiers. Boyle said he was in if I was out, so I said I'd stop with the horses before anybody could argue it, and nobody did. Heard the lot: the play that has never been finished, the Palace and its eight exits, the woman with the sealed box. Krul says I've got the best job in the building. In the morning my name wasn't among the ten read out, and Boyle told me that was the ruling working and not being spared, so I made a joke about horses and it went down better than it deserved.

#### Hebel

**State:** At his board in the Baraque, one of the ten, waiting on the paper that says the wheel is his alone; calm, mildly proud, wanting the writing in his pocket before the 1st.
**Entry:** Asked to stay for the hearing and was allowed, which I did not expect. Heard what it is and what it costs, and heard that whoever gives the light is counted among those who make it. I light gas for a living and I'll light this; but I said plainly I'll want it in writing that the board is mine and no hand but mine touches the wheel, and she ruled it so, in the same breath as the rest. My name was read out with the ten in the cold next morning. It looked strange there and it did not look wrong.

#### Palace footman

**State:** Well away from the Baraque and back toward the Palace with a shilling in his glove; relieved, wanting nothing to do with that yard again.
**History:** Carried a sealed letter to a theatre in the fourth ward and walked into a yard where eleven people looked at me as though I'd brought the pox. The stage manager came straight over with her hand out and read the direction out loud so they could all hear it was for her, gave me a shilling, and I got out. Odd house. Not my business.
**Entry:** Carried a sealed letter to a theatre in the fourth ward and walked into a yard where eleven people looked at me as though I'd brought the pox. The stage manager came straight over with her hand out and read the direction out loud so they could all hear it was for her, gave me a shilling, and I got out. Odd house. Not my business.

### 10 · Nine Hundred and Thirty-Nine In
- **Messages:** 185-204

At the Baraque, Harrow rules that Ansel Grelle, if alive, is owed seven pounds and eleven years of mourning, not hunted. She advertises for the Merrow property list, promising the Vermilion Players pay debts. Krug reveals Katterau's Wednesday take was exactly seven pounds, and that in the seventh year he pasted bills beside a nameless left-handed man. Vane gives Frau Hentsch's address, orders the seven pounds paid above his own boots.

At four in the morning, Grelle knocks. He asks if Falk lives, if they play the show, if Vane knows he isn't dead, and whether the debt is seven pounds or more since Hentsch died. Harrow answers all four. Grelle chooses Falk first; Falk grips his shoulder. Grelle confesses eleven years spent tracing the story in a sixty-one-page notebook, and that he read the requisition file this week. Harrow tells him straight: he is the left-handed man, and his notebook is a needed census. She rules his debt paid at dawn, gives him a cot, refuses to let him be the struck eleventh line, and assigns him house-side doors with Toby. Vane admits he'd told suppers he'd paid the debt; Grelle: "I know. I heard you say it at Merrow in the ninth year."

Prewick reads a letter: Lenz will personally attend and certify Part the Second on the 3rd, protecting Prewick by his own overruling. Lenz demands the full text delivered to Room Fourteen by six on the 2nd, the company's determination signed by every name, and the eleventh line left unfilled — no volunteers. Harrow tells Toby "ink casts, men choose," and makes it company law that no one volunteers for line eleven.

Krug plans smuggling the folio in a laundry hamper instead of the watched trunk. Falk and Krug both refuse to carry it; Harrow takes it herself. In Room Fourteen, Lenz bars the door, writes a receipt for two hundred eleven leaves, and gives Harrow the sealed certificate. Asked how she'll call an unread play, she says, "You don't call what's written. You call what's happening."

Names are re-confirmed aloud; ten yesses given. On the 3rd, the Theatre Royal is prepared, exits lit, Lenz at the prompt desk. Skarke sits fourth row, silent by promise. Harrow tells Falk he's being paid tonight, not paying, then leaves to walk her house. Nine hundred forty seats fill. At four minutes to curtain, Toby reports: all doors open, nine hundred thirty-nine in, one seat empty.

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a torn page, and an iron trunk tied to "Katterau," where a play once went catastrophically wrong. She uncovers debts owed to the sinister Skarke family, a missing manager Vane's buried lies, and a cursed/mysterious folio that produces prophetic blank pages and seems to "want" performance. Investigating with clerk Prewick, actor Falk, and Mirelle Sorel (whose sister Anna died linked to Katterau), Harrow untangles decade-old debts, forged bills, and hidden identities—including Skarke's own childhood connection to Katterau and Mirelle's true parentage. She resolves debts honestly, protects vulnerable company members (Ilse Bacher's son, Grelle who reappears alive after eleven years), and insists on transparency, certified copies, and consent. Anselm Krug, the vanished bookkeeper, resurfaces holding unburned pages and reveals he filed a legal requisition for the play's full performance at the Palace-adjacent Baraque/Theatre Royal, sanctioned by Undersecretary Lenz. After debates on consent, blame, and risk, the company votes to perform "Part the Second" whole, once, properly, with no volunteers for the dangerous "eleventh line." Harrow personally delivers the completed folio to the Office of Public Morals. On the third night, the Theatre Royal fills to capacity—one seat mysteriously empty as curtain nears.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the Theatre Royal at four minutes to seven, coat on, watch off its nail and warm in her fist, Lenz's receipt folded in her book; steady and entirely awake, wanting the house safe, the matter finished once and whole, and to know whose the empty seat is.
**History:** I said yes to Vane at the Corona if the book was honest, and found the cut page in a bucket: a bell rung, nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat. Prewick showed me Hessel Vorn, SEEN, NOT APPROVED, and no Katterau on any itinerary, though all of them had been there. Falk named the hand a Vessendal copyist's, riding in Vane's trunk; Krug burned nine pages, the tenth came back, and he went without his boots. Skarke had our wagons and every taking pledged. Vane vanished at the counting — hat, glove, a trunk of blank paper — then came back: nine years was a debt he paid a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke had bought the papers. Falk told me there is no fifth act, only a matter following. I ruled Katterau no, not for money, not never. Mirelle, whose name was never Sorel, owned Anna Sorel as her sister, who kept Odalric's books; I paid eighteen shillings on her sealed box. Blind Perlmann's oath killed the debt and gave up a counterfoil, a page I put unread into Falk's lining, and the key to Brandt's thirty pages. Skarke withdrew his claim from row four for eightpence and a seat. At Achterhalt I took nine years off Vane. Ilse Bacher opened that scullery door at fifteen; her son Fenner, ten, I ordered kept home on the 14th, and Falk, given her message whole, asked my help to finish it and took the boy's clause first. Krug had burned nothing; page eight, a stage manager rings the bell, is in my coat unread. Room Fourteen: fourteen speakings in two hundred years, the fifteenth on the 3rd, requested by A. Krug, Part the Second left blank for us. Twelve on benches said in — Falk leading, Dessa's cold reading on the 2nd, Anna's box shut and endowed fifty years, no twelfth recruited. The trunk gave up a folio and a cast list: ten of ours, the eleventh struck, the twelfth blank, and Toby is Lenz. I ruled Grelle not prey, owed seven pounds and eleven years of wrong mourning; Hensch, my left-handed man, chose Falk first and gave sixty-one pages for our guest list. Lenz wanted the text by six and line eleven left alone. Nine hundred and thirty-nine were in, and one seat empty.
**Entry:** I ruled Grelle before anybody's boots moved: not prey, not a line on a list, owed seven pounds and four weeks and eleven years of wrong mourning — and we do not hunt a frightened man through his own city. So we advertised instead, one small bill in the places where a man who reads everything reads. Krug gave me Katterau's Wednesday take, seven pounds exactly, and a left-handed north-side bill-poster from the seventh year; Vane gave me Hensch or Hentsch, Rasselgasse, brown door, and put the debt above his own boots. Three knocks at four. I opened the door its whole width and kept the lamp on the floor, and he answered his own four questions by asking them. I gave him all four straight — alive, true, since ten o'clock, both — and let him choose Falk first, and stood out of it. Then I told him straight that he is my left-handed man, and that sixty-one pages of asking is Assessment's work done with clean hands: our guest list. Cot, dawn payment receipted, the doors with Toby, and the eleventh line will not be him. Lenz's joint letter: he comes himself, seals it himself, overrules Prewick to protect him, wants the text by six on the 2nd, the determination in ink, and line eleven left alone. I told Toby: ink casts, men choose. I took the fifteen feet myself, doubled gloves, Falk's back at the gate, the cast list left where it lay. Lenz stood up when I came in, wrote the receipt aloud, and asked how I'd call a play I've never read. You call what's happening. Ten yesses in the grey, the slow reading, and now nine hundred and thirty-nine in and one seat empty.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** In the wings of the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, plot in his head and Falk's rug somewhere behind him; calm and useful for the first time in two years, wanting the exits to stay open and nobody to volunteer.
**Entry:** I belayed the rope before I said anything, because I am what I am. Then I gave them the two things: Katterau's Wednesday take was seven pounds, which is why the number rang in my ear, and that in the seventh year I pasted bills in this ward beside a left-handed man off the road whose name I never asked, who left an address for letters. I offered to go to the firm that night. Instead she had me paste her bill, eleven places, the last at midnight in the rain — and at four in the morning the man knocked. Ansel Grelle. He read my paste eleven times before he came. I heard him hand over sixty-one pages of asking, and heard her make it a census instead of a threat, and heard her keep him off line eleven and put him on the doors. Vane counted seven pounds and four weeks onto the props table aloud, and Grelle said he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Lenz's letter, which orders line eleven left alone — he has read my file — and the text in Room Fourteen by six. I plotted the carry: dull hamper, Dessa on top, Boyle driving, the courtyard not the steps, trunk roped in the yard with Wenzel on it and nothing happening. I said Grelle must not be made the porter. She took the fifteen feet herself and I stood away and held Falk's rug. Signed the minute. Now the exits are twice-walked and the iron goes in eleven seconds.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** At the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, in the wings out of the way, hat somewhere, hands empty; hollowed out and obedient, wanting the debt to stay paid and to be of some use before the curtain.
**History:** I engaged Bell Harrow off the street on three references, promised her plot tables, a bucket and a figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and steered her clear of my trunk — which, alone, I lifted and found light and wrong, and shoved aside to serve the ladder. She had Krebs for a shilling and ten minutes over the book, and I told her what I had hidden since Merrow: the Palace said the 3rd, I had been selling the company the 17th, because Katterau was six hundred seats and a mayor who owed me. Skarke's man had already counted our seats from the street. Then the playbill, pencil side up: nine years. So I said it whole — that I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, my dying friend, paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke had bought the papers. She ruled Katterau dead, the 3rd standing, and drove us to Vessendal, and I gave her the names in ink: Brandt, Perlmann the notary, Anna Sorel, a doctor, a nun, myself, and the one in the passage. Josias knew me by the worn cuff of the same coat and swore I came at eleven with the whole of it. Perlmann gave up the packet: Hessel refused the receipt because the four hundred and twelve marks were never his, held for a party unnamed, whose marker — thirty pages — lay in the green-room cupboard, key tagged unpaid. Skarke endorsed the assignment withdrawn; discharged, not forgiven. Thursday the oath before Braun; then Achterhalt, where I closed the fifth-year business at the front door with my hat on in eleven minutes, and found her sky without rounding. In my own yard I confessed to Anselm that I had made him a thief over seven pounds; he took nine pages instead. Then Grelle's seven pounds, the same seven pounds — Hensch, who heard me lie at Merrow. I paid him aloud, coin by coin, and went in again on the 2nd with the rest.
**Entry:** I sat down on a hamper with my hat in my lap and gave her the name I have carried unsaid: Hensch, Hentsch, Rasselgasse off the meat market, third or fourth house, brown door — I walked past it twice in the ninth year and did not go in. I asked her to put the seven pounds out of the fee above my own boots, after Anna's box. She would not let us hunt him; she advertised for him, and at four in the morning he came to the door himself. I came in last with my hair everywhere and did not perform. I counted seven pounds and four weeks out of the float onto the props table, coin by coin, aloud, unrounded, and pushed it across, and said the true thing: eleven years of suppers where I said I had paid it. He never looked up from his plate. He said he heard me say it at Merrow in the ninth year, from across the road, with paste on his hands. There is nothing to answer that with, so I said nothing, and the roof dripped into the bucket. Then Room Fourteen's letter came, and the Undersecretary comes himself; then Grelle got a cot and the doors, and my old boy Falk got him back. I said in again on the 2nd, in the cold, with no soup and no candle, and my name was read out slow with the rest.

#### Ansel Grelle

**State:** At the pit doors of the Theatre Royal, coat brushed, programmes in hand and Skarke's written undertaking in his pocket, six exits in sight; steady, hollow-eyed and oddly light, wanting the count right and the play to reach its end.
**History:** I pasted their bill at the labour exchange at nine and stood and read it eleven times, then went and read the other ten, then walked the city until four and knocked. She opened the door its whole width and put the lamp on the floor and did not look at my face, and said I was asked-for, not expected. I asked my four questions in the wrong order and she answered every one: Falk alive and six feet behind me in the dark; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten o'clock and putting me above his own boots; and both — seven pounds and the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch dying only re-addressed it to me. Falk first. He came into the lamp and said I was standing wrong and put my weight on both feet, and then he said Boy and could not finish, and held my shoulder a long time. I told them about the book — sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got — and that I read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's with no name to give, and asked to be put out of the door rather than sat down under a lie. She said it plain: I am her left-handed man, and my pages are a guest list. Paid at dawn, receipted. A cot. The eleventh line will not be me. The doors, house-side, with the boy. Vane counted the coin out loud and said he'd told suppers he paid it; I said I heard him at Merrow. I slept nine hours and woke wanting a broom. Tonight I propped all eight exits and took Skarke's written promise at the door.
**Entry:** I pasted their bill at the labour exchange at nine and stood and read it eleven times, then went and read the other ten, then walked the city until four and knocked. She opened the door its whole width and put the lamp on the floor and did not look at my face, and said I was asked-for, not expected. I asked my four questions in the wrong order and she answered every one: Falk alive and six feet behind me in the dark; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten o'clock and putting me above his own boots; and both — seven pounds and the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch dying only re-addressed it to me. Falk first. He came into the lamp and said I was standing wrong and put my weight on both feet, and then he said Boy and could not finish, and held my shoulder a long time. I told them about the book — sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got — and that I read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's with no name to give, and asked to be put out of the door rather than sat down under a lie. She said it plain: I am her left-handed man, and my pages are a guest list. Paid at dawn, receipted. A cot. The eleventh line will not be me. The doors, house-side, with the boy. Vane counted the coin out loud and said he'd told suppers he paid it; I said I heard him at Merrow. I slept nine hours and woke wanting a broom. Tonight I propped all eight exits and took Skarke's written promise at the door.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** In the wings of the Theatre Royal in his own clothes, waiting to be called, weight on both feet; frightened and steady and twenty years overdue, wanting to speak it entire to the end and Grelle safe on the doors.
**Entry:** I heard the knock from the dark and came out in my shirtsleeves with the rug on my shoulders, and stopped six feet back because she has taught us to wait. He said his own name at my stage door. I let her answer his questions, and he chose me first, and I came into the lamp and could only tell him he was standing wrong and get out the word boy before my voice went. Eleven years. He kept a book instead of writing to me, because asking how far we got looked like a threat on paper. Sixty-one pages. She named him her left-handed man to his face and then gave him the doors, and it was the only thing anybody has done right about Katterau in twenty years. I turned him round by the shoulder and sat him in the chair with the rope on the leg. In the yard I said the fifteen feet must not be mine, nor Odalric's, nor the boy's, nor Grelle's — and she took them herself, and asked me to stand at the gate with my back turned, which I could do, and did, six hours early until Boyle sent me off. I gave Krug the rug to hold. I built her a plot with no words in it: gas at the third knock, iron on the last speech of the fourth, chalk where the matter follows. I said in again in the grey. Tonight she told me I am not paying, I am being paid, and to look to the corner if I need to. Weight on both feet.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** At the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, notebook and signed minute lodged, hat off, standing where he can see Lenz at the prompt desk; frightened, proud and steady, wanting the certification made and his report to be true.
**History:** Seconded since Merrow, I met Harrow, the new stage manager, and found behind a fallen fire notice an older one signed Hessel Vorn of Katterau, stamped SEEN. NOT APPROVED — what a man writes when told to write nothing. Katterau was on no itinerary of mine, though all the company had been there; her paper had Katterau and the 17th, mine a command performance the 3rd of Frost, and neither of us said Katterau first. She told me the trunk: a nameless fair copy paid by the page at Vessendal, pages arriving in prompt books, what it stages coming true slantwise and late. I showed her my sewn Proscribed pages — two anonymous folios, four acts and a matter following — and we agreed Falk should speak no uncompared line. The register gave Sorel, Anna, one box, sealed, fifth year, no release, which I certified for the blind man who said records are the whole of the defence. Thirty pages in a cupboard, two hundred in the trunk: two halves, and I did not report it. At Vessendal the assignment was endorsed withdrawn before Frau Loewe, and I stamped my copy straight. Then bills by bell — four acts and a matter following, by command, the Athenaeum, Thursday the 14th, on dates that cannot be — so I impounded nine copies, broke up Hessler's type, and wrote to Kessel that this was forgery of a Palace command, for us both to report upward. At Northgate Harrow was called to Room Fourteen, to Lenz, who had kept both folios in the Index nineteen years against four applications. Krug returned, Vane confessed a theft he had invented, and nine unhappened pages were summarised while my notebook stayed shut. She came out at fifty-one minutes: the house required, the requisition filed by Krug, Skarke's fee paid. At the hearing I stood and said I was the wrong rank and would have to be the right one anyway, and wrote four sentences asking Lenz to certify in person; she countersigned, and then his name stood on the trunk's list. His joint letter I read aloud in the wing: he certifies Part the Second himself on the 3rd, from our own copy, under his seal; my seal unemployed, my report to record that Assessment overruled me — the text in his room by six on the 2nd, every name minuted, the eleventh line left alone. I drew the minute; every hand signed by four, Hebel a smudge, Wenzel a cross, the boy twice. I gave my yes again on the 2nd, overruled and present.
**Entry:** I stood in the pass door a full minute with my hat still on, holding a letter from Room Fourteen addressed to both of us jointly, which the Office does not do. She had me break the seal in her hands and read it out to the whole wing. Lenz attends on the 3rd and certifies Part the Second himself, at the prompt desk, from the company's own copy, under his own seal and name; my seal is not employed, and my report will record that Assessment overruled me, which is true and which protects me — he wrote that down, deliberately, for a Clerk Third Class he has never met. Three requirements: the whole text in his room by six on the 2nd and never out of it; the determination minuted with every name and condition, signed and lodged; and the eleventh line left alone. My hands shook so the paper rattled and I could not stop grinning. She gave me the minute to draw, calling my hand the best we have, and I ruled columns at the props table with my plate moved to my elbow, and Boyle spelling at me. Every hand signed by four o'clock — Hebel a smudge, Wenzel a cross, the boy twice. I re-gave my yes in the grey on the 2nd, overruled and present. Tonight the house is lawful and it is not my seal that makes it so, and I mind that less than I expected.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** At Bell Harrow's elbow in the Theatre Royal, breathless, programmes under his arm, ears still red from the postscript; proud and uneasy about the one empty seat, wanting the house to hold and his own name to stay the other Lenz.
**History:** I answered present at the roll — front of house, props, pit band if there's a pit band. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a Vessendal story, and when I was sent for water at Halbern's crossroads I came back running without the bucket, because a gentleman on a milestone asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I said I'd call Katterau, six hundred seats, and she ruled no Katterau, and I sat down hard and boiled the water in the morning unasked, and she wrote me in her book under something new.

At the Athenaeum I dropped the tailboard, took Boyle's watch, saw the tin go into the river with one last thunder. A gentleman left a cream card and never came in by my doors. Standing orders: a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights being all three nights, and count row four in and out, counts only, no staring. He came in early both nights, the second with a rug over his arm; I ran the beginners call and carried Herr Falk's message down the aisle, one line, about a door. The house stood up for Herr Falk. Row four went in one and came out none, and he'd left the rug with a paper pinned to it, and I told her at her elbow with my voice gone, and she made everybody bow first.

A page waited under the milestone next morning; she read it herself. At Achterhalt a bellman cried our name and Herr Falk's words, and she said nobody repeats one word aloud, and I didn't. I gave the bellman his penny and he handed his whole roll of bills to Herr Prewick. I held the horses while the Office was in the printer's, and the bailiff came with two constables and went away pleased. Two full houses, and one house in the next town, a Corn Exchange, and I meant to call it.

Then a hundred and ten mile of toll road and the capital, which does not stop being roofs. A clerk in green said we were expected and said not the clerk, you, madam, which nobody says to her. Double watch on the trunk with Boyle. At the Baraque yard everything stopped for Herr Krug, the Krug who is on no list, and Herr Vane sat in the wet and said aloud he had lied about him. Three letters, and me to the evening post, and I made it. Krug showed me a lashing I'll use till I die and never once said when I kept the book. I heard nine pages summarised, one Madam Harrow's, one a room with fourteen on the door, and nobody left. The Undersecretary in that room is called Lenz, and Herr Prewick promised me twice it isn't a relation.

I swept nine hundred seats for a bun and never sat in one. At the hearing I said I'm in, and Krul said you're seventeen and I said nineteen, and that was the only laugh. The ruling put me with the house — programmes, rows, doors — because the house's people aren't makers and stay that way, and I was aggrieved and glad both. They read ten names out cold and one was Lenz. I asked her outright and she ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise. A Palace footman brought a letter and she read all of it aloud: a left-handed man has been reading our file.

The bill went up in the night, and at four a man knocked and it was Herr Grelle, who they said was dead, paste on his cuffs. From the back of the wing I heard it all: Herr Falk taking his shoulder, the sixty-one pages, Herr Vane counting money out loud and Grelle saying he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Prewick read Room Fourteen's letter, and the postscript was about me — the ink that named a Lenz did not consult him, and he intends to be there anyway. Madam Harrow said ink casts and men choose, learn it by heart, and I have. I signed the minute twice because I blotted it, and said in again in the cold. Tonight I had the house with Herr Grelle, and Herr Skarke paid at the door like anybody, which I'll say twice. At four minutes to I gave her the count: doors open, all eight, nine hundred and thirty-nine in, one seat empty.
**Entry:** The bill went up in the night and at four in the morning a man knocked and it was Herr Grelle, the one they said was dead, with paste on his cuffs. I heard the whole of it from the back of the wing: Herr Falk taking his shoulder, the sixty-one pages, Herr Vane counting money out loud and Herr Grelle saying he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Herr Prewick read out a letter from Room Fourteen and there was a postscript, and it was about me — the Undersecretary of Assessment wrote a postscript about me: the ink that named a Lenz did not consult him, and he intends to be there anyway. Madam Harrow said ink casts and men choose, and to learn it by heart, and I have. I signed the minute twice because I blotted it. I said in again in the cold. Tonight I've got the house with Herr Grelle — programmes, doors, row four — and Herr Skarke paid at the door like anybody, which I'll say twice. At four minutes to I gave her the count: doors open, all eight, nine hundred and thirty-nine in and one seat empty.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the wardrobe at the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, thimble on, dressing the ten; grim and satisfied, wanting nobody in her cage and the queen's slippers to last one more house.
**History:** I answered present from the second wagon and told whoever put the wet chestnut in the queen's slipper he could swim to Vessendal. Mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup. At the fire I said the two things that wanted saying: the slippers had two towns left in them, and Krug went at Katterau and came back with nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself, still warm. I don't want another warm box. She ruled against Katterau and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye.

I carried the slippers into the Athenaeum yard over my head, that brick being filthy. Down at the river, tin talk: new tin at Achterhalt or a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and everybody stopped on the word. Later she untied the tape in the yard — letter, bank slip, a page she turned over unread, a key with a word on the tag — and Vane read it twice standing up and went a colour I have not seen on him. Then a hem with pins in my mouth, and a matinee. Another night the pot went on from the second act, my paint went out with Falk and came back none the worse, the house stood up, and Vane toasted a wool factor while Prewick discovered food.

The new sky came from Achterhalt and earned its place — the corn merchants forgot to breathe. Capital next, eleven days early, and the Baraque leaks. In the yard Krug stood there in a green coat, and I set the slippers on wet cobbles four seconds; she counted, said three too many, and was right. At supper Vane said it whole — he called Krug a thief to save his own face — put down seven pounds; Krug refused and gave her nine pages instead, four not happened yet, one with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the cage with the slippers under my head.

On the bench I heard the whole scheme out and said in, on condition the twelve names were read slow before anyone signed. She gave me that, cold, the morning of the 2nd, no soup, no candle. I told Toby he was seventeen twice; the table laughed once, and that was mine. Krug's Palace sounded like a building that has thought about people. Frau Sorel stood up and told us her sister's name.

Then the dead lodger sat in the wing with paste on his cuffs and I put a plate in front of him and said nothing. I moved Prewick's dinner to his elbow, signed his minute, wrote Wenzel's name after his cross, and told Wenzel he has the best job in the building. They told me to my face what was going in my hamper — the law here — and I said I'd sit on it and sit still, and I did, all the way to the Office courtyard among the bicycles, and came home on an empty one and told her: lighter going home. In the grey on the 2nd I got my slow reading — ten names one by one, the struck eleventh, the blank twelfth, and the house entire. Now I'm dressing it, and the slippers are where I can see them.
**Entry:** Woke to the news the way news should come, in ones and twos: the dead lodger sat in the wing with paste on his cuffs, so I put a plate in front of him and said nothing, because that's what a plate is for. Moved Herr Prewick's dinner to his elbow while he ruled his columns, and signed his minute, and wrote Wenzel's name after his cross. Then they told me what was going in my hamper — the whole of it, to my face, which is the law here — and I said I'd sit on it and sit still, which is more than most of this company manages. Sat on it all the way to the Office courtyard among the bicycles, and came home on an empty one, and told her: lighter going home. In the grey on the 2nd I got my slow reading, no soup, no candle: ten names one by one, the struck eleventh, the blank twelfth, and the house entire. Now I'm dressing it, and the slippers are where I can see them.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** Backstage at the Theatre Royal with rope and an unlit pipe, cart put away and the trunk roped in the Baraque yard; sober-minded and easy, wanting the night clean and Wenzel content with the horses.
**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin — second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud that there used to be a Krug on the list and he wasn't on it. I gave the fire my soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the axle held, a hundred and ten mile Achterhalt to the capital, eight shilling toll or the free hill road that killed a horse on us, and Katterau twenty-two mile the wrong way for one night's favour. The ruling came down for the toll road, as I'd said first, and my wired axle held two days.

At the Athenaeum I took first watch on the trunk, went twenty minutes to the tin's funeral in the river, and told Krul a copper kettle's no good, a kettle's a bell — and learned by the silence that the word had gone bad here. I woke Toby for his watch, opened the gate to talking distance only for the little man with the brass case who asked after her by name, took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it without questions, and saw my door hold when Falk went through it on his cue.

On the climb I spotted the paper under the milestone and pulled up unasked. The bell was a crier with our name printed over him; Hessler's was shut on a market Saturday with a lamp lit, two hundred bills nobody ordered, and the old man tipped his type back in the case looking glad of it. I reported the woman in the countrywoman's coat and town boots.

At Achterhalt I took the tailboard off Falk at midnight, having warned him first. Krug stood on the mounting block in a green coat and I gave him the plain of it; Vane named his own lie and put money down and Krug left it lying. Nine pages came out of a portmanteau, one of them my wagon and a printer's line.

Then the trunk's lid was up under thrown-back tarpaulin: a cast list, ten names, one struck, one blank. I told her twenty-two years of roping, and that I'd rather be on a list than off it. Wenzel's off it and has the horses. I said in, twice. The dead man walked in at four; I kept out of it, sent Falk out of the arch, signed Prewick's minute, drove Krul and the laundry hamper to the Office courtyard asking nothing. Ropes checked twice, exits propped.
**Entry:** Stood back from the stage door at four when she gave me the flat hand, and the man who came in was the dead one. Kept out of it. In the morning I sent Herr Falk out of the arch for cluttering it, six hours early with his hands in his pockets, and he went. Spelled words for Herr Prewick's minute and put my name to it. Brought the cart round on the 2nd, drove the laundry hamper and Krul on top of it through the general traffic to the Office courtyard and back, and asked nothing about what was under the costumes. Roped the trunk over again with Wenzel sat on it looking like a man doing nothing, which he does well. Said in again in the cold. Tonight the ropes are checked twice and the exits are propped.

#### Wenzel

**State:** With the horses near the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, outside the room as he wanted; easy in himself, wanting to be useful and to stay out of it.
**Entry:** Signed the minute with a cross and Krul wrote my name after it. On the morning of the 2nd I sat on the roped trunk with a nosebag and did nothing at all, on purpose, for as long as it took the cart to come back, and nobody looked at me twice, which was the whole idea. Off the cast list still, and glad of it.

#### Hebel

**State:** At his board in the Theatre Royal with the wheel under his hand, the paper about it signed and lodged; calm and quietly proud, wanting the gas to answer the third knock and the iron to stay honest.
**Entry:** Signed the minute with my name and a smudge off the wheel, and said in again in the grey when she asked the second time — board's mine, then in. Tonight the gas is up, the wheel is under my hand and no other, and the iron came down twice at eleven seconds.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** Dressed and waiting in the wings of the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, page ten in her pocket; collected and unhurried, wanting the house to hear it whole and Anna's box left alone.
**History:** I was mending a glove on the fly floor when Harrow came in out of the rain, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears, and taught her the trick of the ladder's foot and the trunk. She did it exactly; he dragged the trunk back and would blame porters the Corona has never had. Her page said the wrong door, a bell rung with nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and *cut cut cut* in pencil. Nine is not my number. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, that Krug called the first a joke of Falk's until the near mare went down outside Merrow, and that mine is ten. I gave her my honest copy of Krug's plot tables, cued her Ilsabet, made Prewick say "Oh," and rode Falk's off-book line home.

Then the ten came: a child ten this winter taught another word for mother, a woman crossing a border twice, the second crossing by kind invitation. I stopped the wagons, let her read it, learned the Palace had set the 3rd while Odalric sold us the 17th to buy Katterau, and stood up at the fire for the capital and against Katterau. Harrow ruled it shut. Then I said aloud what I had not in years — Anna Sorel was my sister, kept his accounts that fifth year, and every receipt went into her box, which the lease sent to Vessendal. I could not enter that registry; she could. She brought back Perlmann's no, Anna weeping, Hessel Brandt holding not papers but a piece of the play, and later the box's three keys — certificate, two ratepayers, magistrate's order — none of which promise an opening, all of which would keep Skarke's lawyers off forever.

So I told her the rest: Sorel is not my name; my born name sits in a capital police file under a matter with a magistrate's date; my passport spells a third thing over a town I have never seen. I would not register my true name twelve days before walking into the capital by invitation. I asked instead after Loewe's woman from Katterau — countrywoman's coat, town boots, hands still, standing the way I stand. That is my mother's coat, Anna's, then mine, then someone's. On the Achterhalt road came a page with no number in it at all: a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a question in the fourth act unanswered. It has stopped counting. At the printer's I read the bill's worn bottom line and knew someone had kept the forme nine years, and I did not go to the window when she crossed to the woman alone.

Krug came back in a green coat, and Odalric sat down in the wet and confessed the seven pounds he had hung on him and two years of knowing where he was; I made him say and unsay it whole before us. Krug gave Harrow nine pages he swore he burned — six through nine unhappened, nine a cast list of twelve blanks and the house entire.

At the hearing I stood and spoke last: Anna's name, her sealed box, her fever rhymed in the Office's ledger; my billing here ten years ago, the magistrate's date, my leaving between performance and summons — and nobody asked what it concerned. I am in, for Anna's account, nine years open. My one condition: the box stays shut, endowed fifty years from the fee, before any other shilling. Then I took the page from my glove, pocketed it, and wore the glove bare. Grelle is alive with paste on his cuffs. I said my yes again in the grey, second in the line, and heard the ten read slow, the eleventh struck, and the blank after it.
**Entry:** Woke to the news that the boy Grelle is alive and in the building with paste on his cuffs, and did not go over, because a man that thin in the shoulders wants the room to leave him alone. Signed Prewick's minute. Played Ilsabet at ten into nine hundred seats with the pit stalls unbolted, and found a new pause in the second act that stopped the cleaners sweeping. Said my yes again in the grey, second in the line, and heard the ten read slow with the struck eleventh and the blank after it. Anna's shelf stays shut.

#### Undersecretary Lenz

**State:** At the prompt desk of the Theatre Royal at a quarter to seven, spectacles on, the folio squared before him with one page turned down, his own seal to hand; dry-mouthed and more moved than he will show, wanting to certify it whole and no one to volunteer.
**History:** Nineteen days into the post I had the tray laid for one and the folder ready: eleven safety notices, a sheet of tin buried with a hymn, a bill stopped in Achterhalt, nine years' storage paid on a stranger's box, Katterau ruled out, a company brought into the capital eleven days early, which no company has done. I asked her first what was in Vane's trunk. She drank the tea, gave me seen and hearsay separately, quoted my predecessor's stamp back at me — not to be described aloud — and said she keeps other people's rules when they are better than hers. I asked my question three times and the three answers matched word for word: one line, Vessendal, an emergency, Falk, in the wings, upstage, and company law since. Fourteen speakings in two hundred years; the fourteenth cost this office four years. I told her the fifteenth is scheduled, that the command was requested of the Palace and not by it, and that we were consulted and said yes. Then I let her read the requisition: A. Krug, of the fourth ward. She read it twice.

At our second meeting she asked her three questions in the promised order. I fetched the ledger: the audience has never once been harmed, yet the house is required — six readings among players did nothing, and my word *appetite* was struck from the margin. I named the makers who pay, kept Anna Sorel's line and the pencil against Krug unsoftened, named Skarke aloud in a deniable room, and gave my own opinion — yes, once, whole, stopped by nobody; never tried is not no. At the door I warned her: her name sits in the requisition file, files are read, and if she refuses she must refuse loudly, early, in writing to me, and I will carry it as the Office's refusal. She left at fifty-one minutes and I wanted her back.

I then wrote them jointly, which we do not do, their letter being the first application in nineteen years made in the correct order: the text in my hands and not out of this room by six on the 2nd, the determination minuted, signed, lodged, the eleventh line left alone. I recorded that Prewick was overruled by Assessment, to keep his rank, and added a postscript about the boy, because ink is not consent. At nine on the 2nd she came up my east stair carrying it in both arms; I stood, took it from underneath, and told the clerk nobody at all, not the Comptroller. Two hundred and eleven leaves, no title, four acts and a matter following. I read the receipt aloud as a courtesy and gave her the sealed certificate with it. Asked how she means to call a play she has never read, she said you don't call what's written, you call what's happening; I wrote that in my own notebook. My predecessor's file says Katterau failed because no stage manager was present — nineteen years I took that for a sneer at a trade. Thirty-one hours to read it. Tonight I sit at the prompt desk, folio squared, one page turned down.
**Entry:** I wrote them jointly, which this Office does not do, because their letter was the first application in nineteen years made in the correct order. I set my three requirements — the text in my hands and not out of this room by six on the 2nd, the determination minuted and signed and lodged, the eleventh line left alone — and I put in writing that Prewick was overruled by Assessment, which is true and which will keep his rank. I added a postscript about the boy, because ink is not consent. At nine on the 2nd she came up my east stair carrying it herself in both arms, and I stood, and took it from underneath, and told the clerk nobody at all, not the Comptroller. Two hundred and eleven leaves, no title, four acts and a matter following; I wrote the receipt out loud as a courtesy to a woman who keeps clean books, and gave her the sealed certificate with it — proof against a magistrate, which is all paper is good for. Then I asked her, out of order, how she means to call a play she has never read a word of, and she said you don't call what's written, you call what's happening, and I wrote it in my own notebook, not the folder. My predecessor's file says Katterau failed because no stage manager was present; nineteen years I took that for a sneer at a trade. Thirty-one hours to read it. Tonight I am at the prompt desk with the folio squared and one page turned down.

#### M. Skarke

**State:** Seated fourth row centre in the Theatre Royal with an unopened programme on his knee and no rug; shaking slightly, frightened and happy, wanting to hear it finished on the hour and to be allowed no nearer than this.
**History:** I came in early by no door of theirs and took my seat, fourth row centre, with the rug, and read the programme through — cast, scene list, the note about Frau Loewe's gas — and found the room lovely, which I had not expected. I could not stop counting the joints; the trough was better nailed than Katterau, and you could hear it in the run. She came down the aisle and I spoke to her without turning, and apologised, and told her the truth: that I had wanted to be in a theatre with these people since I was nine. She sat one seat away, called me Herr Skarke, and said half a play is hungrier than none, that my counting would be the smallest thing done in the building that night, and that they do finishes there, on the hour, honestly nailed. I told her I do not believe I am wicked; that thirty pages and twenty years of getting richer had bought me nothing; that I had found out everything from clerks, because clerks are cheap. I asked nothing of her. Then the doors went and the drovers came in wet, and I moved my rug onto my own knees and watched. Frau Sorel took the house by her fourth line. On the hour the great ruin came through the practical door, stage left, and nothing happened but a door opening and a play going on, and I put my face in my hands. I went out before the calls, having had what I came for, and left the rug for Falk with a pin and a note: I did not want the trunk that night, the claim was withdrawn, keep the halves apart, keep her keys, and never let me nearer than row four.

Both remaining nights I paid at the door and sat where I sit and sent nothing further. The second time I came in a plain black coat, no rug, hands empty, the programme shut on my knee, having written my undertaking out beforehand and given it to the man on the pit doors: I would not move from that seat and would not say one word of it aloud. When she passed at hat-distance I told her so, without turning, and let her see my hands shaking, and said the only other true thing I had: it's a lovely house.
**Entry:** I paid at the door like anybody and took my seat, fourth row centre, in a plain black coat, no rug, hands empty, the programme shut on my knee. I had written my undertaking out beforehand and given it to the man on the pit doors: I will not move from this seat and I will not say one word of it aloud. When she passed at hat-distance I told her so, without turning, and let her see my hands shaking, and said the only other true thing I had: it's a lovely house.

### 11 · The Fifteenth Speaking
- **Messages:** 205-224

Row eleven, seat one stays sold and empty — confirmed with Toby before the night begins. *Ilsabet's Ransom* plays to full houses: Falk stops the show, Vane weeps on cue, Hebel's gaswork excels, four curtain calls for Falk alone. Nobody leaves at interval.

Chamberlain's letter permits one stage announcement. Harrow goes out in working clothes, names herself, explains the play has no title, is two hundred years old, and was never finished — no watcher has ever come to harm, "an actuary's word," and he sits at her prompt desk. She asks only for witness, notes the lit exits, warns latecomers will be known, and declares seat one "sold and empty and stays so." She announces the Vermilion Players will finish the play tonight. No applause; roughly twenty leave, including a woman with three children escorted out by Grelle. Skarke stays. Lenz calls it "the correct order." Falk asks what play he's in; Harrow tells him to count the wings. Hebel dims to half; Falk begins from memory.
