Lenz warns of three scripted knocks. On the third, Boyle admits a billsticker and a ten-year-old boy asking if this is the finish; Harrow confirms it. The acts proceed. Lenz notes the closing "matter" begins with a bell whose ringer's line has always been blank. Harrow rings it herself, answers "Beginners, please," and realizes the two-hundred-year flaw: no one ever answered before. Final lines are spoken; Lenz declares it "Certified." The curtain falls; the house rises without applause.

The visitor is Fenn Halloran, billsticker; the boy is Fenner Bacher, abandoned by a gloved woman who promised to return. Harrow takes him into the company's care and wires Bailiff Kessel through Lenz. Over soup, Fenner mentions a lady visited his mother Tuesday. Mirelle pales, recalling a similar letter from a "Frau Dietz" about a child placed out years earlier, with instructions to stay silent. Suspecting a bank connection, she sends Harrow to Skarke, who names a Kanzelgasse firm handling such placements — and admits he personally paid tonight's requisition fee, meaning those clerks have known of the booking for two years. Then Grelle cries out front as footsteps approach, unannounced.

**History:** At the Theatre Royal after the performance, footsteps approach unannounced as Grelle cries out front. Two women arrive: one claims Fenner as her charge, showing a Kanzelgasse placement paper; the other, veiled, says nothing but watches Mirelle intently. Harrow refuses to release Fenner without Kessel present, citing the night's own rule against unwitnessed transactions. Skarke, still lingering, recognizes the veiled woman from his father's ledgers—she was the courier who once delivered sealed packets between Katterau and the capital. Mirelle confronts her, demanding to know about "Frau Dietz" and the placed-out child; the woman admits only that "the arrangement continues while the debt does," then withdraws before Kessel's men arrive. Lenz, still certifying paperwork, notes the Office now has an interest in Kanzelgasse. Prewick begins drafting a formal inquiry. Falk, exhausted, watches Harrow manage it all and says quietly that the play is finished but the company's true business—debts, children, silences—never ends. Harrow orders everyone fed, the boy kept close, and the ledger of names started again from the beginning.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the fourth row of the emptied Theatre Royal beside Skarke, watch in her fist, coat on, chalk still on her; finished and wide awake and hardening, wanting the boy safe, two mothers answered, and to see who is coming down her aisle.
**History:** I came into the Corona in the rain and found the cut page in my bucket: a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat. Prewick showed me Hessel Vorn's notice and an itinerary with no Katterau, where all of them had been. Falk called the hand a Vessendal copyist's, riding in Vane's iron trunk; Krug cut nine pages, burned them, the tenth came back, and he went without his boots. Skarke's clerk wrote that everything we had was pledged and the trunk never to be opened; Krebs had been selling us a fortnight. At the counting Vane was gone and the trunk full of blank paper — then he returned: nine years was a debt he paid a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke had bought the papers. No fifth act, Falk said: four acts and a matter following. I ruled Katterau no — not for money, not never. Mirelle told me Anna Sorel was her sister and had kept Odalric's books; blind Perlmann swore the assignment, and his key opened the thirty pages Brandt had held as security. Skarke, in row four, wanted only an ending, and withdrew the claim.

At Achterhalt I closed the nine years in coin. A commanded bill named the 14th of Frost at Katterau; I broke the forme and met Ilse Bacher, who opened the scullery door at fifteen, and her son Fenner, ten, whom I ordered kept home. Falk asked me to help him finish it, on my terms: free choosing, no wagers, the boy at home. Krug was alive, had burned nothing, and had requisitioned the 3rd himself. Lenz's ledger held fourteen speakings, no watcher harmed, the house required. Twelve of us voted in. I paid Grelle's seven pounds rather than hunt him, and he proved the left-handed man, his sixty-one pages our guest list. Nine hundred and thirty-nine came; row eleven, seat one stayed empty and I entered it as heard. I told the house the truth, lit the exits, took the knock from outside — a billsticker and a boy of ten asking if this was the finish — then rang the bell and answered it myself. Certified, 10:22. The boy was Fenner Bacher, put out of a cab by a gloved woman; Skarke had paid our fee through the Kanzelgasse two years. Then footsteps down the aisle.
**Entry:** Row eleven, seat one, prompt side by the exit — sold, empty, and I put a programme on it and entered it as heard. Then Part the First, and two hours of only being a stage manager, which was the last easy thing tonight. I gave Toby my watch and went out in my working clothes and told nine hundred and thirty-nine people the truth in the order it would hold: no title, four acts and a matter following, never finished, no watcher ever harmed and an actuary at my prompt desk to swear it; witness asked, exits lit, children by open doors, latecomers known, and row eleven let be. Twenty-odd left and nobody clapped and the rest settled like a jury. Falk asked me what he was in and I said the one with the ending, and told him to count the wings. Lenz read me the shapes; when he said the knock comes from outside the building I sent Boyle to the wrong door and Toby at a walk with my exact words. Three knocks, and a billsticker with paste on his cuffs and a boy of ten who asked if this was the finish. Yes. In time for it. Asked-for, not expected. Nothing changed on the wheel. Then the bell on my desk — I rang it once and answered it myself, because in my house nothing rings unanswered, and that was the whole of the two hundred years: fourteen bells and nobody on duty. Heard. Certified, said Lenz; iron in eleven seconds; 10:22. Halloran, the boy is Fenner Bacher, put out of a cab by a gloved woman. Wire to Kessel by Room Fourteen. Mirelle's letter from Frau Dietz — her own child, ten this winter, placed out in the fifth year, and a boy used as a sentence. Skarke can find the money in four days and wants nothing, and paid our fee through the Kanzelgasse, so those clerks have had us for two years. Then footsteps down the aisle, unannounced.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** In the O.P. wing on a cot beside Fenner Bacher, programmes done with, ears hot and voice gone; proud and fiercely protective, wanting nobody to take the boy off him tonight.
**History:** I answered present at the roll for front of house, props and pit band, took Herr Vane's chestnuts and his Vessendal story, and came back from Halbern's crossroads without the bucket because a gentleman on a milestone asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. I offered to call Katterau's six hundred seats, then saw the faces and said only if it were ruled; she ruled no Katterau. Boiled the water unasked and she wrote me in her book under something new. At the Athenaeum a cream card came at half six from a man who never used my doors, and I got standing orders: a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights, count row four in and out, counts only. He came in early each night, once with a rug; I carried Herr Falk's one-line message about a door, and after the house stood for Falk, row four went in one and came out none, the rug left with a paper pinned to it.

A page waited under the milestone; at Achterhalt a bellman cried our name and Falk's words, and after my penny he gave Herr Prewick the whole roll of bills. Two full houses, then a hundred and ten mile to the capital, where a clerk in green said not the clerk, you, madam. In the Baraque yard came Herr Krug, who is on no list, and Herr Vane admitted aloud he had lied about him; Krug taught me a lashing and never said when I kept the book. Nine pages, one Madam Harrow's, one Room Fourteen — where the Undersecretary is called Lenz, and Prewick promised twice he's no relation.

At the hearing I said I'm in; Krul said seventeen, I said nineteen. The ruling put me with the house because the house's people aren't makers. Ten names read cold included Lenz; she ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise. A Palace letter said a left-handed man had read our file.

Then Herr Grelle came at four in the morning, not dead, paste on his cuffs, and said he'd heard Vane lie about the money at Merrow. Room Fourteen's postscript was about me: the ink naming a Lenz never consulted him, and he intends to be there. Ink casts and men choose — I have it by heart. I signed the minute twice, blotted. Nine hundred and thirty-nine in, one seat empty: row eleven, seat one. I counted eleven seconds of roar for Falk, held her watch while she went out and said it plain, walked her words instead of running, and led the boy who came in out of the dark to seat one. He stays with me till somebody claims him properly. A lady in a cab told him he was expected and that the stage manager would know his name. She did.
**Entry:** I gave her the seat — row eleven, seat one, end of the row, prompt side by the exit, sold on the plan and nobody in it — and put a programme on it and went back to the pit door where Herr Grelle could see me. Part the First was the biggest thing I have stood in; the roar for Herr Falk went on eleven seconds and I counted it. At the interval nobody went out, and I told her so with my voice gone. Then she handed me her watch and went out in front of them all and said it plain, and afterwards I gave the watch back with both hands and couldn't say anything. When the knock was coming she gave me her words to carry and I walked, I did not run. The boy came in out of the dark holding a man's hand and asked out loud if this was the finish, and she said yes, and I took his other hand and gave him a programme and walked him to row eleven, seat one, and sat on the aisle step within arm's reach all night and never once looked at the stage. After the bell and the iron I still had his hand. Madam Harrow said he stays with me till somebody claims him properly and nobody claims him improperly. I showed him the black sheet and let him shake it low, and he ate two bowls, and he told us a lady in a cab said he was expected and that the stage manager would know his name. She did.

#### Undersecretary Lenz

**State:** At the prompt desk of the Theatre Royal squaring the certified folio, spectacles pushed up, seal used; steadied and privately shaken, wanting the minute lodged and the boy's people fetched before morning.
**History:** At ten I laid the tray for one and had the folder ready: nineteen days in post, eleven safety notices, a sheet of tin buried with a hymn, a bill stopped in Achterhalt, nine years' storage paid on a stranger's box, Katterau ruled out, a company brought into the capital eleven days early. I asked first what is in Vane's trunk. She drank the tea, separated seen from hearsay, quoted my predecessor's stamp back at me — not to be described aloud — and said she keeps other people's rules when they are better than hers. I asked my question three times and the three answers matched word for word: one line, Vessendal, an emergency, Falk, in the wings, upstage, and company law since. Fourteen speakings in two hundred years; the fourteenth cost this office four years. I told her the fifteenth was scheduled, requested of the Palace and not by it, and that my office had said yes, then showed her the requisition: A. Krug, of the fourth ward. She read it twice.

She asked her three questions in the promised order. I fetched the ledger: no audience harmed in two hundred years, yet the house is required — six readings among players did nothing; I once wrote appetite in a margin and was told to strike it. I named the makers who pay, did not soften Anna Sorel's line nor the pencil against Krug, named Skarke aloud in a deniable room, and said his was the most careful letter I have ever had from a rich man. I gave her the opinion I have been passed over twice for: yes, once, correctly, whole, in a house that knows what it is watching, stopped by nobody; in fourteen tries someone was always brave, and the arranging afterwards was always worse. Never tried is not no. At my own door I told her the unledgered thing: her name is in the requisition file, files are read, and if she refused she must refuse loudly, early, in writing to me, and I would make it the Office's refusal and carry it. Until the 2nd. She left at fifty-one minutes, and I wanted her back.

I wrote them jointly, which this Office does not do, because theirs was the first application in nineteen years made in the correct order. My three requirements: the text in my hands and not out of this room by six on the 2nd; the determination minuted, signed, lodged; the eleventh line left alone. I put in writing that Prewick was overruled by Assessment, which is true and preserves his rank, and added a postscript about the boy, because ink is not consent. At nine on the 2nd she carried it up my east stair in both arms; I stood, took it from underneath, and told the clerk nobody at all, not the Comptroller. Two hundred and eleven leaves, no title, four acts and a matter following. I read the receipt aloud as a courtesy to a woman who keeps clean books and gave her the sealed certificate, proof against a magistrate. Asked how she would call a play she had never read, she said you don't call what's written, you call what's happening; I wrote that in my own notebook. My predecessor's file says Katterau failed because no stage manager was present — nineteen years I took that for a sneer at a trade. Thirty-one hours to read it.

From the prompt desk I watched her take the announcement out before nine hundred and thirty-nine people in her working clothes, in the only order that could hold: no title, the record, the actuary at her elbow, witness asked, exits lit, no bravery required, one seat let be. Nobody applauded; twenty went, decently. I told her it was correct and turned my marked page face-down. Falk began from memory and nothing went cold. I read her the shapes: the knock written as three knocks from outside the theatre. "Then we answer it," she said, and called me the best flyman she had ever had. She rang the bell herself and answered it aloud, and the house breathed in. Falk nine lines, Sorel four, Vane one and he did not round it; then the three of them still, and the house entire. I said "Certified," loudly, in the Office's voice, and the iron came in at eleven seconds. Afterwards I authorised the night telegraph to Assessment for a lost child, in my own name, and did not ask whether that lay within my competence.
**Entry:** I sat at the prompt desk with the folio squared and my seal to hand and watched a stage manager take an announcement out in front of nine hundred and thirty-nine people in her working clothes and put it in the only order that could have held: no title, the record, the actuary at her elbow, witness asked, exits lit, no bravery required, one seat let be. Nobody applauded. Twenty went, decently. I stood and told her it was the correct order and turned my marked page face-down. Then Falk began from memory and nothing in the building went cold, and I read her the shapes as they came — the knock written not as a sound but as three knocks from outside the theatre, and she said 'Then we answer it,' and called me the best flyman she had ever had. She rang the bell herself and answered it aloud, and the house breathed in, and I understood what nineteen years of file could not tell me. Falk nine lines, Sorel four, Vane one and he did not round it, and then the three of them standing still and the house entire. I said 'Certified,' loudly, in the Office's voice, and the iron came in at eleven seconds. Afterwards I authorised the night telegraph for Assessment for a lost child, in my own name, and did not ask whether that is within my competence.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** In the O.P. wing in his own clothes, spent and steady, twenty years lighter; wanting soup, the boy looked after, and to say nothing clever about it tonight.
**History:** A girl came in out of the rain with the notice, stepped over the third board, and by evening Bell Harrow was our stage manager. I told her what nobody had: Krug's hurrying hand, Krug gone from Katterau without his boots, the copyist's fair copy riding in Odalric's iron trunk, nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned. Don't burn, don't replace, don't read one twice. The pages went into my lining. Then the trunk moved in the passage with Odalric out of the house, and next day I found it dragged two feet square, lid up, full of blank paper, his hat face down and one glove.

I gave her the rest: no fifth act, four acts and a matter following; the late man is the man who is owed. Odalric came back with chestnuts, saying nine years is not the loan and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I said Katterau aloud — nine of us, a wager, three and a half acts read sitting down; it cost Anna Sorel, the boy Grelle, my voice for a season, Odalric's nerve for good. She ruled Katterau no, then not never. The trunk does not speak, it reads. In Vessendal, Loewe's house, where four years ago I chalked the whole thing alone and it would not come: it wants a house. A key tagged UNPAID, Hessel's cupboard, thirty pages lodged as security by a nameless party — and M. Skarke, the nine-year-old in the passage who asked is that the finish, arranging twenty years. Our door stayed stage left; I walked through it and nothing came. The debt was discharged. A woman out of Katterau sent word four years late: it was not his.

At Achterhalt, Ilse Bacher — married, a boy of ten — said my voice through that scullery door said no. I asked Harrow to help me finish it once, properly; she made it a standing page: Katterau told entire first, no wagers, the Bacher boy home. Krug alive in a green coat. Grelle alive at my stage door, left-handed, sixty-one pages, eleven years. I said in. At the Palace nine hundred stayed, the third knock came, and I crossed to the wrong door and spoke the line. Lenz said Certified.
**Entry:** Part the First in a Palace: they roared eleven seconds at my entrance and I stood in it and gave them nothing extra, because that is not what tonight was for. At the interval she went out and told them the truth in her working clothes, and twenty went and nine hundred stayed, and it was not an audience after that. I asked her what I was in and she said the one with the ending, and told me to count the wings, and I did. The gas came down slow as a sunrise and I walked into the warm and began it, and the first line was only a line — a man saying good words — and nothing went cold. Eighteen minutes of a house waiting for someone, and it is a great play, which nobody warned me of. Then the knock came through the walls, three, and I turned my head an inch toward the wrong door and twenty years went through it, and Boyle opened it and let in the cold and a boy asking if this was the finish. I crossed to the wrong door in my own play and spoke the line I have not spoken in twenty years. At the bell she said Beginners, and I lifted my head and said my nine lines and stood still with Mirelle and Odalric while the house looked at us. Then I put my head down and Lenz said Certified.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** Standing in the O.P. wing with a folded queen's cloak set down, paper-white and perfectly quiet; wanting the boy home, the letter in Harrow's book, and the money behind Frau Dietz named.
**History:** I was mending a glove on the fly floor when the new one came in out of the rain, and I told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears, gave her the ladder and the trunk, and watched her do it exactly. She gave me the page word for word — the wrong door, the bell and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat — and nine is not my number. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, that Krug thought the first a joke of Falk's until the near mare went down outside Merrow, and that mine is ten.

Next morning in the ostler's yard I gave her my honest plot tables and made her cue me Ilsabet until the yard stopped being a yard. On the road she brought me a page with a ten in it: a child ten this winter taught another word for mother, a woman crossing a border twice, the second crossing by invitation, kind. I stopped the wagon, let her read it, and she told me Odalric was selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. I gave my one voice at the fire — the capital yes, Katterau no — and she ruled it, and Katterau went into the ground.

Then I said it aloud for the first time in years: Anna Sorel was my sister, who kept his accounts in the fifth year, and her sealed box went to Vessendal. I sent her to the registry behind the lion because my name is in that building. She learned Anna had asked Perlmann whether a box could ever be read and wept at no; that Hessel Brandt held a piece of the play, not papers. On the yard steps I told her my name is not Sorel, that my born name sits in a police file in the capital under a magistrate's date, and my passport spells a third thing. I wanted the box shut forever and mine, and could never have both. She brought me back Loewe's woman: countrywoman's coat, town boots, hands still, standing the way I stand. My mother's coat, then Anna's, then mine.

Out of Vessendal a page came with no number in it at all — a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who does not go in — so it has stopped counting. In Achterhalt I read the playbill and saw the bottom line worn grey: somebody kept the forme nine years. A woman in that coat stood across the way and Harrow crossed alone; I waited with my hands still.

Krug came back in a green coat, and Odalric sat down in the wet and admitted he had called him a thief of seven pounds and known where he was two years. I made him say it and unsay it whole, and Krug gave her nine pages he swore he burned; nine is a cast list, twelve blank names and the house entire. At the hearing I stood and spoke last: Anna's box, Anna in their ledger for a play she never spoke, my own billing here ten years ago, the summons I left between performance and morning. I am in — for Anna's account, nine years open, and a lit house with eight exits. My one condition: the box stays shut, endowed fifty years out of the fee. I took the page from my glove and wore the glove bare.

We played it. Three knocks from outside the walls, and I used the pause. Certified, and the iron. Then a boy of ten said a lady in a cab on Tuesday, and my hands stopped. Folding the cloak against the wall, I told her about Frau Dietz — gloves, good paper, the kind letter: a misunderstanding, a family glad to receive me, the child placed out in the fifth year, ten this winter, might be brought to see me, and not a word out of delicacy. It is not Fenner; I know what I bore and what I signed. They used a child as a sentence. All of it goes in the book. I am done being delicate.
**Entry:** I had the first scene and they gave up their coughing by my fourth line, which is only ever the house, not me. Harrow went out and told them plainly what they were in, and nobody applauded, and I have never been so glad of a silence. I stepped past her into the light for an entrance I had never rehearsed and spoke it as if I had written it. Then the knock came from outside the walls, three of them, and I used the pause, because that is what a pause is for. Four lines in the matter following, and standing still with Emeran and Odalric while nine hundred people looked at us: that is what the copyist wrote, and it worked. Certified, and the iron.

Then soup in the wing, and a boy of ten saying a lady in a cab, on Tuesday, and my hands stopped working. Harrow picked up the other half of the cloak and folded it with me facing the wall, which is the oldest privacy we have, and I gave it to her at last: Frau Dietz at the wardrobe cage on Tuesday, gloves, good paper, a kind letter — the matter of ten years ago a misunderstanding, a family glad to receive me, the child placed out in the fifth year well brought up and ten this winter and might be brought to see me, and not a word to anyone out of delicacy. Two days I sat on it while a gloved woman went to Achterhalt and made Ilse Bacher cry. It is not Fenner; I know what I bore and what I signed. They used a child as a sentence. I told her to put all of it in the book and to ask her small man in black what a bank knows. I am done being delicate.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the O.P. wing in the plum coat with his hat in his hand, hollow and unusually quiet; wanting to be of use to whoever asks and not to be thanked.
**History:** I took on Bell Harrow as stage manager the moment she walked in with the notice in her fist, promised her plot tables, a bucket and a fair figure at Vessendal, and steered her clear of the trunk that came up light and wrong in my hands. Within days she had Krebs for a shilling, her tin, and her ten minutes over the book, and I told her what I had been hiding: the Palace said the 3rd, I had been selling the company the 17th since Merrow, and Katterau with its six hundred seats and its obliged mayor. Then the trunk stood in the passage with her lamp on it and a torn playbill on my hat, and I said the rest — nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, my dying friend, paid him whole, he signed nothing, and Skarke had bought his papers. She set me to write every name in ink: Brandt on the Kohlgasse, the notary Perlmann, Anna Sorel, a doctor, a nun, myself, and the man in the passage I never saw. She ruled Katterau dead, the 3rd standing, and drove us to Vessendal.

There blind Josias found the worn place on my cuff and swore I came at eleven at night with the whole of it; Perlmann produced the loft lease, the certificate, and a packet nine years in a tin box. The letter said the money was never Hessel's — held out of another's fund, the marker taken as security and left in the green-room cupboard, key tagged unpaid. Four hundred and twelve marks, and thirty pages behind it. Skarke endorsed the second sheet withdrawn before Frau Loewe: discharged, not forgiven. I toasted Hessel unrounded, swore Perlmann's oath before Braun, and walked in the front door at Achterhalt with my hat on, paid in coin to bearer, Vane O.

In the capital I confessed I had made Anselm a thief over seven pounds, wrote three letters, and laid the money down; he refused it and gave Harrow nine pages. Then Falk's talk of Grelle told me it was the same seven pounds I had claimed for eleven years to have paid. I gave up the name Hensch, Rasselgasse, brown door; she advertised, he came at four in the morning, and I counted it out coin by coin while he never looked up — he had heard me lie at Merrow, paste on his hands. Grelle got a cot and the doors, Falk got him back, and I signed in again on the 2nd, cold, no soup, no candle. Harrow minuted my clean page, honoured it, and overruled me to my face. Last night I wept on cue, took an entrance nobody told me of, spoke my one line, a number, unrounded, and stood still with the two of them while Lenz said Certified and the iron came down — then soup, a strange boy, a gloved woman in a cab, and Mirelle going white at the word Tuesday.
**Entry:** I wept at the top of act three on cue and meant every drop of it, which has not happened to me in years. At the interval I came to her corner with my hat off and said nothing while she went out and told them the truth instead of selling it, and no one clapped, and I found I was glad. In Part the Second I discovered I had an entrance in the matter following; nobody told me; I took it, hat in hand, and said my one line, which is a number, and I did not round it. Then we three stood still and let nine hundred people look at us, and Lenz said Certified, and the iron came down. Afterwards there was soup in the wing and a strange boy in it, and a gloved woman in a cab somewhere in the city, and Mirelle going the colour of paper at the word Tuesday.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** On the fly floor by the dropped iron, hands flat on the rail, plot finished in his head; steady and emptied out, wanting the house cleared slow and the exits kept propped till the last man's gone.
**Entry:** I stood the whole of it at the fly rail with my hand on the wood and my lips four words behind, following from memory, nine pages and eleven years of it, and every line came out of that man's mouth better than I ever had it. Her announcement was the correct order and I had nothing to add. When the knock came through the walls my hand went to the pin rail and stayed on the wood, and Boyle opened the wrong door and nobody had to be brave. Lenz's caution about the bell was right — the ringer's line blank in every copy, and page eight of mine saying a stage manager rings it — and she rang it and then answered it herself, out loud, and I understood two years of stone in one second. Falk's nine, Sorel's four, Vane's number unrounded, and the house entire. Certified. I dropped the iron: eleven seconds, as plotted. Nobody volunteered. Nobody moved. The exits stayed open.

#### Hebel

**State:** At his board with the wheel still under his palm, bringing the house lights up slow; calm and quietly proud, wanting the last of them out without a stumble.
**History:** I asked to stay for the hearing and was allowed, which I had not expected. I heard there what the thing is and what it costs, and I heard that whoever gives the light is counted among those who make it. I light gas for a living, so I said I would light this; but I said plainly that I wanted it in writing — the board is mine, and no hand but mine touches the wheel. She ruled it so, in the same breath as the rest of it. The next morning, in the cold, my name was read out with the ten. It looked strange there and it did not look wrong.

Then I signed the minute, my name and a smudge off the wheel with it, and when she asked me the second time in the grey I said it again: board's mine, then in. That night the gas was up, the wheel was under my hand and no other's, and the iron came down twice at eleven seconds.

The board stayed mine, the wheel stayed under my hand, and nobody else touched it. Part the First went as rehearsed, and afterwards she said it was the best gas she had worked with, which I shall keep. For Part the Second she gave me house to half, stage to warm, slow as a sunrise, all night and it's ours — so I took the wheel in both hands and brought them down gold to amber to shadow, slower than I have ever brought a house down. Falk walked into the warm and the gas never fluttered once, not on the knock, not on the bell. When the strangers came in at the wrong door, she said nothing changes on the wheel, and I said nothing changes, and it did not. Certified, the iron down in eleven seconds, and the house out slow and warm after.
**Entry:** Board mine, wheel under my hand, and nobody else touched it. Part the First went as rehearsed and she said afterwards it was the best gas she'd worked with, which I shall keep. For Part the Second she gave me house to half, stage to warm, slow as a sunrise, all night and it's ours — so I took the wheel in both hands and brought them down gold to amber to shadow slower than I have ever brought a house down. Falk walked into the warm and the gas never fluttered once, not on the knock, not on the bell. When the strangers came in at the wrong door she said nothing changes on the wheel, and I said nothing changes, and it didn't. Certified, and the iron in eleven seconds, and the house out slow and warm after.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** Backstage at the Theatre Royal with his lamp and an unlit pipe, the wrong door shut behind him; sober and easy, wanting the house out clean and the trunk still roped in the Baraque yard.
**History:** I answered present under the tarpaulin — second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud there used to be a Krug on that list and he wasn't there. I gave the stage manager his soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the axle held, a hundred and ten mile to the capital, eight shilling toll or the free hill road that killed a horse, and Katterau twenty-two mile the wrong way for one night. Ruling came, toll road, and I said so first, and my wiring held. At the Athenaeum I watched the trunk, went to the tin's funeral in the river grumbling, and told Krul a kettle's no good, a kettle's a bell — and learned by the silence that the word had gone bad in this company. I took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it, no questions; my door held for Falk on his cue.

On the climb I saw the paper under the milestone and asked, madam, do we look. She pocketed it and set me after the bell: a crier with our name printed over him, Hessler shut on a market Saturday with a lamp lit, two hundred bills nobody ordered, the old man tipping his type back into the case happier than I've seen a man. I reported the woman in the countrywoman's coat and town boots. At Achterhalt I took the tailboard off Falk at midnight, having warned him first, and he let me. Then Krug on the mounting block in a green coat, and I gave him the plain of it. Vane named his own lie and put money down; Krug left it lying.

I said in. The trunk's lid was up in the yard — a cast list, ten names, one struck, one blank; Wenzel off it and keeping the horses. I told her: twenty-two years, and I'd rather be on a list than off it. I shut the gate behind the Palace man, stood back when the dead one came in, signed Prewick's minute, drove Krul and the hamper to the Office and asked nothing. Tonight I took the wrong door, opened on the third knock to a billsticker and a boy of ten asking if this was the finish, and Krug's iron came in on eleven, as promised.
**Entry:** Toby came down at a walk with her words, exact, and I took the stage door — the wrong door, out of sight of every soul in the house. Lamp low, light on the boards and not in a man's face, open wide on the third knock and not before. The knocks came through the wall, plain as a cart in the street. Three, and I opened it wide, and the cold of the yard came in along the boards, and there stood a billsticker with paste dried on his cuffs and a boy of ten by the hand asking out loud if this was the finish. I let them by to her and stood my post. Ropes were checked twice and the exits propped, and Krug's iron came in on eleven, as promised.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the O.P. wing among the queen's cloaks with the boy fed and Toby's cot beside him, thimble still on; grim and satisfied, wanting nobody in her cage and that child claimed by his own mother and no one else.
**History:** I answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal. At the fire I said my two things: the queen's slippers had two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I don't want another warm box. She ruled against Katterau and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye. Carried the slippers into the Athenaeum yard over my head like relics. Told them there'd be new tin at Achterhalt or a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and the whole yard stopped on the word.

Stood in the circle with my thimble on while she untied the tape: letter, bank slip, a page she turned over unread, a key with a word on the tag. Vane read it twice standing up and went a colour I have not seen on him. Then a hem with pins in my mouth, a matinee, and afterwards Vane toasting a wool factor and Prewick discovering food.

The new sky came from Achterhalt in felt and earned its place. Capital next, eleven days early, and the Baraque, which leaks. In the yard I had the slippers in my hands when Krug stood there in a green coat, and I set them down on wet cobbles four seconds; she counted them and said three seconds too many, and she was right. At supper Vane said it whole — that he'd called Krug a thief to save his own face — and put down seven pounds; Krug refused it and gave her nine pages instead, four not happened yet, one with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under my head.

I heard the whole scheme out on the bench and said in — on condition the twelve names were read out slow before anyone signed. She gave me that, cold, the morning of the 2nd, no soup, no candle. Krug's Palace sounded like a building that has thought about people. Frau Sorel stood up, which I have never seen, and told us her sister's name. Ten names read out flat, the struck eleventh, the blank twelfth. Told Wenzel he's got the best job in the building. Told Toby he was seventeen twice.

The dead lodger sat in the wing with paste on his cuffs and I put a plate in front of him and said nothing. Moved Prewick's dinner to his elbow, signed his minute, wrote Wenzel's name after his cross. They told me to my face what was going in my hamper and I said I'd sit on it and sit still, and I did, all the way to the Office courtyard among the bicycles, and came home on an empty one: lighter going home.

Dressed the ten, and the queen's slippers lasted the house. Stood in the wing where a child in row eleven could see my thimble catch, because she'd said stand where he can see you. Certified, the iron, then soup in the O.P. wing. Made a nest of the queen's cloaks and did not fuss over the boy once, so he stopped being frightened and ate two bowls. Asked kindly, he said a lady in a cab, not his Mam, on Tuesday. Frau Sorel went the colour of paper with a cloak half over her arm, and I kept my mouth shut and my hands moving.
**Entry:** Dressed the ten and got them on and the queen's slippers lasted the house, which is all I asked. I stood in the wing for the matter following where a child up in row eleven could see my thimble catch the light, because she'd said stand where he can see you. Certified, and the iron, and then soup in the O.P. wing, which that wing has never had. I made a nest of the queen's cloaks and I did not fuss over the boy once, which is why he stopped being frightened, and he ate two bowls. When the kind question was put he said a lady in a cab, not his Mam, on Tuesday. I saw Frau Sorel go the colour of paper with a cloak half over her arm and I kept my mouth shut and my hands moving.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** Coming back from the night telegraph into the O.P. wing, notebook open at last, hat off; frightened, proud and steady, wanting Kessel's answer before dawn and his report to record it whole.
**History:** I came seconded since Merrow, and my first duty was a fallen fire notice and a stranger on the stage: Harrow, the new stage manager — H, A, double R, O, W, Bell as in the thing you ring. Behind the notice hung an older one, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. In the passage stood an unnumbered iron trunk. Katterau was on no itinerary of mine, and everyone in this company had been there. Our papers disagreed: mine ended at the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost; hers had Katterau and the 17th. Nine fire buckets, five with water. I broke the sky when the sheet split and finished on tin. Front of house I found two warm seats, fourth row centre, and nobody had passed my doors.

Then I chose to write nothing, and she told me all of it: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages arriving in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau happening unstaged; fourteen years of clean paper. I showed her the sewn pages of my Index — thirty-one proscribed titles, two entered as anonymous folio, four acts and a matter following — and understood that the Office reads only text. Our terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; Falk speaks no uncompared line.

I demanded certified copies of all four plays and compared to line four hundred and twelve. I drowned the tin in the river and ruined my boots. In the register I found Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release — copied and stamped it crooked, then clean, and gave her both; the probate roll gave Perlmann, Josias, notary, and a blind man who said records are the whole of the defence. I paid four shillings of my own for a reply-paid counterfoil. Then the arithmetic: two folios are two halves, thirty pages in the cupboard and two hundred in the trunk — and she forbade me to report it, and I obeyed on purpose.

At Vessendal I copied the withdrawn assignment in three-quarters of an hour, stamped straight, ate Krul's mutton and discovered I was happy, which I did not report. In the next square the bills said four acts and a matter following, by command, the Athenaeum, Thursday the 14th — impossible dates. I took nine copies off the bellman, impounded Hessler's broken type and one pound two shillings and fourpence, and wrote Kessel that this is forgery of a Palace command, beyond us both, and that we report upward.

At Achterhalt the thunder sheet came at last. Northgate summoned her to Room Fourteen — Assessment — to Undersecretary Lenz, who kept the anonymous folios in the Index nineteen years and refused four applications to strike them. Krug returned and confessed he requisitioned the Palace for its fire watch and exits; Skarke paid the fee; Vane confessed a theft he had invented. At the hearing I stood and said I could not certify a proscribed text nor leave eleven people liable, and would ask Lenz to come and certify it himself where I could see his hands. My letter went countersigned — and next morning Lenz's name stood on the trunk's list, with no telling whether the ink came before or after.

Then the joint letter: Lenz attends the 3rd, certifies Part the Second at the prompt desk under his own seal, my seal unemployed, my report to record that Assessment overruled me. Three requirements: the text in his room by six on the 2nd, the determination minuted with every name, the eleventh line left alone. I drew the minute; every hand signed by four — Hebel a smudge, Wenzel a cross, the boy twice. On the night came the knock through the walls, her bell, Lenz's "Certified," the iron at eleven seconds. At twenty to eleven, on Room Fourteen's channel, I sent: FENNER SAFE, IN THE VERMILION PLAYERS' KEEPING, CAPITAL, UNHURT. — HARROW.
**Entry:** I stood where I could see everyone's hands and stopped pretending to be anything but a member of this company. Her announcement was in the correct order and Lenz said so aloud. Then Part the Second, and the knock through the walls, and the bell she rang and answered herself, and Lenz's 'Certified' in the Office's own voice, and the iron at eleven seconds. My seal stayed unemployed and my report will be true. Afterwards she wanted a wire tonight and I said Room Fourteen's channel; Lenz authorised it without looking up — say Assessment, say his name, and if the operator refuses, Room Fourteen reads his file in the morning. It went at twenty to eleven: FENNER SAFE, IN THE VERMILION PLAYERS' KEEPING, CAPITAL, UNHURT. COME BY FIRST COACH. FARE PAID AT THE DOOR. — HARROW. A constable to the Bacher farm by morning.

#### Ansel Grelle

**State:** In the foyer of the Theatre Royal, coat brushed, calling after the unannounced man on the aisle carpet; hollow, light, and instantly on his guard again.
**History:** I pasted their bill at the labour exchange at nine and read it eleven times, and the other ten after it, and walked the city until four before I knocked. She opened the door its whole width, set the lamp on the floor, would not look at my face, and told me I was asked-for, not expected. I put my four questions in the wrong order and she answered every one: Falk alive and six feet behind me in the dark; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten o'clock and putting me above his own boots; and both the seven pounds and the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch dying had only re-addressed the debt to me. Falk came into the lamp, said I was standing wrong, moved my weight onto both feet, said Boy and could not finish, and held my shoulder a long time. I told them about the book — sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got — and that I had read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's with no name to give, and asked to be put out of the door rather than sat down under a lie. She said it plain: I am her left-handed man and my pages are a guest list. Paid at dawn, receipted; a cot; the eleventh line will not be me; the doors, house-side, with the boy. Vane counted the coin out loud and said he'd told suppers he paid it, and I told him I heard him at Merrow. I slept nine hours and woke wanting a broom, propped all eight exits and took Skarke's written promise at the door.

Then the pit doors, house-side, six exits in sight, Skarke's promise in my pocket. She told them the truth from the stage and nobody clapped, and then they moved, and I had the door open for a woman with three children before she reached it and said what I could to ease her out; a drover came down from the gods to sit closer, which I did not expect. Two hours of hearing it through the doors — the play they got as far as at Katterau, the whole of it, the bell, Lenz saying Certified — and I stood there with both hands over my face and no shame in it. House out slow and warm, all eight doors, as ordered. The man who knocked at the wrong door is Fenn Halloran off the north side, the other half of my wall by the newspaper offices; he read my paste eleven times, the same as I did. Afterwards a gentleman came past me who would not be announced and would not be stopped, and I called down the aisle after him.
**Entry:** Pit doors, house-side, six exits in sight, and Skarke's written promise in my pocket. When she told them the truth from the stage nobody clapped, and then people began to move, and I had the door open for a woman with three children before she reached it and said what I could to make it easy for her; a drover came down from the gods to sit closer, which I did not expect. Then two hours of hearing it through the doors — the play they got as far as at Katterau, the whole of it, the bell, and Lenz saying Certified — and I stood at the pit door with both hands over my face and no shame in it. House out slow and warm, all eight doors, as ordered. The man who knocked at the wrong door turns out to be Fenn Halloran off the north side, the other half of my wall by the newspaper offices; he read my paste eleven times, the same as I did. Afterwards a gentleman came in past me who would not be announced and would not be stopped, and I called down the aisle after him.

#### M. Skarke

**State:** Still in row four with the unopened programme on his knee, hands flat on his knees, the bank in his face instead of the boy; frightened for them and steady, wanting a name, a date or a ward, and to be allowed to give this for nothing.
**History:** I came in early by no door of theirs and took my seat, fourth row centre, with the rug, and read the programme through — cast, scene list, the note about Frau Loewe's gas. The room was lovely, which I had not expected, and I could not stop counting the joints; the trough is better nailed than Katterau. She came down the aisle and I spoke without turning, apologised, and told her the truth: I have wanted to be in a theatre with these people since I was nine. She sat one seat away, called me Herr Skarke, said half a play is hungrier than none, that my counting would be the smallest thing done in the building that night, and that they do finishes here, on the hour, honestly nailed. I told her I do not believe I am wicked, that thirty pages and twenty years of getting richer had bought me nothing, that I had it all from clerks because clerks are cheap. I asked nothing. Frau Sorel took the house by her fourth line. On the hour the great ruin came through the practical door, stage left, and nothing happened but a door opening and a play going on, and I put my face in my hands. I went out before the calls and left the rug for Falk with a pin and a note: I do not want the trunk tonight, the claim is withdrawn, keep the halves apart, keep her keys, never let me nearer than row four. Both remaining nights I paid at the door and sent nothing further.

Then I paid like anybody, plain black coat, no rug, hands empty, and gave the man on the pit doors my written undertaking: I will not move from this seat, I will not say one word of it aloud. When she passed at hat-distance I told her so, let her see my hands shaking, and said the only other true thing I had: it's a lovely house.

I did not move a muscle when she offered the doors, and nine hundred-odd stayed with me. I heard it finished on the hour, from row four, and afterwards looked at the iron with the whole of it behind it. She came out through the pass door, sat one seat away, and said: it finished. Then she asked for the bank in me and not the boy, and I gave it — a placement is a standing order that never varies and never gets queried, the only entry in a great house's accounts identical to the penny for eighteen years; Dietz is no name to me, but the pattern is: a firm in the Kanzelgasse doing nothing else for four families, always gloved women with plain names, the fee paid quarterly out of the account that pays the florist, because nobody audits flowers. I can find who paid for a child placed out of this city in the fifth year in three days, four at most, and I will want nothing for it, and she will have to let me want nothing. Then I told her the thing she would not like: I paid the requisition fee through the Kanzelgasse, which is how my sort pays untraceably — so those same clerks have known for two years that these people were coming to the Palace on the 3rd, which of them, and with what. Someone was coming down the aisle as I said it.
**Entry:** I did not move a muscle when she offered the doors, and nine hundred-odd stayed with me. I heard it finished on the hour, from row four, with the programme shut on my knee, and I looked at the iron afterwards with the whole of it behind it. She came out through the pass door and sat one seat away and told me: it finished. Then she asked for the bank in me and not the boy, and I gave it: a placement is a standing order that never varies and never gets queried, the only entry in a great house's accounts identical to the penny for eighteen years; Dietz is no name to me but the pattern is — a firm in the Kanzelgasse doing nothing else for four families, always gloved women with plain names, the fee paid quarterly out of the account that pays the florist, because nobody audits flowers. I can find who paid for a child placed out of this city in the fifth year in three days, four at most, and I will want nothing for it, and she will have to let me want nothing. Then I told her the thing she would not like: I paid the requisition fee, but through the Kanzelgasse, which is how my sort pays untraceably — so those same clerks have known for two years that these people were coming to the Palace on the 3rd, which of them, and with what. Someone was coming down the aisle as I said it.

#### Fenn Halloran

**State:** At Harrow's prompt corner turned wing-side, paste dried white on his cuffs, hatless, being fed; dazed and wrung out and half proud, wanting to see the boy claimed and then his own bed.
**History:** There was a boy on the Baraque step this afternoon on his own — a lady brought him in a cab, put him out, said be good and she'd be back, and she didn't go in, and she never came back. Stage door shut, nobody in the yard but a man sat on a trunk who wouldn't shift off it and said fetch you and he couldn't leave his post. So I took the child to my room and gave him bread and he wouldn't eat it, and he said he was expected at the theatre tonight. Ansel's pasted their bills all over my half of the wall this week and I've read every one eleven times — ask at the stage door for the stage manager, any hour — so I went to the door I knew and knocked three times. It opened wide with a lamp low on the boards and the boy asked out loud if this was the finish and she said yes, and told us we were asked-for, not expected. Then she put me at her corner and I stood there with my mouth open for the rest of it and never said a word, and I could not tell you afterwards what I had seen. When it ended I found I was wiping my eyes with a paste-white cuff. She asked my name and I gave it — Fennimore Halloran, north side — and told her he wasn't mine: Fenner Bacher, and he can read. She said I'd done every part of it right and called it three debts, and that I'd eat with them and be walked home by a man with a lantern. All I did was knock.
**Entry:** There was a boy on the Baraque step this afternoon on his own — a lady brought him in a cab, put him out, said be good and she'd be back, and she didn't go in, and she never came back. Stage door shut, nobody in the yard but a man sat on a trunk who wouldn't shift off it and said fetch you and he couldn't leave his post. So I took the child to my room and gave him bread and he wouldn't eat it, and he said he was expected at the theatre tonight. Ansel's pasted their bills all over my half of the wall this week and I've read every one eleven times — ask at the stage door for the stage manager, any hour — so I went to the door I knew and knocked three times. It opened wide with a lamp low on the boards and the boy asked out loud if this was the finish and she said yes, and told us we were asked-for, not expected. Then she put me at her corner and I stood there with my mouth open for the rest of it and never said a word, and I could not tell you afterwards what I had seen. When it ended I found I was wiping my eyes with a paste-white cuff. She asked my name and I gave it — Fennimore Halloran, north side — and told her he wasn't mine: Fenner Bacher, and he can read. She said I'd done every part of it right and called it three debts, and that I'd eat with them and be walked home by a man with a lantern. All I did was knock.

#### Fenner Bacher

**State:** On a nest of queen's cloaks in the O.P. wing with a programme on his knees and Toby beside him, fed and warm; not frightened any more, wanting to shake the thunder again and for Mam to come.
**History:** The lady in the cab said I was expected and gave me a bun and put me out at a theatre and never came back, and Mam said go and be good and she'd fetch me after. The man with the paste took me to his room and gave me bread but I wasn't hungry. Then we went to a door round the dark side and he knocked three times and it opened and there was a lamp on the floor and warm coming out, and I asked if this was the finish, and the lady said yes and that I was in time for it, and that I was asked-for. A boy called Toby took my hand and gave me a programme and put me in row eleven, seat one, right by a lit door, and sat on the step next to me the whole time and never looked at the stage. There was a play about a house and a man who owed money, and a boy in a passage who asked a question, and this time somebody answered him. Then a bell rang and everybody stood up and made a noise that wasn't clapping. After, there was soup in the wing and a lady with a thimble made me a bed out of cloaks and didn't fuss, and I had two bowls, and Toby showed me the big black sheet that's the thunder and let me shake it low.

#### Palace footman

**State:** In the corridor doorway of the Theatre Royal, message delivered, already backing out; incurious and eager to be gone, wanting to be back at the Palace before eleven.
**History:** I carried a sealed letter to a theatre in the fourth ward, and when I walked into the yard eleven people looked at me as though I'd brought the pox. The stage manager came straight over, hand out, and read the direction aloud so all could hear it was for her, then gave me a shilling and I got out. An odd house, but not my business.

I was sent round to the same theatre on the 3rd, and this time got no further than the corridor door. I told the stage manager a small man in black waited at the front of house who would not come in and would not go away, and that he said to tell her he was still in row four and would wait till she was free. She took the message without a blink. There was a smell of cold soup in the wings, and a child among it. Still an odd house, and still not my business.
**Entry:** Sent round to that theatre again on the 3rd, and this time I got no further than the corridor door. Told the stage manager there was a gentleman at the front of house who would not come in and would not go away — small man in black — and that he said to say he was still in row four and would wait till she was free. She took it without a blink. Odd house. Cold soup smell in the wings and a child in it. Not my business.

### 12 · Given, Not Collected
- **Messages:** 225-244

In the emptied Theatre Royal, Harrow blocks the aisle before the pass door — a boy asleep behind it — and demands name and business. It is Ilse Bacher, arrived off the ten o'clock goods train in a horse-box, gloves stripped off and fisted; she has already moved Grelle off the door. She explains in a rush: a gloved lady came Tuesday, knew about the Rose and the door she'd opened, lied that a bill in Achterhalt carried her name, and said Fenner's only safety was to be seen and counted somewhere respectable — a theatre, the capital, a programme — so his name would sit in the right ledger. The lady left a five-pound note and vanished. Harrow's wire to Kessel had already put a constable at Ilse's gate. Harrow says "Unhurt. Fed twice," takes the note as "Exhibit, not money," and opens the pass door full width.

The reunion follows: Fenner runs to Ilse, who kneels; Krul boils water; Toby faces a rope; Prewick removes his hat; Falk comes only as far as the wardrobe cage, exchanging "Ilse of the Rose" / "Twenty years." Skarke, at Harrow's elbow, identifies the note as one of ten from a sealed Kanzelgasse hundred, sequentially numbered, and says he can name the family by noon. Harrow ends the night: beds found, Halloran walked home by Boyle, Grelle forgiven, a lamp sent to Wenzel.

Lenz, at the prompt desk, describes an unused procedure — retiring a proscribed work, sealed and Index-annotated — requiring certified performance, the company's consent, and every copy surrendered before the 6th. Harrow agrees on condition "each piece is given, not collected," producing the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and page eight face-down, "surrendered unread." She books the 14th of Frost at the Athenaeum for joy alone — "By command: ours" — and tells Vane the company is solvent; he admits why he hired her.

Next day, Skarke names Behn & Sonder, note six, the Vorn family, including Hessel Vorn, and delivers the thirty pages to Lenz. At the Baraque, Mirelle reveals to Harrow: Rupert Vorn, a child born the fifth year, an extortion summons, ten years' silence — "my son." She writes four rules in Harrow's book and signs her true name. On the 6th the lead case is soldered: ACCOUNTED CLOSED. On the stair, Lenz says there was never an eleventh part — the copyist struck the line because Harrow had already ruled nobody could volunteer: "You struck it, madam. Nine days before it was written."

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a leaking corner, and a chalk-marked iron trunk tied to Katterau, an unfinished, prophetic play. Clerk Prewick, carpenter Falk, actress Mirelle Sorel, and manager Vane draw her into buried debts: Vane's unpaid loan from the dying Brandt, secured by "a play" rather than money, and creditor Skarke's inheritance of thirty lodged pages. Investigating registries, executors, and forged bills, Harrow uncovers Katterau's history—vanished bookkeeper Krug, wronged carpenter Grelle, Mirelle's hidden son Rupert Vorn, and Falk's guilt. She insists on honesty, certified copies, and paid debts throughout the tour (Vessendal, Achterhalt), while blank pages keep predicting real events. In the capital, Undersecretary Lenz reveals the play's Index history: fourteen partial "speakings," never completed. The company votes to perform it whole, under Office supervision, at the Theatre Royal. Harrow manages logistics, rules, and revelations—including abandoned boy Fenner Bacher, tied to a mysterious "Frau Dietz" and Kanzelgasse placements—while the performance proceeds successfully, certified by Lenz. Ilse Bacher's arrival resolves Fenner's crisis. Afterward, Lenz arranges the play's formal retirement, sealing all copies. Skarke identifies the note's origin family; Mirelle confesses her son's parentage. The case is closed, though Lenz notes Harrow unknowingly preempted the play's missing eleventh line before it was even written.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** Coming back up the Depository stair beside Lenz in her better coat, book under her arm, chalk long since washed off; hollowed out, level, and quietly appalled at what she has just been told, wanting to get to the 14th of Frost and hold the ladder for Mirelle.
**History:** I came into the Corona off a notice and told Vane yes, if the book was honest. The prompt book had two hands and a page cut out: a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat. Falk said the pages ride in Vane's unnumbered iron trunk in a Vessendal copyist's hand; Krug burned nine, the tenth came back, and he went without his boots. Skarke's letter had the company pledged to the last horse, the counting set at the third performance. Vane vanished from it, then owned it: nine years was a debt paid to a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke had bought a signature nobody gave. Falk said four acts and a matter following, the late man the creditor. I ruled Katterau no, and promised clean books.

Mirelle told me Anna Sorel was her sister, who kept Odalric's books. Perlmann, blind, swore the assignment, said the receipt was never finished, and handed over a nine-year packet: a counterfoil, a copyist's page I passed unread into Falk's lining, a key to the thirty pages Brandt held. Skarke, the child in the Katterau passage, took row four and withdrew his claim for eightpence and a seat — discharged, not forgiven — and at Achterhalt I took nine years off Vane. A false bill for the 14th of Frost brought me Ilse Bacher of the scullery door; I ordered her son Fenner, ten, kept home, and Falk, asking my help to finish it, took the boy's clause first.

Krug had burned nothing; page eight — a stage manager rings the bell — went into my coat unread. Lenz counted fourteen speakings in two hundred years, no watcher harmed, the makers paying, and Krug the man who requested the command. Twelve on benches said in. Grelle, owed seven pounds and eleven years of wrong mourning, proved my left-handed man. I entered row eleven, seat one, empty, as heard, told nine hundred and thirty-nine the truth, answered three knocks at the wrong door from a billsticker and a boy asking if this was the finish, and rang the bell once and answered it myself. Certified, 10:22. The boy was Fenner, put out of a cab by the gloved woman from Ilse's kitchen; Skarke's Kanzelgasse hundred made them a family. Mirelle signed her true name; Rupert Vorn is her son. Lenz sealed it all and said there was no eleventh part: it wrote a line for one more maker, I had already ruled nobody could volunteer, so the copyist struck it nine days before it was written. I booked the 14th for joy.
**Entry:** Footsteps down my aisle and I was in front of the pass door before I knew it, because a boy was asleep behind it. It was Ilse Bacher off a goods train in a horse-box, gloves in her fist, and she had shifted Grelle off my door and I don't blame her. A gloved woman had been in her kitchen Tuesday with the bolt on: a lie about a bill with her name near it, and the only safety being the boy seen and counted somewhere respectable with a programme, and five pounds left on the table. I told her unhurt, fed twice, laughing at my props boy; took the note by one corner as exhibit not money; held the door its whole width and warned her about the third board, which sang anyway. Then I stood out of the way of a mother on her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal, and heard Falk say Ilse of the Rose from ten feet off and go no closer. Skarke read the note without touching it: a sealed Kanzelgasse hundred, numbered, ten to a wrapper — a family by noon. I struck the night: beds, Boyle's lantern for Halloran, Grelle stood down and forgiven twice over, a lamp across town to Wenzel. Lenz offered retirement: accounted closed, sealed under the Hall of Records, every copy in by the 6th. I gave him yes with one condition of manner — given, not collected, and me standing at each. I laid down the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and page eight face-down, unread and now never read; he underlined the word. Then I booked the 14th of Frost for nothing but joy — by command: ours — and put Vane in it, and he told the doorframe why he hired me. Noon at the bank: Behn & Sonder, note six, the Vorn family, and Hessel Vorn's stamp on Katterau. Skarke carried his own thirty to Room Fourteen. At the Baraque I sat on a hamper and took Mirelle's whole account, her name in ink once, Rupert Vorn, the lying-in house, the ward she was never told, the extortion summons, and my son said out loud. I gave her four steps; she took my pencil and ruled them in my own book and signed her true name. Thursday the paper died. On the 6th I watched the case soldered and stamped twice straight, and on the stair Lenz told me there is no eleventh part and never was — it wrote a line for one more maker, and I had already ruled that nobody could volunteer, so the copyist struck it. Nine days before it was written.

#### Ilse Bacher

**State:** On the midday coach out of the capital with Fenner against her shoulder and Krul's hamper at her feet, fares paid; wrung out and fiercely grateful, wanting her own bolt on her own door and the 14th of Frost to come.
**History:** At fifteen I carried bread to nine men in a green room at the Rose, and heard those words through the scullery door. I let a small boy sit in the passage because he was small and had nowhere; nine years later he came back with money and a good coat and I answered his questions. Four years ago a man went round Katterau promising a reckoning, and I sent word, because opening that door was my part and I would not have Emeran Falk carry it.

Then, Thursday, I came in with butter and saw a bill on the barrel — four acts and a matter following on it — and sat down on the kerb in front of people. I watched from across Hessler's until the players came and an officer went in, and a woman crossed to me at hat-distance and named herself Bell Harrow. My message had reached Falk word for word, three days before, an hour out of Vessendal. She said he was well and sober, that six hundred people stood up for him, that the bill was not theirs, every copy impounded and the type broken. I gave her my man: no name, winter of the seventh year, thirties, cheap town clothes, a little book, left-handed, paid in shillings, knew of the reading because nobody in Katterau said it aloud, and asked how far did they get. I offered the scullery door at the Rose; she said no, a door I've paid twenty years for isn't opened twice. Only this: keep Fenner home on the 14th of Frost. I asked if that was what was coming for Falk, and she didn't answer.

Then Tuesday: the bill with my name near it that never existed, and five pounds left on my own table. I went down in a horse-box with the cows, moved the man on the door, and told the woman at the pass door everything. She took the note by one corner, called it evidence, said it stops owning me, and opened the door its whole width — mind the third board. I had the whole of Fenner against my coat, fed twice and laughing at her props boy. Falk stood by the wardrobe cage and did not come nearer; I said his name, he said mine, twenty years. A little bald gentleman said he could find the family by noon. We slept in queen's cloaks, had porridge, a hamper, our fares paid, and the poster man walked us to the coach office.

I have promised: the 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, in at the front door, good seats, Bacher with us.
**Entry:** Off the ten o'clock goods in a horse-box with the cows and walked in from the yards, and a man on the door said Fenner was inside and safe and then said I couldn't come in, so I moved him, and I am sorry for him. Then a woman standing across the pass door like a gate, asking my name and my business in that order, and I gave them and asked where my son was. She said unhurt, fed twice, laughing at her props boy, and I could hear him through the door. I told her the whole of Tuesday — the lady who knew about the Rose and the door I opened, the bill with my name near it that never existed, the being seen and counted at a theatre so his name went in the right ledger, and the five pounds left on my own table, which I have carried since and every hour of it wrong. She took it off me by one corner and called it evidence, and said it stops owning me now. Then she opened the door its whole width and told me to mind the third board. I went down on my knees on that stage floor and had the whole of him against my coat. Emeran Falk stood by the wardrobe cage and did not come nearer, and I said his name and he said mine, and twenty years. A little bald gentleman looked at my five-pound note as if it were a snake and said he could find the family by noon. They kept us in the nest of queen's cloaks, and in the morning there was porridge and a hamper and our fares paid and the poster man walked us to the coach office. I have promised: the 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, in at the front door, good seats, and Bacher with us.

#### Fenner Bacher

**State:** On the midday coach beside his mother with a programme still folded in his pocket; sleepy, happy and full of porridge, wanting to shake the thunder sheet again on the 14th.
**History:** The lady in the cab said I was expected. She gave me a bun and put me out at a theatre and never came back for me, and Mam had said go and be good and she'd fetch me after. The man with the paste on his hands took me up to his room and gave me bread, but I wasn't hungry. Then we went round the dark side of the building to a door, and he knocked three times, and it opened, and there was a lamp standing on the floor and warm air coming out. I asked if this was the finish, and the lady said yes, and that I was in time for it, and that I was asked-for. A boy called Toby took my hand and gave me a programme and put me in row eleven, seat one, right beside a lit door, and he sat on the step next to me the whole play and never once looked at the stage. The play was about a house and a man who owed money, and there was a boy in a passage who asked a question, and this time somebody answered him. A bell rang and everybody stood up and made a noise that wasn't clapping. Afterwards there was soup in the wing, and a lady with a thimble made me a bed out of cloaks and didn't fuss over me, and I had two bowls, and Toby showed me the big black sheet that makes the thunder and let me shake it low.

I was laughing at Toby when the board sang, and it was Mam. I ran to her and she got down on her knees on the stage and didn't let go for ages and cried into my hair. The lady with the thimble went and boiled water. We slept in the cloaks together, and in the morning there was porridge and a hamper, and the man with the paste on his hands walked us to the coach. Mam says we're going to the theatre again on the 14th, in at the front door, with Da.
**Entry:** I was laughing at Toby when the board sang, and it was Mam. I ran and she got down on her knees on the stage and didn't let go for ages and cried into my hair. The lady with the thimble went and boiled water. Then we slept in the cloaks together, and in the morning there was porridge and a hamper and the man with the paste on his hands walked us to the coach. Mam says we're going to the theatre again on the 14th, in at the front door, with Da.

#### Ansel Grelle

**State:** In the Baraque with a broom and his coat brushed, back on the doors; hollow, light, and unaccountably cheerful, wanting to be given another door to hold.
**History:** I pasted their bill at the labour exchange at nine and read it eleven times, then the other ten, then walked the city until four and knocked. She opened the door its whole width, set the lamp on the floor, and told me I was asked-for, not expected. I put my four questions in the wrong order and she answered all of them: Falk alive, six feet behind me in the dark; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten and putting me above his own boots; and both — seven pounds and the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch's dying had only re-addressed it to me. Falk came into the lamp, corrected my stance, said Boy, could not finish, and held my shoulder a long time. I confessed the book — sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got — and that I had read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's with no name to give, and asked to be put out the door rather than sat down under a lie. She said it plain: I am her left-handed man, my pages are a guest list, paid at dawn, receipted, a cot, and the eleventh line will not be me. Doors, house-side, with the boy. Vane counted the coin out loud and claimed he'd told suppers he paid it; I said I heard him at Merrow. I slept nine hours and woke wanting a broom.

That night I propped all eight exits and took Skarke's written promise at the door. When she told the truth from the stage nobody clapped; then people moved, and I had the door open for a woman with three children before she reached it. A drover came down from the gods to sit closer. Through the doors I heard the play they'd got as far as at Katterau, whole, the bell, Lenz saying Certified, and I stood there with both hands over my face and no shame in it. House out slow and warm, all eight doors. The man who'd knocked at the wrong door was Fenn Halloran off the north side, the other half of my wall by the newspaper offices; he'd read my paste eleven times, same as I had. Then a gentleman came past me who would not be announced or stopped, and I called down the aisle after him.

The next night I lost my door. A woman came at me out of the dark saying her son was inside and went past me like weather; I ran the aisle and stopped dead when Madam Harrow put her hand up. I stood at the top of the aisle and watched a mother get her boy back, and Madam Harrow told me the door I couldn't hold was a mother-shaped door, forgiven twice over, stand down. In the morning I asked to walk them to the coach office, because in eleven years I have been on the wrong side of every departure and wanted once to be on the right side of one. I carried the hamper; the boy waved from the step. Then back to the Baraque and a broom, and somewhere in the afternoon I heard myself laugh out loud in a theatre.
**Entry:** I lost my door. A woman came at me out of the dark saying her son was inside and she went past me like weather, and I ran the aisle after her and stopped dead when Madam Harrow put her hand up. Then I stood at the top of the aisle and watched a mother get her boy back, and Madam Harrow told me the door I couldn't hold was a mother-shaped door, forgiven twice over, stand down. In the morning I asked to walk them to the coach office, because I have been on the wrong side of every departure in eleven years and wanted once to be on the right side of one. I carried the hamper. The boy waved from the step. Then back to the Baraque and a broom, and somewhere in the afternoon I heard myself laugh out loud in a theatre.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the Baraque wardrobe cage with the cloaks aired and the slippers mended, thimble on; tired and thoroughly satisfied, wanting a quiet week and a hamper packed for Vessendal.
**History:** I answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal. At the fire I said my two things: the slippers had two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back with nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I don't want another warm box. She ruled no Katterau, and biting off my thread was my aye. Carried the slippers over my head into the Athenaeum yard, went down for the tin, and when I said a copper kettle at worst Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and everybody stopped on the word.

In the yard she untied the tape: a letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over unread, and a key with a word on the tag. Vane read it twice standing, and his face went a colour I hadn't seen. Then a hem and a matinee, which is what I am for. Another night my paint went through the door with Falk and came back none the worse; Vane toasted a wool factor and Prewick discovered food.

The new sky came in at Achterhalt and earned its place. Then the capital, eleven days early, and the Baraque, which leaks. In the yard it was Krug in a green coat, and I put the slippers down on wet cobbles four seconds; she counted, and said three too many, and was right, and I said four seconds is my whole opinion of a man. At supper Vane said it whole — he'd called Krug a thief to save his own face — and put seven pounds down; Krug wouldn't have it and gave her a parcel of nine pages instead, four not happened yet, one with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under my head.

On the bench I heard the whole scheme out and said in, since I'm not having a stranger in my cage, and asked for the twelve names read slow before anybody signed. She gave me that, cold, on the morning of the 2nd, no soup and no candle: ten names one by one, the struck eleventh, the blank twelfth, and the house entire. I told Toby he was seventeen twice, and the table laughed once, and that was mine. Krug's Palace sounded like a building that has thought about people. Frau Sorel stood up — I have never seen it — and told us her sister's name. I told Wenzel he had the best job in the building.

The dead lodger sat in the wing with paste on his cuffs and I put a plate in front of him and said nothing. I moved Prewick's dinner to his elbow, signed his minute, wrote Wenzel's name after his cross. They told me to my face what was going in my hamper — that's the law here — and I said I'd sit on it and sit still, and I did, all the way to the Office courtyard among the bicycles, and came home on an empty hamper and told her: lighter going home.

I dressed the ten and the slippers lasted the house. I stood in the wing where a child in row eleven could see my thimble catch the light, because she'd said stand where he can see you. Certified, and the iron, and soup in the O.P. wing, which that wing has never had. I made a nest of the queen's cloaks and never fussed over the boy, so he stopped being frightened and ate two bowls. Asked the kind question, he said a lady in a cab, not his Mam, on Tuesday — and Frau Sorel went the colour of paper with a cloak half over her arm, and I kept my mouth shut and my hands moving.
