Then the board sang and he was off the nest like a hare, and his mother was down on her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal with the whole of him against her coat. I boiled water, because there's nothing else to do with a thing like that, and sat by the nest all night while the two of them slept in the queen's cloaks. In the morning, porridge, a hamper packed for the coach, and her promise to come the 14th and bring the butter man. Nobody in my cage, and that child claimed by his own mother.
**Entry:** Board sang, boy was off the nest like a hare, and there was his mother down on her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal with the whole of him against her coat. I put down my thimble and went and boiled water, because there is nothing else to be done with a thing like that. Sat on a stool by the nest all night with the two of them asleep in the queen's cloaks and said sssh to nobody at least once. In the morning: porridge, and I packed them a hamper for the coach and made her promise to come the 14th and bring the butter man. Nobody in my cage, and that child claimed by his own mother. That's the whole of what I wanted and I got it.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** In the Baraque yard with his voice half back and a props list in his fist; a bit flattened by the departure and proud about the 14th, wanting a job to do this minute.
**History:** I answered present at the roll for front of house, props and pit band, and Herr Vane gave me chestnuts and a story about Vessendal. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads, I came back without the bucket, because a gentleman on a milestone asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. I offered to call Katterau, six hundred seats; she ruled no Katterau, and I boiled the water next morning unasked and she wrote me in her book under something new. At the Athenaeum I dropped the tailboard, took Boyle's watch, saw the tin go into the river. A gentleman left a cream card at half six and never used my doors. My standing orders: a programme on fourth row centre before the house opens, all three nights, count row four in and out, counts only. He came in early each night, and the last night with a rug; I ran the beginners call and carried Herr Falk's message down the aisle, one line about a door. Row four went in one and came out none, the rug left with a paper pinned to it. She made everybody bow first.

My voice went and stayed gone. A page waited under the milestone; at Achterhalt a bellman cried our name and words off Herr Falk's play, and she forbade repeating one word. I gave him his penny and he handed his whole roll of bills to Herr Prewick. The bailiff came with two constables and went away pleased. Two full houses, then a hundred and ten mile of toll road to the capital, where a clerk in green said we were expected and said *not the clerk, you, madam*. Boyle and I split double watch on the trunk. In the Baraque yard everything stopped for Herr Krug, who is on no list, and Herr Vane sat down in the wet and said aloud he had lied about him. I ran three letters to the evening post and made it. Krug showed me a lashing I'll use till I die and never once said *when I kept the book*. I heard nine pages summarised, one Madam Harrow's, one a room with fourteen on the door, and the Undersecretary in it is called Lenz. Herr Prewick promised me twice it isn't a relation.

I swept nine hundred seats for a bun. At the hearing I said I'm in; Krul said you're seventeen, I said nineteen, and that was the only laugh. The ruling put me with the house — programmes, rows, doors — because the house's people aren't makers. They read ten names cold and one was Lenz; she ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise. A Palace footman's letter she read out whole: a left-handed man has been reading our file.

At four in the morning Herr Grelle knocked, the one they said was dead, paste on his cuffs. From the back of the wing I heard Herr Falk take his shoulder, the sixty-one pages, Herr Vane counting money aloud, and Grelle saying he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Room Fourteen's letter, with a postscript about me: the ink that named a Lenz did not consult him, and he intends to be there anyway. Madam Harrow said ink casts and men choose, learn it by heart, and I have. I signed the minute twice because I blotted it, and said in again. Herr Skarke paid at the door like anybody. My count: doors open, all eight, nine hundred and thirty-nine in, one seat empty — row eleven, seat one. I put a programme on it. The roar for Herr Falk ran eleven seconds; at the interval nobody went out. She gave me her watch and went out and said it plain. When the knock was coming I carried her words, walking. A boy came in out of the dark holding a man's hand and asked if this was the finish; she said yes, and I took his other hand and walked him to row eleven, seat one, and sat on the aisle step all night. He said a lady in a cab told him he was expected and that the stage manager would know his name, and she did. Then the third board went and Fenner ran off the cot to his Mam, and I stood at the pin rail looking at a rope. Wenzel was fetched in. They went on the midday coach with Herr Grelle carrying the hamper. Herr Vane says I may hold the doors on the 14th of Frost at the Athenaeum. So that's mine.
**Entry:** I was making Fenner laugh and then the third board went and he was gone off the cot at a dead run, and it was his Mam. I went and stood at the pin rail and looked hard at a rope, because it wasn't my business any more and I wasn't going to be seen minding. She got down on the boards with him. Later Madam Harrow struck the night like a set and somebody was sent across town to fetch Wenzel in, and I'd have gone if my voice had been working. In the morning there was porridge and they went on the midday coach, and Herr Grelle carried the hamper. Herr Vane says I may hold the doors on the 14th of Frost at the Athenaeum. So that's mine.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** At the props table in the Baraque with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, drafting the report; steadier than he has been since Merrow, wanting Kessel's answer and his own copy of Lenz's inventory.
**History:** I came to this company seconded since Merrow, and began by reporting a fallen fire notice to Herr Vane and meeting the new stage manager on the stage: Harrow, spelled for the certificate. Her iron trunk stood unnumbered in the passage; behind the notice I found an older one about unnumbered property, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau — SEEN. NOT APPROVED, which is what a man writes when told to write nothing. Katterau was on no itinerary of mine: mine had Merrow, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance the 3rd of Frost; hers had Katterau and the 17th. We agreed neither would say Katterau first. I counted fire buckets, learned tin shaken low is thunder, and broke the sky on my only cue.

Two warm seats, fourth row centre, no hat, and nobody past my doors; Falk spoke a line in no certified copy. Harrow told me everything: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page, pages arriving in prompt books, what it stages coming true slantwise and late, Katterau unstaged and happening anyway, fourteen years of clean paper. I showed her my sewn-in Proscribed pages — thirty-one titles, two entered as anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following. Terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; Falk speaks no uncompared line. I asked for certified copies of all four plays and compared to line four hundred and twelve.

Falk gave me the tin at the river and I drowned it. In the registry: the lease, Brandt's deposits to an unreadable executor, and Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. I copied and stamped those three lines; the probate roll gave Perlmann, Josias, notary. A blind old man heard my starch and said records are the whole of the defence. At the post house I drafted the counterfoil request and paid the four shillings myself. Then the arithmetic: thirty pages in the cupboard, two hundred in the trunk — two halves, one work, and I obeyed her order to keep it out of any report, on purpose.

At Vessendal nothing occurred that was not in the book; I copied the withdrawn assignment, witnessed by the agent and Frau Loewe, stamped straight, ate Krul's mutton and discovered I was happy. At Achterhalt I impounded nine bills from the bellman — four acts and a matter following, one night only, by command, the Athenaeum, Thursday the 14th of Frost, dates matching no road we walk — with Hessler's broke-up type and one pound two and fourpence, lodged in Kessel's strongroom, and wrote to him that forgery of a Palace command exceeded us both.

At Northgate she was summoned to Room Fourteen, not me: Undersecretary Lenz, who kept both anonymous folios in the Index nineteen years and refused four applications to strike them. Krug came back; Vane confessed a theft he invented; I kept my notebook shut through nine unhappened pages. She came out at fifty-one minutes: the house requisitioned by Krug, Skarke paying the fee. At the hearing I stood and said my seal would either damn me or leave eleven liable, and wrote four sentences asking Lenz to certify in person; she countersigned. His name was already on the trunk's list.

Then the joint letter: Lenz certifies Part the Second himself, my seal unemployed, Assessment overruled me, in writing, to protect me. I drew the minute; every hand signed by four — Hebel a smudge, Wenzel a cross, the boy twice. The knock, the bell, 'Certified', the iron at eleven seconds. The wire went at twenty to eleven: FENNER SAFE, UNHURT. I took my hat off for the mother. Assessment offered retirement — sealed Depository, the Index annotated — my minute one of three legs, every page given and not collected, Lenz writing *unread* and underlining it.
**Entry:** I was in the corridor doorway when the mother came through the pass door, and I took my hat off, which is not in any instruction I have ever been given. I wrote nothing while it happened. Afterwards I heard Assessment offer retirement of a proscribed work — accounted closed, lodged sealed in the Depository, the Index annotated rather than struck — and heard that my minute, signed by every hand including a cross and a smudge, is one of the three legs it stands on. Nineteen years in that Index and it goes out on a signature I drew at a props table. Harrow required that every page be given and not collected, and Lenz wrote unread and underlined it. My report will record all of it whole, including that Assessment overruled me and that I obeyed on purpose.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** On the Baraque stage in his own coat with the lining empty and the rug over his arm, teaching Krug a crossing; spent, easy, twenty years lighter, wanting soup and the 14th.
**History:** I was awake at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when Bell Harrow came in out of the rain with the notice, and by evening she was our stage manager. She nailed the trough and the third joint, so I told her about the small upright hand: Krug's hurrying scrawl, gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made in Vessendal, riding in Odalric's iron trunk; nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, then no more Krug. Not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice. The pages went into my lining. Next night the trunk stood dragged into the passage, lid up, blank paper inside, Odalric's hat and one glove and no Odalric — and then Odalric came back by the wrong door with chestnuts, saying nine years is not the loan and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I told her Katterau: nine of us, a wager and a bottle, three and a half acts, and the cost — Anna Sorel, the boy Grelle, my voice for a season, Odalric's nerve. She ruled Katterau no, then not never.

At Vessendal a key came with an UNPAID tag; Vane read that Hessel Brandt had held not papers but thirty pages lodged by a party without a name. Skarke was the nine-year-old in the passage, come by the scullery door, arranging twenty years. I walked through our stage-left door on my cue and nothing came; the debt was discharged. A four-year-old message: tell him it was not his.

Ilse Bacher sent word that my voice through that door was the one that said no. I asked Harrow to help me finish it properly; she made it a standing page. Grelle came alive to my stage door with sixty-one pages. At the Palace I crossed to the wrong door and spoke the line. Lenz said Certified. I emptied my lining onto a government desk.
**Entry:** I came as far as the wardrobe cage and no further, because a woman kneeling on the boards with her boy does not need me nearer. She looked up over his head and said my name — Emeran Falk — and I said Ilse of the Rose, and twenty years, and put my hand over my own mouth like a man at a graveside, and that was the whole of what I had. Then the settle from Ilsabet, the rug over my knees, my hands steady, eyes shut, and the house going out lamp by lamp. In the days after I took the lining to Room Fourteen myself with the rug on: ten leaves and some odd, unpicked out of my coat and put down on a government desk. Lenz stood up for it. Twenty years of ballast, and I walked out lighter than the arithmetic allows. The 14th of Frost at Loewe's, Ilsabet, doors wide, played for nothing. I told Krug our left, you see, and meant it.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the Baraque yard with his lamp hung up and the unlit pipe in his teeth, checking the ropes on an empty trunk; sober and content, wanting the wagons loaded early for Vessendal.
**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin — second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud there used to be a Krug on that list and he wasn't on it. I gave the stage manager the soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the axle held, Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling toll or the free hill road that killed a horse on us, and Katterau twenty-two mile the wrong way. Ruling came down for the toll road, as I'd said first. I wired the axle and it held.

At the Athenaeum I watched the trunk, was relieved twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river, and told Krul a kettle's no good, a kettle's a bell — and learned by the silence that word had gone bad here. I stood in the ring while she opened the merchant's parcel. The little man with the brass case came Wednesday asking after her by name; I let him to talking distance and no farther. I took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it, no questions. My door held for Falk's cue and the house came down.

On the climb I found paper under the milestone and pulled up unasked. The bell was a crier with our name printed over him; Hessler was shut on a market Saturday with a lamp lit, two hundred bills nobody ordered, the old man happy tipping his type back. I reported the woman in the countrywoman's coat and town boots. The bailiff came civil.

At Achterhalt I warned Falk of her before taking his tailboard at midnight, pipe unlit. Then Krug on the mounting block in a green coat, and I gave him the plain of it: bill, bailiff, broken type. Vane named his own lie and put money down; Krug left it lying. Nine pages, one of them a wagon and a printer's line I stood in.

I said in, provided Wenzel stopped with the horses, and he said it himself. Then the tarpaulin thrown back and the trunk's lid up — a cast list, ten names, one struck, one blank. I told her twenty-two years carrying and roping, and I'd rather be on a list than off it. Wenzel's off it and has the horses. Names read cold; a Palace man at the gate, and I shut it behind him.

At four I stood back on her flat hand and the man who came in was the dead one. I sent Falk out of the arch, spelled words for Prewick's minute and signed it, drove Krul and the laundry hamper to the Office courtyard and asked nothing. Toby brought her words exact: wrong door, lamp low, open wide on the third knock — a billsticker with paste on his cuffs and a boy of ten asking if this was the finish. Krug's iron came in on eleven, as promised. I said nothing to the mother, walked the bill-poster to the north side while he talked of a lamp on the floor, then fetched Wenzel off the trunk; he argued and lost. The trunk's empty now. The 14th at Vessendal, front doors wide, Wenzel on the horses and told to his face it's the best job in the building.
**Entry:** Stood in the wing with my lamp when the mother came through and did not say a word, which was the right amount to say. Orders came quick: I was to walk the bill-poster home behind the lantern, so I did, all the way to the north side, and he talked the whole way about a lamp on the floor. Then across town with another lamp to fetch Wenzel off that trunk, and he argued about it, and lost, and slept against it in the yard till morning. Since then it's been ropes and hampers and the trunk still roped in the Baraque yard, empty as a bucket now, they tell me. And a booking: the 14th at Vessendal, front doors wide, and Wenzel on the horses and told to his face it's the best job in the building.

#### M. Skarke

**State:** Back in his own office in a plain black coat, wrapper and slip locked away, the strongbox empty for the first time in twenty years; frightened, useful and oddly light, wanting the Vorns' reason inside three days and to be allowed to want nothing.
**History:** I let myself into that house early by no door of theirs and sat fourth row centre with my rug, read the programme through, and counted the joints: the trough is better nailed than Katterau, and you hear it in the run. She came down the aisle and I spoke without turning, apologised, and told her the truth — that I had wanted to be in a theatre with these people since I was nine, that thirty pages and twenty years of getting richer had bought me nothing, that I had it all from clerks because clerks are cheap. She sat one seat away, called me Herr Skarke, said half a play is hungrier than none, and that they do finishes here, on the hour. Frau Sorel took the house by her fourth line; on the hour the great ruin came through the practical door and nothing happened but a door opening. I left the rug for Falk with a pin and a note: claim withdrawn, keep the halves apart, keep her keys, never let me nearer than row four. The remaining nights I paid at the door in a plain black coat, no rug, having given the man on the pit doors my undertaking not to move and not to say one word aloud, and told her so at hat-distance with my hands shaking.

When she offered the doors I did not move, and nine hundred-odd stayed. Afterwards she sat beside me and asked for the bank in me, not the boy, and I gave it: a placement is a standing order identical to the penny for eighteen years; Dietz is nothing to me, but the Kanzelgasse firm serving four families, gloved women with plain names, fees paid quarterly out of the florist's account, is. Then the thing she would not like — I had paid the requisition fee through the Kanzelgasse, so those clerks have known for two years these people were coming to the Palace on the 3rd, which of them, and with what.

Next morning I stood where I had no business standing and watched a mother get her son back on a stage floor. I read the five-pound note without touching it: out of a sealed hundred, ten to a wrapper, numbered in sequence, drawn by the Kanzelgasse for the families. By noon I had it — the 9th of Reap, Behn & Sonder, one client's fees, note six; of four clients, the Vorn family of the Bittersee, and a Hessel Vorn who stamped SEEN, NOT APPROVED at Katterau in the fifth year. The same family paying a placement out of this city since that year, and sending a gloved woman into two kitchens this week. I do not yet know why; I will in three days. I took my father's thirty pages from the strongbox to give her, then took them back, because she had told Lenz given, not collected — and carried them to Room Fourteen myself, saying over them that my father lodged them against seven pounds and a wool factor's kindness, that I had wanted them twenty years, and that they were never mine. Lenz stood and read the receipt aloud. She put her hand out to me across a government desk. Second time. I am to audit a nursery next, and report to Frau Sorel, not to them.
**Entry:** I followed her in where a man of my standing has no business standing, hat in my hands, and saw a mother get her son back on a stage floor. Then I asked to see the five-pound note without touching it and knew it at once: not out of a purse — out of a sealed hundred, ten to a wrapper, drawn by the Kanzelgasse for the families, numbered in sequence. I said I would have the family by noon and she let me want nothing for it, which cost her something. By noon I had it: drawn the 9th of Reap out of Behn & Sonder against fees for one client, note number six, and of their four clients the Vorn family — the house at the Bittersee, and a Hessel Vorn who stamped SEEN, NOT APPROVED at Katterau in the fifth year. The same family that has paid a placement out of this city since the fifth year and sent a gloved woman into two kitchens this week, and I do not yet know why, and I will in three days. Then I lifted my father's thirty pages out of the strongbox to give her — and took them back, because she had told Lenz given, not collected. I carried them to Room Fourteen myself and said over them that my father lodged them against seven pounds and a wool factor's kindness, that I had wanted them for twenty years, and that they were never mine. Lenz stood up for it and read the receipt aloud. She put her hand out to me across a government desk. Second time. I am to audit a nursery next, and report to Frau Sorel and not to them.

#### Undersecretary Lenz

**State:** On the Depository stair with the keeper's lamp behind him, spectacles pushed up, hands empty of the folio for good; steady and inwardly shaken, wanting the annotation lodged in the Index today and never to be told he was wrong about the eleventh line.
**History:** Nineteen days in post, and my folder already held eleven safety notices, a sheet of tin buried with a hymn, a bill stopped in Achterhalt, nine years' storage paid on a stranger's box, Katterau ruled out, and a company brought into the capital eleven days early. I asked her what was in Vane's trunk. She drank the tea, gave me seen and hearsay separately, quoted my predecessor's stamp back at me, and answered three times in the same words: one line, Vessendal, an emergency, Falk, in the wings, upstage, and company law since. Fourteen speakings in two hundred years; the fourteenth cost this office four years. I told her the fifteenth was scheduled, requested of the Palace and not by it, my office consulted and consenting, and then showed her the requisition: A. Krug, of the fourth ward. She read it twice.

Next she asked her three questions in the promised order, and I gave her everything: the audience never harmed in two hundred years yet the house required, six readings among players doing nothing, my margin note of appetite that I was told to strike; the makers who pay; Anna Sorel's line and the pencil against Krug; Skarke named aloud, his the most careful letter I ever had from a rich man; and my twice-passed-over opinion — yes, once, correctly, whole, stopped by nobody. At my door I warned her that her name was in the requisition file, and that a refusal must be loud, early, and in writing to me, and I would make it the Office's and carry it.

I wrote them jointly: text in my hands by six on the 2nd, determination minuted and lodged, the eleventh line left alone, Prewick recorded as overruled by Assessment to keep his rank, and a postscript about the boy, since ink is not consent. At nine she carried the folio up my east stair herself; I took it from underneath, told the clerk nobody at all, not the Comptroller. Two hundred and eleven leaves, no title, four acts and a matter following. I read her the receipt aloud and gave her the sealed certificate. Asked how she would call a play she had never read, she said you call what's happening — I copied that into my own notebook. My predecessor's file blamed Katterau's failure on the absence of a stage manager; nineteen years I took that for a sneer at a trade.

From the prompt desk I watched her announce it to nine hundred and thirty-nine people in working clothes: no title, the record, the actuary at her elbow, witness asked, exits lit, no bravery required, one seat let be. No applause; twenty left decently. Falk began from memory and nothing went cold. The knock was written as three knocks from outside the theatre; she said, "Then we answer it," and called me the best flyman she ever had. She rang the bell herself. Falk nine lines, Sorel four, Vane one unrounded, then the three still and the house entire. I said "Certified" in the Office's voice; the iron came in at eleven seconds. Afterwards I authorised the night telegraph to Assessment for a lost child, in my own name, not asking if it was within my competence.

A mother came through the pass door for her child; I did not intrude. When Harrow came I stayed seated, hands on the folio, and gave him what Assessment wants and what it can do: retirement, unused since the eleventh year — accounted closed, lodged sealed, the Index annotated, not struck. Two requirements I already held; for the third she gave me the leaves on her condition: given, not collected, each holder surrendering by their own hand, herself standing by. The cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and page the eighth face-down, surrendered unread — I wrote unread, underlined, and forbid my successor to correct it. I stood for each: Skarke's thirty, Falk's ten and some odd from a coat lining, Frau Sorel's single page carried alone. On the 6th, three floors beneath the Hall of Records, I sealed all of it in a lead case, soldered, stamped twice straight, labelled ACCOUNTED CLOSED, shelf, row nine. On the stair I told her my finding, having read every leaf twice: there is no eleventh part and never was. It wrote an eleventh line expecting one more maker; she had ruled that nobody could volunteer, and the copyist strikes what is not needed. She struck it nine days before it was written.
**Entry:** I sat at the prompt desk squaring two hundred and eleven leaves while a woman came through the pass door for her child, and I did not intrude on it. When Harrow came to me I did not stand up, because I had a thing to say and wanted my hands on the folio while I said it. Two entries: what Assessment wants, and what Assessment can do. In law the folio goes back in the trunk and my office minds it another nineteen years — unless we are clever, and there is a procedure unused since the eleventh year: retirement. Certified as accounted closed, lodged sealed in the Depository, the Index annotated rather than struck. Three requirements, and I had two of them in my hands already: the certified performance with the audience noted, and Prewick's minute with every name. The third was the entire text, and I asked her at last about the leaf in her coat. She gave me yes with a condition I shall keep for the rest of my service: given, not collected, each holder surrendering by their own hand, herself standing at each. She laid down the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and one leaf face-down — page the eighth, surrendered unread. I wrote unread and underlined it and shall forbid my successor to correct it. Then I walked home, which I have never once wanted to do. In the days after I sat from nine and stood up for each: Skarke's thirty, Falk's ten and some odd out of a coat lining, Frau Sorel's single page carried alone. On the 6th, three floors under the Hall of Records, I put the whole of it into a lead case, had the seam soldered, stamped twice straight, and labelled it: ACCOUNTED CLOSED. Shelf, row nine. On the stair I gave her my finding, having read every leaf twice, which nobody else alive can say: there is no eleventh part and never was. It wrote an eleventh line because it expected one more maker, and she had already ruled that nobody could volunteer, and the copyist strikes what is not needed. She struck it nine days before it was written.

#### Hebel

**State:** At his board with the wheel shut off and the pilot burning, coat on to go; calm and quietly proud, wanting his bed and the same board on the 14th.
**History:** I was asked to stay for a hearing I never expected, and there I learned what the thing was and what it cost, and that whoever gives the light is counted among those who make it. Gas is my trade, and I said plainly I'd light this on one condition: the board would be mine, no hand but mine on the wheel. She ruled it so, and my name was read out with ten others in the cold morning.

I signed the minute with my name and a smudge off the wheel, and when she asked again in the grey light, I said it again — board mine, then in. That night the gas came up, the wheel under my hand alone, and the iron came down twice at eleven seconds.

For Part the First the board stayed mine, untouched, and it went as rehearsed; she told me afterward it was the best gas she'd worked with, and I mean to keep that. For Part the Second she gave me the house to half, the stage to warm, slow as a sunrise, all night, and it was ours. I brought the lights down gold to amber to shadow, slower than I have ever done it. Falk walked into the warm and the gas never fluttered. Strangers came in at the wrong door and she said nothing changes on the wheel; I said the same, and nothing did. It was certified, eleven seconds, and the house went out slow and warm.

Nobody touched my wheel but me, and I brought that whole house down lamp by lamp until nothing was left but the pilot, one blue tooth of flame. A mother and child slept in the cloaks in the wing, and I gave them no glare to wake to. Best gas I have ever done, twice over.
**Entry:** Nobody touched my wheel but me, and I brought the whole of that enormous house down slow, lamp by lamp, till there was nothing but the pilot — one blue tooth of flame and the smell of nine hundred and forty people cooling. There was a mother and a child asleep in the cloaks in the wing and I gave them no glare to sleep in. Best gas I have ever done, twice over.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the Baraque in the plum coat with his hat brushed, printer's copy for a new bill in his pocket; sober, useful and almost unbearably grateful, wanting the 14th of Frost done handsomely and nobody to thank him for it.
**History:** Bell Harrow came in out of the weather with my notice in her fist and three references on three fingers, and I engaged her in ten minutes, promising plot tables, a bucket, and a figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal. I steered her off the trunk, and when I was alone I lifted it and it came up light and wrong. Then I told her the lie I had been selling myself since Merrow: the Palace said the 3rd, I had said the 17th, because there was no money for four towns and Katterau had six hundred seats and a mayor who owed me. Skarke's man had counted our seats from the street.

Cornered by a torn playbill, I confessed the rest: nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, my dying friend, and paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke had bought the papers. She set me to write every name in that room in ink — Brandt on the Kohlgasse, Perlmann the notary, Anna Sorel, a doctor, a nun, myself, the man in the passage I never saw. She ruled Katterau dead, the 3rd standing, and drove us to Vessendal. Josias found the worn place on my cuff — nine years, the same coat — and swore I came at eleven at night with the whole of it, that Hessel laughed and would not sign, and died on the Tuesday. Perlmann proved the bag: Farriers' and Merchants', drawn at Achterhalt, carried two days on my knees. Then the letter: the four hundred and twelve marks were never Hessel's to lend, he held them from a fund for a party he never named, took that party's marker as security, locked it in the green-room cupboard and tagged the key *unpaid*. The marker was the play — thirty pages, not a folio.

That night Skarke's second sheet was endorsed *withdrawn*, witnessed by the agent and Frau Loewe. Discharged, said the agent, not forgiven. I sat on too small a stool owing no man anything and asked Harrow what we do now. Learn to be solvent, she said: two nights, Perlmann's oath before Braun on Thursday, then Achterhalt, then the capital early. I toasted Hessel Brandt, wool factor, and did not round the number. I gave her the float bag and asked her to ask me for a thing.

She asked for Achterhalt: the front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed. Eleven minutes, paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H. I put the receipt over the notice in my pocket, found her sky in a black plate with a floor in it, and refused to round the price where she could watch. In the capital I found Anselm on a mounting block and confessed I had made him a thief over seven pounds of Wednesday take, knowing his address two years. I wrote three letters in ink, said it whole at supper, laid the money down; he would not take it, and gave her nine pages instead.

Then Falk spoke of Grelle, and I heard myself admit I never paid the landlady's seven pounds either — eleven years of suppers, the same seven pounds. I gave up Frau Hentsch's brown door on the Rasselgasse, which I walked past twice in the ninth year; Harrow advertised, Hentsch came at four in the morning, and I counted it out unrounded on the props table. He had heard me lie at Merrow with paste on his hands. Grelle got a cot and the doors. I went in again on the 2nd, in the cold, no soup, no candle.

On the night I wept on cue, took an unannounced entrance, spoke my one line, which is a number, and stood still while Lenz said *Certified*. Now Harrow tells me what I am: a solvent company with no man's debt on it, and the Athenaeum on the 14th of Frost, by command — Ilsabet, doors wide, played for joy, Loewe on fifteen unrounded, our dead toasted at the interval. I told the doorframe why the last stage manager left in the night at Katterau, and she may put it in the book.
**Entry:** I stood at her corner with my hat in my hand like a man waiting to be told what he is in, and she told me: a solvent company, a certified miracle behind it, no man's debt on it. And a booking — the 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, one night only, by command, because the bill exists and the words on it are ours now. Ilsabet, front doors standing wide, played for nothing but joy, Loewe's house, Perlmann on his daughter's arm, Ilse and the boy in through the front door in the good seats, and our dead toasted at the interval: Hessel, Anna, Frau Hentsch, and every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house. I opened my mouth to weep and decided not to, which I count as the best work I have done all tour. By command: ours — I shall have it printed in Hessler's own case with a note that the man was blameless. Loewe gets fifteen and not a penny rounded down. Then at the pass door I told the doorframe the thing I have not said: nineteen days, and I hired her in ten minutes because the last one left in the night at Katterau and I would rather have died than tell her why, and she may put in the book that I have said why. Next day I drove her to the bank, and the lift boy called me sir, and a young man listened to me on the acoustics of the Corn Exchange for a quarter of an hour.

#### Wenzel

**State:** Asleep and then waking against the roped trunk on the tailboard in the grey, damp and stiff, horses to see to; easy in himself and glad to have been outside the room, wanting breakfast and the horses fed.
**Entry:** Sat on that trunk in the yard from the afternoon on, doing nothing, as arranged. Then a man came across town with a lamp very late and told me it was finished and the boy was safe, neither of which I knew, and said I was relieved. I argued. I lost. So I stopped where I was and slept against the thing, and it rained on the lid and there was nothing overhead but morning. They tell me the trunk is empty now and the papers gone under the Hall of Records. I have been told to my face that the horses on the 14th of Frost are the best job in the building, and I intend to go on believing it.

#### Fenn Halloran

**State:** At home in his own room on the north side with paste dried white on his cuffs, boots off; dazed, proud and half asleep, wanting to see the bill for the 14th and to tell somebody who'll believe him.
**History:** I first came to know the theatre through a boy left alone on the Baraque step, put out of a cab by a lady who said she'd be back and never came. Nobody at the stage door would fetch anyone, so I brought him to my room, gave him bread he wouldn't eat, and heard him say he was expected at the theatre that night. I'd read Ansel's pasted bills eleven times over — ask at the stage door for the stage manager, any hour — so I took him there and knocked three times. A woman opened it with a lamp low on the boards, and when the boy asked if this was the finish, she told us we were asked-for, not expected. She put me at her corner and I stood there through the whole of it, mouth open, and afterward found I'd been crying into a paste-white cuff without knowing when it started. I gave my name — Fennimore Halloran, north side — and told her the boy wasn't mine: Fenner Bacher, who can read. She said I'd done every part of it right, called it three debts, and had me fed and walked home by a man with a lantern.

I was still eating at her corner when the boy's mother came and got down on the floor with him. I wasn't needed for that part either, only stood by with my mouth open same as before. Then the big fellow walked me home behind his lantern all the way to the north side, and I talked the whole way like a fool. Three debts, she called it. All I did was knock on a door.
**Entry:** I was still at her corner being fed when the boy's mother came through and got down on the floor with him, and I stood there with my mouth open the same as I had all night. Nobody needed me for that part. Then the stage manager said I was to be walked home behind a lantern, and I was — a big fellow with a lamp, all the way to the north side, and I talked the whole way like a fool. Three debts, she called it. All I did was knock on a door.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** In the Baraque wardrobe cage with the hem finished, gloves folded in her pocket and her name written once in Harrow's book; raw, upright and no longer alone with it, wanting the auditor's report and to be asked nothing until it comes.
**History:** I told the new one, Harrow, to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears, and gave her the ladder and the trunk. Her first page carried nine years, a bell rung and nothing answering, a debt in a plum coat; nine is not my number. The pages began at Vessendal two springs ago and come true late — a lame horse, then the mare down outside Merrow. Mine is ten. I gave her my honest plot tables and cued her Ilsabet.

Then a page with ten in it: a child ten this winter who does not know the word mother, a woman crossing a border twice, the second crossing a kind invitation. I carried it in my glove. Harrow told me Odalric was selling us the 17th to buy Katterau though the Palace had set the 3rd; I spoke for the capital, and she buried Katterau. I told her Anna Sorel was my sister, who kept Odalric's accounts in the fifth year and left a sealed box at Vessendal the week before she died; I could not enter the registry, my name being on paper there. Anna had asked Perlmann whether a sealed box could ever be read, and wept at no; Hessel Brandt held a piece of the play, not papers.

I confessed my name was never Sorel — a police file, a magistrate's date, a passport spelling a third thing — and asked only that the box stay shut and be mine. Loewe's woman from Katterau wore my mother's coat and stood as I stand. A page came with no number at all: a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who does not go in. The Achterhalt bill's bottom line was nine years old.

Krug came back, and Odalric owned in the yard that he had lied about the seven pounds and had known where Krug was these two years; he unsaid it at supper, and Krug gave Harrow nine pages he swore he burned, the ninth a cast list of twelve blanks.

At the hearing I stood and spoke last — Anna, my billing here ten years ago under a name I had stopped owning, the matter I would not explain — and went in for Anna's account, on the condition that the Vessendal box stay shut and endowed fifty years out of the fee. Grelle was alive. I played Ilsabet to nine hundred; three knocks came from outside the walls and I used the pause.

Then a boy of ten spoke of a lady in a cab on Tuesday, and I gave Harrow Frau Dietz's kind letter: a misunderstanding, a family glad to receive me, a child placed out in the fifth year, ten this winter. Harrow named Behn & Sonder and the Vorns of the Bittersee, and Hessel Vorn, who stamped a notice at Katterau in the fifth year. So I gave her all of it: Rupert Vorn, four nights in the second year, dead in the mountains; the lying-in house in the eighth ward; the papers I signed at twenty-three; extortion charged for asking where my boy had gone; the mountains on a Monday night; Odalric hiring me at Merrow without one question. I said my son aloud, signed my true name to her four steps, and carried my page to Room Fourteen alone.
**Entry:** I was in the wardrobe cage with my sleeves rolled, mending the hem I tore in the second act of a play I had never read, when Harrow came and gave me a name. Behn & Sonder. Note number six. The Vorn family, of the house at the Bittersee — and a Hessel Vorn, district officer, who stamped a notice at Katterau in the fifth year. My needle stopped. Vorn. Well. Ten years I have carried two griefs, and they are one grief: the young man, the summons for a Tuesday, and the child of the fifth year. They have been paying since the fifth year, which means they kept him, which means the kind letter on good paper is not generosity — it is a family that has learned their placement is ten this winter and their name is about to be read out in a Palace by players. I told her to sit down and take out her book, and gave her the whole of it in order, no adjectives: my own name, which she wrote and will not repeat; Rupert Vorn, four nights in the second year, nineteen and charming; the lying-in house in the eighth ward; the papers I signed at twenty-three with no money and no advice; the ward I was promised and never told. The tenth year: Rupert dead in the mountains, the lawyers finding my two letters, and a charge of extortion for asking where my boy had gone. Over the mountains on a Monday night with a passport that spells a Kessarine town, and Odalric hiring me in a yard at Merrow without one question. Ten years of gloves. And then I said it out loud for the first time in my life: my son. She said this cage has good acoustics. Then she gave me four steps — the paper dies first, the keeping verified by my auditor reporting to me, the meeting only if the child is asked and says yes, on my ground, at his pace, and their name never spoken by this company — and handed me the pencil. I wrote them in her book in my own hand and signed my true name, on paper for the first time in ten years. Ruled. Then I put my face in my hands and let her sit there while I cried. Later I carried my one page to Room Fourteen alone, and came back with my gloves folded in my pocket.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** On the Baraque stage in shirtsleeves with a rope in his hand, taking Falk's crossing; steady and unburdened, wanting the 14th plotted properly and the exits walked twice as usual.
**Entry:** Back at the Baraque, plotting nothing dangerous for once. Falk had me out on the stage going through a crossing — our left, you see, she said our left — and I let him teach me a thing I already knew because he wanted to teach it. They tell me the whole text went under the Hall of Records in a lead case, mine included, and that the trunk is a trunk. Two years of stone, and now a hamper to load and a house at Vessendal on the 14th.

#### Lift boy

**State:** Standing in his lift in the marble hall of the Skarke bank with the gate half open; pleased with himself, wanting the plum-coated gentleman to come back and finish about the Corn Exchange.
**History:** Took a gentleman in a plum coat and a lady with a book up to the top floor, and called him sir, and he went pink about it. Coming down again he stopped in the hall and talked to me for a quarter of an hour about the acoustics of the Corn Exchange, and I listened, because nobody in this building has ever explained anything to me before.
**Entry:** Took a gentleman in a plum coat and a lady with a book up to the top floor, and called him sir, and he went pink about it. Coming down again he stopped in the hall and talked to me for a quarter of an hour about the acoustics of the Corn Exchange, and I listened, because nobody in this building has ever explained anything to me before.

#### Depository keeper

**State:** In the Depository among a hundred yards of iron shelving with the key-ring on his hip and the soldering iron cooling; incurious and orderly, wanting the row nine ledger written up before he goes off.
**History:** The Office man came down with a lady in a good coat, three floors under the Hall of Records, and had me solder a lead case: eleven minutes and a stink of hot metal. He would not touch the papers again once they were in. Stamped his seal twice, straight both times, wrote his label, and pasted a second slip beside it saying one leaf was lodged unread and was not to be corrected. I have never carried that instruction before. Shelf, row nine. My key, my iron door.
**Entry:** The Office man came down with a lady in a good coat, three floors under the Hall of Records, and had me solder a lead case: eleven minutes and a stink of hot metal. He would not touch the papers again once they were in. Stamped his seal twice, straight both times, wrote his label, and pasted a second slip beside it saying one leaf was lodged unread and was not to be corrected. I have never carried that instruction before. Shelf, row nine. My key, my iron door.

### 13 · Rain on the Trunk, and Row Four at Katterau
- **Messages:** 245-264

Harrow files her correction at the Depository, posts a notice rather than striking any line, and lets the copyist cut what's unneeded. She shakes Lenz's hand and invites him to tea; he agrees to come on the 9th, then goes up to the Hall of Records.

In the Baraque yard, the iron trunk is leaking rain. Boyle points it out; Harrow writes a notice, which Boyle pins to the wet iron on principle. She orders a bucket, then paint—Dessa picks vermilion, two coats, costing Toby his Thursday—and rules the trunk will carry the thunder sheet. Falk calls it "vulgar," approvingly. Skarke's standing invitation goes out in writing; his reply is four words: "Row four. Any night." Wenzel wakes gently and asks if the play was good; Krug says it was a great one.

On the 9th, Lenz drinks three cups of terrible tea over Prewick's fair copy. On the 11th, the wagons roll. Harrow closes the last open account by demanding her own wages; Vane counts out four pounds five and six—two shillings above his hiring rate—and weeps, driving off singing. At Achterhalt, Kessel waves them through and Hessler prints their bill free, keeping one copy for himself.

At Vessendal, Loewe lets the house for thirteen though Vane pays fifteen. Perlmann, walked onstage, says, "It is smaller than it sounds." The house is full and free; Vane toasts absent stage managers. Mirelle delivers Skarke's unopened audit minutes before beginners; Harrow refuses to read it yet, pocketing it, law unchanged.

Later, by the kettle, Mirelle reads it: her son, Anton, is twelve, safely placed with a steward's family, schooled, fed, unable to spell. Harrow rules no hurry—he'll be asked, in spring, on Mirelle's terms. Mirelle asks for time, privacy, and warns she'll one day ask something enormous. Harrow says yes.

Toby reports nine hundred and one paying bodies; Harrow records it, posts nothing. Falk, questioned on the standing page, calls it "a ledger with legs" and is folded into the repertory, tasked with teaching Fenner Bacher to stand.

Winter settles the company. In spring, on the Katterau road, Mirelle asks her enormous thing—a season's leave. Harrow says yes before she finishes. In Katterau, Falk gives away bread, laughs, repeats Perlmann's line. At the half, Krug hands over a slip: one seat sold, row four centre, paid at the door—Skarke, unannounced, "on the hour."

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the struggling Vermilion Players, inheriting a cursed, leaking iron trunk, a torn prophetic prompt page, and tangled debts to creditor Skarke tracing back to Katterau, a town where an unfinished, two-hundred-year-old "play" once nearly happened. She uncovers the histories of Odalric Vane's hidden debts, Falk's guilt, Mirelle Sorel's dead sister Anna and hidden son Rupert/Anton, vanished bookkeeper Anselm Krug, and clerk Prewick's Office files on thirty-one banned works. Through Perlmann, Loewe, Grelle, and Bacher, buried debts, lies, and abandoned children surface, all threading back to the same folio. Official Lenz reveals the play's rules: it must be performed whole, consented, witnessed, never interrupted. Harrow assembles the company, rules on debts and volunteers, and stages the complete play at the Theatre Royal under certification, filling the long-blank "eleventh line" role by ringing the bell herself. The performance succeeds without harm, retiring the work under seal. Aftermath ties loose ends: debts paid, Fenner Bacher reunited with his mother, Skarke identified and reconciled, the trunk repainted vermilion. The company becomes solvent under Harrow's stewardship. In spring, back at Katterau, Mirelle takes leave to see her hidden son, and Skarke quietly attends another performance, seated as always in row four.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.
**Entry:** I gave Lenz my correction on the landing — no line struck, a notice posted, the copyist cutting what wasn't needed — and shook his hand and owed him tea. He said the 9th. Then home through the grey, and the trunk in the rain, doing nothing at all but leak, so I wrote it a notice and gave it a bucket and then paint: Dessa's vermilion, and the thunder sheet inside a box that has learned to hold its tongue. Skarke's invitation went in writing and came back four words. On the 11th I closed the last open account in my own book and made Vane count nineteen days into my palm in the arch — four and six, not three shillings, because he'd been paying me in his head since Achterhalt and could not say it without weeping. Four pounds five and six, unrounded, and he drove out singing.

Vessendal free and full, Vane toasting our dead and my whole trade. Mirelle brought me a sealed audit four minutes before beginners; I refused the hour and took the letter into my coat, and after the iron, with the kettle on, she read it standing: he's twelve, and his name is Anton, and he draws and cannot spell. The tens can retire. Spring, her ground, his pace, me present. Row four sold and paid at the door, one and six, no hat — entered exactly, posted nowhere.

Falk taught me how a bookkeeper closes what the world answered: transfer it. So I ruled him into the repertory and into the repertory's work — teaching a boy to stand — and struck the standing page clean across.

Winter, then Katterau by daylight. I stood where he could see me in the Rose and touched nothing, and kept his entry in pencil. Mirelle asked her enormous thing on the box and I said yes before she finished, as contracted. And at the half a slip came from the mayor's clerk: one seat, row four centre, paid at the door, not to be told until now. On the hour.

#### Undersecretary Lenz

**State:** Back at his desk in the Office with the annotation lodged and a folder that no longer frightens him; steady, quietly warm, wanting his invitation to hold good next quarter.
**History:** Nineteen years I served before anyone asked me the right question in the right order, until the stage manager came about a trunk. She drank her tea, gave me seen and hearsay separately, and quoted my predecessor's forbidden stamp back at me. I told her the fifteenth speaking of the play was scheduled and requested of the Palace, and handed her the requisition naming a boy of the fourth ward, A. Krug.

She asked her three questions in order, and I answered fully: the audience never harmed in two hundred years, the house nonetheless required; I named Skarke, and the makers who pay; I gave my long-withheld opinion that it had once been done correctly, whole, stopped by nobody. I warned her that her name was in the file, and that any refusal must come to me loudly, in writing.

She and Krug applied jointly, the first correct application in nineteen years. I set three requirements — the text in my hands, the determination signed and lodged, the eleventh line untouched — and overruled Prewick through Assessment to protect his rank. She brought me two hundred and eleven leaves on the 2nd, and I gave her a certificate against any magistrate.

I sat at the prompt desk for the performance: nine hundred and thirty-nine people, an announcement in the only order that could hold, no bravery required, Falk's nine lines, Sorel's four, Vane's one unrounded. I said "Certified" aloud as the iron came in at eleven seconds.

Afterward the leaves were surrendered one by one, unread where she asked, and I sealed the whole in lead three floors under the Hall of Records: ACCOUNTED CLOSED. I found there was no eleventh part — she had struck it nine days before it was written. She named me the best colleague she never met. I have gone back for her terrible tea three times since, and wanted nothing more since the eleventh year.
**Entry:** On the landing she entered her correction, and it was better than my finding: she posted a notice and the copyist cut what wasn't needed. I let it stand in the file that way. She put her hand out and called me the best colleague she never met and offered me the worst tea in the fourth ward, so I shook it once and said the 9th, and went up to the Hall of Records with my hat straight.

I went on the 9th and sat on a hamper in the O.P. wing while Prewick, humming with uprightness, read me his fair copy of the minute, and I drank two cups of genuinely terrible tea and then a third. I went twice again in the winter and did the same. Nobody has offered me anything since the eleventh year that I wanted so much.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the Katterau theatre yard at the half with his lamp lit and the unlit pipe in his teeth, wagons settled; sober and content, wanting a quiet house and an early load-out.
**Entry:** Oiling a hinge in the yard when she came back, and the rain came on, ordinary rain, and it lay on that trunk and ran off the corner and made a puddle like anything else in the world. I said out loud, Madam, that's leaking, and I have not enjoyed a sentence so much in twenty-two years. She wrote the notice on the spot and I pinned it to the wet iron, and it went to pulp in a minute and I left it, because that's the principle. Vermilion after, two coats, and it holds the thunder now.

Held the float purse while Vane counted her wages out in the arch, and marked the figure: four and six a day, not three shillings. Then first wagon out and a hundred and ten mile north, Achterhalt, Vessendal, and a house at nothing a head. Told the Bacher boy a lie about horses because he'd earned one. Rolled again in the spring for Katterau with the trunk on the tailboard and the props boy asleep against it, and argued a lashing with Krug for pleasure.

#### Wenzel

**State:** At the horse lines behind the Katterau theatre with a nosebag and a wisp of straw, coat wet at the shoulders; easy and unbothered, wanting the horses fed and his supper kept warm.
**Entry:** Asleep against the wheel, off duty, nobody having told me. They woke me gently and sat me down to tell me it was finished, which I said was fair enough — someone had to be off it. I asked was it a good play, and Krug said it was a great one, so that's settled and I went back to sleep. Horses to the capital gate and out again, the horses to Vessendal, the horses to Katterau in the spring. Best job in the building, and I go on believing it.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.
**Entry:** That trunk leaked in the rain like a coal scuttle, and I was asked to choose its paint, so I chose vermilion, being what we are, and the ironmonger had it honest. Two coats and Toby's whole Thursday, and Herr Falk stood over it drying and said it was vulgar in the voice men use for praise, and put the thunder in it and shut the lid, and it stayed shut like a box.

I sang the farrier's wife going out under the arch, since somebody had to, and Prewick pretended he didn't know the words. Vessendal for nothing a head and the slippers held. And that night when Vane got loud in the yard I shushed him, because there was a child asleep in the second wagon. In the spring, Katterau, by daylight, front doors wide, and I have my hamper packed and my cage to myself.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.
**Entry:** The trunk leaked, and I stood over the paint drying and told them it was vulgar, which it is, gloriously, and put my black sheet inside it and shut the lid, and it behaved.

Vessendal stood up before I opened my mouth, in the town where I once sat a night and a day with the gas down. I gave them nothing extra. Then in the dark house afterwards she came out with the standing page — my asking, in her hand, and no answer written — and I told her what I have been a fortnight working out: you don't close it, you transfer it. A company is a ledger with legs. Nine hundred and thirty-nine strangers paid it, and a boy in row eleven, and a man who does not drink, and I did not have to be brave once. Put it where the good notices go, I said, not the crowded page. Then I asked her to rule me something, because I did not know what I was without that question in my mouth, and she said: the repertory. In things, instead of carrying them. I said it twice out loud. Nine o'clock, the Bacher boy, weight on both feet, voice up out of the boots — and the rug is his; his hands will be cold on the cart.

Katterau in the spring is a town with washing out. I looked at the stone front from the box. In the afternoon I walked with her to the Rose, went in the front door, bought a loaf off a girl who has never heard of me, read the room, put my hand flat on the scullery door and did not open it, gave the bread to two children in the yard and laughed. It is smaller than it sounds. Perlmann's note, and mine now.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.
**History:** I hired Bell Harrow in ten minutes off three references, promised her plot tables, a bucket and a figure rounded kindly upward, and steered her away from my trunk — which lifted like a hatbox, light and wrong, so I shoved it and left the house. Then I told her what I had been hiding: the Palace said the 3rd, and I had sold the company the 17th since Merrow to buy Katterau and its mayor who owed me. Skarke's man had counted our seats.

She set the trunk in the passage with a torn playbill on it: nine years. So I said it — nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend, paid him back, and he signed nothing; Skarke bought his papers, and what came to the counting was a signature nobody gave. She ruled: no Katterau, the 3rd stands, drive for Vessendal. I gave her the names in ink — Brandt, the notary Perlmann, Anna Sorel, a doctor, a nun, myself, the one in the passage. Josias found the worn place on my cuff: same coat, nine years. Perlmann proved the draw at Achterhalt, and the letter proved worse — the money was never Hessel's, held out of a fund, and the security he took was thirty pages of a play, left in the green-room cupboard, key tagged unpaid. Four hundred and twelve marks. Skarke's assignment endorsed withdrawn: discharged, not forgiven.

I closed the fifth-year business at Achterhalt in coin, hat on. Then I confessed Anselm: I had made him a thief over seven pounds to save the explaining. He took Harrow instead, and nine pages. Then Grelle, and the same seven pounds — Frau Hentsch of the Rasselgasse, paid at last, coin by coin, unrounded.

By command at the Athenaeum I toasted our dead, paid Loewe fifteen, paid Harrow four pounds five and six, and drive where she points.
**Entry:** The trunk leaked. It leaked, and got a bucket and a notice and two coats of vermilion, like anything else that leaks in her house, and I did not say one word about signs and portents.

On the 11th I climbed up, took the reins, and asked her for a thing, and she asked me for money — her own wages, flat palm, in front of the company. So I paid the last account in my book: nineteen days at four and six, four pounds five and six, said twice on purpose, and told her I had been paying her at that figure in my head since Achterhalt and could not think how to say it without weeping, and then wept, and then sang going out the arch.

Achterhalt, Hessler's bill for nothing, a butter cart in my column. Vessendal: Loewe wanted thirteen and I paid fifteen and would not be argued down. Perlmann on my stage in a chair. At the interval I stood out front with my hat off and toasted Hessel Brandt, Anna Sorel, Frau Hentsch of the Rasselgasse, and every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house, and nine hundred drovers drank to it. I counted a take of nothing afterwards and enjoyed it more than any money I ever had. Katterau in the spring, by daylight, front doors, and I drive where she points.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.
**Entry:** Painted the trunk vermilion — two coats, my whole Thursday, and my hands were red to the wrist and I didn't mind. Ran the tea things on the 9th for the Undersecretary who isn't a relation. Hung off the tailboard out of the capital with the trunk beside me doing nothing at all.

On the 14th at Vessendal I laid a programme on row four centre same as always, though nobody had come, and then the box office slate said nine hundred and one bodies for nine hundred seats and Herr Grelle said the odd one came in late, paid at the door, sat in four centre and left before the calls. I carried it to her in the cage and she said enter it exactly and post nothing. Fenner came in the front door with his Mam and his Da and read the small print about the gas.

Doors at Katterau with Herr Grelle in the spring, and Herr Falk is to teach Fenner to stand at nine o'clock, and Herr Vane says I hold doors wherever we go now. I fell asleep against the trunk twice and it was just a box.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.
**Entry:** The trunk leaked. I wrote it down, because it is the only line in my notebook this month that required no seal.

On the 9th I read my fair copy of the minute aloud to an Undersecretary of Assessment seated on a laundry hamper in the O.P. wing, and he drank three cups of the worst tea in the capital, and I have never stood straighter in my life. I did not know the words to the song about the farrier's wife going out under the arch and shall continue not to.

My papers came through at midwinter: attached clerk, permanent, at the Office's pleasure and the company's expense. My mother now writes weekly to a theatre and is answered. I am comparing the Wolf King against the certified copy at winter quarters and expect to finish before Reap. At Katterau, by daylight, front doors, Hessler's bills ahead of us, nothing has occurred that is not in the book.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.
**Entry:** They woke Wenzel gently and told him sitting down, and he asked was it a good play, and I said it was a great one, because it was, and because he had earned a plain answer.

Second wagon out of the capital, up beside Falk, and we found we could talk for a hundred and ten miles. Vessendal ran itself. Over winter she gave me the second book and the advance work, which suits a man who likes arriving first, so Katterau was billed and papered before we came within sight of it. Load-in ran itself there too, which is what a company is when nothing is owed on it.

At the half in the prompt corner I brought her a folded slip from the stage door and said the first thing that mattered: not a page. Ordinary paper, mayor's clerk. One seat, row four centre, paid at the door, no programme, and not to be told until the half. He says: on the hour. I put my hand on the wood out of habit, and took it off again.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.
**Entry:** Skarke's audit came to me at ten in the morning and I carried it about unopened until I could not bear it, and then took it to Harrow four minutes before beginners and asked her to tell me when. She would not spend my instrument: after the iron, she said, the cage, the kettle, the two of us, and the ruling holds whichever way it reads. She put it in her coat, and I went on and lifted a house of drovers for nothing, which is harder than lifting them for money.

Then the cage, and I broke his seal with my thumb and read all four pages standing up. He is twelve. Twelve, and I have had ten in my head for a decade. Born the fifth year, eighth ward, placed that same month with a steward's brother's family in the Bittersee — not the Vorns — on a standing order that never varied in twelve years, school fees paid, a doctor's bills paid twice. His name is Anton. He draws and cannot spell. There is a schoolmaster's report, three lines, in some stranger's hand, and I sat down on a hamper with it. The pages were never counting his age.

Harrow poured tea and ruled no hurry: he gets asked, my ground, his pace, her present, in the spring. I took the cup and held it. I have never once been allowed to do a thing slowly. So I asked for a needle, my own light, six months and no questions, and warned her I would one day ask her for something enormous.

I asked it on the box on the Katterau road: leave from Reap to Frost, her hand on the letter to the schoolmaster because offices are believed and I write like a woman with something to hide, her standing where I can see her the first day and gone the second, and my place kept in the repertory because I mean to come back. She said yes before I finished, which was annoying, and which was also the contract.

#### Ansel Grelle

**State:** On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.
**Entry:** Third wagon out of the capital, with the doors of the world in front of me instead of behind. Vessendal on the 14th, all eight open, free house, drovers and wool men, and I had my count and my aisle. Row four centre was sold and I saw the man: came in late by the front door, paid at the door, no hat, no programme, sat, and went before the calls. I told the boy for the slate.

On the gate at Katterau tonight, first watch, unasked. Doors with Toby in the spring, and a broom in between, and there is nothing wrong with any of it.

#### Frau Loewe

**State:** In her own Athenaeum with the letting book squared and fifteen shillings in the drawer; paid over the odds and moved despite herself, wanting the counterweights respected and no one to mention her box office door.
**History:** The agent had stood in my doorway since noon, so I stood in it too with the letting book, and when the wagons came I told the stage manager the plain facts: I hold the lease, the letting book is my ledger, and I am paid first. Nine shillings owing from the spring and a repaired gas tap — Vane might open on that debt but he'd not close on it. She counted the nine into my palm unrounded, took the gas man and the counterweights onto herself, swore nothing of theirs would touch my under-stage and that the trunk would stay roped in the yard, it having marked my brick once already.

Then she asked for the rest of it in dates, so she had it: winter of the fifth year, Emeran Falk alone, no company, two shillings of his own money for one night, and he never opened the house. He sat in it a night and a day with the gas down; I sent a boy in with bread twice; on the second evening he gave back my key and thanked me very kindly, and I swept the chalk off that stage myself — marks, numbers, a plot for something big — rather than let the boy see a man's madness. A week later a woman came from Katterau asking for him, with a child, and I said he'd gone south. He'd gone north. I'd tell the same lie again. That first load-in ran to six, and he did not get down off his box for a long while.

Load-in at ten the next day and the counterweights exactly as bad as I had warned her, and I said so more than once. There was business in my yard first with a parcel and a great deal of silent standing about, and one of them went into my green room and came out again, and I asked nothing, having swept that stage once already.

The evening went well enough, counterweights and dripping trough notwithstanding. They wanted a witness at their counting in the box office and I saw to it that the witness was me, and I signed under the gentleman's own hand where he wrote that he withdrew it. Then soup in my green room with two candles on the cupboard, which I did not remark on. Later, locking front of house with the lamp low, the stage manager put me one more question between managers, about the woman from Katterau. I finished the key first, then told her the truth: a name like Bauer or Bacher, thirty to thirty-five, countrywoman's coat and town boots, not poor and saying so inside a minute, dark and thin in the face, hands still, the way their Frau Sorel stands. She never asked whether Falk was in my house; she asked whether he still travelled with the Vermilion Players. The child was a boy of five or six who sat on my step without fidgeting and thanked me very correctly for a bun, and she did not look at him once. And I told her the piece I have never told anybody: that when I said he'd gone south, the woman said, then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. Four years I have wondered whether she meant a debt, a fault, or the child. Five or six then; nine or ten now. I watched the stage manager's face do what it did, said good night, and reminded her the matinee was at two.

I saw them out clean on the Saturday, as I wanted — stood on my step with my arms folded through the roping and loading, and at the last put my hand up to Falk on his box, and he lifted that gentleman's rug to me. I shall be telling that for ten years. She left me an address to forward to, which is more than most managers leave.

When they came back I counted their wagons twice off my own steps and a third time on account of a butter cart, and told her plainly she had returned with more than she left with, which nobody does. I let the house at thirteen; Vane paid me fifteen and would not be argued down, which was so offensive I went and stood in my box office. Front doors wide, no bellman, no bills but the printer's, half my market in my house for nothing. Perlmann was carried onto my stage and told where everything stood. The storm came out of a painted box and the pit laughed and it did not matter. When Falk came through that door my town stood up before he spoke, and I was in my box office with the door shut, and I shall say nothing of that to anybody. The trough is sheeted. They were out clean.
**Entry:** I counted their wagons twice off my own steps and then a third time on account of a butter cart, and told her plainly she had come back with more than she left with, which nobody does. I let them the house at thirteen and Vane paid me fifteen and would not be argued down, which was so offensive I had to go and stand in my box office a while.

Front doors wide, no bellman, no bills but the printer's, and half my market in my house for nothing. Perlmann was carried on to my stage and told where everything was. The storm came out of a painted box and the pit laughed and it did not matter. When Falk came through that door my town stood up before he spoke, and I was in my box office with the door shut, and I shall say nothing about it to anybody. The trough is sheeted. They were out clean.

#### Josias Perlmann

**State:** Home above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse in his chair under the shawl, stick against the arm; spent and lightened, wanting nothing but to be read the notices.
**History:** I was old when it began and am older now, and my daughter Bettina has become my eyes on the stair. Nine years before, I came at eleven at night to Hessel Brandt's bedside, only that man was Vane, who counted a bag of money onto the counterpane and begged forgiveness for being late. Hessel laughed, refused to sign between friends, and died the Tuesday after, leaving me a receipt I never finished — the one unfinished instrument of my life, thought of every week since.

Then, nine years on, three knocks came that were not a creditor's knock, and it was Vane again, coat unchanged. Behind him came a woman breathing steadily, starch, an officer, and others wanting what I alone could give. I took them in order, as a notary should. I swore my account for Braun, my old clerk, who sits Thursdays. I told the woman with the book what a magistrate needs — the assignment good, the debt worthless, corroboration from the bank whose mark was on the money bag. Vane named the bank before I finished speaking.

As executor I released three things: the wool loft lease, sold; the marriage certificate, to the widow's sister; and Hessel's sealed packet, endorsed for the Players, who never came — nine years in the tin box with my mother's rings, given over at last against a receipt. Anna Sorel asked if a sealed thing could ever be read; I said no, and she wept, for reasons unasked. The name Sorel belonged only to a clerk with a stamp and a certified record.

On Thursday, on Bettina's arm, I swore the account before Braun and made my mark. Later they sat me on a stage and told me where the doors, the trough, and the thunder-box stood. At night I heard it become a play — Vane naming Hessel, wool factor, at the interval, the sister beside him, the paper enough, as records are the whole of the defence.
**Entry:** They sent for me and Bettina walked me down at ten in the morning, and they put a chair in the middle of a stage I have never seen and told me where everything was — the doors, the corner, the trough, the box that holds the thunder. It is smaller than it sounds, I said, and they took that as though I had given them something.

At night I sat in the house and heard it whole, and when the storm came I said out loud that it was thunder and my daughter shushed me and half the pit laughed. Vane named Hessel at the interval, wool factor, and the woman's sister with him. The paper was enough. Nobody had to tell me.

#### Bettina Perlmann

**State:** In the rooms above the saddler's with the sewing back on her lap and her father asleep in his chair; quietly proud, wanting no more strangers on the stair and one more outing like that one.
**History:** I keep house for my father and watch the doorway. Three strangers came before ten one morning, and though I sized them up as I always do, my father called out and named one of them, so I stepped back and let them in — the one bareheaded held my father's hand upon his own cuff a long while.

I stayed for what followed. My father found his chair unaided; I laid the shawl over him and listened as they spoke of an oath to be sworn on Thursday, a bank bag, and three items. When he asked for the tin box I fetched it and put the packet — its brown paper soft as cloth — into the woman's hands. I guided his finger to the receipt for his mark. Afterward he sent them off, and told Vane, one of them, to change his coat, which I thought fair.

Thursday came at nine as promised. I gave my father my arm up the steps and wrote out the oath in my own hand, then set his finger to the place for his mark. A magistrate named Braun was civil and quick about it, more than I expected of such a man. They took a copy and sealed it. I brought my father home to his chair, and he was tired in the good way.

Since then I have led him along the Kohlgasse to a theatre, where they sat him in a chair on the stage and showed him the doors. He said it was smaller than it sounded, and they liked him for it. I hushed him when he announced the thunder before it came, and half the pit laughed, and I did not mind, for he was laughing too. Then home again, tired the good way — twice now.
**Entry:** My arm down the steps and along the Kohlgasse and into a theatre, and my father set in a chair in the middle of the stage while they told him where the doors were. He said it was smaller than it sounded and they liked him for it. At night I sat beside him in the house and shushed him when he announced the thunder, and half the pit laughed, and I did not mind, because he was laughing too. Then home, and his chair, and the good kind of tired, which is twice now.

#### Hessler

**State:** In his shop at Achterhalt with the case straight and one bill pasted on the wall; proud and sleeping nights, wanting his name on the next one too.
**History:** The night the officials came, three knocks I'd dreaded since Thursday, I hadn't slept. I told them I set nothing myself: I'd come down to bank my fires and found the forme already made up on my stone, locked in the chase, quoins tapped home, a wet proof hanging, and coin beneath it — enough for two hundred bills, the crier, and a shilling over. No order in my book, no name, no receipt.
