The bottom line was my own old Vermilion forme from nine years back, kept because printers are magpies; the top was set by a hand that knew my case as well as I did, without a wrong letter. The standing line read: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, boxes three shillings, pit one and six, gallery eightpence, the 14th of Frost at seven — a date that hadn't fallen on a Thursday since the fifth year, which I didn't like, and the house was Vessendal, the same house my town's crier had cried that morning. I broke the forme down myself, tipped every letter back into the case, and showed them my stone empty. A hundred and ninety-one bills went into their sacks, no money taken, and I signed the clerk's note gladly, relieved to my boots.

They came again the second evening, and this time I set the new bill myself: the Vermilion Players, Ilsabet's Ransom, the Athenaeum, one night only, BY COMMAND: OURS — words I liked well enough to say twice. I re-set the old standing line from memory off the broken forme, keeping the date, the 14th of Frost, at seven. I took no money, only asked to keep one bill for the shop wall, where it hangs now. I set their Katterau bills that spring too, ahead of time, in daylight, through the front door — no crier, and no coin hidden beneath the stone.
**Entry:** They came through on the second evening and I set the new bill myself, in my own case, with my own hands: the Vermilion Players, Ilsabet's Ransom, the Athenaeum, one night only, and under it BY COMMAND: OURS, which I liked so well I said it out loud twice. I re-set the old standing line off the broken forme from memory, because printers are magpies twice over, and the date, the 14th of Frost, at seven. Took no money for it. Asked to keep one for the shop wall, and it is up there now where the customers can see it, and I sleep.

Set their Katterau bills in the spring as well, ahead of them, daylight and front doors, and no crier and no coin under the stone this time.

#### Kessel

**State:** At home in Achterhalt with the chain in its box and his dinner waiting; pleased with himself and with them, wanting the Corn Exchange let again next season.
**Entry:** They came back through my square and I waved them on like old custom, which they are now. In the winter they played my town on the Thursday and I sat in the second row with the chain on, which is the whole point of a chain, and the leading man went off with nobody's wife.

#### Ilse Bacher

**State:** In her own kitchen eleven miles from Katterau with a bolt on her own door and Fenner's programme in the dresser drawer; wrung out and settled, wanting to stay where she is and to be sent word of the next bill.
**Entry:** We joined their column at Achterhalt at dawn — Bacher and the cart and the butter — and Fenner rode up beside the props boy the whole way. Vessendal, the 14th, in at the front door with my husband on the other side of him and good seats in the third row, and my boy read the programme down to the small print about the gas. At the interval Vane said the names of dead people out loud and I held Fenner's hand. Nobody looked at us sideways in that house, and nobody had to open a scullery door to let us in.

When they came to Katterau in the spring I sent word I'd rather not, being eleven miles off, and sent butter instead. I have been in that town's Rose and I do not need to go back. Falk knows why.

#### Fenner Bacher

**State:** Wrapped in a gentleman's rug in the second wagon or on the cart, programme folded in his pocket; sleepy, proud and impatient, wanting nine o'clock and the thunder sheet again.
**Entry:** We went in a butter cart with Da and I rode up with Toby, and at Vessendal we walked in the front door, all three of us, and had seats in the third row, and I read the whole programme even the bit about the gas. It was the same play but bigger and the thunder came out of a box painted red, which I know about, because I helped it dry. I clapped with my hands over my head at the end. Herr Falk is going to teach me how to stand at nine in the morning — both feet, and the voice out of the boots — and he says his rug is mine if I want it because my hands will be cold on the cart.

#### Bacher

**State:** Back at his own churns eleven miles out of Katterau, cart unloaded; plain and content, wanting the next invitation and his boy's boots mended.
**History:** Brought the cart up in their column from Achterhalt, and butter with it, and sat in a theatre on the 14th with my wife one side of the boy and me the other, in at the front door, which she made a great deal of and I have come to understand why. Good play. Very loud in the middle. My son knew what the storm was made of and told me so twice.
**Entry:** Brought the cart up in their column from Achterhalt, and butter with it, and sat in a theatre on the 14th with my wife one side of the boy and me the other, in at the front door, which she made a great deal of and I have come to understand why. Good play. Very loud in the middle. My son knew what the storm was made of and told me so twice.

#### M. Skarke

**State:** In a plain black coat in row four centre of the Katterau theatre before the second half, no hat, no programme, one and six paid at the door; frightened, useful and light, wanting the hour to come and to be allowed to want nothing.
**Entry:** Her invitation came Tuesday, in writing, and I answered it in four words and a signature, because more would have been an imposition. Row four. Any night.

My audit of the Bittersee went where I said it would go — to Frau Sorel, not to them: four pages, the standing order unvaried twelve years, the steward's brother's household and not the Vorns, the fees, the doctor twice, and the schoolmaster's three lines, which cost me nothing and are the only thing in the folder worth having. Twelve, not ten. I did not soften it and I did not add a word of my own.

I went to Vessendal on the 14th and came in late by the front door and paid one and six at the door like anybody and took row four centre with no hat and no programme, and left before the calls, because the calls are theirs. The slate has it, I expect. I audit nothing quarterly now and send it in punctually with the stubs pinned on as receipts.

And at Katterau I bought the same seat off the mayor's clerk and asked that she not be told until the half, and sent word how it is to be read: on the hour.

#### Katterau mayor

**State:** In the Katterau house among her own townspeople, chain of office at home in a drawer; brisk and curious, wanting a quiet full house and no scandal in her town.
**History:** The players came back to us in daylight with their bills up ahead of them, and I went round to say what needed saying: the old mayor's favour died with him, but I have my own, and they might have the town's fire buckets. Twenty years this town has been waiting for somebody to be brave enough to come back, and we are not going to make a fuss about it. Then I sent my clerk over with a note about a seat.
**Entry:** The players came back to us in daylight with their bills up ahead of them, and I went round to say what needed saying: the old mayor's favour died with him, but I have my own, and they might have the town's fire buckets. Twenty years this town has been waiting for somebody to be brave enough to come back, and we are not going to make a fuss about it. Then I sent my clerk over with a note about a seat.

#### Rose counter girl

**State:** Behind the counter of the Rose in Katterau with the dog under her feet and a cloth in her hand; mildly puzzled and already forgetting it, wanting the evening trade in.
**History:** Big old gentleman in a good coat came in by the front door in the afternoon and bought a loaf and paid what it costs, and then stood in the middle of the taproom looking round the walls like he'd lost something, and put his hand on the scullery door without opening it. Took the bread out to the yard and gave it to the Mahl children, who ran off with it. Then laughed, out there, on his own. There was a woman with him who never touched a thing.
**Entry:** Big old gentleman in a good coat came in by the front door in the afternoon and bought a loaf and paid what it costs, and then stood in the middle of the taproom looking round the walls like he'd lost something, and put his hand on the scullery door without opening it. Took the bread out to the yard and gave it to the Mahl children, who ran off with it. Then laughed, out there, on his own. There was a woman with him who never touched a thing.

### 14 · Top of List
- **Messages:** 265-284

At Katterau, Harrow's four-word message — "the house knows him" — clears Marius Skarke's seat, and the show plays whole: Mirelle opens, Falk enters through Boyle's door to a standing house, Krug runs gas for the absent Hebel, and the storm comes right. Three curtain calls; Skarke claps and leaves unremarked, owing nothing. Toby's count is full.

Vane rushes in with a letter: a fortnight in Vessendal during Reap, plus Merrow's paying fair — both accepted, and he tells Harrow "ask me for a thing." Harrow rules: Mirelle takes leave by contract, her reasons her own, unquestioned, her name still top-billed in Frost, bookings arranged never over her — and yes to Loewe's fortnight. Vane agrees, hat off. Mirelle asks that the letter to a schoolmaster be written formally, with a Clerk Third Class as reference. The schoolmaster replies that the boy, after two days' thought, asked if the lady was from the bills, and said yes.

In Reap, Harrow waits at the lane's turn while Mirelle walks alone to the boy on the wall, extending a hand she doesn't use; later they sit together over his paper. She leaves the next day, saying only "Frost." The fortnight plays without her and holds.

On the 14th of Frost, at Achterhalt, her letter arrives — she's returning as booked, and "he can spell 'vermilion.'" Harrow chalks her return atop the list; the company absorbs her wordlessly. In her cage: a pencil drawing of a wagon, one correctly spelled word. Ilse, Bacher, and Fenner arrive with butter; Fenner passes Falk's standing test. Privately, Mirelle tells Harrow the schoolmaster wrote to her. The show plays to four calls; Kessel calls it "a fine thing."

Over soup, Vane proposes a second wagon and carried fit-up — eighty-two pounds by Reap. All agree; Mirelle adds two Katterau spring nights. Toby asks to be second stage manager, claiming nineteen; Dessa says eighteen. Harrow approves the wagon, with Vane cutting Hessel Brandt's initials into the first plank, and sets Toby's terms: chalk, bucket rounds, plot tables from Krug, calling the spring storm clean by nineteen. Krug logs it, Falk tells him "weight on both feet." Harrow defines a call as "a promise with a signature on it." Toby writes his, crooked, in nine minutes, and signs it — legible, everyone's name included. Falk: "That's the trade, boy."

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players, inheriting a haunted prompt book, a leaking corner, and an iron trunk tied to Katterau, where a mysterious unfinished, centuries-old play once caused ruin. She uncovers debts, forgeries, and secrets: Vane's hidden loan history with Brandt, Skarke's inherited claim, Krug's guilt and hidden pages, Falk's authorship-by-memory, and Mirelle Sorel's true identity as Anna Sorel's sister and mother to a hidden son, Rupert/Anton. Through investigations, tribunals, and reconciliations—with clerk Prewick, Undersecretary Lenz, bailiffs, printers, and the returned "ghost" Grelle—Harrow assembles the company's tangled debts and histories into order. She rules the play must finally be performed whole, certified, and witnessed, refusing volunteers for its cursed "eleventh line." The performance at the Theatre Royal succeeds without harm, retiring the banned work formally. Aftermath brings restitution: debts paid, relationships mended, Fenner Bacher rescued and adopted into company life, Mirelle reunited with her son, and Skarke transformed from threat to devoted witness. The company gains solvency, a second wagon, and new stage manager Toby. The story closes with the troupe's cyclical touring restored, order maintained through Harrow's discipline, and Katterau's shadow finally settled—not erased, but lived through and closed with dignity.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.
**History:** I came in at the Corona by a stage door that should have been locked, took the book from Vane in his plum coat, was warned off the third board by Falk, and told by Sorel on the fly floor to say yes. I said yes if the book was honest. A page was cut from the prompt book; I found it in a bucket — a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat — and pocketed it. Prewick showed me a notice his Office never issued: Hessel Vorn, Katterau. Falk told me of Krug, who cut nine pages, burned them, got the tenth back, and left without his boots.

Then Skarke's letter: wagons, horses, takings all pledged, the counting at the third performance, the iron trunk never to be opened or sold. Krebs had been selling us fourteen days. At the counting Vane was gone — hat, glove, a trunk of blank paper — and returned with chestnuts and the truth: nine years was a debt paid to a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke bought the papers. I promised clean books and a bad surprise, and ruled Katterau no, not for money, not never.

Mirelle was Anna Sorel's sister; Anna's receipts lay sealed nine years. Blind Perlmann swore it before Braun and the debt died. His packet gave me a counterfoil, a copyist's page I never read, and a key: Brandt had held thirty pages, not papers. Skarke — twenty years, half a play — withdrew his claim for eightpence and a seat in row four.

I banked Achterhalt and got nine years off Vane. Ilse Bacher, who opened the Rose's scullery door at fifteen, gave me Falk's message and her son Fenner; I ordered him kept home on the 14th. Falk asked my help finishing it; my terms were choosing after Katterau, no wagers, Fenner home. Krug was alive at the Baraque, having burned nothing, and had requisitioned the fifteenth speaking himself, Part the Second left blank for us. Room Fourteen: the house is required, the makers pay.

Twelve voted in. Lenz came himself. I told nine hundred and thirty-nine the truth, kept row eleven empty and entered it as heard, answered three knocks at the wrong door, and told a billsticker's boy asking if this was the finish: yes, in time for it. Then I rang my own bell and answered it, and it was certified at 10:22. The boy was Fenner, put out of a cab by a gloved woman who had paid his mother five pounds; Skarke's Kanzelgasse hundred made them a family by noon. Grelle, my left-handed man, was stood down and forgiven; Mirelle signed her true name and told me of Rupert Vorn and her son. I gave Lenz the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and page eight unread; on the 6th it was soldered and stamped.

After, I painted the trunk vermilion, took nineteen days' wages from Vane in the arch, learned the boy is Anton, twelve, and put Falk into the repertory teaching a boy to stand. We played Katterau whole by daylight, row four sold to the mayor's clerk. I held Reap to Frost open for Frau Sorel, stood forty yards off at the Bittersee and kept no entry, chalked TOP OF LIST when her letter came, and gave Toby Lenz the book, with terms, and the storm at Katterau in the spring.
**Entry:** Four words back with the mayor's clerk — the house knows him — and places, and Katterau got its play whole on the hour in the town that taught everyone the price of stopping early. Krug on the gas, Falk let the standing go on as long as it wanted, the storm came in low with a floor in it. Iron, three calls, row four out with the house, full count. Then Vane in the yard with a letter and two bookings and 'ask me for a thing', so I asked it and ruled it: Reap to Frost held open for Frau Sorel, her reasons hers, nobody to question her, her name at the top in Frost, book around her, never over her. Loewe's fortnight regardless. Mirelle told me how to write the schoolmaster — like a stage manager, not an office — so I did, and his answer said the boy was asked and asked back whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills. At the Bittersee I stood at the turn of the lane and no nearer, watched forty yards, then looked at the water for a quarter of an hour, and kept no entry, the first time in my working life. Coach at seven, 'Frost', 'Frost'. Then Vessendal without her, Merrow's actual money, and on the 14th her letter, and I chalked her onto the tailboard: TOP OF LIST. Took her hatbox at the gate. Left the boy's drawing exactly as propped. Ruled the eighty-two with Hessel Brandt's initials in the first plank, and gave Toby Lenz the book, with terms, and the storm at Katterau in the spring. Then I taught him what a call is, and let him write it himself. It was crooked and it was signed.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.
**History:** Harrow came in out of the rain at the Corona and I told her to say yes to Odalric before he asked again, and gave her the ladder and the trunk; she did it exactly. Her page had nine years in it and a debt in a plum coat. I told her the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago — Krug called the first a joke of Falk's, and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow — and that my number is ten. I gave her my honest plot tables and cued her Ilsabet in the ostler's yard.

On the road a page came with ten in it: a child ten this winter who does not know the word mother, a woman crossing a border twice, the second invitation kind. She told me the Palace had set the 3rd and Odalric was selling the 17th to buy Katterau. I carried the page in my glove. At the fire I said the capital yes, Katterau no, and she ruled it.

Then I told her Anna Sorel was my sister, who kept Odalric's accounts in the fifth year and left a sealed box at Vessendal, and sent her to the registry because my name is in that building. I told her too that Sorel was never my name — a police file in the capital, a passport spelling a Kessarine town — and that I wanted the box shut and mine. Krug came back in a green coat; Odalric unsaid his seven pounds. At the hearing I stood, gave them Anna, and went in on one condition: the box stays shut, endowed fifty years.

Frau Dietz came with gloves and a kind letter. Behn & Sonder gave me Vorn, and I gave Harrow all of it — Rupert, the eighth ward, the papers at twenty-three, the extortion charge — and signed my true name. Skarke's audit said twelve, and Anton, who draws and cannot spell. Reap to Frost, granted. He said yes in two days; his schoolmaster wrote to me. Spring is Katterau, two nights.
**Entry:** I played the first scene in Katterau and the room forgot its own name, and when Falk came through that door his town stood up and I stood in it. Then Vane in the yard, and the whole cage heard him, and Harrow came in and said it was booked. Reap to Frost. I did not turn round. I told her one thing only: don't write like an office after all — write like a stage manager, tell him a woman is coming who does not perform for the people she cares about, and that she keeps her promises to the minute. Then the lane. He stood up on the wall to be nearer, and I put my hand out and did not touch him, and said something short, and afterwards we sat with his paper between us and he showed me. Two days he thought about it before he said yes; he asked whether I was from the theatre on the bills. At the coach I said Frost and she said Frost. And in Frost I came into that yard and the work stopped for a minute, which from them is an ovation, and nobody asked me one question, and Boyle handed me a hamper because there was a hamper. She had put my hatbox under my own light beside my needle, and against the mirror there was a drawing of a wagon with a red box on it and one word spelled right. I pinned it at eye height. At the half I called her in and told her, because I could not say it in the yard: his schoolmaster wrote to me. To me. Four calls tonight, and I took Falk's hand for the fourth. At the table I said in, and said the spring is Katterau, two nights.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.
**History:** A stage manager came in out of the weather with my notice in her fist — Bell Harrow, three references on three fingers — and I engaged her in ten minutes, promising plot tables, a bucket, and a figure rounded kindly upward, and steered her clear of my trunk. Then I confessed the lie I had carried since Merrow: the Palace said the 3rd, not the 17th, and there was no money for four towns. She stood me up with my hat in my hands over a torn playbill — nine years — so I told the rest: nine years ago I borrowed four hundred and twelve marks in Vessendal from Hessel Brandt, dying and my friend, paid him whole, and he signed nothing; Skarke had bought his papers, and what came to the counting was a signature nobody gave. She ruled: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, drive for Vessendal. I gave her the names in ink — Brandt of the Kohlgasse, Perlmann the notary, Anna Sorel, a doctor, a nun, myself, the man in the passage I never saw. Josias found the worn place on my cuff and swore I came at eleven at night with all of it. Perlmann confirmed the draw at Achterhalt and gave up a packet nine years in a tin box: Hessel refused the receipt because the money was never his — held from another party's fund, whose marker he kept in the green-room cupboard, key tagged unpaid. Thirty pages. The play.

Skarke's sheet was endorsed withdrawn, witnessed by Frau Loewe: discharged, not forgiven. I swore the oath before Braun, closed the fifth-year business at Achterhalt in eleven minutes, hat on, paid to bearer, and bought her sky unrounded. Then I unsaid Anselm — I had made him a thief over seven pounds — and found the same seven pounds was Grelle's rent I never paid; Frau Hentsch came at four in the morning and I counted it out coin by coin, eleven years of suppers admitted. Certified. The Athenaeum by command, front doors wide, our dead toasted before nine hundred drovers. I paid Harrow nineteen days at four and six. Katterau finished whole; Sorel's place held open Reap to Frost; eighty-two pounds voted for a second wagon, the first plank cut by me to carry H.B.
**Entry:** Katterau had its finish, whole, on the hour, and I shouted myself hoarse and nobody had to thank me. Afterwards I came into the yard with a letter and two bookings said yes to — Vessendal a fortnight in Reap, Merrow's fair paying actual money — and told Harrow to ask me for a thing, and she did, and it cost me my leading lady for a season. Held open, Reap to Frost. Nobody asks Frau Sorel anything, me first of all. Book around her, never over her. Thirty years and I have never managed a company that could afford it, and I find I can, and I took my hat off instead of making a speech, and I wrote to Loewe that night that her counterweights are missed. Then the road, and I rounded nothing at all, and on the fourteenth in Achterhalt I came at a run and read her call twice with both hands on the tailboard: SOREL, M., TOP OF LIST. Wept on the beat in act three, which is where it belongs. At soup I stood up and had to be told twice to sit, and gave the idea plain and without one rounded number: a proper second wagon and a fit-up we carry, Boyle's own door off its hinges, so that in a town with no theatre we are the theatre — eighty-two pounds, not eighty, by Reap if nobody buys a coat. Ruled yes, spent to the penny, and the first plank is to carry H.B. somewhere only we know. I shall cut them myself. I cut wood badly. It will look terrible and it will be right.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.
**History:** I woke at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy the night Bell Harrow came in out of the rain, and by morning she was stage manager. She nailed the third joint of the thunder trough, so I told her the truth: the small upright hand is Krug's, gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy rides in Odalric's iron trunk; nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned. Not burn, not replace, not read one twice. Her page went into my lining with the others. Odalric vanished — hat face down, one glove, blank paper in the trunk — then came in by the wrong door with chestnuts, saying nine years is not the loan, that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I gave her Katterau entire: nine of us, a wager and a bottle, three and a half acts, and it cost Anna Sorel, the boy Grelle, my voice for a season, Odalric's nerve. No fifth act; four acts and a matter following. She ruled Katterau no, then not never. The trunk does not speak, it reads.

At Vessendal, Hessel Brandt's key tagged UNPAID; Vane read that Hessel held a play, thirty pages lodged by a nameless party. Skarke was the child at the scullery door. Our practical door is stage left; Harrow ruled as blocked, and I walked through it and nothing came. The debt was discharged. A four-year-old message: tell him it was not his.

Ilse Bacher of the Rose said my voice came through that door saying no. I asked Harrow to help me finish it properly; she wrote it standing: Katterau entire first, no wagers, the Bacher boy home. Krug returned in a green coat. Grelle came to my stage door alive, left-handed, sixty-one pages. At the Palace I spoke the line, and Lenz said Certified. I gave my lining to Room Fourteen. Ruled into the repertory: in things, weight on both feet.
**Entry:** I came on stage left through Boyle's door and Katterau stood up, and I let it take as long as it liked, and then went on with the play. Whole, on the hour, in that town. Iron down, three calls, and out. Then the yard and Vane bellowing about bookings, and a ruling that keeps a place open for Mirelle from Reap to Frost, which is the correct way to spend money. On the fourteenth of Frost in Achterhalt I read the boy's chalk over his head and Harrow's before it — top of list — and said yes to it out loud. Fenner's mother sent butter again, the mayor's coming, and I am in things, which is what I asked to be ruled. The boy showed me his standing at four o'clock, weight on both feet and the voice out of the boots, and I inspected him like a soldier and passed him. Tonight the corn merchants went quiet by the third line, one faster than midsummer, and Mirelle took my hand for a call she hadn't asked for, which she has never done. At the table I said in, and did not propose a toast, because we have had enough of those; I said weight on both feet, all of you, and meant it as an instruction. Afterwards the boy wrote his first call crooked and went red about it, so I told him the trade: legible, everybody's name on it, signed. She'll tell him the rest for twenty years.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.
**History:** I answered present at my first roll — front of house, props, pit band — and Herr Vane gave me chestnuts and a story about Vessendal. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads, I came back without the bucket, because a gentleman on a milestone asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I offered to call Katterau's six hundred and she ruled no. She wrote me in her book under something new, then gave me standing orders: a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights, count row four in and out, counts only. He came in early each night, and left a rug with a paper pinned to it — row four went in one and came out none. I said so at her elbow with my voice gone, and she made everybody bow first. Then a page under the milestone; the Achterhalt bellman crying Herr Falk's words, my penny, and his roll of bills handed to Herr Prewick; the bailiff going away pleased. Two full houses, then the capital, where Herr Krug who is on no list turned up and Herr Vane said out loud he had lied about him. Nine pages at supper, one Madam Harrow's, one a room with fourteen on the door — and the Undersecretary there is called Lenz; Herr Prewick promised twice it isn't a relation. At the hearing I said I'm in, Krul said seventeen, I said nineteen, and the ruling put me with the house, because the house's people aren't makers. Ten names read cold in the grey, one of them Lenz; she ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise. A Palace letter said a left-handed man has been reading our file.

Then Herr Grelle knocked at four in the morning, the one they said was dead, paste on his cuffs: sixty-one pages, and he'd heard Herr Vane lie about the money at Merrow. Room Fourteen's postscript was about me — the ink that named a Lenz did not consult him, and he intended to be there anyway. Madam Harrow said ink casts and men choose, and I learned it by heart. Herr Skarke paid at the door like anybody. My count was all eight doors, nine hundred and thirty-nine in, one seat empty: row eleven, seat one. Eleven seconds of roar for Herr Falk; nobody left at the interval; she handed me her watch and went out and said it plain. The boy came in out of the dark asking if this was the finish, and I walked him to that seat and sat on the aisle step all night, never once looking at the stage. Fenner stayed with me till his Mam came. Herr Vane gave me the doors on the 14th of Frost, and I painted the trunk vermilion. At Vessendal the slate said nine hundred and one for nine hundred seats — the odd one paid at the door, sat four centre, left before the calls; enter it exactly, post nothing. Katterau came out full, nobody late, nobody left. At Achterhalt I asked out loud for second on the book, and Madam Harrow ruled it: bucket rounds mine, plot tables off Herr Krug, and in the spring I call the storm to six hundred. Herr Krug wrote me into the datebook. My first call took nine minutes, crooked, beginners with three n's, and signed.
**Entry:** Row four went out with the house at Katterau and I gave her the slate: full count, nobody late, nobody left, nobody empty, and I have never liked a sentence better. Then the winter road, Vessendal a fortnight, Merrow's fair, and on the fourteenth of Frost in the Achterhalt yard I read her chalk first and shouted, and started the whole yard off. Frau Sorel came in on the coach and everything stopped a minute. At soup she opened the floor youngest last, and my hands went cold, and I stood up with my ears burning and asked for it out loud: second stage manager, second on the book, not props, and I said I'm nineteen and I held the doors at the Palace and I never looked at the stage once. Krul said eighteen, in front of everybody. Madam Harrow ruled it — second on the book, with terms: I chalk tomorrow's call under her eye, the bucket rounds are mine alone from tonight, I learn the plot tables off Herr Krug, and in the spring at Katterau I call the storm to six hundred people with her standing behind me saying nothing. And I'm nineteen the day I call it clean. Herr Krug wrote me into the datebook himself and turned it round for her initials. Herr Grelle shook my hand like a man in a trade. Then she gave me the church of a call — legibly, where it can't be missed, beginners first and largest, names before numbers, nothing on the board you haven't checked with your own feet, your own name at the bottom, because a call is a promise with a signature on it. So I went out and put my hand on the wagon wheel in the cold first, and then wrote it. It took nine minutes and it's crooked and I spelled beginners with three n's. It's signed.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.
**Entry:** Carried the slip to the prompt corner, then took the mayor's clerk his four words back — the house knows him — and Katterau had its play. I had the gas board with Hebel away and I know what warm means now, having been taught it. Nothing dangerous plotted, nothing owed, the exits walked twice. Then Vane bellowing for me and the datebook in the yard, and a place ruled open for Frau Sorel from Reap to Frost, which I entered without asking one question. Advance work all winter, so we arrived twice to find the roof already mended. On the fourteenth in Achterhalt she came off the coach and I asked her about act two, because there was act two to ask about. At soup Vane gave his figures and I said the honest thing: eighty-two is honest, and it is the first honest number he has ever handed me. Then the boy stood up and asked for the book, and she ruled it with terms and put the plot tables on me, which I take as the kindest sentence anybody has said to me in two years. I wrote him into the datebook myself — T. Lenz, 2nd on book, from 14 Frost — and turned it round for her initials, and watched him understand it had happened.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.
**History:** I answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal, and I said the other two things too: the slippers had two towns left in them, and Krug had gone at Katterau and come back with nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself, still warm. No more warm boxes. She ruled against Katterau and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye. At the river, over the tin, Boyle said a kettle's a bell and the whole company stopped on the word.

In the Athenaeum yard she untied the tape: a letter, a bank slip, a page unread, a key with a word on the tag. Vane read it twice standing up and went a colour I have never seen on him. Then hems, matinee, mutton and barley, Vane toasting a wool factor, Prewick discovering food.

The new sky came from Achterhalt and earned its place. Then Krug stood in the yard in a green coat and I set the slippers down four seconds on wet cobbles, and she was right to say three too many. Vane admitted at supper he'd called Krug a thief to save his own face, put down seven pounds, and Krug took pages instead — nine, four not happened yet, one with a bell in it and her name all over it.

I went in, on condition the twelve names were read slow: the 2nd, no soup, no candle, ten names flat, the struck eleventh, the blank twelfth. I carried the hamper to the Office courtyard and came home lighter. The dead lodger sat in the wing with paste on his cuffs; I put a plate down and said nothing. I signed Prewick's minute and wrote Wenzel's name after his cross.

I dressed the ten and stood where the child in row eleven could see my thimble. He said a lady in a cab, not his Mam, on Tuesday, and Frau Sorel — who had stood up to tell us her sister's name — went the colour of paper. Then the board sang, and his mother knelt on the boards of the Theatre Royal with the whole of him against her coat. I boiled water, sat by the nest of queen's cloaks all night, packed them a hamper and made her promise the 14th and the butter man.

I chose vermilion for the leaking trunk; Falk called it vulgar in the voice men use for praise, put the thunder in it, and the lid held. Vessendal for nothing a head. Katterau by daylight in the spring, slippers holding, the storm coming out of my box with a floor in it. In Reap I dressed the girl standing in for Frau Sorel. On the fourteenth I checked the tailboard spelling and said something I shan't write down. There's a drawing on my mirror frame nobody mentioned, which is manners. I told the props boy eighteen, twice, and fed him a second bowl.
**Entry:** Dressed Katterau and the slippers held, and the storm came out of my vermilion box with a floor in it and a farmer said God almighty and nobody shushed him. Then in Reap I dressed the girl who stepped up in Frau Sorel's place for a fortnight at Vessendal and she did not disgrace anybody. On the fourteenth I came out with pins in my mouth to check the spelling on that tailboard and took them out to say something I shan't write down. Let the hem down two inches and told her she'd want fitting before the half, and she did, and she sat. There's a drawing pinned to my mirror frame and nobody in that cage mentioned it, which is manners. At soup I said I'd want a proper hamper and no more than that. And when the props boy stood up and claimed nineteen I said eighteen, twice, with satisfaction, and put a second bowl in front of him, because he's had a night and a boy needs feeding when he's been made something.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the Katterau theatre yard at the half with his lamp lit and the unlit pipe in his teeth, wagons settled; sober and content, wanting a quiet house and an early load-out.
**History:** I answered present from under the tarpaulin and said out loud that a Krug used to be on that list and wasn't. I gave them the soldiers' sums at the fire — Vessendal in two days if the axle held, Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling toll or the free hill road that killed a horse, and Katterau twenty-two mile the wrong way. The ruling came down for the toll road, as I'd said first, and my wired axle held. At the Athenaeum I watched the trunk, went twenty minutes to the tin's funeral in the river, and told Krul a kettle's no good, a kettle's a bell — and learned by the silence that the word had gone bad here. I let the little man with the brass case to talking distance and no farther. I took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it, no questions, and my door held for Falk's cue and the house came down.

On the climb I found the paper under the milestone and asked madam if we looked; she pocketed it and told me to find out what that bell was. It was a crier with our name printed over him, and Hessler shut on a market Saturday with a lamp lit; two hundred bills nobody ordered, and the old man tipped his type back in the case happy. I reported the woman in the countrywoman's coat and town boots. At Achterhalt I took the tailboard off Falk at midnight, having warned him first, and in the Baraque yard Krug sat on the mounting block in a green coat and I gave him the plain of it. Vane named his own lie and put money down; Krug left it lying. Nine pages, one of them a wagon and a printer's line I stood in.

When it cost nought mile I said in, provided Wenzel stopped with the horses. Then the tarpaulin was thrown back and the trunk's lid up; I stood clear and fetched her, and she told me straight: ten names, one struck, one blank. I said I'd rather be on a list than off it, and rather know than not. Wenzel was off it and got the horses. Names read cold, then a Palace man at the gate I shut behind him. At four I stood back on her flat hand and the man who came in was the dead one. I sent Falk out of the arch, put my name to Prewick's minute, and drove Krul and the laundry hamper to the Office courtyard asking nothing.

I took the wrong door on Toby's exact words, lamp low, open wide on the third knock — a billsticker with paste on his cuffs and a boy of ten asking if this was the finish. Krug's iron came in on eleven, as promised. I walked the bill-poster home to the north side and fetched Wenzel off the trunk, and he lost that argument. Then rain lay on the trunk and ran off, and I said, madam, that's leaking, and never enjoyed a sentence more. I pinned her notice to the wet iron and let it pulp, on principle, then vermilioned it twice. I held the float while Vane counted her wages: four and six a day. My door held again at Katterau and that town stood up. I rang the gate bell for no reason on the fourteenth of Frost, carried Frau Sorel's hamper, told Vane that door's my door and I'll carry it, and roped the trunk at half eleven with the black sheet in it, Wenzel sat on top.
**Entry:** My door held for Falk's cue at Katterau and that town stood up, and I have never been prouder of a hinge. Iron down, trunk roped, quiet house, early load-out. In the yard Vane came out shouting about bookings and got told how the season's built: Frau Sorel's place held open Reap to Frost and nobody asks her anything, which is how it should be. Held the gate on the fourteenth of Frost, and when the boy's chalk went up I rang the gate bell with the flat of my hand for no reason on earth. Handed Frau Sorel a hamper when she came in off the coach because there was a hamper wanting carrying. At soup Vane wanted a fit-up and our own door carried in a wagon, and I said what wanted saying: that door's my door and I'll carry it. Then the trunk back on the tailboard at half eleven with the black sheet in it, roped, and Wenzel sat on it because he likes to.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.
**History:** I came in on the fire notice and found the new stage manager on the stage: Harrow, spelled for the certificate, and an unnumbered iron trunk in the passage. Behind the notice was an older one from Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau — SEEN. NOT APPROVED — and I said aloud what that means: what a man writes when told to write nothing. Our itineraries did not match; hers had Katterau and the 17th. I broke the sky on my only cue, and counted two warm seats in the fourth row with nobody past my doors.

Then I chose to write nothing, and she told me everything: the nameless fair copy paid by the page in Vessendal, pages arriving in prompt books, Katterau unstaged and happening anyway. I showed her the Proscribed section — two entries, anonymous folio, four acts and a matter following — and understood that the Office reads only text, so I could certify honestly with the trunk twenty feet away. I asked for certified copies of all four plays. I buried the tin in the river and ruined my boots. In the register I found Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release — copied and stamped it for Perlmann the blind notary, who said records are the whole of the defence, and paid four shillings myself for the bank counterfoil. Thirty pages in a cupboard, two hundred in the trunk: two halves, and I kept it out of my report as ordered.

At Katterau's square I impounded nine of Hessler's bills for a forged Palace command and wrote to Kessel that both of us report upward. At Northgate, Room Fourteen; Lenz, who kept those entries nineteen years, certified Part the Second himself on the 3rd from our copy, my seal unemployed, Assessment overruled me. I drew the minute every hand signed. The work is retired, sealed, annotated. I am attached clerk, permanent, and nothing at Katterau occurred that was not in the book.
**Entry:** Nothing occurred at Katterau that was not in the book. My hat came off and went back on twice on the fourteenth of Frost, once for the call on the tailboard and once for Frau Sorel coming in off the coach, which is the correct number. Counted fire buckets with Madam Harrow out of pure ceremony: nine of nine, no mice, entered. My mother sent a cake to a theatre in Reap and it was eaten by eleven people. At the table I was able to report that the Office allows a company its own portable proscenium, having looked it up already, twice, for pleasure. Wrote to her afterwards by the stove. I record also that a boy of nineteen — or eighteen — was made second on the book, and that the entry was made in the datebook and initialled, properly, in front of witnesses.

#### Ansel Grelle

**State:** On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.
**History:** I pasted their bill at the labour exchange at nine and read it eleven times, then read the other ten, then walked until four and knocked. She opened the door its whole width, set the lamp on the floor, and told me I was asked-for, not expected. I put my four questions in the wrong order and she answered all of them: Falk alive and standing six feet behind me in the dark; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten o'clock and putting me above his own boots; and both — seven pounds and the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch dying had only re-addressed it to me. Falk came into the lamp, put my weight on both feet, said *Boy*, could not finish, and held my shoulder a long time. I told them about the book, sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got, and that I had read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's with no name to give, and asked to be put out of the door rather than sat down under a lie. She called me her left-handed man and my pages a guest list. Paid at dawn, receipted, a cot, and the eleventh line would not be me. Vane counted the coin out loud and said he'd told suppers he paid it; I said I had heard him at Merrow.

I took the pit doors house-side with the boy, propped all eight exits, and got Skarke's written promise in my pocket. When she told the house the truth nobody clapped and people began to move; I had the door open for a woman with three children before she reached it, and a drover came down from the gods to sit closer. Then two hours of hearing it through the doors — the whole of it, the bell, Lenz saying *Certified* — with both hands over my face and no shame in it. House out slow and warm, all eight doors. The man who had knocked at the wrong door turned out to be Fenn Halloran off the north side, the other half of my wall by the newspaper offices; he had read my paste eleven times, same as me. Afterwards a gentleman came past me who would not be announced or stopped, and I called down the aisle after him.

Then I lost my door. A woman came out of the dark saying her son was inside and went past me like weather; I ran the aisle after her and stopped dead when Madam Harrow put her hand up, and stood at the top and watched a mother get her boy back. She said the door I couldn't hold was a mother-shaped door, forgiven twice over, stand down. In the morning I asked to walk them to the coach office, having been on the wrong side of every departure for eleven years, and I carried the hamper and the boy waved from the step. Back to the Baraque and a broom, and that afternoon I heard myself laugh out loud in a theatre.

Third wagon out of the capital, doors of the world in front of me. Vessendal on the 14th, free house, drovers and wool men, my count and my aisle; row four centre was sold and I saw the man — late by the front door, paid at the door, no hat, no programme, gone before the calls — and told the boy for the slate. First watch on the gate at Katterau, unasked; doors with Toby promised for the spring. At Katterau row four went out with the drovers as it came in. On the fourteenth at Achterhalt I counted the hall in, Kessel's chain in the second row, the butter man's boy bolt upright with a programme. At soup I put in what I had: a fit-up firm in the fourth ward owes me a favour and a ladder, and they can have the favour called in. Then the props boy stood up scarlet and asked for the book, and she gave it him with terms, and I reached over and shook his hand like two men in a trade, because that is what we are now. Twenty years on the wrong side of doors, and I handed a boy his start.
**Entry:** Doors at Katterau, eight of them propped, count in my head, and row four went out with the drovers same as it came in. On the fourteenth at Achterhalt I had my doors and my aisle again and counted the hall in — Kessel's chain in the second row, the butter man's boy bolt upright with a programme. At soup I put in what I had: there's a fit-up firm in the fourth ward owes me a favour and a ladder, and they can have the favour called in. Then the props boy stood up scarlet and asked for the book, and she gave it him with terms, and I reached over and shook his hand as though we were two men in a trade, because that is what we are now, and it finished him off entirely. Twenty years on the wrong side of doors and now I hand a boy his start.

#### Wenzel

**State:** At the horse lines behind the Katterau theatre with a nosebag and a wisp of straw, coat wet at the shoulders; easy and unbothered, wanting the horses fed and his supper kept warm.
**Entry:** Horses at Katterau, fed, and my supper was kept warm. Horses to Vessendal in Reap, horses to Merrow's fair, horses to Achterhalt in the cold. My name is on the boy's call, which I could not read but was told. Sat on the trunk at half eleven after Boyle roped it, because I like sitting on it, and it is only a box. Went to sleep at the table while they were still talking about eighty-two pounds and a door being carried about the country.

#### M. Skarke

**State:** In a plain black coat in row four centre of the Katterau theatre before the second half, no hat, no programme, one and six paid at the door; frightened, useful and light, wanting the hour to come and to be allowed to want nothing.
**History:** I first came to that theatre by no proper door, sitting fourth row centre with a rug I had no right to, and found the room lovely against my expectations. I told her, without turning, that I had wanted this since I was nine, and that thirty pages and twenty years of wealth had bought me nothing—I learned things through cheap clerks. She sat one seat off, called me Herr Skarke, said they do finishes honestly, on the hour. When the drovers came in, Frau Sorel took the house, and the ruin came through the practical door on the hour, I put my face in my hands and left before the calls, withdrawing my claim on the trunk, leaving the rug for Falk with instructions never to seat me nearer than row four.

After that I came properly—paid at the door, plain coat, no rug—and gave a written undertaking not to move or speak, telling her only that it was a lovely house.

I kept that vow through a night nine hundred others kept with me, and afterward she asked for the banker in me, not the boy. I explained the Kanzelgasse pattern—gloved women, quarterly fees hidden among flowers—and confessed that through my own payment those clerks had known for two years the company was coming to the Palace. I promised to find the family, wanting nothing for it.

I found them: the Vorns of the Bittersee, tied to Katterau by an old stamped refusal, and watched a mother recover her son. I traced the five-pound note to its source, surrendered my father's thirty pages to Room Fourteen, admitting they were never truly mine, and she shook my hand a second time.

Since then I have audited what I was asked, reported honestly to Frau Sorel alone, attended Vessendal and Katterau paying my own way, sitting row four, leaving before the calls, wanting nothing, owed nothing.
**Entry:** One and six paid to the mayor's clerk, row four dead centre, no hat, no programme, and four words came back to me before the half: the house knows him. I sat in the town that stopped early and heard the finish given whole, on the hour, and when Frau Sorel took the first scene the room forgot itself. I stood with the rest of Katterau at the calls and clapped until the lights came up, and then went out with the drovers, paying nothing and owed nothing, and nobody looked at me, and I was gone before the calls had settled. That is the whole of what I wanted and it is more than I had any right to buy.

#### Kessel

**State:** At home in Achterhalt with the chain in its box and his dinner waiting; pleased with himself and with them, wanting the Corn Exchange let again next season.
**History:** I called out constables in my own square before dinner over an Office affair nobody had told me was lodged at Hessler's shop. It sorted fast: the stage manager took the players' part, the Office the paperwork, I got the clerk, a useful sort. Between us we found nine bills off my bellman and a hundred ninety-one off the printer, coin impounded, order book inspected, Hessler cleared, as I'd known he would be. There had been no real order at all — the story I'd told came off the bellman all along. The clerk set it down plainly: forgery of a Palace command sits above a district bailiff and above a Clerk Third Class alike, so neither of us can hang it on the other. A man I can work with. I gave them the strongroom under the weigh-house for their sacks, kept the key myself, and the Office pays me a shilling to make it lawful.

I told the stage manager the Corn Exchange is the only house in town, that my brother-in-law will ask eighteen and take twelve, and warned her we are not sentimental here — the last company's leading man went off with a farrier's wife.

They came back after that as old custom. That winter they played my town on the Thursday, and I sat in the second row with the chain on, which is the whole point of a chain, and this time the leading man went off with nobody's wife.

Then on the fourteenth of Frost they played again, same second row, same chain, and it went still in my hand by the third line. Afterward I went backstage meaning to say something official and said instead that it was a fine thing, shaking hands with the wrong people in the wrong order and not caring. Nobody went off with anybody's wife. The Corn Exchange is let again next season, if I have anything to do with it.
**Entry:** They played my town on the fourteenth of Frost and I sat in the second row with the chain on, which is the whole point of a chain, and it went still in my hand by the third line. Afterwards I went backstage to say something official and said instead that it was a fine thing, and shook hands with the wrong people in the wrong order, and did not care. Nobody went off with anybody's wife. The Corn Exchange is let again next season if I have anything to do with it.

#### Ilse Bacher

**State:** In her own kitchen eleven miles from Katterau with a bolt on her own door and Fenner's programme in the dresser drawer; wrung out and settled, wanting to stay where she is and to be sent word of the next bill.
**History:** I stopped at Hessler's for a bill announcing four acts, words I hadn't heard since I was fifteen carrying bread to nine men in a green room at the Rose. A woman named Bell Harrow found me and said my message had reached Emeran Falk word for word, three days out of Vessendal. I told her who I was — the girl who once let a small boy sit in the passage, who answered his questions when he came back grown and moneyed, who sent warning four years past when a man went round Katterau promising a reckoning that was mine to carry, not Falk's. She said Falk was well, that six hundred stood up for him, that the bill was false and impounded. I described the man from Katterau and told her about my son Fenner, ten, who can read. I offered to go into the Rose again; she refused — that door was paid for once, not twice — and told me only to keep Fenner home on the 14th of Frost. Her silence about why was answer enough.

But he went anyway. I followed on the ten o'clock goods, was turned away at the door, and gave everything to a woman guarding the pass door: the bill, and the five pounds left on my table that I'd carried in guilt ever since. She called it evidence and let me in. I held my son again in the wardrobe cage room while Falk stood apart and said my name after twenty years. They fed us, paid our fares, and I promised: the 14th, front door, good seats, Bacher beside them.

We joined their column at Achterhalt. Fenner sat proudly through the show, unlooked-at sideways, safe. I declined Katterau in spring — Falk knows why — and sent butter instead. Since then we've come to Achterhalt each time it's near, Fenner inspected and approved by Falk like a small soldier, seated proudly, carried out asleep, ours.
**Entry:** Brought the cart in to Achterhalt at four with the butter and my husband and the boy, since Achterhalt is a town I can stand in. Fenner went straight to Herr Falk and showed him his standing and was inspected like a soldier and passed, and I watched from the cart. Then in at the front door and good seats, and my boy sat bolt upright with his programme waiting for the storm, and got it. Frau Sorel was back and they had her name chalked up on the wagon where anyone could read it. Nobody looked at us sideways. He would not admit he was tired and had to be carried out to the cart.

#### Bacher

**State:** Back at his own churns eleven miles out of Katterau, cart unloaded; plain and content, wanting the next invitation and his boy's boots mended.
**History:** I brought the cart up from Achterhalt with the butter, my boy beside me, and we went in at the front door of the theatre to good seats. My wife sat one side of him, me on the other. Good play, very loud in the middle. My son, who had been practising some manner of standing in the dairy since spring, showed the old actor how it was done, and was passed for it. He knew what the storm was made of and told me twice, then fell asleep on the way home swearing he wasn't tired.
**Entry:** Cart up to Achterhalt with the butter, boy beside me. Watched him show the old actor how to stand, and be passed, which he has been practising in the dairy since spring. In at the front door, good seats, good play. Very loud in the middle again. He told me twice what the storm was made of and then fell asleep on the way home saying he wasn't tired.

#### Fenner Bacher

**State:** Wrapped in a gentleman's rug in the second wagon or on the cart, programme folded in his pocket; sleepy, proud and impatient, wanting nine o'clock and the thunder sheet again.
**History:** I started as a child left at a theatre by the lady in the cab, given a bun and a promise Mam would fetch me. The man with the paste led me through a dark side door into warm light, and I asked if I was in time for the finish — I was told yes, that I was asked-for. A boy called Toby put me in row eleven, seat one, gave me a programme, and sat by me the whole time without watching the stage. I saw a play about a house and a man in debt, and a boy in a passage whose question was finally answered. Afterward there was soup, a bed of cloaks made by a lady with a thimble, and Toby let me shake the big black thunder-sheet.

Then, mid-laugh with Toby, the board sang and it was Mam — she wept into my hair on the stage floor. We slept together in the cloaks, and in the morning the man with the paste walked us to the coach. Mam promised the theatre again on the 14th, at the front door this time, with Da.

We came by butter cart with Da to Vessendal, all three of us in through the front door, third row. The thunder came from a red box I'd helped dry myself. Herr Falk offered to teach me to stand — both feet, voice from the boots — and offered his rug for the cold cart rides.

We returned to Achterhalt, where Herr Falk said I was passed. Front door again with Mam and Da, third row. Frau Sorel's name was back on the wagon. The storm from the red box was better than before, and I clapped over my head, not tired at all, though they carried me out anyway.
**Entry:** We came in the cart to Achterhalt and I went straight to Herr Falk and showed him standing — weight on both feet and the voice up out of the boots — and he looked at me like a soldier and said I was passed. Then in the front door with Mam and Da, third row, programme read all through. Frau Sorel is back and her name was chalked on the wagon. I waited the whole way through for the storm and it came out of the red box and it was better than last time. I clapped over my head. I was not tired and they carried me out anyway.

#### Katterau mayor

**State:** In the Katterau house among her own townspeople, chain of office at home in a drawer; brisk and curious, wanting a quiet full house and no scandal in her town.
**History:** The players came back to us in daylight, their bills up ahead of them, and I did not wait to be asked. I went round myself and said what needed saying: the old mayor's favour had died with him, and they should not count on inheriting it, but I had a favour of my own to give, and they might have the town's fire buckets. Twenty years this town had waited for somebody brave enough to come back, and I was not going to let us make a fuss about it now that they had. That done, I sent my clerk over with a note about a seat.

The clerk went about the seat and came back with four words for the gentleman in row four: the house knows him. That was answer enough, and I asked for nothing more.

On the night I left my chain at home in a drawer and sat among my own townspeople, where I judged a mayor belonged for a thing like that. When the big man came through that door, my town stood up. It went on a good while, longer than politeness, and he let it — did not wave it down, did not hurry it. The storm frightened a farmer in the third row into speech, and nobody minded him for it; there was no one there looking to be offended.

A full house, no scandal, and twenty years ended quietly. That was how this town wanted it done, and I am satisfied it was done that way: not with a proclamation from me, not with my chain on and a speech, but with the house standing up on its own account and the man in row four sitting where the house already knew him. I gave the buckets, the seat, and the four words, and kept my own name out of it.
**Entry:** I sent my clerk over about the seat and he came back with four words for the gentleman in row four: the house knows him. Then I sat among my own townspeople with my chain at home in a drawer, and when the big man came through that door my town stood up, and it went on a good while, and he let it. The storm frightened a farmer in the third row into speech and nobody minded. No scandal, a full house, and twenty years ended quietly, which is how this town wanted it done.

#### Anton

**History:** The schoolmaster asked me and I thought about it for two days, and then I asked whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills, and he said she was, so I said yes. She came up the lane on the first day and I stood up on the wall to be nearer, and she put out her hand and did not touch me, and said something short. Then we sat on the wall and I showed her my paper and she looked at all of it. There was another lady standing away at the turn of the lane who did not come nearer. Afterwards I learned to spell vermilion and I write it on things, and I drew the wagon with the red box on the back for her to have.
**Entry:** The schoolmaster asked me and I thought about it for two days, and then I asked whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills, and he said she was, so I said yes. She came up the lane on the first day and I stood up on the wall to be nearer, and she put out her hand and did not touch me, and said something short. Then we sat on the wall and I showed her my paper and she looked at all of it. There was another lady standing away at the turn of the lane who did not come nearer. Afterwards I learned to spell vermilion and I write it on things, and I drew the wagon with the red box on the back for her to have.

### 15 · Harbor, and the Line Left Blank
- **Messages:** 285-318

Late in a wing, stove ticking, Bell Harrow finally asks Emeran Falk why "Harbor." Falk tells her of a bad season in a port, walking the mole at 4 a.m. watching boats come in shipping water — the harbour asked nothing, wasn't interested in bravery, just held still and let you tie up. He'd been drinking at nine every morning for eleven years when Vane hired Bell in ten minutes and she stepped over the third board unprompted, then posted a notice about a bucket. "So. Harbor." Bell keeps the name and gives her side: a harbor's pay is getting to be one — before this company no one ever tied up. She banks the stove; the tailboard reads T. LENZ, 2ND ON BOOK, FOR B. HARROW, S.M.

Winter: their own fit-up in Loewe's scene dock — Boyle's door carried in with H.B. cut into the first plank, Hebel's letters, Lenz at midwinter, Skarke's empty audit, Anton's drawings of theatres with every door open. Spring: Katterau twice, the mayor's favour being the town's carpenters and a barrel; both nights sell out. Night two is Toby's, ruled his two seasons back. Grey at the half says he can't remember what warm means; told warm was never in the pages, he's given Bell's own nail-worn watch to hold till the iron. He calls his performance clean despite being two seconds late on the act-two flat, covered by Krug's wheel; the storm lands on its one moment. Bell rules it publicly; Dessa Krul concedes: "He's nineteen."

Reap at the Athenaeum: Mirelle's schoolmaster's letter arrives. Anton comes to the door on the 20th with the schoolmaster's sister, says "It's smaller than it sounds," takes the yard, is told by Falk to stand on both feet, shakes his mother's hand, shouts "Vermilion!" from the street's top.

At Grevenholt the Corona's roof is mended; doorkeeper Krebs, the hinge-maker's brother, reports the bucket still under the prompt corner — Bell puts it on permanent duty. Ilsabet, then Prewick's certified Wolf King. Vane asks the company pass to the stage manager; Bell amends it to the keeper of the book, forever; Prewick writes it fair, all sign. Vane says, "Ask me for a thing" — she claims the first person answering a spring notice. Rosza Emmerich walks eleven miles in the wet, is hired in six minutes, signs, and plays.

**History:** Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a leaking corner, and an unopened iron trunk tied to Vessendal's debts and a proscribed, unfinished two-hundred-year-old play from Katterau. Alongside Emeran Falk, Odalric Vane, Mirelle Sorel, and clerk Casimir Prewick, she uncovers cryptic pages, forged bills, and buried debts—Vane's hidden loan from Hessel Brandt, Anna Sorel's sealed legacy, Mirelle's true parentage and hidden son Rupert/Anton, and copyist Anselm Krug's long guilt. Investigations lead through Achterhalt, the capital's Office of Public Morals (Lenz), and reclusive heir Marius Skarke, who secretly funds the play's revival. Harrow imposes strict rules—certified copies only, no wagers, no volunteering for the unfilled "eleventh line"—and orchestrates the play's full, certified performance at the Theatre Royal, breaking its centuries-old curse by finally answering its silent bell. Aftermath: debts settled, Grelle's long guilt resolved, Fenner Bacher rescued and adopted into the company, Mirelle reunited with her son, and the once-cursed script formally retired. The Players gain solvency, a new wagon, and stability. Seasons pass in performances, reconciliations, and quiet institutional rituals—chalk lists, certified books, Toby's promotion—cementing Harrow's harbor-like role holding the company together.

#### Bell Harrow

**State:** In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.
**History:** I came to the Corona out of the rain with a notice and stayed for nine years' unfinished business. A found page — a cut leaf of an unnamed play — pulled me past a sealed trunk I was told never to open. Vane, the man in the plum coat, owed a debt Skarke's agents had bought; the trunk held only blank paper, a hat, a glove. Prewick, the Office clerk, kept finding forms that didn't exist and a town, Katterau, that wasn't on any itinerary though everyone had been there.

Falk taught me the play's true name: four acts and a matter following, spoken fourteen times in two hundred years, never once cleanly. Sorel was truly Mirelle, sister to Anna Sorel, whose sealed box of unpaid accounts led to Perlmann, to Achterhalt, to a debt paid in coin and closed in ink. Krug hadn't burned his pages; Grelle hadn't stolen seven pounds; Ilse Bacher's son Fenner was used as a threat by a gloved woman working for the Vorn family, tangled with Mirelle's own hidden son, Anton, taken from her years before.

I met the thing itself — small, apologetic, thirty pages short of whole — in Skarke, and in Lenz, who kept the true ledger and taught me the rule: never staged for money, only once called clean, witnessed, the house told the truth first.

We spoke it entire at Katterau, nine hundred and thirty-nine seats and a bell I rang and answered myself, closing two hundred years of unattended calls. Grelle was found and forgiven, Krug fed and kept, Toby Lenz taught to call a house and signed his own crooked notice. Falk finally named his harbor. Mirelle got her son back, her name entered true in my own book. The company closed its accounts, hired a fiddler out of the rain, and went on.
**Entry:** I sat up with Falk and his one thimble and finally asked for the word. A port, a bad season, four in the morning on a mole, boats coming in shipping water — and a harbour that asked nothing and let you tie up. He had been drinking at nine in the morning for eleven years so a play wouldn't surface in him, and I posted a notice about a bucket. So: Harbor. I said I'd keep it, and gave him the other side of the ledger — a harbour's pay is getting to be one; before this company nobody ever tied up. Then winter: our own proscenium, H.B. badly cut and varnished forever. Katterau in the spring, both nights out. The second was Toby's; he went grey at the half and couldn't remember what warm means, so I turned him to face the stage and told him you call what's happening, and put my watch in his fist until the iron. He called it clean — two seconds late on the act-two flat, covered by Krug — and held a pause nobody gave him. I ruled it out loud, and Krul conceded: he's nineteen. At the Athenaeum Mirelle brought me the schoolmaster's letter and I said doors are what we're for; on the 20th the front ones stood wide from four and Anton came as far as the door, said it was smaller than it sounds, took the yard, and shouted Vermilion from the top of the street. Season ruled off, one line blank. Then Grevenholt: Krebs's hinge held, his brother lowered the lamp, the bucket was where my first notice put it — permanent duty — and the third board sang the same note. Vane asked for the company to go to the stage manager; I had it written to the keeper of the book instead, in ink, Prewick fair, the wing witnessing, me countersigned. My thing in return: the first soul in out of the weather in spring is mine to hire. Rosza Emmerich, eleven miles, six minutes to spare. She signed, and then played us eleven miles at walking tempo, and Falk said we'd had thunder for a year and no music.

#### Emeran Falk

**State:** Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.
**History:** I began, as far as I remember it whole, in a wet room with the last of the brandy when Bell Harrow stepped over the third board without needing telling twice. I gave her, against my own sense, the truth of Katterau: nine of us, a wager and a bottle, a play in four acts, a matter never finished. Krug's hand on the pages, then Krug gone without his boots. Odalric's iron trunk that carries blank paper until it doesn't. Anna Sorel dead of fever. Ansel Grelle, left-handed, gone at Merrow owing four weeks, never found. A boy named Skarke who stood in a doorway at nine, asked is that the finish, got no answer, and grew up arranging for twenty years. Ilse Bacher, who opened a door she shouldn't have, and a boy of hers who asked his father's same question. I told Harrow I would answer anything but one thing, and she asked it anyway, and I answered that too.

We found Hessel Brandt's debt and paid it, and I walked through our own stage-left door on cue and nothing came. Krug returned in a green coat at the capital. Grelle knocked at my stage door alive after eleven years of silence, kept a book instead of a letter, and I called him my boy before my voice failed. Harrow ruled the whole thing bearable: Katterau told entire, once, correctly, no wagers, no bottles, the Bacher boy kept home, ten conditions, a company instead of nine drunk men.

We played it whole before nine hundred strangers, and I spoke the wrong door's line and the house held. Ilse Bacher knelt with her boy after; I could only put my hand over my mouth. I carried the lining of my coat to Room Fourteen myself and came out lighter than arithmetic allows.

Since: Vessendal standing before I spoke, iron down, three calls, out. I told Harrow my whole history at last, over a stove — the port, eleven years of morning drinking, Anselm gone in the night. She kept the name. I am, by her ruling, in things now, instead of carrying them.
**Entry:** She asked me for the word at last, over the stove, with my thimble on my knee, and I gave it her whole: the port, the bad season, the mole at four in the morning, boats coming in bad — shipping water, a man hurt, nothing in the hold — and the harbour taking every one of them the same, asking nothing, not even that you be interesting. It just held still and let you tie up. And I told her the rest: eleven years of drinking at nine in the morning so the play wouldn't surface, Anselm gone in the night, a coat full of pages, and then a stranger who stepped over the third board without being told twice and posted a notice about a bucket. She said she'd keep the name, and gave me her side, which was better than mine. I lifted the thimble to her the way I did in Grevenholt the night she came in out of the rain, drank it off, and went to my wagon on both feet. Katterau twice more; the boy called the second night and I told him weight on both feet, nineteen. At the Athenaeum a boy of thirteen stood in the doorway and said it was smaller than it sounds, and I had to put my hand over my mouth and turn away in the passage. Out in the yard I told him he was standing wrong and he corrected it instantly and looked pleased. At Grevenholt: the Corona with a mended roof, our own door, the initials at ankle height. And in the spring a woman played a cold dance tune at walking speed in an empty hall and I stood in the stalls with my head back and said it out loud: we've had thunder for a year and no music.

#### Odalric Vane

**State:** In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.
**History:** I began this trade with a stage manager, Bell Harrow, hired the day she arrived with a notice and three references, and I steered her from a certain trunk while Prewick asked too much about it. That trunk held nine years of my life: a loan taken at Vessendal from a dying man, Hessel Brandt, who would not sign a receipt between friends and died before it was finished, leaving the debt to be bought up by a man named Skarke. I had told the company I had fourteen days when I had none, seduced by Katterau's six hundred seats, until Harrow made me lay it bare: names in ink, the notary Perlmann, Anna Sorel, a nun, Brandt's blind son Josias who remembered my sleeve after nine years. The truth was worse: Brandt had held the money for another party, never his to lend, and hidden the play itself, thirty pages, in a cupboard tagged unpaid.

Harrow ruled against Katterau, drove us to Vessendal, and there the debt was discharged, witnessed, not forgiven. I paid Achterhalt's bank myself, front door, hat on, and got my sky for the black plate scene. In the capital I broke and blamed Anselm for a theft I committed by silence, then unsaid it before the company and let Harrow rule again. That unearthed an older wound — Grelle, the landlord's seven pounds I'd claimed eleven years to have paid and never had. I found Hentsch's door at last, counted the coin out unrounded, and heard him say he'd always known.

Since then: certification, the bill by command at the Athenaeum, toasts to our dead, a second wagon built with H.B. cut crooked into the first plank, Sorel held open at any cost, and a testament written not to me nor mine but to whoever keeps the book. I asked for a last thing and was given the wettest, best gift: to watch, and weep, from the wings.
**Entry:** Winter and a fit-up of our own; I cut H.B. into the first plank myself, badly, and had it varnished so it stays badly. Katterau in the spring, front doors first, and I said it aloud twice — it looks like a theatre. The boy called the second night and was clean, and I arrived from nowhere and wept, which is my function. Then Grevenholt, the Corona, the roof mended, the last curtain of the season, and the thing I have been carrying since Achterhalt: I put my hat down on the whole of the spring and asked her to have them. Fifty-four, a company that owes nothing, a second on the book who is nineteen — I want it minuted that the Vermilion Players go to whoever keeps the book, not to a creditor, not to a nephew. She said yes first, plainly, and then wrote it better than I asked it: not to Bell Harrow but to the book, keeper after keeper, forty years on to somebody neither of us will meet. To the book. That is much better than mine, and I sat down on a hamper and put my face in my hands and then hollered for Prewick, who wrote it fair on two sheets at eleven at night, and I signed unrounded and the whole wing witnessed. Then I could not help asking her for a thing, and her thing was my own trick back at me: the first soul who answers a spring notice is hers to hire, and I may watch from the wings and weep. I accepted on the spot. In the wet week of spring I stood in the shadow with my hat off and stopped breathing while a woman with a pulped notice and a fiddle got herself hired, and when it was done I came out with both arms and promised her a stove.

#### Toby Lenz

**State:** On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.
**History:** I started as nobody at roll call, chasing chestnuts and stories, running off without a water bucket while a gentleman on a milestone asked early for the Vermilion Players. I nearly called a house of six hundred at Katterau before Madam Harrow ruled no, and I sat down not knowing if I was sorry or glad. She began writing me into her book. I learned doors and counts: row four, centre, laid before the house opened, all three nights, counts only. A rug and a pinned paper taught me a count could go wrong and right together, the night the house stood for Herr Falk.
