There were voices, bells, bailiffs, a bellman's penny, Achterhalt's two full houses, the capital, the Baraque yard where Herr Vane confessed a lie about Herr Grelle, Krug's lashing story, nine pages summarised at supper, and a Room Fourteen with the name Lenz on the door that wasn't, Prewick swore, my relation. I demanded to be a maker at the hearing and was ruled to the house instead. Ink named a Lenz; a left-handed man was reading our file; a postscript from the Undersecretary of Assessment named me by name. Herr Grelle came back from the dead with paste on his cuffs. I gave my empty seat, row eleven, to a lost boy who asked if this was the finish, and sat with him all night until his Mam found him. I painted the trunk vermilion, held doors at the Palace and Vessendal, and asked for advancement at Achterhalt over Krul's objections about my age. Madam Harrow ruled me second on the book, with terms. Months of plot tables followed until I called the storm at Katterau myself, holding her own watch, missing "warm" but finding truth instead. It came in clean. I signed the minute: T. Lenz, second on book.
**Entry:** Winter was plot tables until Herr Krug said he dreamt in them. Then Katterau, and the second night was mine, ruled two seasons ago. I was up at five, walked the plot four times, checked a wagon I didn't need to check, and wrote the call so straight it looked printed, and at the half I went grey and told Madam Harrow the storm was on page nine and I couldn't remember what warm means. She turned me round to face the stage, not the book, and said warm was never in my pages — you call what's happening: Herr Falk's shoulders, Frau Sorel's hands, the house breathing. Then she put her own watch in my fist and closed my fingers on it, mine for tonight, to be given back at the iron. I stopped shaking all at once. Beginners, please, and my voice went where I sent it. I took the act-two flat two seconds late and Herr Krug covered it on the gas and nobody but the three of us will ever know. I held a pause nobody told me to hold and brought the light after Frau Sorel and not with her. In act four six hundred people leaned forward and I never looked at page nine: storm — go. It came in low with a floor in it and somebody in the gods laughed from fright. Iron down, three calls. I held the watch out on my palm and couldn't say one word. She weighed it, put it back on its nail, and ruled it in the wing out loud: clean. Krul said he's nineteen, and the whole wing went up. Later I went out with a lantern and stood with my hand on a wheel before I wrote a number down. At Grevenholt I called the load-in, and I signed the new minute last — T. Lenz, 2nd on book — and read it twice before I understood it. In the spring I wrote the new name on the call, spelled right, because I asked her twice.

#### Dessa Krul

**State:** In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.
**History:** I started with a queen's slippers and a needle that never stopped moving, and a fear I named plainly: no Katterau, because Krug went there and came back to nothing, not even his boots, and I packed his empty box with my own hands still warm. She ruled against it, and I bit off my thread on that, glad.

The slippers travelled everywhere with me, guarded from filth. When Krug turned up alive in a green coat, I set them down for four seconds in shock, and stood by that as my whole opinion of the man, even after Vane confessed he'd called Krug a thief to save face, and Krug refused payment, giving pages instead — nine of them, unfinished, one with a bell and her name all through it.

We took on new company under my condition: the twelve names read slow before signing. I got that reading cold, without soup or candle, on the morning of the 2nd — ten names, a struck eleventh, a blank twelfth. I sat on a secret about my own hamper's contents all the way to the Office courtyard and came home lighter, as told.

A dead lodger got a plate and silence. A lost boy got a nest of the queen's cloaks, two bowls of soup, and no fuss, until his mother found him kneeling on the boards of the Theatre Royal. I boiled water because there was nothing else to do, and made her promise to return on the 14th.

I painted a trunk vermilion, ugly, and it held through storms in Katterau and beyond. I dressed a girl who stepped into Frau Sorel's place and did not disgrace anybody. I settled the props boy's age at eighteen, twice, and fed him after. A fiddle case now steams beside the slippers in my cage, which I permit and will not discuss.
**Entry:** Watched the whole of the boy's act from the wardrobe doorway with pins in my mouth, and when she looked past his shoulder at me for the arithmetic I took the pins out one at a time and said it to the whole wing: he's nineteen. Then bedlam, as it should be — Boyle bellowing, Vane weeping on cue, Wenzel joining in without knowing why. At the Athenaeum I showed the schoolmaster's boy the queen's slippers and he didn't touch them, not being asked to, which is manners. He looked at the hamper properly. Later, a fiddle case steaming in my cage beside the slippers, which I have decided is acceptable and will not be discussing. Pins in the tin, and a new girl in the book who walked eleven miles.

#### Anselm Krug

**State:** In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.
**History:** I began in the Baraque yard, come back to answer for the seven pounds Odalric said I stole. He confessed he'd made me a thief because I wouldn't say why I left; I told him three companies had refused me, the truer shame. Frau Sorel ruled it, Harrow made him write letters and made me eat, and I gave over the nine pages of the play I'd claimed I'd burned. I hadn't yet told her the rest: two years before, friendless, with page eight in my pocket, I'd filed a fire-safety requisition on the Palace theatre, believing that if fate meant to arrange me I'd choose the room myself. When she found my hand on the Palace paper I confessed it. She named it a design, not a betrayal, and gave me first word at the hearing; the company voted me in. I plotted the Palace exits and the iron drop precisely, and it held—nine hundred and forty seats emptied without anyone needing to be brave.

Along the way I learned that Katterau's seven-pound Wednesday take, and a left-handed bill-paster I'd once worked beside without learning his name, were the same man: Ansel Grelle, who came asking questions and was made a doorman instead of a threat. I helped carry the hidden trunk to safety without letting Grelle bear it. At the Palace I stood at the fly rail while the true author spoke his own lines, dropped the iron on cue, and watched Frau Sorel ring and answer the warning bell herself. The text was sealed under the Hall of Records afterward.

Since then: ordinary work, chosen. Advance man and second book, Vessendal and Katterau papered before arrival, Wenzel told gently of the ending, a boy named T. Lenz signed into the datebook in my own hand, eighty-two honest pounds from Vane, and a night I closed the datebook simply to listen to music.
**Entry:** Went ahead on the Wednesday and pasted Katterau myself, so the bills were up before we came in sight of the town. Fit-up in five hours. First night ours; second night the boy's, and I had the gas board, so when he came two seconds late on the act-two flat I covered it and said nothing until she said it for me — and I told him from the board, without turning round, that he owed me a Katterau drink, which is the expensive kind. Advance work all winter, the datebook fattening. At the Corona at the end of the season the datebook lay open with eleven towns in it, and Vane put his hat over the whole spring and asked for something that wasn't a booking, and I signed my name to it in the wing with everybody else. In the spring I shut the datebook to listen to a woman play a dance tune at walking speed in a half-built house, and did not plot one dangerous thing all evening.

#### Ottmar Boyle

**State:** In the Katterau theatre yard at the half with his lamp lit and the unlit pipe in his teeth, wagons settled; sober and content, wanting a quiet house and an early load-out.
**History:** I am Ottmar Boyle, twenty-two years carrying, roping, and standing on tailboards for this company. It started with lists and axles: a Krug missing from the roster, a wheel-rim wired back together, and word that Katterau was back on the books — twenty-two mile out and twenty-two home, four days for one night I'd rather not have walked. The ruling sent us the toll road instead, eight shilling, and I said so first. I stood watch on the trunk many nights, called kettle a bell when the word had gone bad, and learned to open doors only to talking distance until told otherwise. I banked the bag from Vane without asking questions, fed horses, roped tarpaulins twice, because twice is the number.

I found paper under a milestone and said, madam, do we look; found Hessler's shop shut on a market Saturday with two hundred unordered bills printed against us, and a woman watching who wasn't ours to chase. Krug came back in a green coat on a mounting block, and Vane confessed his own lie before us all and put money on it, which Krug let lie. A cast list turned up in the trunk — ten names, one struck, one blank — and I told her straight I'd rather be on a list than off it. Wenzel was struck and given the horses instead, which suited him better than sparing would have.

I've walked billstickers home behind lanterns, fetched Wenzel off a trunk he wouldn't leave, held a stage door for a mother who said nothing and a boy asking if this was the finish. I watched rain leak through that trunk and enjoyed saying so more than anything in twenty-two years. My door held for Falk's cue at Katterau, and I've never been prouder of a hinge. I've argued with a beam and lost, and kept holding it anyway.
**Entry:** My door taken off its hinges and carried about the country like a relic, with the initials cut in the plank badly, which is the right way to cut them. Katterau in the daylight, five hours to a fit-up, both nights out; the boy called the second and I bellowed as loud as anybody when the wardrobe woman said he was nineteen. Told the schoolmaster's lad in Loewe's yard what every rope was for, properly, with knots, and he listened. At Grevenholt I swore at the arch as usual and put my name to Vane's paper. In the spring I lost an argument with a beam, and was still holding it when the new woman played, and I stood in the O.P. entrance with the beam in my hands until she finished.

#### Casimir Prewick

**State:** At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.
**History:** I entered service as a clerk of the Office, seconded since Merrow, and came to the company, where I met Harrow, its new stage manager, and Sorel. I found an unnumbered iron trunk and an older fire notice signed by Hessel Vorn of Katterau, marked SEEN. NOT APPROVED. The company's true itinerary disagreed with mine; Katterau was erased from my own papers. I learned what the trunk held: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, whose pages arrived unbidden and came slantwise true, and the Proscribed section of my own Index, thirty-one titles, two of them one work split in error into anonymous folios. I chose to serve it knowingly rather than blindly, and was let choose. I helped drown a broken thunder sheet with something like reverence, hunted Sorel's sealed box through registries and probate rolls to a blind man who called records the whole of the defence, and impounded Hessler's forged bills for a false command performance, sending the matter upward beyond my rank. At Achterhalt I delivered Harrow to Room Fourteen and to Undersecretary Lenz, who had guarded that same Index entry nineteen years. I wrote him a countersigned letter asking him to certify Part the Second himself, and he came and did, overruling my seal to protect me, while I drew the minute every hand in the company signed. I witnessed a stolen boy, Fenner, restored to his mother, hat off, unbidden. Assessment retired the proscribed work sealed rather than destroyed, my minute one of its three legs. My papers came through at midwinter: attached clerk, permanent, at the Office's pleasure and the company's expense. I finished certifying the Wolf King, saw a boy of nineteen made second on the book, and at Reap, hollered from bed, wrote fair in my own hand the instrument settling the company's name, wagons, properties, and debts, with goodwill passing to each keeper of the book in turn — Vane signing unrounded, Harrow countersigning, myself as scrivener, where such things belong.
**Entry:** The winter fit-up I inspected as one inspects a text, and Undersecretary Lenz did the same at midwinter over three cups. At Katterau I applauded the boy at regulation volume with my hat off, and wrote to my mother about a second on the book who is nineteen. At the Corona my Wolf King comparison was finished, certified, stamped straight, my seal on the paper at last, and I stood at the back of the O.P. side through act one with my hat off and my mother's cake in the wing. Then, at eleven at night on the props table, I was hollered for and wrote the instrument fair in my own hand and read it aloud twice: the name, the wagons, the properties, the fit-up, the debts if any, and the goodwill pass upon death or retirement to the keeper of the company's book, and thereafter to each keeper in turn. Two sheets, numbered. Vane signed unrounded, Harrow countersigned, the wing witnessed, and I signed as scrivener. It goes in the book, which is where such things belong.

#### Ansel Grelle

**State:** On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.
**History:** I pasted their bill at the labour exchange, walked the city until four, and knocked. The woman with the lamp said I was asked-for, not expected. I asked my four questions and got answers: Falk alive, behind me; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten, putting me above his own boots; both debts — seven pounds and four weeks — re-addressed to me since Frau Hentsch's death. Falk came into the lamplight, told me I stood wrong, held my shoulder a long time. I told them of my book, sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got. I was made her left-handed man, paid at dawn, given a cot, the house-side doors, a boy under me. Vane counted the coin aloud, claiming credit I knew was false, and let it pass. I propped all eight exits that first night and took Skarke's written promise.

At the pit doors I got a woman with three children out early; a drover came down from the gods to sit close. Through the doors I heard the play at Katterau, the bell, Lenz saying *Certified*, and stood with my hands over my face. Fenn Halloran turned out to be the man who'd knocked at the wrong door. I lost my door once to a mother running for her son; Madam Harrow forgave it, called it a mother-shaped door. I walked them to the coach office, carried the hamper, watched the boy wave.

We went out third wagon from the capital — Vessendal, Katterau, Achterhalt — doors propped, counts kept, Kessel's chain and the butter man's boy noted. I called in a favour for ladders. The props boy got the book from her with terms; I shook his hand as a man in the trade now. At the Athenaeum, the Corona, I propped pass doors instead of standing outside them, signed Vane's paper, and once held a door with my shoulder for no one at all, and did not mind.
**Entry:** Doors at Katterau both nights, and I had my hand on the boy's shoulder when the wing went up for him. At the Athenaeum in Reap I propped the pass door because that is what I do now instead of standing outside one. Signed Vane's paper in the wing at the Corona. In the spring, when the fiddle woman played, I held the pass door open with my shoulder although there was nobody to keep out, and did not mind at all.

#### Wenzel

**State:** At the horse lines behind the Katterau theatre with a nosebag and a wisp of straw, coat wet at the shoulders; easy and unbothered, wanting the horses fed and his supper kept warm.
**History:** I took the second wagon out for eleven shillings with an honest axle, six days on the road, whistling four notes without noticing. Later I turned up for soup and ended on a bench at a company hearing, meaning only to play at soldiers. Boyle said he was in if I was out, so I took the horses before anyone could argue, and heard talk of an unfinished play, a Palace with eight exits, and a woman with a sealed box. Krul called mine the best job in the building. My name wasn't read among the ten chosen, which Boyle told me was the ruling working, not me being spared.

I signed a minute with a cross, Krul writing my name after it, and sat a whole morning on a roped trunk doing nothing on purpose, glad to be off the cast list. I kept that watch through an evening too, until a man came with a lamp very late to tell me it was finished and the boy was safe — news to me, and that I was relieved. I argued and lost, slept against the trunk in the rain. Later I learned the trunk was emptied, its papers gone under the Hall of Records. I was told again the horses were the best job in the building, and I mean to keep believing it.

They woke me once to say the play was finished, and Krug called it a great one, so that settled it. Since then: horses to the capital gate, to Vessendal, to Katterau, to Merrow's fair, to Achterhalt, supper always kept warm. My name appeared on the boy's call, though I couldn't read it. I heard talk of eighty-two pounds and a door carried about the country, and fell asleep before it finished. A boy at the Athenaeum argued with me about the size of a horse and thought better of it. I put my cross to Vane's paper too, and slept once through a woman's fiddle in an empty hall.
**Entry:** Horses through the winter and the spring, supper kept warm. Woke in the middle of the wing cheering the boy without knowing what for, which was fair enough. At the Athenaeum a lad of thirteen looked at the wagon and said the horse was too small, so I told him the horse is the right size and the wagon's too big, and he thought about it very seriously and said nothing, which I took as agreement. Put my cross to Vane's paper and Krul wrote my name after it. Fell asleep somewhere I shouldn't have while a woman played a fiddle in an empty hall.

#### Mirelle Sorel

**State:** In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.
**History:** I began as a mender of gloves in low light, keeping the company's small order — Odalric's debts, Falk's mockeries, the bucket under the star trap that had waited since Katterau. Then Harrow came in out of the rain, and I taught her the trade: the ladder, the trunk, the arts of asking and going away. She showed me a page with nine in it; I told her mine was ten, and that pages come slantwise, tin only, never the trough in houses under forty foot. I gave her Krug's plot tables, cued her Ilsabet, and hid a page with ten in it inside my mended glove. Through her I learned Odalric had sold the 17th to buy Katterau, and I refused Katterau — Halbern was enough backwards-walking for one life. I told her of my sister Anna Sorel, who kept Odalric's accounts and left a sealed box in Vessendal's registry. I would not go near that building; my name there is one I cannot afford to meet. Harrow found the box, found Hessel Brandt, found a countrywoman's coat that was my mother's, then Anna's, then mine. At Halbern the pages stopped counting. Krug returned; Odalric confessed a theft; nine pages surfaced, one a cast list of twelve. At the hearing I gave my whole history aloud — Anna, the magistrate's matter, the summons — and joined the company on one condition: Anna's box stays shut forever, paid for first.

Then came Rupert Vorn, the lying-in house, papers signed at twenty-three, the son I was told never to look for, the extortion charge that drove me over the mountains. Harrow's audit found him — a steward's brother's family in the Bittersee, a boy named Anton, twelve, who draws and cannot spell. I asked for slowness and got it: a letter in Harrow's hand, not an office's. He came, at five, tall, satchel on his shoulder, shook my hand, and shouted Vermilion at the whole street. I mended gloves longer than ever that night, and in spring I stopped my needle to hear the new woman play.
**Entry:** Katterau twice more, top of the list, and Falk gave me his fourth call and I gave it to the house. Mid-fortnight at the Athenaeum I came to the corner before the half with the schoolmaster's letter and no gloves at all: term ended, and the boy had asked in his own words, spelling his one word right, whether he might come as far as the door of the theatre where the wagon lives. She read it whole and said doors are what we're for, name the day, the front ones will stand wide. I named the 20th, Loewe's last Thursday, the coach, the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible and briefed. As far as the door — not a seat, not the house — and I said that was the wisest thing anybody in this business has said in ten years. I folded the letter in three and put it in my pocket, not my glove. He came at five, tall now, with a satchel, not wanting his hand held, and stood in the doorway and looked a long time and said it was smaller than it sounds. He took the wagon, the horse, the ropes, the hamper; Falk told him to stand on both feet and he looked pleased. Twenty-five minutes. I stood where I could see him and did not perform for him once. He thanked four people in the wrong order, and stopped in front of me and put out his hand, and I shook it. At the top of the street he turned and shouted Vermilion at the whole street. Then the yard was very quiet and I stood in it with my hands at my sides. I mended that night longer than anyone. Signed Vane's paper at the Corona, and in the spring stopped my needle to hear the new woman play.

#### Frau Loewe

**State:** In her own Athenaeum with the letting book squared and fifteen shillings in the drawer; paid over the odds and moved despite herself, wanting the counterweights respected and no one to mention her box office door.
**History:** I have held this house a long time, and I keep my letting book straight, whatever else runs crooked. In the winter of the fifth year, Emeran Falk came alone and hired my house for one night, two shillings, and never opened it — sat in the dark, gave back the key, and left chalk marks I swept myself, so no boy should see a man's madness. A week later a woman came from Katterau asking after him, with a child, and I told her he had gone south, when he had gone north. I would tell the same lie again.

Years on, the Vermilion Players came — Vane, her stage manager, their counterweights exactly as bad as I said. I stood witness at their box-office counting and signed under a gentleman's own hand where he withdrew money. Over soup, the stage manager asked about the woman from Katterau, and I told the truth I had kept four years: her name near Bauer or Bacher, a boy of five or six who thanked me correctly for a bun, and her words when I lied to her — *then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his.* I have never known whether she meant a debt, a fault, or the child.

I saw them out clean that Saturday, and Falk lifted his rug to me from his box, which I shall tell for ten years. They left me an address, more than most leave.

They came back richer, and Vane overpaid me on purpose, which offended me thoroughly. Perlmann was carried onto my stage; when Falk came through my door, my whole town rose before he spoke, and I sat shut in my box office and said nothing.

Then they wintered in my scene dock, mending my gas tap, building their theatre out of my dust. On my last Thursday the doors stood open for no reason given, and a tall boy off the coach said the house was smaller than it sounds — the truest thing said in it all year. I kept out of the yard, and afterward told them only that the gas tap was a disgrace, and went inside.
**Entry:** Their winter in my scene dock, building themselves a theatre out of my dust, and the counterweights sound and the gas tap mended and the brick in the passage scrubbed pale. In Reap the front doors stood wide from four o'clock on my last Thursday and nobody would tell me why, so I stopped asking, as I do. A woman in brown and a tall boy off the coach; he stood in my doorway and looked at my house and said it was smaller than it sounds, which is the truest thing said in it this year. They took him through to the yard and I kept out of it. When it was over and the yard went quiet I said doors open at half six and the gas tap is a disgrace, and went inside so as to be no trouble.

#### Anton

**History:** I asked to go and see the lady from the theatre bills, and after two days' thought I said yes to the schoolmaster. She came up the lane, put out her hand but did not touch me, and we sat on the wall while she looked through all my paper. Another lady stood off at the turn of the lane and never came nearer. Afterwards I learned to spell vermilion, wrote it on things, and drew a wagon with a red box on the back for the lady to keep.

She wrote back, and I went by coach with the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible, and I did not have my hand held. At the theatre the doors stood open, and I looked at the gas and the boxes and the empty stage, and said it was smaller than it sounds. The stage manager agreed, and said it was bigger than it looks, and told me the wagon lived through the yard door, and that my pace was the law inside those walls. I went only as far as the wagon. I said the horse was too small, as in my drawing, but the man on the bale said the horse is right and the wagon is too big, and I said I would think on that. The big man showed me what all the ropes are for, with their knots. The lady with the pins showed me the queen's slippers, and I did not touch them. Herr Falk came out with a rug on his arm and told me I was standing wrong, weight on both feet; I fixed it, and he saw me fix it. It lasted twenty-five minutes, and then there was the six-forty train to catch. I thanked four people and shook my mother's hand. At the top of the street I shouted Vermilion as loud as I could.
**Entry:** The lady wrote back and I came on the coach with the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible, and I did not have my hand held. The theatre where the wagon lives had its front doors wide open and it was warm and dark inside, and I stood in the doorway and looked at the gas and the boxes and the empty stage, and I said it was smaller than it sounds. The stage manager said it was smaller than it sounds and bigger than it looks, and told me where the wagon lives, through the yard door, and that my pace was the law inside the walls. So I went as far as the wagon. The horse is too small, as I said in my drawing; the man on the bale said the horse is right and the wagon is too big, and I shall think about that. The big man told me what all the ropes are for, with knots. The lady with the pins showed me the queen's slippers and I did not touch them. Herr Falk came out with a rug on his arm and said I was standing wrong, weight on both feet, and I fixed it and he saw me fix it. Twenty-five minutes and then the six-forty. I said thank you to four people. I shook my mother's hand. At the top of the street I shouted Vermilion as loud as I could.

#### Schoolmaster's sister

**History:** Brought the boy on the coach as arranged, set him down at the top of the street, and stood by while he went as far as the door and no further, which was the whole of the agreement. Twenty-five minutes in a theatre yard, ropes and a horse and an old actor telling him to stand up straight. I looked at my watch and said the six-forty, and we caught it.
**Entry:** Brought the boy on the coach as arranged, set him down at the top of the street, and stood by while he went as far as the door and no further, which was the whole of the agreement. Twenty-five minutes in a theatre yard, ropes and a horse and an old actor telling him to stand up straight. I looked at my watch and said the six-forty, and we caught it.

#### Katterau mayor

**State:** In the Katterau house among her own townspeople, chain of office at home in a drawer; brisk and curious, wanting a quiet full house and no scandal in her town.
**History:** I remember when the players came back to us, their bills already up around town, pasted by their own man before I ever met them. I went to the square and met them myself, and I gave them my favour: the loan of the town's carpenters and a barrel for the company. They had a theatre standing inside five hours. Two nights, six hundred each, both out, and the town went in at the front doors and came out satisfied. Nothing wanted a chain or a speech that time.

They came back to us again in daylight, with their bills up ahead of them as before, and I went round to say what needed saying. I told them the old mayor's favour had died with him, but I had my own, and they might have the town's fire buckets. I reminded myself, and them, that twenty years this town had been waiting for somebody to be brave enough to come back, and that we were not going to make a fuss about it. I sent my clerk over after with a note about a seat.

My clerk came back with four words for the gentleman in row four: the house knows him. I sat among my own townspeople that night with my chain left at home in a drawer, and when the big man came through the door my town stood up, and it went on a good while, and he let it happen. A storm frightened a farmer in the third row into speech, and nobody minded that either. There was no scandal, a full house, and twenty years ended quietly, which is exactly how this town wanted it done.
**Entry:** Their bills were up before they were, pasted by their own man on the Wednesday. I met them in the square and gave them my favour, which was the loan of the town's carpenters and a barrel for the company, and they had a theatre standing inside five hours. Two nights, six hundred each, both out. The town went in at the front doors and came out satisfied, and nothing wanted a chain or a speech.

#### Krebs the doorkeeper

**History:** Three soft knocks, unhurried, and I came with the lamp and two bolts. A woman said she was Bell Harrow, stage manager of the Vermilion Players, so I lowered the lamp to the boards and not in her face, and told her she'd be the one that posted the notices, and that my brother did their hinge — which bites its frame still. Then I told her the thing I have been keeping: there's a bucket under her prompt corner, there since the other Katterau, the one before hers, and nobody has dared move it. She came in over the third board on purpose and let it sing, and then she ruled the bucket on permanent duty, dry or not, the oldest notice in their church. I set my lamp on the prompt shelf beside it and looked at the pair of them, and said I'd tell the gas boy, who has been trying to fill it with rags since June. Then she gave me the news like a present: two nights, Ilsabet first, and the second a debut — the Wolf King, certified at last, with a storm in it that has a floor.
**Entry:** Three soft knocks, unhurried, and I came with the lamp and two bolts. A woman said she was Bell Harrow, stage manager of the Vermilion Players, so I lowered the lamp to the boards and not in her face, and told her she'd be the one that posted the notices, and that my brother did their hinge — which bites its frame still. Then I told her the thing I have been keeping: there's a bucket under her prompt corner, there since the other Katterau, the one before hers, and nobody has dared move it. She came in over the third board on purpose and let it sing, and then she ruled the bucket on permanent duty, dry or not, the oldest notice in their church. I set my lamp on the prompt shelf beside it and looked at the pair of them, and said I'd tell the gas boy, who has been trying to fill it with rags since June. Then she gave me the news like a present: two nights, Ilsabet first, and the second a debut — the Wolf King, certified at last, with a storm in it that has a floor.

#### Rosza Emmerich

**History:** I read the notice four times in the wet before going in — eleven miles walked, boots finished, fiddle under my coat. The stage door stood open, and when I said it shouldn't be, Bell Harrow, the stage manager, told me it was open on purpose, turning her lamp so the light fell on the boards, not my face. My ten minutes began when I stepped on the singing board. She said I could answer her three questions in any order. I told her: I am Rosza Emmerich; four years at a dancing school where tempo is the whole job; two years in a Kessarine pit band until it stopped paying; a winter of weddings and a funeral a week, which teaches you to change a tune when a room changes. I read music, transpose while playing, don't drink at work, and can mend a bow — nothing else. I said they should take me because hers was the only bill that said ask for the stage manager, meaning somebody kept a book, and I'd been paid from hats for two years and wanted to be written down. She counted my three good signs on three fingers, then gave me terms — posted, unrounded wages, a line in the book, a bunk in the second wagon, four sentences of house rules — and I signed my full name and asked what hour beginners were. A weeping man in plum came from the wing promising me a stove; she ruled it harmless before supper. Then she told me to play. I tuned badly, then properly, and played a cold dance tune at the tempo of eleven miles. Nobody clapped. An old man in the stalls said they'd had thunder for a year and no music. Later, case steaming beside the queen's slippers, I found the third board again and asked once more what hour beginners were.
**Entry:** Four days that notice sat on a board with a horse auction and two lost dogs, and I read it four times in the wet before I went in. Eleven miles, boots finished, fiddle under my coat. The stage door opened without a knock and I said so — it shouldn't have been open — and she said it was open on purpose, and turned her lamp down so the light was on the boards and not in my face. Bell Harrow, stage manager, and my ten minutes had started when I stepped on the singing board. She asked three things in any order I liked, so I thought about the order first: Rosza Emmerich; four years for a dancing school where you learn nobody is watching you and the tempo is the whole job; two years in a Kessarine pit band until it stopped being paid; a winter of weddings and a funeral a week, which teaches you to change a tune when a room changes. I can read, I transpose while playing, I don't drink at work, I can mend a bow and nothing else. And why they should carry me: because hers is the only bill I ever saw that said ask for the stage manager, which told me somebody in there keeps a book, and I have been paid out of hats for two years and would like to be in a book. She counted my three good signs back at me on three fingers, gave me terms — wages posted and unrounded, a line in the book, a bunk in the second wagon, and a church of four sentences — and I signed my whole name and asked what hour beginners were. Then a large weeping man in plum came out of the wing promising me a stove, and she ruled that harmless before supper. Then she told me to play, so I tuned badly and then properly and played a cold dance tune at the tempo of eleven miles, and the house gave it back bigger than me, and nobody clapped, and the old man in the stalls said they'd had thunder for a year and no music. Late, my case steaming beside the queen's slippers, I found the third board again in the dark and asked once more what hour beginners were.

What we ask of you is the oldest thing a theatre asks: witness. Stay, if you choose. Leave, if you choose — now, or at any moment; the exits are lit, all eight, and this play will not stop for a leaver, and nobody in this building is required to be brave tonight. Any child here sits by an open door, and any child who'd rather have the foyer and a bun has my note for both. If anyone comes in late, by any door, the house will know them — we keep count here. One seat in row eleven is sold and empty and stays so; let it be. That's everything I know how to tell you honestly, and it's all of it."
